n.0: Monetary policy is the Bank of England's role, not FCA guidance.
n.2: Prudential standards are set by rules and the PRA, not guidance.
n.3: Pension trustees are regulated by TPR, not Handbook guidance.

q: A bank subject to the PRA is reviewing broad expectations such as acting with integrity and prudence. What type of provision in the PRA Rulebook sets out these high-level expectations for firms?
o: Discussion responses
Conduct standards
Technical annexes
Fundamental rules
Guidance papers
w: The PRA Rulebook includes fundamental rules, which set out broad expectations for firms, such as acting with integrity and prudence.

n.1: Conduct standards are FCA requirements, not PRA fundamental rules.
n.4: Guidance papers do not have binding status.
n.2: Technical annexes may supplement rules but are not high-level principles.
n.0: Discussion responses do not form part of the Rulebook.

q: A compliance manager is looking for handbook material that indicates steps which tend to show a rule has been met. Which type of provision in FCA and PRA handbooks sets out these practical details of compliance?
o: Rules, which are optional and carry no disciplinary effect
Principles, which give detailed step-by-step compliance instructions
Guidance, which is legally binding and overrides the rules
Codes of practice, issued for firms by HM Treasury
Evidential provisions, indicating steps that tend to show compliance
w: Evidential provisions give practical examples of how compliance can be achieved, helping firms apply the rules in practice.

n.0: Rules are mandatory and binding; breach can lead to disciplinary action.
n.2: Guidance is not binding and does not override the rules.
n.1: Principles are high-level statements, not detailed compliance steps.
n.3: Codes of practice are not issued by HM Treasury.

q: A newly authorised firm is reviewing the FCA's high-level requirements such as integrity, skill, care and diligence. Which FCA provisions are based on these high-level principles for business?
o: Training and Competence Handbook
Conduct of Business Rules
Supervisory Statements
Principles for Businesses
Capital Adequacy Requirements
w: The FCA’s Principles for Businesses are high-level requirements such as integrity, skill, care, and diligence, applicable to all authorised firms.

n.1: Conduct of Business Rules are detailed, not high-level principles.
n.0: The Training and Competence Handbook sets staff requirements, not firm principles.
n.4: Capital adequacy is a PRA provision, not FCA principles.
n.2: Supervisory Statements are PRA tools, not FCA high-level rules.

q: A trade body has produced sector guidance that the FCA has confirmed. A compliance officer asks how binding it is. What is the status of FCA-approved industry guidance?
o: Able to override the FCA's own rules where they conflict
Fully binding and directly enforceable like a statutory rule
Not binding, but adherence may be treated as persuasive evidence
Legally equivalent to primary Acts of Parliament
Of no regulatory significance and never referred to at all
w: Sector guidance approved by the FCA is not binding, but regulators may consider adherence as evidence of compliance with rules.

n.1: Approved industry guidance is not binding or directly enforceable.
n.4: It does carry weight; regulators may treat compliance as evidence.
n.0: Guidance cannot override the FCA's rules.
n.3: Guidance is not legislation and has no statutory force.

q: A PRA-regulated insurer is looking for the regulator's published expectations on how to approach prudential requirements. Which PRA publication sets out its expectations for firms' approaches to prudential issues?
o: FOS case studies
Discussion papers
The UK Corporate Governance Code
Supervisory statements
FCA guidance notes
w: The PRA issues supervisory statements to clarify its expectations of firms’ approaches to meeting prudential requirements.

n.4: FCA guidance notes relate to conduct, not prudential issues.
n.1: Discussion papers invite comment but do not set expectations.
n.2: The Corporate Governance Code is issued by the FRC, not PRA.
n.0: FOS case studies relate to consumer complaints, not prudential supervision.

q: A firm chose not to follow relevant FCA guidance and is now facing scrutiny over a rule breach. What is the effect of failing to follow FCA guidance?
o: It always leads to criminal prosecution of the directors
It automatically results in a financial penalty being imposed
It may be used as evidence in enforcement or disciplinary cases
It has no possible consequences of any kind for the firm
It renders all of the firm's consumer contracts void
w: While not binding, FCA guidance may be used as evidence of whether a firm took reasonable steps to comply with rules.

n.3: Non-compliance can still be cited as evidence, so consequences exist.
n.1: There is no automatic penalty simply for departing from guidance.
n.0: Departing from guidance is not itself a criminal offence.
n.4: Failure to follow guidance does not void consumer contracts.

q: A compliance officer is identifying the FCA Handbook material that expresses overarching standards such as integrity and treating customers fairly. Which type of provision sets out these high-level regulatory standards?
o: Rules
Supervisory statements
Guidance
Principles
Discussion papers
w: Principles are overarching high-level standards, such as integrity and treating customers fairly, which underpin all FCA regulation.

n.0: Rules are detailed and binding, but not broad principles.
n.2: Guidance interprets, rather than sets, standards.
n.1: Supervisory statements are PRA publications, not FCA principles.
n.4: Discussion papers seek input but are not binding standards.

q: A large bank falls under both the PRA and the FCA and is checking which rulebooks apply. What is the relationship between PRA rules and FCA rules for dual-regulated firms?
o: FCA rules automatically override PRA rules in all cases
Firms must comply with both PRA prudential and FCA conduct rules
Only one regulator's rules apply to the firm at any time
PRA rules automatically override FCA rules in all cases
Neither regulator's rules are binding on dual-regulated firms
w: Dual-regulated firms, such as large banks and insurers, must comply with both PRA prudential rules and FCA conduct rules simultaneously.

n.3: Neither regulator's rules override the other; both apply.
n.0: FCA rules do not override PRA rules; both must be met.
n.2: Both sets apply simultaneously, not one at a time.
n.4: Both PRA and FCA rules are binding on such firms.

q: A consumer group is reviewing older legislation aimed at standard-form contracts weighted against consumers. What was the main purpose of the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999?
o: To monitor mergers and enforce UK competition law
To regulate the collection of corporation tax from firms
To set the minimum capital ratios that banks must hold
To supervise the funding of occupational pension schemes
To protect consumers from unfair terms in standard contracts
w: The UTCCRs 1999 were designed to protect consumers against unfair terms in contracts they signed with businesses, ensuring balance and transparency.

n.1: The UTCCRs concern consumer contract terms, not corporation tax.
n.3: Pension funding is TPR's area, not the UTCCRs.
n.2: Bank capital ratios are prudential rules, not the UTCCRs' subject.
n.0: Competition law is the CMA's domain, not the UTCCRs.

q: A firm's legal team is confirming which agreements the UTCCRs 1999 actually applied to. Which contracts were primarily covered by the UTCCRs 1999?
o: Agreements between governments
Consumer contracts with businesses
Contracts between large corporations
Employment contracts
International treaties
w: The UTCCRs applied specifically to contracts made between a business and a consumer, not business-to-business or international agreements.

n.2: UTCCRs did not apply to B2B contracts.
n.0: Government agreements are outside consumer law.
n.3: Employment contracts are governed by employment law.
n.4: International treaties are a matter of public international law.

q: A firm is reviewing a standard clause that heavily favours the business over the customer. Under the UTCCRs, when could such a term be considered 'unfair'?
o: If it merely created extra administrative work for the business
If it had not first been approved by a government minister
If it related in any way to the reporting of the firm's tax
If it caused a significant imbalance to the consumer's detriment
If it had not been physically signed by both of the parties
w: A term was considered unfair if it caused a significant imbalance between the rights of the consumer and the trader, to the detriment of the consumer.

n.0: Inconvenience to the business is not the test of unfairness.
n.1: No ministerial approval of contract terms is required.
n.2: Tax reporting is irrelevant to whether a term is unfair.
n.4: A missing signature does not make a term unfair under the UTCCRs.

q: A firm is confirming which clearly stated, prominent terms were outside the UTCCRs' fairness test. Which type of terms were exempt from assessment of fairness under the UTCCRs?
o: Terms setting out the parties' respective employment provisions
Warranties contained within general insurance contracts
Core terms on price or subject matter, provided they are transparent
Terms that operate to restrict competition between businesses
All clauses that impose a penalty on the consumer for default
w: Core terms, such as price and the main subject matter, were exempt from fairness assessment as long as they were transparent and prominent.

n.4: Penalty clauses were not the exempt category; core terms were.
n.0: Employment provisions are outside the UTCCRs.
n.3: Competition restrictions are not the exempt terms.
n.1: Insurance warranties are not the exempt core-terms category.

q: A student is tracing which body policed unfair contract terms before functions passed to the CMA in 2014. Which authority enforced the UTCCRs 1999 in the UK?
o: Prudential Regulation Authority
Financial Ombudsman Service
Bank of England
Upper Tribunal
Office of Fair Trading
w: The Office of Fair Trading (OFT) was the primary body responsible for enforcing UTCCRs before its functions transferred to the CMA in 2014.

n.2: The Bank of England focuses on monetary and financial stability, not contracts.
n.0: The PRA handles prudential regulation, not consumer contract law.
n.1: The FOS resolves disputes but did not enforce UTCCRs.
n.3: The Upper Tribunal hears appeals but does not enforce regulations.

q: A compliance reviewer is scanning a standard contract for a clause that would fail the UTCCRs. Which example could be classed as an unfair term under the UTCCRs?
o: A clause restating the consumer's statutory right to a refund
A transparent clause stating the total price the consumer will pay
A clearly explained repayment schedule agreed by both parties
A clause letting the business change terms unilaterally without reason
A term requiring the consumer to give written notice to cancel
w: Terms giving one party a one-sided power to change conditions, without justification, were considered unfair under UTCCRs.

n.1: A clear price term is not unfair; core price terms are usually exempt.
n.2: An agreed, transparent repayment schedule is fair.
n.4: Requiring reasonable written notice to cancel is not unfair.
n.0: Restating a statutory refund right benefits the consumer, so it is fair.

q: A consumer discovers a clause in their contract was unfair under the UTCCRs and asks what that means for them. What was the effect of an unfair term under the UTCCRs 1999?
o: It triggered compensation from the FSCS
It required referral to the High Court
It became a criminal offence
It automatically voided the entire contract
It was not binding on the consumer
w: An unfair term was not binding on the consumer, though the rest of the contract could still stand if capable of operating without it.

n.3: The whole contract did not necessarily become void; only the unfair term lost effect.
n.1: Not every case required High Court referral.
n.0: The FSCS deals with firm failure, not unfair terms.
n.2: Unfair terms were not a criminal offence; they were civil law matters.

q: A compliance officer is tracing the European measure that the UK transposed into the UTCCRs 1999 to protect consumers from unfair terms. Which EU directive did the UTCCRs implement?
o: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive (MiFID)
Insurance Distribution Directive
Prospectus Directive
Council Directive 93/13/EEC on unfair terms
Data Protection Directive
w: The UTCCRs implemented Council Directive 93/13/EEC, which required Member States to protect consumers from unfair contract terms.

n.0: MiFID regulates financial markets, not consumer contracts.
n.4: The Data Protection Directive deals with privacy, not contracts.
n.1: The Insurance Distribution Directive is unrelated to UTCCRs.
n.2: The Prospectus Directive regulates securities, not consumer contracts.

q: A firm is updating training to reflect that the UTCCRs have since been superseded by consolidated consumer law. Which later legislation replaced the UTCCRs 1999?
o: Companies Act 2006
Financial Services Act 2012
Pensions Act 2004
Consumer Rights Act 2015
Banking Act 2009
w: The Consumer Rights Act 2015 consolidated consumer law and replaced the UTCCRs with updated protections against unfair terms.

n.0: The Companies Act relates to company law, not consumer contract terms.
n.1: The Financial Services Act 2012 reorganised regulators, not consumer rights.
n.4: The Banking Act 2009 focuses on bank resolution, not contract law.
n.2: The Pensions Act 2004 governs pensions, not contracts.

q: A tutor is explaining why the UTCCRs mattered where consumers had little bargaining power over standard contracts. Why were the UTCCRs considered important for consumer protection?
o: They reformed the regulation of occupational pensions
They fixed the interest rates charged on consumer lending
They introduced new rules governing company mergers
They placed a statutory cap on companies' tax liabilities
They addressed the imbalance of power between firms and consumers
w: The UTCCRs limited unfair advantage taken by businesses in standard form contracts, where consumers had little bargaining power.

n.1: The UTCCRs did not set lending interest rates.
n.3: They did not cap corporate tax liabilities.
n.0: Pensions regulation was not the UTCCRs' purpose.
n.2: Merger control is a competition-law matter, not the UTCCRs'.

q: A firm is briefing staff on legislation covering goods, services and digital content that brought older consumer law together. What was the main purpose of the Consumer Rights Act 2015?
o: To create the rules governing company merger control
To consolidate and simplify the UK's consumer protection law
To reform the collection of corporation tax from firms
To set the UK's monetary policy and interest rates
To supervise the solvency of UK insurance companies
w: The CRA 2015 consolidated and simplified previous consumer legislation, covering contracts for goods, services, and digital content.

n.3: Monetary policy is the Bank of England's role, not the CRA's.
n.4: Insurer solvency is a PRA matter, not the CRA's purpose.
n.0: Merger control is competition law, not consumer law.
n.2: The CRA concerns consumer rights, not corporation tax.

q: A compliance officer is confirming which earlier unfair-terms regime the Consumer Rights Act 2015 absorbed and updated. Which area of law did the CRA 2015 replace and update?
o: The Banking Act 2009 and its resolution regime
The Pensions Act 2004 and scheme funding rules
The Companies Act 2006 governing company law
The Financial Services Act 2012 and the FCA
The Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999
w: The CRA 2015 replaced the UTCCRs 1999, incorporating and updating protections against unfair terms in consumer contracts.

n.0: The Banking Act 2009 concerns bank resolution, not consumer terms.
n.2: The Companies Act 2006 governs companies, not consumer contracts.
n.3: The 2012 Act reformed financial regulation, not consumer law.
n.1: The Pensions Act 2004 covers pensions, not the UTCCRs.

q: A software retailer is checking which category of product the CRA 2015 explicitly brought within consumer protection for the first time. What new category of contract did the CRA 2015 explicitly cover?
o: Digital content
Pension scheme rules
International treaties
Corporate loan agreements
Employment contracts
w: The CRA 2015 was the first major UK consumer law to explicitly cover contracts for digital content such as software and downloads.

n.4: Employment contracts are governed by employment law.
n.3: Corporate loans are governed under financial services law, not CRA.
n.2: International treaties are outside consumer law.
n.1: Pension rules are regulated separately, not under the CRA.

q: A customer buys a faulty appliance and wants a full refund shortly after purchase. What right does the CRA 2015 give consumers if goods are faulty?
o: A complete exemption from paying VAT on the goods
An automatic award of criminal compensation from the trader
A short-term right to reject faulty goods within 30 days
A guaranteed top-up to the consumer's pension entitlement
A personal right to bring an action under competition law
w: The CRA gives consumers a statutory right to reject faulty goods within 30 days for a full refund, a key protection.

n.1: The CRA gives a civil right to reject, not criminal compensation.
n.0: Faulty goods do not exempt a consumer from VAT.
n.4: Competition law is not a consumer remedy for faulty goods.
n.3: Pension top-ups are unrelated to faulty-goods rights.

q: A firm's legal team is assessing whether a contract term is fair under current consumer law. What is the test of fairness for contract terms under the CRA 2015?
o: Whether the term first received approval from the FCA
Any inconvenience the term causes to the trader's business
Whether the contract was registered at Companies House
A significant imbalance in rights, to the consumer's detriment
Whether the term was approved in advance by HM Treasury
w: A term is unfair if it causes a significant imbalance between consumer and trader rights, to the detriment of the consumer.

n.1: Inconvenience to the business is not the CRA's fairness test.
n.0: FCA approval of individual terms is not required.
n.4: HM Treasury does not approve consumer contract terms.
n.2: Contracts need no Companies House registration to be fair.

q: A student is confirming which body now enforces unfair contract terms after the OFT was abolished. Which enforcement body took over from the OFT under the CRA 2015?
o: The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)
The Bank of England's financial policy arm
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
The Pensions Ombudsman service (PO)
The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)
w: The Competition and Markets Authority became responsible for enforcing unfair contract terms after the OFT was abolished.

n.2: The FCA regulates financial conduct, not general unfair contract terms.
n.4: The PRA is a prudential regulator, not the OFT's successor.
n.1: The Bank of England did not take over the OFT's consumer role.
n.3: The Pensions Ombudsman handles pension disputes, not the OFT's work.

q: A consumer's downloaded software is defective and they ask what they are entitled to. What remedy does the CRA provide if digital content supplied is faulty?
o: An automatic increase in the consumer's pension
A right to repair, replacement or a price reduction
An exemption from the operation of competition law
A rebate on the income tax the consumer has paid
A referral of the dispute to compulsory arbitration
w: Consumers have the right to repair, replacement, or a price reduction if digital content provided under contract is faulty.

n.0: Pension increases have nothing to do with faulty digital content.
n.4: The CRA does not force disputes into compulsory arbitration.
n.3: No tax rebate arises from faulty digital content.
n.2: Competition law exemptions are not a consumer remedy.

q: A firm is redrafting its consumer contracts so terms are clear, understandable and not buried. Which principle guides transparency under the CRA 2015?
o: Only orally agreed contracts are treated as valid
Every term must be individually negotiated with the consumer
Contracts must be registered with Companies House
All contracts must first be approved by HM Treasury
Terms must be plain, intelligible and prominent to the consumer
w: The CRA requires contract terms to be transparent—plain, intelligible, and prominent—so consumers can understand their effect.

n.1: The CRA does not require every term to be individually negotiated.
n.3: HM Treasury does not approve consumer contracts.
n.0: Written contracts are valid; the CRA does not require oral ones.
n.2: No Companies House registration is required for consumer contracts.

q: A clause in a consumer contract is found to be unfair under the CRA 2015, and the consumer asks about the rest of the agreement. What happens if a term is deemed unfair under the CRA 2015?
o: It requires referral to the Supreme Court
It voids the entire contract automatically
It triggers criminal liability for the trader
It mandates repayment of all previous contracts
It is not binding on the consumer
w: An unfair term is not binding on the consumer, although the remainder of the contract can still be enforced if workable.

n.1: The whole contract is not automatically voided.
n.0: Cases do not go straight to the Supreme Court.
n.2: Unfair terms are not criminal offences under CRA.
n.3: The CRA applies per contract, not retroactively to all agreements.

q: A revision note needs a one-line summary of what the Consumer Rights Act 2015 achieved. Which phrase best summarises the impact of the CRA 2015?
o: It overhauled the prudential supervision of banks
It created the UK's regime for merger control
It introduced new occupational pension funding rules
It set the country's official interest rate policy
It modernised and consolidated UK consumer protection law
w: The CRA 2015 modernised consumer protection by consolidating previous law, addressing digital content, and clarifying unfair terms provisions.

n.3: Interest rate policy is the Bank of England's role, not the CRA's.
n.2: The CRA did not create pension funding rules.
n.0: Bank supervision is a PRA matter, not the CRA's effect.
n.1: Merger control is competition law, not the CRA's.

q: A trustee is confirming which regulator's focus is safeguarding members and promoting sound scheme administration. What is the main role of The Pensions Regulator in relation to occupational pension schemes?
o: To issue government bonds and manage public borrowing
To enforce UK competition law against merging firms
To protect members' benefits and promote good scheme administration
To handle individual consumers' financial complaints
To collect income tax from pension scheme members
w: The Pensions Regulator (TPR) is responsible for protecting pension scheme members’ benefits, promoting good scheme administration, and reducing the risk of calls on the Pension Protection Fund.

n.0: Issuing gilts is the Debt Management Office's role, not TPR's.
n.3: Consumer complaints are the FOS's function, not TPR's.
n.4: Income tax is collected by HMRC, not TPR.
n.1: Competition enforcement is the CMA's role, not TPR's.

q: An employer is checking whether both its final-salary and money-purchase workplace schemes fall under The Pensions Regulator. Which schemes fall under TPR's remit?
o: Workplace occupational pension schemes, both DB and DC
Consumer credit and personal loan agreements
Retail bank deposit and current accounts
Individuals' personal ISAs and share dealing accounts
General insurance policies sold to consumers
w: TPR oversees occupational pension schemes, including defined benefit and defined contribution workplace pensions.

n.3: ISAs are savings products regulated by the FCA, not TPR.
n.2: Bank deposits fall under the PRA and FCA, not TPR.
n.4: Insurance policies are regulated by the FCA/PRA, not TPR.
n.1: Consumer credit is an FCA matter, not within TPR's remit.

q: A trustee who has mismanaged a scheme is concerned about the regulator's enforcement reach. Which power does The Pensions Regulator hold over scheme trustees?
o: It can approve or block corporate merger deals
It can set the solvency rules for insurance firms
It can levy income tax penalties on the trustees
It can impose fines and remove or prohibit scheme trustees
It can set the Bank of England's monetary policy
w: TPR has enforcement powers to issue fines, remove or prohibit trustees, and require corrective action to protect members’ benefits.

n.4: Monetary policy is the Bank of England's role, not TPR's.
n.2: Tax penalties are imposed by HMRC, not TPR.
n.0: Merger approval is a CMA function, not TPR's.
n.1: Insurer solvency rules are set by the PRA, not TPR.

q: A defined benefit scheme is running a deficit and must agree a plan to address it. What funding-related rules does The Pensions Regulator oversee?
o: The caps imposed on companies' dividend payments
The capital adequacy requirements applied to banks
The maximum limits placed on consumer lending
Defined benefit scheme funding and deficit recovery plans
The collection of value added tax from employers
w: TPR ensures defined benefit schemes are properly funded, requiring recovery plans where deficits exist, to safeguard member benefits.

n.4: VAT collection is an HMRC matter, not TPR's.
n.1: Bank capital adequacy is set by the PRA, not TPR.
n.2: Consumer lending limits are an FCA matter, not TPR's.
n.0: TPR does not cap company dividend payments.

q: A newly appointed trustee is reviewing the standards of conduct The Pensions Regulator expects. What is the objective of TPR's governance requirements?
o: To handle and resolve individual consumer complaints
To supervise the pricing of consumer insurance policies
To ensure trustees act in the best interests of members
To set the rates of corporation tax that firms pay
To regulate and approve corporate merger activity
w: TPR sets governance standards requiring trustees to act prudently, honestly, and in the best interests of pension scheme members.

n.3: Corporation tax rates are set by government, not TPR.
n.4: Merger control is the CMA's role, not TPR's.
n.1: Insurance supervision is an FCA/PRA matter, not TPR's.
n.0: Consumer complaints are resolved by the FOS, not TPR.

q: A scheme administrator is checking what must be provided to members about their benefits and funding. What disclosure obligations does TPR enforce on schemes?
o: Giving members clear and timely information about their benefits
Reporting the amount of corporation tax the scheme has paid
Disclosing the outcomes of competition law investigations
Filing periodic reports on the conduct of monetary policy
Publishing the details of national interest rate policy
w: TPR requires trustees to give members clear, accurate, and timely information about their benefits and scheme funding.

n.4: Interest-rate policy is not a TPR disclosure obligation.
n.2: Competition rulings are unrelated to TPR.
n.1: Corporation tax reporting is not the obligation.
n.3: Monetary policy reporting is not TPR's remit.

q: A tutor is explaining how The Pensions Regulator lowers the chance that failing schemes end up as a claim on the Pension Protection Fund. How does TPR reduce risks to the PPF?
o: By regulating how insurers underwrite their policies
By collecting additional tax contributions from employers
By setting the minimum capital ratios that banks hold
By requiring schemes to manage funding and governance properly
By supervising the conduct of consumer credit lenders
w: TPR enforces funding and governance rules for occupational schemes, reducing the risk of schemes collapsing and passing liabilities to the PPF.

n.1: TPR does not collect tax to protect the PPF.
n.4: Consumer credit supervision is an FCA role, not TPR's.
n.2: Bank capital ratios are set by the PRA, not TPR.
n.0: Insurance underwriting is regulated by the FCA/PRA, not TPR.

q: A finance director is briefed that recent legislation lets The Pensions Regulator pursue those who deliberately harm a scheme. What criminal powers were given to TPR under the Pension Schemes Act 2021?
o: Power to enforce the collection of employers' taxes
Power to regulate the fairness of consumer contracts
Power to authorise and supervise retail banks
Power to prosecute reckless or wilful conduct harming a scheme
Power to set the Bank of England's base interest rate
w: The 2021 Act strengthened TPR’s powers, allowing it to bring criminal prosecutions against those who recklessly or wilfully endanger pension schemes.

n.4: Setting interest rates is the Bank of England's role, not TPR's.
n.1: Consumer contract fairness is a CMA/FCA matter, not TPR's.
n.0: Tax enforcement is HMRC's role, not TPR's.
n.2: Authorising banks is the PRA's role, not TPR's.

q: A first-time trustee is unsure how much they must understand about pensions law and funding. What requirement does TPR place on scheme trustees regarding knowledge?
o: Trustees must have appropriate knowledge and understanding of pensions
Trustees must enforce the rulings of competition authorities
Trustees must follow the rules governing corporation tax
Trustees must publish regular monetary policy updates
Trustees must personally approve new insurance products
w: Trustees are legally required to demonstrate adequate knowledge and understanding of pensions law, funding, and governance standards.

n.2: Trustees' duty concerns pensions knowledge, not corporation tax.
n.3: Monetary policy is not a trustee responsibility.
n.1: Competition rulings are enforced by the CMA and courts, not trustees.
n.4: Approving insurance products is not a trustee duty.

q: A revision card needs a one-line summary of The Pensions Regulator's mission. Which phrase best summarises TPR's approach to occupational pension regulation?
o: Regulate, tax and collect from occupational schemes
Borrow, lend and spend to support the pension sector
Protect members' benefits, promote good administration, reduce risk
Compete, merge and acquire on behalf of members
Issue, supervise and dissolve occupational schemes
w: TPR’s mission is to protect members’ benefits, promote good administration, and reduce risks to the PPF — often summarised as protect, promote, and reduce risk.

n.1: TPR does not borrow, lend or spend; that is not its mission.
n.0: TPR does not levy or collect taxes.
n.3: Mergers and acquisitions are not TPR's mission.
n.4: TPR does not issue or routinely dissolve schemes as its aim.

q: A new CISI member is reviewing the framework of ethical standards expected of securities and investment professionals. What is the main purpose of the CISI Code of Conduct?
o: To supervise the solvency and capital of banks
To enforce the collection of corporation tax
To set ethical standards for securities and investment professionals
To issue government bonds and manage borrowing
To regulate the fairness of consumer contracts
w: The CISI Code of Conduct provides a framework of ethical standards for securities and investment professionals to uphold integrity, honesty, and fairness in their work.

n.0: Bank solvency is a PRA matter, not the CISI Code's purpose.
n.4: Consumer contract fairness is a legal/CMA matter, not the Code's.
n.1: Tax enforcement is HMRC's role.
n.3: Bond issuance is unrelated to the CISI Code.

q: An adviser is identifying the CISI Code principle that demands honesty, fairness and transparency in all dealings. Which principle requires professionals to act with honesty and fairness?
o: Integrity
Monetary policy
Pension regulation
Tax compliance
Confidentiality
w: Integrity is the first principle of the CISI Code, requiring professionals to act with honesty, fairness, and transparency in all dealings.

n.4: Confidentiality is important but not the same as integrity.
n.3: Tax compliance is managed by HMRC, not CISI principles.
n.1: Monetary policy is set by the Bank of England.
n.2: Pensions are overseen by The Pensions Regulator.

q: A candidate is confirming how many core principles make up the CISI Code of Conduct. How many core principles are in the CISI Code?
o: Four
Eight
Six
Ten
Twelve
w: The CISI Code of Conduct contains eight core principles that set professional and ethical expectations for members.

n.0: There are more than four principles.
n.3: There are not ten principles; the correct number is eight.
n.2: There are more than six principles.
n.4: The Code does not contain twelve principles.

q: A member is planning their continuing professional development to meet the Code. Which CISI Code principle emphasises maintaining knowledge and competence?
o: Ensuring fairness in the firm's consumer contracts
Holding sufficient regulatory capital at all times
Maintaining knowledge and competence through ongoing development
Enforcing competition rules against rival firms
Meeting all of the firm's corporation tax duties
w: The Code requires members to maintain and improve their knowledge and competence through continuous professional development.

n.0: Consumer contract fairness is not the CPD principle.
n.1: Capital adequacy is a prudential rule, not a competence principle.
n.4: Tax duties are not part of the CISI competence principle.
n.3: Competition enforcement is not a CISI Code principle.

q: A member who has breached the CISI Code asks what action the institute may take. What is the consequence of breaching the CISI Code of Conduct?
o: Tax penalties from HMRC
Automatic criminal prosecution
Disciplinary action by CISI
Revocation of Bank of England licence
Loss of pension entitlements
w: Breaching the Code may lead to disciplinary action by CISI, which can include warnings, suspension, or expulsion from membership.

n.1: Criminal prosecutions are not automatic under the Code.
n.0: HMRC deals with taxation, not CISI Code breaches.
n.4: Pension entitlements are not linked to CISI membership.
n.3: The Bank of England does not license CISI professionals.

q: An adviser is unsure when they may disclose client information under the Code. Which CISI principle requires professionals to uphold client confidentiality?
o: Tax transparency, presented as safeguarding client data
Capital adequacy, said to require keeping client data secret
Respecting the confidentiality of client information held
Monetary stability, described as protecting client information
Consumer redress, framed as a duty of client secrecy
w: Respect for confidentiality is a principle requiring members to safeguard client information unless disclosure is legally required.

n.1: Capital adequacy is a prudential rule, not the confidentiality principle.
n.3: Monetary stability is unrelated to client confidentiality.
n.4: Consumer redress concerns compensation, not confidentiality.
n.0: Tax transparency is not the CISI confidentiality principle.

q: A professional realises a personal interest could clash with a client's interests on a transaction. Which principle of the CISI Code relates to managing conflicts of interest?
o: Identifying, managing and avoiding conflicts of interest
Maintaining the bank's minimum capital ratio
Keeping the financial system's competition neutral
Ensuring the good governance of pension schemes
Guaranteeing the consumer a full refund on request
w: The Code requires professionals to avoid conflicts of interest and to act in clients’ best interests where conflicts may arise.

Exempt persons under Exemption Order 2001

Public companies issuing shares
Government departments acting commercially
w: Exempt persons under the Exemption Order 2001 include certain professional firms who can operate without FSMA authorisation.

n.2: Unit trust managers must be authorised and are not exempt under FSMA.
n.0: Approved persons are individuals within authorised firms, not exempt firms themselves.
n.3: Public companies issuing shares still require compliance with FSMA and are not exempt.
n.4: Government departments acting commercially are not listed as exempt under FSMA orders.

q: A firm begins advising on investments without ever obtaining FCA permission. Under FSMA 2000, how is carrying out regulated activity without authorisation classed?
o: A criminal offence
An unenforceable contract term
A civil tort only
A permitted exemption
A minor administrative breach
w: Engaging in regulated activities without authorisation is a criminal offence under FSMA 2000.

n.4: It is not treated as minor administration; it is criminally sanctioned.
n.2: It goes beyond civil liability and is a criminal offence under FSMA.
n.3: Exemptions apply only to specific categories, not unauthorised activities generally.
n.1: While contracts may be unenforceable, the act itself constitutes a criminal offence.

q: An unauthorised firm arranges an investment for a client and later tries to hold the client to the deal. What is the legal status of that agreement?
o: The regulator must later approve it for it to bind
The agreement is unenforceable against the client
The agreement remains fully valid and binding on both
It is automatically void and treated as cancelled
It converts into an ordinary civil debt owed
w: FSMA states agreements by unauthorised persons are unenforceable against clients, protecting consumers from unlicensed activity.

n.2: FSMA makes such agreements unenforceable against the client, not binding.
n.0: No later regulator approval validates the agreement.
n.3: It is unenforceable, not void; the client may still choose to enforce it.
n.4: It does not convert into a civil debt.

q: An individual prosecuted for conducting regulated activity without authorisation raises a defence. Which defence is available to such a person under FSMA?
o: That they gained no financial benefit from the activity
That they reported the activity to the FCA afterwards
That they were supervised by a senior manager
That they reasonably believed they were exempt from FSMA
That they acted only on the client's instructions
w: A defence exists if the person reasonably believed they were exempt or not breaching FSMA.

n.4: Acting on client instructions is no defence to unauthorised activity.
n.0: Making no profit does not provide a FSMA defence.
n.2: Manager supervision does not excuse unauthorised activity.
n.1: Reporting after the event is not a statutory defence.

q: A compliance officer is unsure whether a new service crosses the regulatory perimeter and looks for official guidance. Who issues guidance on the scope of regulated and exempt activities under FSMA?
o: The Bank of England in monetary policy reports
The Serious Fraud Office via prosecution notices
The FCA through the Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG)
HM Treasury through annual budgets
The Prudential Regulation Authority via Basel guidance
w: The FCA provides detailed guidance on regulated and exempt activities through the Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG).

n.0: The Bank of England handles monetary policy, not FSMA perimeter guidance.
n.4: The PRA focuses on prudential matters, not defining regulated activities.
n.3: HM Treasury sets policy but PERG guidance is issued by FCA.
n.1: The SFO prosecutes crime, not regulatory activity definitions.

q: A firm has obtained Part 4A permission and now conducts regulated business. Under FSMA, who is classed as an authorised person?
o: A bank director acting privately
Any individual employed in finance
A shareholder in a listed company
An overseas entity trading shares
A firm with Part 4A permission
w: An authorised person is a firm with Part 4A permission granted by the FCA or PRA.

n.1: Employment in finance alone does not confer authorised person status.
n.3: Overseas entities need UK authorisation to be classed as authorised persons.
n.0: Private actions of directors do not count as firm authorisation.
n.2: Shareholding does not make an individual an authorised person under FSMA.

q: A compliance manager is explaining to a trainee why certain specified bodies need no FSMA authorisation. What is the effect of the Exemption Order 2001?
o: It exempts specified persons from needing FSMA authorisation
It removes all criminal liability arising under FSMA
It ends the PRA's prudential oversight of firms
It exempts foreign regulators from UK financial law
It automatically authorises every bank operating in the UK
w: The Exemption Order 2001 allows specified persons or bodies to operate without FSMA authorisation.

n.4: The Order grants exemptions to persons; it does not authorise all banks.
n.1: It does not remove criminal liability under FSMA.
n.2: It does not end PRA oversight.
n.3: It does not exempt foreign regulators from UK law.

q: Which action constitutes an offence under FSMA?
o: Managing the treasury of a public authority
Advising on investments without the required authorisation
Operating a bank under a proper statutory licence
Providing general, non-specific financial education
Publishing factual financial news articles
w: Giving investment advice without authorisation is a criminal offence under FSMA.

n.3: Generic financial education is not a regulated activity offence.
n.4: Publishing financial news is not itself a FSMA offence.
n.2: A properly licensed bank is acting lawfully.
n.0: Managing a public authority's treasury is not an FSMA offence.

q: A firm is unsure whether a borderline service falls inside the regulatory perimeter and seeks the FCA's interpretation. Which document clarifies how FSMA applies to borderline cases of regulated activity?
o: The Insolvency Act 1986 on winding up
The Financial Reporting Council's audit code
The FCA's Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG)
The Bank of England Act 1998
The Companies Act 2006 on company law
w: The FCA’s Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG) provides clarity on borderline cases of regulated activities under FSMA.

n.4: The Companies Act governs company law, not the FSMA perimeter.
n.3: The Bank of England Act concerns the central bank, not the perimeter.
n.0: The Insolvency Act deals with insolvency, not regulated-activity scope.
n.1: The FRC code concerns audit, not the FSMA perimeter.

q: A trainee asks how an exempt person differs from an unauthorised one under FSMA. What is the main feature of an exempt person?
o: They may carry on regulated activities without direct authorisation
They set the prudential requirements applied to banks
They may impose fines on other authorised firms
They automatically become members of the FSCS
They must approve every firm's financial promotions
w: Exempt persons can perform specified regulated activities without direct authorisation under FSMA due to statutory exemption.

n.2: Exempt persons cannot fine authorised firms.
n.3: Exemption does not make a person an FSCS member.
n.1: Exempt persons do not set banks' prudential rules.
n.4: Exempt persons do not approve firms' financial promotions.

q: An adviser operates under the authorisation of a principal firm rather than holding his own permission. Which of the following is an example of an exempt person under the FSMA Exemption Order 2001?
o: Insurance underwriters pricing and accepting risks
Appointed representatives acting under an authorised principal
Independent investment advisers giving retail advice
Retail bank branch managers handling deposits
Shareholder activists campaigning at company meetings
w: Appointed representatives are exempt as their activities are covered by their principal’s authorisation under FSMA.

n.2: Independent advisers must be authorised, not exempt.
n.3: Bank managers work within authorised firms; they are not exempt persons.
n.0: Underwriters operate within authorised insurers, not as exempt persons.
n.4: Shareholder activists are not exempt persons under FSMA.

q: An appointed representative sells products under a larger firm's permissions. Who assumes regulatory responsibility for an exempt appointed representative?
o: The representative's local council or authority
The Bank of England's supervisory arm
The Financial Ombudsman Service
The authorised firm acting as their principal
Parliament's Treasury Select Committee
w: The authorised principal firm takes full regulatory responsibility for its appointed representatives’ conduct.

n.0: A local authority does not take regulatory responsibility for an AR.
n.2: The FOS resolves complaints; it does not supervise ARs.
n.1: The Bank of England does not take responsibility for an AR.
n.4: A parliamentary committee does not supervise ARs.

q: A trainee questions why FSMA lets appointed representatives trade without their own authorisation. Why does FSMA allow certain exempt persons to operate without direct authorisation?
o: They operate exclusively outside of the United Kingdom
They make direct financial contributions to the government
They are supervised directly by Companies House
They provide only charitable, non-commercial services
Their conduct is overseen indirectly through an authorised principal
w: Exemption exists because oversight is effectively achieved through the authorised principal firm that supervises their conduct.

n.1: Exemption is not granted because of contributions to government.
n.3: Exempt representatives are not limited to charitable services.
n.2: Companies House does not supervise regulated conduct.
n.0: Exempt representatives commonly operate within the UK.

q: A client dealing with an appointed representative asks who would be answerable if things went wrong. What is the regulatory risk of dealing with an exempt appointed representative?
o: They are barred from trading in any regulated market
The authorised principal firm is liable for their actions
They must submit their reports directly to the FCA
They are entirely immune from all client complaints
They can never be investigated by the regulators
w: The authorised principal assumes full liability for the actions of its exempt appointed representatives.

n.0: ARs can carry on the regulated activities permitted by their principal.
n.2: ARs report through their principal, not directly to the FCA.
n.3: ARs are not immune from client complaints.
n.4: ARs can be investigated by regulators.

q: Which legislation underpins the definition of exempt persons?
o: FSMA Exemption Order 2001
Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
Companies Act 2006
Banking Act 2009
Financial Services Act 2012
w: The FSMA Exemption Order 2001 specifies categories of exempt persons under UK regulation.

n.4: The 2012 Act reformed regulators but did not define exempt persons.
n.2: The Companies Act deals with company law, not FSMA exemptions.
n.3: The Banking Act addresses crisis management, not exemptions under FSMA.
n.1: The Proceeds of Crime Act relates to money laundering, not exemptions.

q: A compliance officer is sorting entities into those that count as exempt persons and those that do not. Which of the following would NOT qualify as an exempt person?
o: The Bank of England carrying out its functions
A member of a recognised investment exchange
An appointed representative acting under a principal
A person exempted by a statutory instrument
An unauthorised firm acting without any principal firm
w: A firm acting without a principal and without authorisation is committing an offence, not operating as an exempt person.

n.2: An AR under a principal is exempt, so it does qualify.
n.1: Members of recognised investment exchanges are exempt persons.
n.0: The Bank of England is an exempt person under FSMA.
n.3: A person exempted by statutory instrument does qualify as exempt.

q: A client asks how the conduct of an exempt appointed representative is ultimately kept in check. Who ultimately supervises the conduct of an exempt person?
o: The local trading standards authority
The Treasury Select Committee
The High Court
The FCA via the authorised principal
The Competition and Markets Authority
w: The FCA supervises through the authorised principal, which is responsible for its exempt representatives’ conduct.

n.0: Trading standards regulate consumer goods, not FSMA exemptions.
n.2: The High Court adjudicates disputes but does not supervise exempt persons.
n.4: The CMA focuses on competition, not FSMA exemptions.
n.1: The Treasury Select Committee reviews policy, not individual supervision.

q: A firm is documenting where liability sits between an appointed representative and the firm it acts for. Which best describes the relationship between an exempt appointed representative and their principal?
o: The representative supervises the principal's own compliance
The representative is immune from any FCA enforcement
The FCA supervises both of them separately and directly
The principal is liable for all regulated activities the AR performs
The principal and representative share liability equally
w: The principal is fully liable for all regulated activities conducted by its appointed representative.

n.0: The principal supervises the AR, not the other way round.
n.4: Liability is not shared equally; the principal bears it.
n.2: The AR is overseen via the principal, not directly by the FCA.
n.1: ARs are not immune from FCA enforcement.

q: Before dealing with a new counterparty, a firm checks whether that counterparty is an exempt person. Why must firms confirm whether a counterparty is an exempt person?
o: To improve the effectiveness of the firm's marketing activities
To avoid the firm having to pay levies towards the FSCS
To confirm the voting rights attaching to a counterparty's shares
To ensure regulatory obligations are met through the correct oversight
To reduce the firm's filing requirements at Companies House
w: Identifying exempt persons ensures firms understand regulatory responsibility and oversight channels.

n.0: The check is about correct regulatory treatment, not marketing.
n.2: It is unrelated to shareholder voting rights.
n.4: It does not affect Companies House filings.
n.1: It is not a way to avoid FSCS levies.

q: A firm starts arranging deals in investments before its FCA permission is granted. What offence is committed if a firm undertakes regulated activities without authorisation under FSMA?
o: Ignoring the FCA's client classification rules
Failing to maintain the required capital adequacy
Failing to publish the firm's audited annual accounts
Carrying on regulated activities without authorisation
Breaching the UK's data protection principles
w: Undertaking regulated activities without authorisation is a criminal offence under FSMA.

n.2: Not publishing accounts is a Companies Act matter, not this offence.
n.0: Mis-classifying clients is a conduct breach, not the general prohibition.
n.4: Data protection breaches are an ICO matter, not this FSMA offence.
n.1: A capital shortfall is a prudential breach, not unauthorised activity.

q: A firm faces criminal proceedings after conducting business without authorisation. Which body prosecutes criminal offences under FSMA?
o: The Financial Conduct Authority
The Bank of England
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Competition and Markets Authority
The London Stock Exchange
w: The FCA has the power to prosecute criminal offences under FSMA.

n.2: The PRA regulates prudentially but does not prosecute FSMA offences.
n.1: The Bank of England oversees systemic stability, not FSMA prosecutions.
n.4: The LSE is a market operator, not a prosecutor of FSMA offences.
n.3: The CMA enforces competition law, not FSMA criminal offences.

q: A director is warned about the sanctions his firm could face for trading without FCA permission. What is the potential penalty for carrying on unauthorised regulated activities?
o: The loss of the firm's FSCS protection
The automatic dissolution of the company
An award of civil damages and nothing more
A temporary suspension of the firm's trading only
Imprisonment and/or an unlimited fine on conviction
w: Unauthorised regulated activity can result in criminal prosecution with imprisonment and/or an unlimited fine.

n.3: The penalty is criminal, not merely a trading suspension.
n.1: Conviction does not automatically dissolve the company.
n.2: The offence carries criminal penalties, not only civil damages.
n.0: Loss of FSCS cover is not the penalty for this offence.

q: An employee who deliberately helped his firm operate without authorisation asks whether he too can be prosecuted. When is an individual personally liable under FSMA?
o: If they delay holding the annual general meeting
If they are knowingly involved in unauthorised regulated activity
If they fail to file the company's tax returns on time
If they neglect to communicate with shareholders
If they breach their company secretarial duties
w: Individuals knowingly involved in unauthorised activity can be criminally liable under FSMA.

n.2: Late tax returns are an HMRC matter, not FSMA personal liability.
n.0: Delaying an AGM is a company-law issue, not this FSMA liability.
n.4: Company secretarial breaches are not FSMA offences.
n.3: Poor shareholder communication is not a FSMA offence.

q: A student asks why FSMA attaches criminal sanctions to operating without authorisation. Why does FSMA criminalise unauthorised regulated activity?
o: To protect consumers and safeguard market integrity
To reduce the audit costs borne by firms
To promote the growth of international trade
To increase the tax revenue collected by government
To encourage the formation of new companies
w: Criminalisation deters unauthorised activity and protects consumers and financial markets.

n.2: Criminalisation is about protection, not promoting international trade.
n.4: It is not aimed at encouraging company formation.
n.3: Raising tax revenue is not its purpose.
n.1: Reducing audit costs is not the reason for criminalisation.

q: A compliance quiz asks staff to spot the odd one out from a list of possible wrongdoings. Which of the following is NOT an offence under FSMA?
o: Carrying on regulated activity without authorisation
Market abuse through insider dealing
Making false statements to the FCA
Issuing misleading financial promotions
Failing to notify shareholders of dividends
w: Failing to notify shareholders of dividends is a corporate law matter, not a FSMA offence.

n.3: Misleading promotions are offences under FSMA.
n.0: Carrying on without authorisation is a FSMA offence.
n.2: False statements to FCA are offences under FSMA.
n.1: Market abuse including insider dealing falls under FSMA offences.

q: A prosecutor is preparing a case against a firm alleged to have breached FSMA. What must a prosecutor prove to secure a FSMA offence conviction?
o: That the firm suffered a loss of profitability
That the firm had breached UK employment law
That the firm had clients based overseas
That the firm's shareholders suffered financial losses
That a regulated activity was carried on without authorisation
w: The offence is established once a regulated activity is carried on without authorisation, regardless of financial loss.

n.0: Loss of profit need not be proved for the offence.
n.3: Shareholder loss is not an element of the offence.
n.1: Employment-law breaches are irrelevant to this offence.
n.2: Having overseas clients is not an element of the offence.

q: Several people were involved in a firm's unauthorised business and wonder who could face charges. Which individuals are at risk of FSMA prosecution?
o: Anyone at all who is employed by any bank
Those knowingly involved in the unauthorised regulated activity
Every shareholder of the regulated firm
All directors of any non-financial company
Only the senior auditors of listed companies
w: Anyone knowingly involved in unauthorised regulated activity may be prosecuted under FSMA.

n.0: Mere employment by a bank does not create FSMA liability.
n.2: Ordinary shareholders are not liable simply for holding shares.
n.4: Liability is not confined to auditors of listed companies.
n.3: Directors of non-financial firms are not automatically at risk.

q: A client who contracted with an unauthorised business asks whether the deal binds him. How does FSMA treat agreements made by unauthorised businesses?
o: They are enforceable once both parties consent
They are valid once approved by the firm's auditors
They are automatically valid and binding contracts
They become valid as soon as they are notarised
They are unenforceable against the other party
w: Contracts made through unauthorised regulated activity are unenforceable against the counterparty under FSMA.

n.2: Such agreements are unenforceable against the client, not valid.
n.0: Consent does not make them enforceable by the unauthorised firm.
n.3: Notarisation does not validate the agreement.
n.1: Auditor approval does not make the agreement enforceable.

q: A student notes that FSMA breaches can bring both damages claims and criminal charges and asks why. Why might FSMA offences include both civil and criminal consequences?
o: To simplify enforcement under the Companies Act
To remove shareholders' oversight of the firm
To replace the role of employment tribunals
To give regulators flexibility in deterrence and consumer redress
To reduce reliance on professional membership bodies
w: FSMA includes civil and criminal sanctions to deter misconduct and provide remedies to affected parties.

n.4: The dual approach is about deterrence and redress, not professional bodies.
n.0: It does not exist to simplify Companies Act enforcement.
n.2: It does not replace employment tribunals.
n.1: It is not intended to remove shareholder oversight.

q: An unauthorised firm attempts to enforce an investment agreement against its client in court. What is the default legal status of that agreement under FSMA?
o: It is valid only if approved by a court
It is valid once reported to the FCA
It is automatically enforceable in all circumstances
It is enforceable if both parties agree verbally
It is unenforceable against the other party
w: Contracts entered into by unauthorised firms are unenforceable against the counterparty under FSMA.

n.2: FSMA explicitly denies automatic enforceability for unauthorised business contracts.
n.0: Court approval cannot retroactively validate unauthorised contracts under FSMA.
n.1: FCA reporting does not cure unenforceability of unauthorised agreements.
n.3: Verbal consent does not override FSMA’s statutory unenforceability rule.

q: A trainee asks the rationale behind making unauthorised firms' contracts unenforceable. Why does FSMA make agreements by unauthorised firms unenforceable?
o: To encourage firms to cut their operating costs
To protect consumers from unauthorised financial dealings
To improve competition between rival firms
To assist with the process of incorporating companies
To simplify the firm's tax reporting duties
w: The rule protects consumers from unauthorised dealings by making such contracts unenforceable by the unauthorised firm.

n.0: The rule protects consumers, not to help firms cut costs.
n.4: It is unrelated to tax reporting.
n.2: It is not aimed at improving competition.
n.3: It has nothing to do with company incorporation.

q: A consumer who dealt with an unauthorised firm wants to know whether he can still hold it to the deal. Which party may still enforce an agreement with an unauthorised business?
o: The private counterparty who contracted with the firm
HM Treasury, stepping in to enforce the terms
The Bank of England, acting on the agreement
The unauthorised business that carried on the activity
The FCA, enforcing the contract on the client's behalf
w: The counterparty retains the right to enforce, but the unauthorised firm cannot enforce against them.

n.3: The unauthorised firm cannot enforce the agreement.
n.4: The FCA does not enforce private contracts for clients.
n.1: HM Treasury does not enforce such agreements.
n.2: The Bank of England does not enforce private contracts.

q: A court hears a dispute over an unenforceable contract made by an unauthorised firm. What remedy may the court provide?
o: Automatic validation of the unenforceable agreement
A criminal conviction imposed on the counterparty
Restitution, returning money or property transferred
A requirement for shareholders to approve the deal
Conversion of the agreement into a loan contract
w: Courts may order restitution to restore parties to their original position when a contract is unenforceable under FSMA.

n.0: The court does not validate the agreement; it may order restitution.
n.1: The innocent counterparty is not criminally convicted.
n.3: Shareholder approval is not the court's remedy.
n.4: The agreement is not converted into a loan.

q: An unauthorised firm's contract is unenforceable, yet it hopes a court may still recognise value it provided. In what circumstance might it still benefit from the agreement?
o: If the firm registers with Companies House
If the court allows restitution
If an auditor confirms fair value
If both parties agree to continue
If the FCA issues a temporary waiver
w: Courts may allow restitution to prevent unjust enrichment, even where a contract is unenforceable.

n.4: The FCA cannot waive statutory unenforceability provisions.
n.3: Consent does not cure statutory unenforceability.
n.0: Companies House registration does not affect FSMA enforceability rules.
n.2: Auditor confirmation cannot override statutory provisions of FSMA.

q: A consumer worries about the consequences of having signed a contract with an unauthorised business. How does unenforceability affect consumers contracting with unauthorised businesses?
o: It protects the consumer from being sued on the agreement
It removes the consumer's right to complain to the Ombudsman
It lets the unauthorised firm enforce the contract in court
It requires the consumer to repay any money already received
It cancels any FSCS protection the consumer would have
w: Consumers cannot be sued on unenforceable agreements, giving them statutory protection against unauthorised firms.

n.2: The reverse is true: the agreement is unenforceable against the consumer, not enforceable by the firm.
n.3: The consumer can recover money and compensation, not repay it, under FSMA.
n.1: Unenforceability does not affect Ombudsman eligibility.
n.4: Unenforceability does not remove FSCS protection.

q: A compliance officer is identifying which of a firm's dealings are most exposed to unenforceability. Which contracts are most at risk of being unenforceable under FSMA?
o: Service contracts between a company and its own directors
Contracts of carriage covering the transport of goods
Ordinary retail purchase contracts for everyday consumer goods
Agreements for regulated activities made by unauthorised firms
Employment contracts held by staff of authorised firms
w: Contracts involving unauthorised regulated activity are unenforceable under FSMA.

n.2: Ordinary consumer goods sales are not regulated activities under FSMA.
n.4: Employment contracts are outside the FSMA regulated-activity regime.
n.0: Directors' service contracts are governed by company law, not FSMA enforceability.
n.1: Carriage of goods contracts are unconnected to regulated activities.

q: Before signing with an investment firm, a consumer wants to be sure any agreement would be enforceable. How can a consumer check if a firm's agreement will be enforceable?
o: By obtaining a credit reference from the firm's own bank
By checking the firm's authorisation on the FCA register
By asking the firm's shareholders to confirm its status
By requesting a certificate of good standing from Companies House
By reviewing the marketing brochures the firm has produced
w: Consumers can confirm enforceability by checking if a firm is authorised on the FCA register.

n.3: Companies House confirms incorporation, not FCA authorisation.
n.0: A bank reference says nothing about regulatory authorisation.
n.4: Marketing material can be misleading and is not proof of authorisation.
n.2: Shareholders cannot verify a firm's regulatory permissions.

q: An unauthorised firm sues a client to enforce an investment agreement. What happens if it tries to enforce the agreement in court?
o: The court will refuse enforcement
The court imposes only a civil fine
The court must validate the contract
The Ombudsman rules on the enforceability
The case is transferred to Companies House
w: Courts refuse enforcement of agreements entered into by unauthorised firms under FSMA.

n.2: Courts cannot validate unenforceable agreements under FSMA.
n.1: Civil fines are not the statutory remedy; unenforceability applies.
n.4: Companies House has no role in FSMA contract enforcement.
n.3: The Ombudsman resolves complaints, not enforceability of FSMA contracts.

q: A regulator explains how the unenforceability rule underpins trust in the financial system. Why is the enforceability rule critical to market confidence?
o: It removes the need for firms to maintain compliance departments
It simplifies the preparation of firms' annual audit reports
It works to reduce the overall number of retail investors
It operates to guarantee a level of profit for authorised firms
It reassures consumers that only authorised firms can legally enforce contracts
w: The rule builds confidence by ensuring enforceable contracts can only be made by authorised firms.

n.3: The rule does not guarantee firm profits.
n.1: It is unrelated to audit-report preparation.
n.2: It does not aim to reduce retail investor numbers.
n.0: It does not remove the need for compliance functions.

q: A defendant charged with unauthorised regulated activity puts forward a defence at trial. Which defence is available to a person accused of unauthorised regulated activity under FSMA?
o: That the business was highly profitable during the period
That they reasonably believed they were not contravening FSMA
That Companies House was supervising the firm's conduct
That the firm was correctly registered for VAT purposes
That the firm's shareholders had approved the activity
w: A valid defence is a reasonable belief that the activity did not contravene FSMA requirements.

n.0: Profitability is irrelevant to whether an offence was committed.
n.4: Shareholder approval cannot authorise unlawful regulated activity.
n.2: Companies House does not supervise regulated financial conduct.
n.3: VAT registration has no bearing on FSMA authorisation.

q: Someone prosecuted under FSMA argues he had no idea his activity needed authorisation. What is a recognised defence against allegations of carrying on unauthorised regulated activity?
o: That the person complied fully with health and safety law
That the person filed annual tax returns on time
That the company's directors had approved the activity
That they neither knew nor could know the activity was regulated
That the person held a current personal bank account
w: A person may defend themselves if unaware the activity required authorisation under FSMA.

n.4: Holding a bank account is irrelevant to a FSMA defence.
n.1: Filing tax returns has no bearing on regulated-activity offences.
n.0: Health and safety compliance is unrelated to FSMA.
n.2: Directors cannot approve unauthorised regulated activity.

q: A law student asks why FSMA builds in statutory defences to its offences. Why are statutory defences included in FSMA?
o: To encourage authorised firms to maximise their trading profits
To promote the overseas expansion of UK financial firms
To reduce the level of competition in financial markets
To simplify the external auditing requirements for firms
To avoid unfairly criminalising people who made genuine mistakes
w: Defences exist to prevent criminalisation where individuals made genuine mistakes about regulatory requirements.

n.0: FSMA is not designed to boost firms' profits.
n.2: FSMA aims to protect markets, not reduce competition.
n.3: Statutory defences have nothing to do with audit requirements.
n.1: Defences are unrelated to overseas expansion.

q: A defendant lists several arguments hoping one will excuse his FSMA breach. Which of the following is NOT a defence under FSMA?
o: Lack of awareness that activity was regulated
Due diligence checks undertaken
Approval by FCA for the activity
Consent from a counterparty
Proof of reasonable belief of compliance
w: Counterparty consent does not provide a defence under FSMA for unauthorised activity.

n.4: Reasonable belief in compliance is a recognised defence under FSMA.
n.0: Lack of awareness can be a statutory defence in FSMA cases.
n.2: FCA approval validates activities, making a defence unnecessary.
n.1: Evidence of due diligence can support a defence of reasonable belief.

q: A firm prosecuted for a FSMA breach argues it did everything it reasonably could to comply. What defence may a firm use if prosecuted for breach of FSMA?
o: That it employed appropriately qualified and experienced staff
That it was a member of a recognised trade association
That it filed its statutory accounts before the deadline
That it maintained strong profits throughout the period
That it took all reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence
w: Due diligence demonstrating compliance efforts can form a defence against FSMA breaches.

n.2: Timely filing of accounts is not a FSMA defence.
n.3: Profitability does not excuse a regulatory breach.
n.0: Qualified staff alone is not a statutory defence.
n.1: Trade association membership provides no defence.

q: In a FSMA prosecution, the accused relies on his honest view that no permission was needed. When might the defence of 'reasonable belief' apply?
o: When the firm was the market leader in its sector
When the accused genuinely believed no authorisation was required
When the firm maintained an unusually large base of clients
When the firm achieved consistently high client satisfaction scores
When the firm's directors were widely respected in the industry
w: The defence applies where the accused reasonably believed authorisation was not required for their activity.

n.3: Client satisfaction is irrelevant to the reasonable-belief defence.
n.0: Market position does not establish a defence.
n.4: A director's reputation is not a legal defence.
n.2: Client numbers have no bearing on the defence.

q: An individual who unknowingly breached FSMA seeks a statutory protection limiting his liability. Which statutory protection limits liability for inadvertent FSMA breaches?
o: A blanket exemption granted under the Companies Act 2006
An automatic waiver of liability granted by the FCA
An indemnity provided to the firm by its shareholders
The defence of having acted without knowledge of the breach
Protection gained by relying on professional tax advice
w: The statutory defence of acting without knowledge protects individuals who were unaware their conduct breached FSMA.

n.1: The FCA does not grant automatic liability waivers.
n.2: A shareholder indemnity does not remove FSMA liability.
n.0: The Companies Act grants no FSMA exemption.
n.4: Relying on tax advice is not a statutory FSMA defence.

q: A compliance officer explains why the due diligence defence matters even when a breach still happens. Why is the due diligence defence important under FSMA?
o: It shows the firm tried to prevent a breach that still occurred
It releases the firm from its regulatory reporting duties
It raises profits by cutting the firm's compliance spending
It automatically grants the firm the authorisation it needs
It allows the firm to avoid external audits of accounts
w: The defence demonstrates a firm took reasonable care to comply, even if a breach occurred.

n.2: Due diligence is about compliance effort, not cutting costs.
n.4: The defence does not exempt a firm from audits.
n.3: A defence never confers authorisation.
n.1: Reporting obligations remain regardless of the defence.

q: A firm intends to rely on a due diligence defence at trial and asks what it must establish. What must a defendant demonstrate to succeed with a due diligence defence?
o: That they obtained client approval for the activity beforehand
That they were the leading firm in their market sector
That they achieved a high level of customer satisfaction
That they held current ISO quality-management certification
That they took all reasonable steps to prevent the breach
w: The defence requires evidence of reasonable steps taken to avoid FSMA contraventions.

n.0: Client approval cannot authorise a breach of FSMA.
n.2: Customer satisfaction is irrelevant to the defence.
n.1: Market leadership is not a legal defence.
n.3: ISO certification is unrelated to a FSMA defence.

q: A student asks why FSMA pairs strict offences with statutory defences. Why does FSMA balance strict offences with statutory defences?
o: To encourage greater shareholder activism within firms
To lessen the sector's reliance on tax legislation
To replace other duties owed under general company law
To ensure fairness where a breach was genuinely unintentional
To promote the export of UK financial services abroad
w: Statutory defences ensure fairness by distinguishing genuine mistakes from deliberate misconduct.

n.4: Statutory defences are not an export-promotion tool.
n.0: They have nothing to do with shareholder activism.
n.2: FSMA defences do not replace company-law duties.
n.1: They are unrelated to tax legislation.

q: The FCA decides that a former adviser is no longer fit and proper and takes action against him personally. What is the purpose of a prohibition order under FSMA?
o: To cancel a company's incorporation at Companies House
To cap the amount a firm may spend on advertising
To limit the number of shareholders a firm may have
To stop an individual from performing regulated functions
To dissolve an authorised financial services firm entirely
w: A prohibition order stops an individual from carrying out regulated functions if they are not fit and proper.

n.4: A prohibition order targets individuals, not firm dissolution.
n.1: It does not restrict advertising budgets.
n.2: It does not limit shareholder numbers.
n.0: It cannot cancel a company's incorporation.

q: The FCA is considering a prohibition order and reviews who can fall within its reach. Against whom can the FCA issue a prohibition order?
o: Only directors of authorised firms
Any auditor working in financial services
Any individual deemed not fit and proper
Only shareholders with over 5% stake
Only employees of the FCA
w: The FCA may prohibit any individual considered not fit and proper from performing regulated activities.

n.0: Orders are not restricted to directors; they apply to any individual.
n.3: Shareholding level is irrelevant to prohibition orders.
n.4: FCA staff are not the intended targets of prohibition orders.
n.1: Auditors are regulated differently; prohibition orders apply more broadly.

q: A retail client suffers loss after a firm breaches FCA rules and looks to FSMA s.138D for redress. What recourse does a private person have?
o: They can suspend the firm’s authorisation
They can cancel the firm’s shares
They can fine the firm directly
They can sue for damages
They can issue their own prohibition order
w: FSMA s.138D allows private persons to bring actions for damages when a firm breaches FCA rules.

n.4: Only the FCA can issue prohibition orders, not private persons.
n.0: Suspension of authorisation is a regulatory power, not private action.
n.2: Private individuals cannot levy fines; only regulators can.
n.1: Share cancellation is unrelated to FSMA remedies.

q: A compliance officer is confirming which FSMA provision underpins the FCA's power to ban individuals. Which FSMA section empowers the FCA to make prohibition orders?
o: Section 56
Section 71
Section 59
Section 118
Section 138D
w: FSMA section 56 gives the FCA power to make prohibition orders.

n.1: Section 71 deals with enforceability of agreements, not prohibition orders.
n.4: Section 138D concerns damages claims, not prohibition orders.
n.2: Section 59 relates to approval of controlled functions, not prohibition orders.
n.3: Section 118 addresses market abuse, not prohibition orders.

q: The FCA moves to ban an individual from performing regulated functions. Why might the FCA issue a prohibition order against an individual?
o: Because they operate outside the UK
Because they hold dual citizenship
Because they criticised FCA policy
Because they are not fit and proper
Because they failed to file company accounts
w: Prohibition orders are issued if an individual is not fit and proper to perform regulated activities.

n.4: Failure to file accounts is a Companies Act issue, not FSMA prohibition grounds.
n.1: Citizenship is irrelevant to fitness and propriety tests.
n.2: Criticism of FCA policy does not justify prohibition.
n.0: Operating abroad does not itself warrant prohibition.

q: A firm applying for an individual to take on a controlled function checks the relevant FSMA power. Which FSMA section allows FCA approval of individuals performing controlled functions?
o: Section 118
Section 71
Section 59
Section 138D
Section 56
w: Section 59 FSMA provides the FCA with power to approve controlled functions.

n.4: Section 56 concerns prohibition orders, not approvals.
n.1: Section 71 deals with unenforceable agreements, not controlled functions.
n.3: Section 138D permits damages actions, not approval powers.
n.0: Section 118 addresses market abuse, not controlled functions approval.

q: An approved person acts while subject to a breach of the approval requirement, and a client questions the deal. What is the effect of FSMA section 71 on agreements made in breach?
o: The agreement may be unenforceable against the other party
The agreement takes effect only with Ombudsman approval
The agreement is converted into a civil monetary penalty
The agreement guarantees the counterparty full FSCS coverage
The agreement automatically becomes valid and fully binding
w: Section 71 confirms agreements made in breach may be unenforceable against the counterparty.

n.4: Breach makes agreements unenforceable, not automatically valid.
n.2: Agreements are not converted into penalties.
n.3: Unenforceability does not trigger FSCS coverage.
n.1: The Ombudsman does not approve agreements.

q: A client harmed by a firm's rule breach considers a civil claim under FSMA. Which of the following best describes the right of action for damages under FSMA s.138D?
o: Auditors may impose financial penalties directly on firms
The Treasury may annul rules that the FCA has made
Shareholders may void decisions taken by the company's board
Firms may automatically reclaim their losses from competitors
Private persons may claim damages for a firm's breach of FCA rules
w: Section 138D allows private persons to seek damages for FCA rule breaches by firms.

n.3: s.138D gives no automatic right to reclaim from competitors.
n.2: It does not empower shareholders to void board decisions.
n.0: Auditors cannot impose penalties on firms.
n.1: The Treasury does not annul FCA rules via s.138D.

q: A consumer group is explaining why s.138D matters to ordinary investors. Why is FSMA s.138D significant for consumer protection?
o: It gives private persons a legal right to claim damages
It guarantees consumers a minimum return on investments
It exempts consumers from paying tax on their investments
It prevents authorised firms from paying any dividends
It requires shareholder approval for consumer contracts
w: Section 138D enhances consumer protection by providing a direct right to sue for damages.

n.2: s.138D grants no tax exemption to consumers.
n.1: It does not guarantee investment returns.
n.3: It does not restrict firms paying dividends.
n.4: It does not require shareholder approval for contracts.

q: A regulator is describing how banning unfit individuals and allowing damages claims work together. What is the combined effect of prohibition orders and damages actions?
o: They operate to guarantee the future profitability of authorised firms
