n.3: It does not become newspaper advice.
n.0: The overseas exemption does not apply.
n.4: It is not a joint enterprise.

q: A compliance officer must decide whether a trustee's actions are exempt or regulated advice. How does the law distinguish between the two?
o: By examining whether the actions are fiduciary or commercial
By reviewing pre-approval documents issued by the FCA
By confirming the tax status of the trust in question
By checking whether the trustee charges any fees
By assessing whether the activity is carried on overseas
w: The key test is whether the trustee’s actions are fiduciary in nature or commercial advice requiring authorisation.

n.3: Charging fees is not the distinguishing test.
n.4: Whether it is overseas is not the relevant test.
n.1: The FCA does not issue pre-approval documents for this.
n.2: The trust's tax status is irrelevant to the test.

q: An employer sets up a share scheme for its own staff. Why are employee share schemes excluded from FCA authorisation requirements?
o: Because they arise within the employer-employee relationship
Because they always involve securities issued overseas
Because they are always managed by independent trustees
Because they never involve any investment activity at all
Because they are operated and overseen by newspapers
w: Employee share schemes are excluded as they are part of the employment relationship rather than public investment business.

n.1: They do not necessarily involve overseas securities.
n.3: They can involve shares, which are investments.
n.2: They are not necessarily managed by trustees.
n.4: Newspapers do not operate employee share schemes.

q: A compliance officer is deciding whether an internal arrangement qualifies as an employee share scheme under PERG 2.9.13 so that authorisation is not needed. Which feature would characterise such a scheme?
o: It operates as a joint enterprise with another company
It markets a range of investments widely to the public
It gives staff shares or options as part of their pay
It provides regulated mortgage contracts to members of staff
It promotes regulated advice services to external clients
w: Employee share schemes give staff shares or options as part of employment benefits and are excluded from FCA authorisation.

n.1: Marketing to the public is not an employee share scheme feature.
n.3: Providing mortgages to staff is a separate regulated activity.
n.0: It is not a joint enterprise arrangement.
n.4: Promoting advice externally is not part of such a scheme.

q: A firm's MLRO is reviewing several share arrangements to see which can rely on the employee share scheme exclusion. Which of these would NOT fall within that exclusion?
o: Granting shares under a staff incentive plan
Running a tax-advantaged company share option plan
Providing options to staff as part of bonuses
Offering shares to the general public
Allocating stock to employees under a savings scheme
w: Public offers are regulated activity; only schemes within employment relationships are excluded.

n.2: Staff bonuses through options are covered by the exclusion.
n.0: Incentive plans within employment are excluded.
n.4: Savings schemes for employees are excluded.
n.1: Tax-advantaged option plans remain excluded.

q: A start-up wants to offer shares to its own staff without becoming FCA authorised. Which exclusion would let it do so without needing permission?
o: Employee share schemes
Trustee exemption
Group enterprise exemption
Overseas person exemption
Newspaper advice exemption
w: Employee share scheme exclusions cover offers of shares to staff as part of employment benefits.

n.1: Trustee exemption applies to fiduciary roles, not share offers.
n.4: Newspaper advice relates to media content, not share schemes.
n.2: Group exemptions concern intra-group services, not staff benefits.
n.3: Overseas person rules apply differently, not to employee schemes.

q: A paraplanner is asked how a firm's tax-advantaged share option plan for its employees is treated for regulatory purposes. What is the correct treatment?
o: They need trustee approval before the exemption can apply
They require full FCA authorisation before they can operate
They are authorised automatically by HM Treasury
They are regulated under the joint enterprise exclusion rules
They are excluded from authorisation as employee share schemes
w: Tax-advantaged share option plans are covered under the employee share scheme exclusion from FCA authorisation.

n.1: Such plans do not require full FCA authorisation.
n.3: They are not governed by the joint enterprise rules.
n.0: Trustee approval is not required for the exemption.
n.2: HM Treasury does not grant automatic authorisation.

q: An adviser is confirming which of a company's arrangements is exempt under the employee share scheme rules. Which of the following would be an exempt activity?
o: Providing regulated mortgage advice to members of staff
Publishing detailed investment advice in a paid newsletter
Offering shares for sale to the public through an IPO
Allocating shares to staff under a Save-As-You-Earn plan
Arranging overseas securities for external retail clients
w: Save-As-You-Earn schemes for staff are explicitly exempt as employee share schemes.

n.2: A public IPO is a regulated offer, not an exempt scheme.
n.1: Paid newsletter advice is regulated, not an employee scheme.
n.0: Mortgage advice to staff is a separate regulated activity.
n.4: Arranging securities for external clients is regulated.

q: A trainee asks a compliance officer why employee share schemes are not treated as risky as public investment offers. What is the correct explanation?
o: Because they involve no financial instruments whatsoever
Because they require approval from a regulator overseas
Because they are supervised and overseen by newspapers
Because they guarantee the staff a profit on their shares
Because they are limited to the employees of the firm
w: The scope is limited to employees, so systemic risks and public exposure are reduced.

n.3: Such schemes do not guarantee staff a profit.
n.0: They can involve shares, which are financial instruments.
n.2: Newspapers do not supervise these schemes.
n.1: No overseas regulator approval is required.

q: A firm is reviewing its share plan and wants to keep the employee share scheme exclusion. Which of these actions would invalidate that exclusion?
o: Allocating free shares to members of the firm's staff
Offering the scheme to external clients beyond staff
Offering discounted shares internally to employees
Granting share options to staff as an annual bonus
Running a Save-As-You-Earn plan for existing employees
w: The exclusion fails if shares are offered to external clients beyond employees.

n.4: An SAYE plan for employees keeps the exclusion valid.
n.0: Free shares to staff fall within the exclusion.
n.3: Share options as a staff bonus remain within scope.
n.2: Discounted internal shares to staff stay exempt.

q: A compliance officer must explain the underlying rationale for the employee share scheme exemption to the board. Which regulatory principle best explains it?
o: They are restricted only to participants based overseas
They are excluded because of the joint enterprise rules
They are automatically overseen by independent trustees
They never involve any securities whatsoever
They are employment benefits, not public investment services
w: Employee share schemes are classed as employment benefits rather than regulated investment services.

n.2: They are not necessarily overseen by trustees.
n.3: They can involve shares, which are securities.
n.0: They are not restricted to overseas participants.
n.1: The joint enterprise rules are not the basis for exclusion.

q: An adviser is listing tax-advantaged staff schemes that fall within the exclusion in PERG 2.9.13. Which of these is an example of such an exempt scheme?
o: Joint enterprise bond sale
Trustee managed investment club
Public retail bond issue
Newspaper subscription service
Company Share Option Plan
w: Company Share Option Plans are explicitly included within the employee share scheme exclusion.

n.2: Retail bond issues are public offers and regulated.
n.3: Newspaper services fall under a different exclusion.
n.1: Trustee clubs are not part of employee share schemes.
n.0: Joint enterprises are treated separately under PERG 2.9.9/10.

q: A firm based abroad is checking when it can rely on the overseas person exclusion in PERG 2.9.15. In which situation does that exclusion apply?
o: When firms co-operate under the joint enterprise rules
When a firm's own employees give advice internally
When a trustee administers an estate based in the UK
When activities are carried on from abroad with no UK place of business
When a newspaper publishes an investment column
w: The overseas person exclusion applies when activities are conducted from outside the UK without establishing a place of business here.

n.1: Internal employee advice is a different matter entirely.
n.2: UK estate administration is the trustee exclusion.
n.4: Newspaper columns fall under the newspaper exclusion.
n.0: Joint enterprise co-operation is a separate exclusion.

q: A compliance team is assessing which arrangement best qualifies for the overseas person exclusion. Which situation would qualify?
o: A London firm advising clients based in Manchester
A journalist writing tips on UK stocks from London
A UK bank offering mortgages to borrowers nationwide
A US broker dealing with UK clients from New York
A trustee managing assets that are located in the UK
w: A US broker dealing with UK clients from abroad falls under the overseas person exclusion.

n.0: A London firm operating in the UK is not an overseas person.
n.2: A UK bank has a UK establishment, so the exclusion fails.
n.4: A UK-based trustee is not an overseas person.
n.1: A UK journalist is not carrying on business from abroad.

q: An overseas broker currently relies on the overseas person exclusion and wants to keep it. Which factor would remove the benefit of that exclusion?
o: Serving all of the firm's clients from outside the UK
Providing execution-only services entirely from abroad
Communicating with clients by email from abroad
Establishing a permanent place of business in the UK
Restricting the services offered to overseas clients only
w: Once an overseas person sets up a permanent UK presence, the exclusion no longer applies.

n.0: Serving clients from abroad is consistent with the exclusion.
n.4: Restricting to overseas clients does not remove the exclusion.
n.2: Emailing from abroad does not create a UK establishment.
n.1: Execution-only services from abroad keep the exclusion.

q: A student asks why FSMA sets out a specific exclusion for overseas persons. What is the reason for it?
o: To avoid regulating foreign firms with no UK establishment
To guarantee a profit for investors based in the UK
To grant an automatic exemption to all trustees
To reduce the tax liabilities faced by UK firms
To simplify the structure of domestic corporate groups
w: The exclusion ensures FSMA does not regulate firms without a UK establishment.

n.1: The exclusion does not guarantee UK investors a profit.
n.2: It is not a trustee exemption.
n.3: It is unrelated to reducing UK firms' tax.
n.4: It does not concern domestic group structures.

q: A compliance officer is checking which foreign firm can no longer rely on the overseas person exclusion. Which of these would NOT be covered by it?
o: A Hong Kong adviser opening a London office
A Japanese bank offering services from Tokyo
A US asset manager emailing UK clients
A Canadian broker executing trades remotely
A Swiss bank advising UK clients from Geneva
w: Opening a London office constitutes a UK establishment, which removes the overseas exclusion.

n.4: Advising from abroad without UK presence is covered by the exclusion.
n.3: Remote execution from abroad remains exempt under the exclusion.
n.2: Remote email contact from overseas is still exempt.
n.1: Services from Tokyo without UK presence qualify for the exclusion.

q: The FCA is assessing whether a foreign firm counts as an overseas person. What test is applied to determine that status?
o: Whether the person operates an employee share scheme
Whether the person forms part of a corporate group
Whether the person maintains an establishment in the UK
Whether the person provides trustee or nominee services
Whether the person publishes articles in UK newspapers
w: The key test is whether the person has a UK establishment; if so, the exclusion does not apply.

n.4: Publishing in UK newspapers is not the overseas-person test.
n.1: Group membership is not the relevant test.
n.3: Providing trustee services is a different exclusion.
n.0: Running a share scheme is unrelated to overseas status.

q: An adviser is picking an example that correctly illustrates use of the overseas person exclusion. Which scenario does so?
o: A financial journalist providing share tips to readers
A trustee in the UK holding assets for beneficiaries
A UK branch of a foreign bank offering mortgages here
A US broker executing UK trades from New York, with no UK branch
An employer offering shares to its own members of staff
w: Conducting business from abroad without a UK establishment fits the overseas person exclusion.

n.2: A UK branch is a UK establishment, so the exclusion fails.
n.1: A UK trustee is not an overseas person.
n.4: An employer share offer is the employee scheme exclusion.
n.0: A journalist's tips fall under the newspaper exclusion.

q: An overseas person opens a UK office to serve local clients but does not apply for authorisation. What risk does this create?
o: They automatically qualify under the exemption available to trustees
They are exempt from FSMA provided their services are supplied free of charge
They fall within the joint-enterprise exclusion by default
They remain automatically exempt from FSMA by virtue of being overseas
They may breach FSMA by carrying on regulated activities without permission
w: Once a UK office is established, FCA authorisation is required; failure to apply is a breach of FSMA.

n.3: Overseas status does not confer automatic FSMA exemption.
n.0: The trustee exemption does not apply on these facts.
n.2: The joint-enterprise exclusion is not automatic.
n.1: Providing services free does not remove the need for permission.

q: A policy analyst is explaining how the overseas person exclusion helps international financial markets. Why does it support them?
o: They apply to all forms of marketing aimed at the public
They grant an automatic exemption to all UK trustees
They guarantee a return on the investments UK clients make
They reduce the taxes payable by foreign investors
They let foreign firms serve UK clients with no UK establishment
w: Overseas exclusions enable cross-border services without requiring local authorisation if no UK establishment exists.

q: A trainee asks a compliance officer why FSMA section 19 imposes a general prohibition. What is the purpose of it?

q: A firm has been carrying on a regulated activity without authorisation. What is the consequence of breaching the FSMA section 19 general prohibition?

n.2: Companies House registration does not cure a s.19 breach.

n.3: Each regulator approves the SMFs it designates; dual approval does not apply to the same SMF16.
n.4: The firm’s Board cannot approve SMFs; regulator approval is required.
n.2: SMF16 is not a Certification Function; it requires regulator pre-approval.

q: A firm is compiling a Form A application for a new SMF holder. Which item must accompany the application?
o: A notarised copy of the candidate’s passport
A Statement of Responsibilities for the individual
The firm’s annual bonus policy
A written reference covering the last two years only
A copy of the candidate’s employment contract
w: An up-to-date Statement of Responsibilities (SoR) is mandatory and must clearly set out the SMF holder’s responsibilities. Firms must also obtain appropriate criminal records checks and regulatory references (typically covering the previous six years) as part of fit-and-proper assessments.

n.4: Employment contracts are not mandated as part of the regulatory submission.
n.2: Bonus policies are unrelated to SMF approval documentation.
n.0: Proof of identity may be part of vetting, but a notarised passport copy is not a universal regulatory requirement.
n.3: Regulatory references normally cover six years, not just two.

q: A trainee is learning how SMF approval differs from the Certification Regime. Which statement best describes the boundary between the two?
o: Only certification staff are certified each year by the regulator
Neither SMF holders nor certification staff need approval or certification
SMF holders need regulator approval; certification staff are certified by the firm
Both SMF holders and certification staff are approved by the regulator
SMF holders are approved by the firm; certification staff by the regulator
w: SMF roles require prior regulator approval (e.g., via Form A). Certification Functions do not require regulator approval; instead, the firm must assess fitness and propriety and issue annual certification.

n.3: Certification staff are certified by the firm, not the regulator.
n.0: The firm, not the regulator, certifies certification staff.
n.1: SMF holders do require prior regulator approval.
n.4: This reverses the roles: the regulator approves SMF holders.

q: Before appointing a new SMF, a firm is completing its fit-and-propriety checks. Which check is it specifically expected to carry out under SM&CR?
o: Regulatory references typically covering six years
A single character reference from a colleague
An attestation that the candidate will not trade personally
Submission of the firm’s remuneration report to the FCA
Only an internal interview with no external checks
w: Firms must conduct robust fit-and-proper assessments, including obtaining regulatory references (usually for the preceding six years) and a criminal records check for SMF candidates, alongside assessing honesty, integrity, competence and financial soundness.

n.4: Regulators expect external checks (e.g., regulatory references, criminal records), not just an internal interview.
n.1: One informal reference is insufficient for a fit-and-proper assessment.
n.2: Personal dealing attestations are not a substitute for mandated checks such as regulatory references and criminal records.
n.3: Submitting a remuneration report is unrelated to pre-approval fit-and-proper checks for an SMF hire.

q: An SMF holder's duties have been substantially reorganised following a restructure. When must the firm submit a revised Statement of Responsibilities?

Only when the SMF holder resigns from the firm
Only when it is specifically requested by the FCA
Once every three years as a routine refresh

n.3: It is not only on FCA request.
n.2: It is not limited to resignation.
n.4: There is no fixed three-year cycle.

n.3: HM Treasury legislates but does not approve individual SMF roles.

o: If staff request it informally

Once at hiring only
Every ten years
At regular intervals
w: Training needs must be assessed at the outset and then at regular intervals throughout employment.

n.2: One-time assessment at hiring is insufficient under TC rules.
n.3: A ten-year gap is far too long; regular reviews are required.
n.1: Training reviews are ongoing, not only tied to discipline.
n.0: Informal requests alone are not sufficient; formal reviews are required.

q: A compliance officer is checking the firm's duty under TC 2.1.12. What does this rule require the firm to do?

Ensure that employees receive an annual pay rise
Guarantee the firm's staff pension contributions
Take appropriate steps to maintain employee competence
Reduce staff training hours year on year

n.2: Pension contributions are not the TC 2.1.12 requirement.
n.4: Firms must maintain, not cut, training.

q: A firm needs a document proving one of its advisers holds a valid qualification under the TC rules. Which document demonstrates this?

The adviser's personal curriculum vitae
The adviser's signed employment contract
A Statement of Professional Standing
The adviser's most recent annual tax return

n.2: An employment contract does not evidence qualification.
n.1: A CV is not proof of a valid qualification.
n.4: A tax return does not evidence competence.
n.0: An internal log is not the required evidence.

q: An adviser needs their Statement of Professional Standing renewed before continuing to give retail investment advice. Which type of body must issue it?
o: The Bank of England
An FCA-accredited professional body
The Financial Ombudsman Service
The individual adviser's own employer
HM Revenue and Customs

n.3: The employer does not issue the SPS.
n.4: HMRC does not issue the SPS.
n.0: The Bank of England does not issue the SPS.

q: An adviser wants to keep a valid Statement of Professional Standing. What must they complete each year to retain it?

Reapply each year for FCA authorisation
Undertake an annual government health check
Attend the firm's annual shareholder meeting
Complete at least 35 hours of CPD each year

n.0: Payslips are not submitted to the FCA.
n.3: Attending shareholder meetings is not required.
n.2: No government health check is required.

q: A firm is explaining why TC 2.1.11 requires training needs to be reassessed at regular intervals. What is the reason?

To keep competence current as roles evolve
To meet the firm's annual tax deadlines
To cut the firm's staff recruitment costs
To adjust the firm's office rent payments

n.2: Reassessment is about competence, not tax deadlines.
n.3: It is not about recruitment costs.
n.0: It is not about holiday entitlement.
n.4: It is not about office rent.

q: A firm is checking what TC 2.1.13 requires it to do to maintain employee competence. What does the rule call for?
o: Weekly financial disclosures made to HMRC
Monthly physical fitness tests for all staff
Annual submission of the firm's profit forecasts
Quarterly publication of all client complaints
Ongoing training and development activities

n.2: Profit forecasts are not a competence requirement.
n.3: Publishing complaints quarterly is not required.
n.0: Weekly HMRC disclosures are not required.
n.1: Fitness tests are not a competence requirement.

q: An adviser assumes his competence is judged by his clients. Who is actually responsible for assessing an adviser's competence under the TC rules?
o: The Financial Ombudsman Service
The authorised firm that employs the adviser
The adviser's own retail clients
The Bank of England
HM Treasury
w: The employing firm is responsible for assessing and maintaining the competence of its advisers.

n.2: Clients do not assess adviser competence.
n.0: The Ombudsman does not assess competence.
n.3: The Bank of England does not assess competence.
n.4: HM Treasury does not assess competence.

o: Consumer harm and breaches of the rules
A reduction in staff travel expenses
A fall in the number of corporate events
An increase in staff holiday requests
Lower spending on the firm's office supplies

n.1: Travel expenses are not the competence risk.
n.3: Holiday requests are not the risk.
n.2: Corporate events are unrelated to the risk.
n.4: Office supply costs are not the risk.

q: An adviser asks which ongoing activity is essential to keep her competent under the TC rules. Which type of development is required?
o: A personal physical fitness programme
Creative writing workshops
Weekend cookery lessons
Continuing professional development
Language classes taken for holidays
w: Continuing professional development is required to maintain competence in regulated activities.

n.0: Fitness training does not maintain regulatory competence.
n.4: Holiday language classes are not relevant.
n.1: Creative writing is not relevant to competence.
n.2: Cookery lessons are not relevant to competence.

q: A firm is onboarding an adviser into a retail investment role. Which exam requirement applies before they can start?
o: Securing a ministerial letter
Completing five years’ industry experience
Passing an FCA-approved qualification
Publishing an academic paper
Obtaining shareholder consent
w: Before starting certain retail investment roles, individuals must pass an FCA-approved exam to demonstrate competence.

n.1: Experience alone does not replace mandatory exam requirements.
n.4: Shareholder consent is unrelated to competence exams.
n.3: Academic publications are not required under TC 2.1.6.
n.0: Government letters are not part of competence verification.

q: A client asks what an adviser's Statement of Professional Standing actually confirms. What is a key feature of an SPS?
o: It guarantees the adviser's future investment returns
It confirms the adviser's shareholder voting record
It lists the adviser's current annual salary
It states the adviser's personal tax code
It confirms the adviser met qualification and ethical standards
w: An SPS confirms an adviser holds the required qualifications and complies with ethical standards.

n.0: An SPS does not guarantee investment performance.
n.2: It does not list salary.
n.3: It does not state a tax code.
n.1: It does not record voting.

q: A firm is confirming which of its people must hold a valid SPS to give retail investment advice. Which staff are these?
o: Reception staff
External auditors
Retail investment advisers
Administrative clerks
IT-services contractors
w: Retail investment advisers must hold a valid SPS to demonstrate qualification and ethical compliance.

n.3: Administrative clerks do not need an SPS.
n.4: IT contractors do not need an SPS.
n.0: Reception staff do not need an SPS.
n.1: External auditors do not need an SPS.

q: A compliance officer explains why the firm carefully documents its competence assessments under the TC rules. What is the reason?
o: To reduce the firm's insurance premiums
To support staff salary negotiations
To evidence compliance with FCA competence standards
To improve the firm's canteen catering
To justify staff annual holiday requests
w: Documenting assessments provides evidence that firms comply with FCA competence standards.

n.4: Records are for compliance evidence, not holidays.
n.1: They are not for salary negotiations.
n.0: They are not for reducing insurance premiums.
n.3: They are not for catering.

q: Which activities are specifically covered by the FCA’s TC Appendix 1?
o: Drafting the firm's press releases
Organising the firm's corporate events
Filing the firm's corporation tax returns
Advising on retail investments
Managing the firm's staff holidays
w: TC Appendix 1 lists retail investment advice as one of the activities subject to training and competence requirements.

n.4: Holiday management is not a TC Appendix 1 activity.
n.2: Tax filing is not a TC Appendix 1 activity.
n.0: Press releases are not a TC Appendix 1 activity.
n.1: Event organising is not a TC Appendix 1 activity.

q: A firm is mapping which of its activities fall under TC Appendix 1 competence rules. Which of the following requires competence?
o: Providing office catering
Supervising car park staff
Advising on mortgages
Designing company logos
Cleaning office facilities
w: Mortgage advice is one of the regulated activities covered under TC Appendix 1 competence requirements.

n.0: Catering is not a regulated activity under TC rules.
n.1: Car park supervision is unrelated to financial services competence rules.
n.3: Designing logos is marketing, not covered by TC Appendix 1.
n.4: Cleaning services are not within the regulatory scope of TC rules.

q: A firm is confirming which product advice sits within TC Appendix 1 competence rules. Which type is covered?
o: Office stationery purchases
Building maintenance contracts
Company uniform supply
Packaged investment products
Travel expense reimbursements
w: Packaged investment product advice is specifically covered by TC Appendix 1 competence requirements.

n.0: Stationery purchases are operational, not regulated advice.
n.4: Expense reimbursements are internal processes, not regulated activities.
n.1: Building contracts are not regulated financial advice under TC rules.
n.2: Uniform supply is unrelated to competence rules in TC Appendix 1.

q: A firm is checking which insurance advice falls within the scope of TC Appendix 1. Which type is covered?
o: Life insurance
Car parking insurance for employees
Office contents insurance
Health insurance provided as a perk
Travel insurance for holidays
w: Life insurance advice is one of the regulated activities requiring competence under TC Appendix 1.

n.1: Car park insurance is not listed as a regulated retail activity in TC Appendix 1.
n.4: Holiday travel insurance is not a core competence requirement under TC Appendix 1.
n.3: Perk-based health insurance is not part of regulated retail activities under TC rules.
n.2: Office contents insurance is corporate cover, not retail advice regulated by TC.

q: A firm has staff advising on retail investment products. What must it ensure about these employees under TC Appendix 1?
o: That they take an unpaid internship first
That they own shares in the firm
That they submit their tax code each year
That they live close to the office
That they meet the TC competence standards
w: Firms must ensure staff advising on retail investments are competent in line with TC Appendix 1.

n.1: Share ownership is not a TC requirement.
n.0: An internship is not required.
n.3: Living near the office is not required.
n.2: Submitting a tax code is not required.

q: A firm is identifying which of its activities require professional standards under TC Appendix 1. Which of these is such an activity?
o: Handling cafeteria supplies
Providing office cleaning services
Organising company sports teams
Advising on pension transfers
Negotiating office lease contracts
w: Advising on pension transfers is a regulated activity that falls under TC Appendix 1 competence rules.

n.1: Cleaning services are not regulated activities.
n.2: Sports teams are recreational and not regulated under TC rules.
n.4: Office lease negotiations are commercial contracts, not retail regulated activities.
n.0: Cafeteria supplies are not regulated financial advice.

q: A compliance officer is explaining why TC Appendix 1 lists the activities to which the T&C rules apply. What is the purpose?
o: To ensure clients receive competent advice in sensitive retail areas
To bring about a reduction in the rates of corporation tax
To advertise and promote available financial services jobs
To set out the holiday and leave policies applying to staff
To place a limit on the rate of staff turnover within firms
w: TC Appendix 1 ensures staff giving retail advice on sensitive areas like pensions or investments meet competence standards.

n.1: T&C is about competence, not corporation tax.
n.4: It is not a staff-turnover measure.
n.3: It does not set holiday policy.
n.2: It is not a recruitment advertising tool.

q: A firm is reviewing which of its advice roles falls under the TC Appendix 1 rules. Which role is covered?
o: IT system administrators
Office maintenance staff
Press officers
Legal clerks
Retail investment advisers
w: Retail investment advisers are included under TC Appendix 1 and must meet competence standards.

n.1: Maintenance staff are not covered by TC Appendix 1.
n.0: IT administrators are not covered.
n.3: Legal clerks are not covered.
n.2: Press officers are not covered.

q: A firm is identifying which TC Appendix 1 activity relates to advising on home finance. Which activity is it?
o: Advising on staff recruitment
Advising on office relocations
Advising on pension schemes for directors only
Advising on corporate branding
Advising on regulated mortgage contracts
w: Advising on regulated mortgage contracts is covered under TC Appendix 1 competence requirements.

n.1: Office relocation advice is not regulated by TC Appendix 1.
n.3: Corporate branding is a marketing function, not regulated advice.
n.0: Recruitment advice is not a TC-regulated activity.
n.2: Director-only pension advice must still be competent but is separate from Appendix 1 scope.

q: A firm notes that one of its activities is listed under TC Appendix 1. What is the effect of that listing for the staff involved?
o: Staff are certified each year by the PRA instead of the firm
Staff automatically become FCA-approved persons on appointment
Staff are supervised only until they pass an initial exam
Staff must hold a Level 6 qualification before any client contact
Staff must meet competence and qualification standards for their activity
w: Being listed under TC Appendix 1 means staff must meet regulatory competence and qualification standards for their activity.

n.1: FCA approval is a separate SM&CR process, not conferred by a TC listing
n.0: Certification is done by the firm, not the PRA, under SM&CR
n.2: The competent-employees rule requires ongoing supervision, not just an initial exam
n.3: TC sets exam standards per activity, not a blanket Level 6 requirement

q: A compliance officer is locating the FCA sourcebook that sets out whistleblowing arrangements for firms. Which one is it?
o: MAR
SYSC
COBS
ICOBS
CASS
w: Whistleblowing arrangements are set out in SYSC 18 of the FCA Handbook.

n.2: COBS covers conduct of business, not whistleblowing.
n.4: CASS relates to client asset protection, not whistleblowing rules.
n.3: ICOBS regulates insurance conduct, not whistleblowing provisions.
n.0: MAR covers market abuse, not internal whistleblowing arrangements.

q: A firm is setting up its whistleblowing arrangements under SYSC 18. What is the main purpose of these rules?
o: To replace a firm's internal grievance procedures entirely
To require firms to publish every whistleblowing report they receive
To transfer whistleblowing oversight from the firm to the FCA
To protect staff who raise regulatory concerns from reprisal
To make anonymous reporting to the police compulsory for staff
w: Whistleblowing rules ensure staff can raise concerns safely, with protection from unfair treatment.

n.1: SYSC 18 requires confidential internal channels, not public disclosure of reports
n.2: Oversight stays with the firm via the whistleblowers' champion, not the FCA
n.4: Routes are internal or to the regulator, not compulsory police reporting
n.0: It supplements, and does not replace, existing grievance procedures

q: A compliance officer is confirming the wider UK statute underpinning whistleblowing protection. Which law provides the legal basis?
o: Bribery Act 2010
Companies Act 2006
Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
Data Protection Act 2018
Financial Services Act 2012
w: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 provides the legal framework for whistleblowing protections in the UK.

n.1: The Companies Act 2006 governs company law, not whistleblower protection
n.4: FSA 2012 restructured the regulators; it did not create whistleblowing rights
n.0: The Bribery Act 2010 addresses bribery offences, not whistleblowing protection
n.3: The DPA 2018 governs personal data, not whistleblowing protection

q: A firm is putting its whistleblowing arrangements in place under SYSC 18.4.4. Which role must it appoint?
o: A client money officer
An external tax adviser
A remuneration committee
A shareholder liaison officer
A whistleblowers’ champion
w: Firms must appoint a whistleblowers’ champion to oversee internal arrangements.

n.1: Tax advisers are not mandated by SYSC 18.4.4.
n.0: Client money officers fall under CASS rules, not whistleblowing.
n.2: Remuneration committees are governance bodies, not whistleblowing requirements.
n.3: Shareholder liaison is not specified in whistleblowing provisions.

q: A firm has appointed a senior manager as its whistleblowers' champion under SYSC 18. What is the role of this individual within the firm?
o: To act as the firm's money laundering reporting officer
To approve the firm's financial promotions before publication
To sign off the firm's regulatory capital calculations
To personally investigate every whistleblowing report received
To oversee whistleblowing arrangements and report to the board
w: The whistleblowers’ champion oversees whistleblowing arrangements and ensures effective reporting to senior management.

n.3: The champion oversees the arrangements' integrity, not each individual case
n.1: Approving promotions is a compliance function, unrelated to the champion
n.0: The MLRO is a separate SM&CR function from the whistleblowers' champion
n.2: Capital calculations sit with finance and risk, not the champion

q: Under SYSC 18.3 a firm is putting in place a facility for its staff to speak up about wrongdoing. What must the firm provide to its employees?
o: Internal arrangements for employees to raise whistleblowing concerns
Firm-funded external legal representation for any grievance
A guaranteed financial reward for every disclosure that is made
Anonymity that cannot be lifted even during an investigation
Direct access to the FCA's own board for all members of staff
w: SYSC 18.3 requires firms to provide internal arrangements that allow employees to raise concerns safely.

n.1: SYSC 18.3 requires internal channels, not firm-funded external legal representation
n.2: UK whistleblowing is not reward-based; no mandatory payment is required
n.4: Staff escalate internally or to regulator channels, not to the FCA board
n.3: Confidentiality is protected but may be limited where disclosure is legally required

q: A firm is designing its whistleblowing procedures. Which regulator must staff be able to report concerns to under them?
o: Financial Ombudsman Service
Companies House
London Stock Exchange
FCA or PRA
HMRC
w: Whistleblowing procedures must allow staff to report concerns directly to the FCA or PRA.

n.1: Companies House records company data, not whistleblowing cases.
n.4: HMRC focuses on tax matters, not whistleblowing reports.
n.0: The Ombudsman resolves client complaints, not internal whistleblowing.
n.2: The Stock Exchange handles trading venues, not whistleblowing.

q: An employee is considering raising a public-interest concern. What protection does the Public Interest Disclosure Act give whistleblowers?
o: Protection from dismissal or victimisation
Free legal aid for all cases
Automatic pay rises
Exemption from disciplinary action for misconduct
Guaranteed promotion
w: The Public Interest Disclosure Act protects whistleblowers from dismissal or victimisation when reporting concerns in the public interest.

n.2: Pay rises are not guaranteed protections under PIDA.
n.4: Promotion is not automatically granted for whistleblowing.
n.3: PIDA protects against unfair treatment but does not excuse unrelated misconduct.
n.1: Free legal aid is not guaranteed by whistleblowing law.

q: A firm is designing the whistleblowing training it gives to staff under SYSC 18. What must this training explain to employees?
o: How to raise concerns internally and to the regulator externally
How to obtain written FCA approval before raising a concern
How to claim financial compensation for making a disclosure
How to report all suspicions directly to the police first
How to negotiate a settlement before reporting any misconduct
w: Training must explain how staff can raise concerns internally and externally under whistleblowing procedures.

n.4: Training covers raising concerns, not negotiating settlements first
n.3: Routes are internal then regulator; there is no police-first requirement
n.2: UK whistleblowing gives protection, not a compensation entitlement
n.1: No prior FCA approval is needed to raise a whistleblowing concern

q: A firm's whistleblowers' champion is preparing their yearly submission to the board. What must this annual report cover?
o: The names of all employees who raised any concern that year
The total number of financial promotions approved that year
The effectiveness of the firm's whistleblowing arrangements
The firm's progress against its annual sales and revenue targets
The regulatory capital held against operational risk
w: The whistleblowers’ champion must provide an annual report to the board on the effectiveness of whistleblowing arrangements.

n.1: Promotions approvals are unrelated to the champion's annual report
n.3: Sales targets are commercial matters outside the report's scope
n.0: The report protects identities; it does not name whistleblowers
n.4: Capital reporting is a separate prudential process, not this report

q: A compliance officer is confirming the status of the UK Market Abuse Regulation after the UK left the EU. Which statement best describes its current legal position?
o: An onshored UK regime, amended for EU exit and supervised by the FCA
Non-binding guidance that carries no FCA enforcement powers at all
An EU regulation still administered by ESMA for UK trading venues
A regime fully replaced by the Criminal Justice Act 1993 in 2020
A regime applying only to instruments traded on EU venues
w: Post-Brexit, the UK retained MAR by onshoring it into domestic law and amending it via The Market Abuse (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. The FCA is responsible for supervision and enforcement in the UK. This ensures continuity of the substantive framework while allowing UK-specific amendments over time.

n.2: MAR was onshored into UK law; ESMA no longer administers it for the UK
n.1: UK MAR is directly enforceable by the FCA, not mere guidance
n.3: MAR was retained, not replaced by the CJA 1993, which is a criminal statute
n.4: UK MAR applies to UK venues and instruments, not only EU venues

q: A firm's surveillance team is scoping the behaviours captured by UK MAR. Which behaviours fall within its market abuse framework?
o: Benchmark rigging, cartels, and anti-competitive mergers
Fraud, money laundering, and the financing of terrorism
Insider dealing, unlawful disclosure, and market manipulation
Mis-selling, unfair contract terms, and pension liberation
Bribery, tax evasion, and false accounting by companies
w: UK MAR targets three core behaviours: dealing on the basis of inside information, unlawfully disclosing such information, and manipulating markets (e.g., spoofing, disseminating false signals). These behaviours undermine market integrity and investor confidence.

n.1: These are financial-crime offences under POCA and terrorism law, not MAR
n.4: Bribery and tax evasion fall under other statutes, not the MAR framework
n.3: These are conduct and consumer matters governed by COBS, not MAR
n.0: Competition matters fall to the CMA; MAR covers abuse of markets

q: An analyst is assessing whether a piece of information counts as 'inside information' under UK MAR. Which combination of attributes must it have?
o: Precise, publicly disclosed, and prepared by a firm's authorised investment analyst
Concerning scheduled macroeconomic data due to be released by a government body
Contained in an issuer's audited financial statements before they are signed off
Precise, non-public, related to an issuer or instruments, and likely to move the price significantly
Capable of being either true or false, provided it could move a price if acted upon
w: Inside information is defined as precise, non-public information concerning an issuer or its financial instruments (directly or indirectly) that, if made public, would likely have a significant effect on price. All elements must be present.

n.0: Inside information must be non-public; once publicly disclosed it is no longer inside information.
n.4: Inside information must be precise; imprecise or speculative material does not qualify.
n.2: Being in draft accounts does not by itself make information inside information under the MAR test.
n.1: Routine scheduled macroeconomic releases are not, of themselves, inside information about an issuer.

q: Unusual order activity has been flagged on a trading desk. Which party is obliged to submit a Suspicious Transaction and Order Report to the FCA without delay?
o: An issuer whenever its share price falls sharply during the day
Any retail client who suffers a loss on one of their trades
A share registrar that maintains the company's shareholder register
A financial journalist reporting on an unusual price movement
An investment firm that reasonably suspects possible market abuse
w: Firms arranging or executing orders must have surveillance systems to detect potential abuse and must submit a STOR to the FCA without delay where there is a reasonable suspicion that a transaction or order may involve market abuse.

n.1: STOR duties fall on firms arranging or executing orders, not losing clients
n.0: Issuers need not file a STOR for ordinary price movements
n.3: Journalists have no STOR duty; it rests with market intermediaries
n.2: Registrars maintain registers and have no STOR obligation

q: The FCA decides to pursue a trader for market abuse using its civil, rather than criminal, powers. Which outcome is available to the regulator under that civil toolkit?
o: Criminal conviction and custodial sentence decided by the FCA
Revocation of UK citizenship of the offender
Automatic delisting of the issuer from the trading venue without process
Imposition of significant financial penalties and public censure
Only private warnings with no financial penalty
w: The FCA’s civil toolkit for market abuse includes financial penalties, disgorgement, and public censure, applied through its enforcement process and decision-making procedures outlined in DEPP and related guidance.

n.0: Criminal convictions and imprisonment are matters for the criminal courts, not FCA civil action.
n.2: Delisting involves the trading venue and listing authority processes, not an automatic FCA sanction for market abuse.
n.4: The FCA regularly imposes financial penalties where appropriate; it is not limited to private warnings.
n.1: Citizenship is outside the FCA’s sanctioning powers.

q: Which legislation primarily creates the criminal offence of insider dealing in the UK?
o: Companies Act 2006, Part 15
UK Market Abuse Regulation (onshored) alone
Criminal Justice Act 1993, Part V
Financial Services Act 2012, Sections 89–92
Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
w: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 (Part V) sets out the main criminal offences of insider dealing in the UK, including dealing, encouraging others to deal, and unlawful disclosure by insiders.

n.3: FSA 2012 Sections 89–92 address misleading statements and impressions; insider dealing is covered by the CJA 1993.
n.0: The Companies Act focuses on company law and reporting, not the insider dealing offence.
n.4: POCA deals with money laundering and confiscation, not the creation of insider dealing offences.
n.1: UK MAR provides the civil market abuse framework; criminal insider dealing is set out in the CJA 1993.

q: A compliance officer is testing staff understanding of unlawful disclosure under UK MAR. Which statement best describes it?
o: Releasing information already announced via a regulatory news service
Sharing price data with clients after an official announcement is made
Circulating compliance-approved marketing materials to investors
Repeating market commentary that later proves inaccurate despite care
Disclosing inside information other than in the normal course of duties
w: Unlawful disclosure occurs when an insider reveals inside information outside the normal course of their duties, exposing the market to selective disclosure and potential misuse of non-public, price-sensitive information.

n.3: Inaccurate commentary is not unlawful disclosure; it must be inside information
n.0: Information already public through an RNS is no longer inside information
n.1: Post-announcement information is public, so sharing it is not disclosure
n.2: Approved marketing of public information is not disclosure of inside information

q: A surveillance analyst is reviewing trading conduct against UK MAR. Which of the following is an example of market manipulation?
o: Placing and cancelling large orders to fake demand (spoofing)
Carrying out due diligence before joining a share placing
Routing an order via a smart router to achieve best execution
Receiving a routine trade confirmation from an executing broker
Submitting a genuine order through the firm's DMA after the open
w: Layering/spoofing involves placing orders without genuine intent to trade to mislead market participants about supply or demand, thereby sending false or misleading signals—conduct captured by the market manipulation limb of MAR.

n.4: A genuine DMA order placed normally is not market manipulation
n.1: Due diligence before a placing is legitimate, not manipulative
n.2: Seeking best execution via a smart router is a lawful practice
n.3: Receiving a trade confirmation is administrative, not manipulation

q: A compliance officer is briefing traders on the criminal offences in the Financial Services Act 2012. Which conduct relating to markets does that Act criminalise?
o: Publishing a securities prospectus that has been approved by the listing authority
Making misleading statements or creating a misleading impression as to investments or benchmarks
Failing to publish a routine trading update during a scheduled closed period
Issuing forward-looking guidance that is properly qualified with appropriate caveats
Holding client money in a designated account at an approved credit institution
w: Sections 89–92 of the Financial Services Act 2012 create criminal offences for misleading statements, misleading impressions, and offences relating to benchmarks, complementing the civil market abuse regime.

n.2: Silence during a closed period is not the s.89-91 misleading-statements offence.
n.3: Properly caveated forward-looking guidance is lawful.
n.4: Correctly holding client money is compliant, not an offence.
n.0: An approved prospectus is lawful, not a criminal misleading statement.

q: An issuer's broker is running a buy-back programme and wants to know if it can rely on a defence under the market abuse framework. Which of the following is a recognised safe harbour when the conditions are met?
o: Placing identical opposing orders to create volume
Trading while in possession of any confidential information regardless of its price sensitivity
Stabilisation and buy-back programmes conducted in accordance with prescribed rules
Delaying disclosure of inside information indefinitely for reputational reasons
Trading based on a colleague’s tip received in a private chat
w: Stabilisation and issuer buy-back programmes can benefit from safe harbours where strict conditions (including disclosure, limits, and record-keeping) are observed, reflecting legitimate market-supporting activities.

n.4: Tips can involve unlawful disclosure and dealing on inside information, which is prohibited.
n.0: Creating artificial volume or prices is a hallmark of manipulation.
n.3: Disclosure delays are strictly conditioned; indefinite delay on reputational grounds is not permitted.
n.1: Confidentiality alone is insufficient; the regime focuses on non-public, precise, price-sensitive information.

q: A trading firm's head of compliance is deciding how to meet the MAR obligation to detect and prevent market abuse. Which firm-level control best supports that requirement?
o: Surveillance with calibrated alerts, documented investigation and timely STOR escalation
Circulating a quarterly market-conduct newsletter to clients and counterparties
Excluding cross-venue activity from monitoring to keep the alert volume manageable
Relying on individual traders to identify and self-report their own suspicious orders
Ceasing all proprietary trading so that the firm has no positions capable of abuse
w: Effective MAR compliance requires proportionate surveillance that monitors orders and trades across venues, tuned alerting, thorough investigation records, and prompt STOR submissions where reasonable suspicion arises.

n.4: Stopping proprietary trading is disproportionate and does not address client or agency flow.
n.3: Self-reporting alone is not an adequate surveillance control.
n.1: A client newsletter is not a market-abuse detection control.
n.2: Cross-venue activity must be monitored; excluding it creates blind spots.

q: An MLRO is explaining to a new analyst how the FCA's civil market abuse regime differs from criminal insider dealing. Which statement best captures that distinction?
o: The criminal regime applies the balance of probabilities standard and results only in prohibition notices.
The criminal regime is limited to behaviour on regulated markets while the civil regime covers only unregulated venues.
The civil regime applies the balance of probabilities standard and can result in unlimited fines and public censure.
Both regimes require proof beyond reasonable doubt and can result only in fines.
The civil regime requires proof beyond reasonable doubt and can result in imprisonment.
w: The civil market abuse regime (FCA MAR/FSMA s.123) is pursued by the FCA using the civil standard of proof (balance of probabilities). Sanctions include unlimited financial penalties, public censure, and prohibitions. The criminal regime (CJA 1993 Part V and Financial Services Act 2012 ss.89–91) requires the criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt) and can lead to imprisonment and/or fines.

n.3: Criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt; the civil regime does not. Civil penalties are not limited to fines alone.
n.4: The civil regime does not use the criminal standard and cannot impose imprisonment; imprisonment arises only in criminal proceedings.
n.0: The criminal regime uses the criminal standard of proof and can include imprisonment; prohibition notices can also arise from civil/regulatory action.
n.1: Venue distinctions are not that narrow. Both regimes can capture behaviour across a range of venues depending on the instrument and conduct.

q: Under the FCA’s Decision Procedure and Penalties manual (DEPP 6), which of the following is one of the core steps in calculating a financial penalty for market abuse?
o: Apply a fixed statutory percentage of firm revenue.
Cap the penalty at the higher of £1 million or 10% of turnover.
Multiply the daily value at risk (VaR) by a fixed factor.
Disgorge any financial benefit derived from the misconduct.
Offset the penalty fully against future remediation spend.
w: DEPP 6 sets out a structured, step-based approach. One of the initial steps is disgorgement of any financial benefit gained from the misconduct, followed by assessing seriousness, factoring aggravating/mitigating elements, adjusting for deterrence, and applying any settlement discount.

n.0: DEPP 6 does not rely on a single fixed statutory percentage of revenue; it uses a multi-step framework keyed to seriousness and benefit.
n.2: VaR is not a prescribed input in DEPP 6’s penalty steps.
n.1: There is no universal statutory cap in DEPP 6 of this form; penalties can be unlimited in serious cases.
n.4: Remediation spend does not provide a full offset; it may mitigate but does not eliminate penalties.

q: The FCA is considering a criminal charge under sections 89 to 91 of the Financial Services Act 2012. Which behaviour falls within those offences?
o: Notifying the FCA of a personal account deal after the firm's internal deadline has passed
Operating a price stabilisation mechanism during the permitted period following an IPO
Making a false or misleading statement intending to induce another person to deal
Failing to keep an insider list of all employees with access to confidential firm information
Publishing a periodic financial report a short time before its scheduled release date
w: FS Act 2012 ss.89–91 create criminal offences around false or misleading statements and impressions (including benchmarks) where done knowingly or recklessly to induce dealing or create a false/misleading impression of the market.

n.3: An incomplete insider list is a systems failing, not one of the s.89-91 criminal offences.
n.0: Late internal notification of a PA deal is a conduct breach, not a s.89-91 offence.
n.1: Stabilisation within the permitted period is expressly lawful, not an offence.
n.4: Early publication of a report is not among the s.89-91 misleading-statement offences.

q: A firm's compliance team is reviewing exposure under Part V of the Criminal Justice Act 1993. Which statement accurately describes the insider dealing offences it creates?
o: Only the person who deals using inside information can be liable; encouraging another is not covered.
Possession of inside information alone automatically creates a criminal offence without any dealing or disclosure.
A person cannot be liable if the trading occurred outside the UK.
Disclosing inside information other than in the proper course of employment can itself constitute an offence.
The offences are enforced solely by civil penalty from the FCA.
w: Part V CJA 1993 criminalises dealing in price-affected securities while in possession of inside information, encouraging another to deal, and disclosing inside information otherwise than in the proper course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.0: Encouraging another to deal is specifically captured under the CJA 1993.
n.2: Territorial application is nuanced; conduct with a UK nexus can still be within scope.
n.1: Mere possession without dealing, disclosure, or encouragement does not in itself complete the criminal offence.
n.4: These are criminal offences; enforcement can involve prosecution and imprisonment, not only civil penalties.

q: A case involving suspected insider dealing and offences under the Financial Services Act 2012 is being escalated for prosecution. Under FSMA s.402, which body is empowered to institute criminal proceedings?
o: The Competition and Markets Authority
The London Stock Exchange
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Takeover Panel only
The Financial Conduct Authority
w: FSMA s.402 provides the FCA with the power to institute criminal proceedings for specified offences, which include insider dealing under the CJA 1993 and false/misleading statements and impressions under the FS Act 2012.

n.3: The Takeover Panel is not the prosecuting authority for these criminal offences.
n.0: The CMA focuses on competition matters, not prosecutions for insider dealing or FS Act 2012 offences.
n.1: The exchange is not the criminal prosecuting body for these offences.
n.2: The PRA’s remit is prudential regulation; it does not prosecute market abuse crimes.

q: The FCA decides to pursue a market abuse matter through the civil regime rather than criminal prosecution. Which outcome is available under the civil regime but is not a criminal sentence?
o: Community sentence
Confiscation order following conviction
Criminal record
Public censure by the FCA
Imprisonment
w: Civil market abuse outcomes include public censure, unlimited fines, and prohibitions. Imprisonment and criminal records arise from criminal proceedings, not civil action.

n.4: Imprisonment is a criminal sanction, not a civil outcome.
n.2: A criminal record results from conviction, not from a civil market abuse finding.
n.1: Confiscation orders are tied to criminal convictions and proceeds of crime frameworks.
n.0: Community sentences are criminal penalties, not civil outcomes.

q: A compliance officer explains the scope of the FCA's civil market abuse regime under MAR 1.1.3. Which categories of behaviour fall within that civil regime?
o: Only conduct that causes identifiable consumer detriment
Only conduct that also satisfies every element of a criminal offence
Only conduct by authorised firms, never by individuals
Insider dealing, improper disclosure, and market manipulation
Only conduct that takes place away from a trading venue
w: The civil regime captures a broad range of market abuse behaviours including insider dealing, improper disclosure, and market manipulation/manipulative practices, regardless of whether the conduct also satisfies the elements of a criminal offence.

n.1: The civil regime applies whether or not criminal elements are also met
n.4: The civil regime covers conduct on and off trading venues alike
n.2: The civil regime applies to any person, including individuals, not just firms
n.0: Market abuse needs no proof of consumer detriment to fall within the regime

q: A trainee is learning which sanctions attach to which market abuse regime. Which pairing correctly matches a regime with a sanction available under it?
o: Criminal false or misleading statements — private warning only
Criminal insider dealing — supervisory visit
Civil market abuse — imprisonment
Civil market abuse — criminal record
Civil market abuse — public censure
w: Civil market abuse outcomes include public censure, financial penalties, and prohibitions. Imprisonment and criminal records are consequences of criminal proceedings, not civil action.

n.2: Imprisonment is a criminal sanction, not a civil one.
n.1: A supervisory visit is a supervisory tool, not a criminal sanction for insider dealing.
n.0: Criminal offences under FS Act 2012 can lead to imprisonment and fines; a private warning alone is not the typical outcome.
n.3: A criminal record arises from conviction, not from a civil market abuse finding.

q: The FCA is weighing whether to pursue criminal prosecution rather than civil action in a market abuse case. Consistent with the Enforcement Guide (EG 12.3), which factor most supports criminal prosecution?
o: Investors have already filed a parallel private civil claim
The firm has already paid full redress to the affected clients
The behaviour occurred over six years ago with no market impact
The case shows minor systems lapses with no personal culpability
The misconduct is especially serious or dishonest, needing deterrence
w: EG 12.3 indicates that, among other factors, seriousness, dishonesty, and the need for general deterrence may justify criminal prosecution rather than civil action.

n.3: Minor lapses without culpability point away from criminal prosecution
n.1: Paying redress does not by itself justify criminal rather than civil action
n.2: Age and lack of impact weigh against pursuing a criminal prosecution
n.0: A private civil claim is not an EG 12.3 factor for choosing criminal action

q: A trader is convicted of insider dealing in the Crown Court under the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What is the maximum custodial sentence typically available for that offence?
o: Ten years
Two years
Fourteen years
Seven years
Five years
w: The CJA 1993 provides for a maximum custodial sentence of up to seven years for insider dealing, alongside the possibility of an unlimited fine.

n.1: The statutory maximum is higher than two years.
n.4: The statutory maximum exceeds five years.
n.0: Ten years is above the typical statutory maximum historically associated with CJA 1993 insider dealing.
n.2: Fourteen years is not the stated maximum for this offence.

q: A trader's conduct could be pursued civilly by the FCA or prosecuted criminally. Which statement best reflects how the two regimes interact for the same market abuse conduct?
o: Only one of the civil or criminal regimes can ever apply to any given set of facts
A criminal prosecution must always be concluded before any civil enforcement action can begin
Civil action becomes available only after a jury has acquitted the defendant in a criminal trial
Once the FCA opens civil action, criminal prosecution of the same conduct is legally barred in every case
The same conduct can engage both regimes, but authorities avoid duplicative punishment
w: Conduct may be addressed under the civil market abuse framework or prosecuted criminally where appropriate. The FCA and prosecuting authorities coordinate to avoid double punishment for the same conduct while choosing the route that best protects market integrity and deters misconduct.

n.3: Civil action does not automatically bar criminal prosecution of the same conduct.
n.1: There is no rule that criminal proceedings must precede civil enforcement.
n.0: The same facts can engage both the civil and criminal regimes.
n.2: Civil action does not depend on a prior criminal acquittal.

q: A paraplanner is confirming which statute sets out the specific criminal offences for insider dealing in the UK. Which is it?
o: Criminal Justice Act 1993
Fraud Act 2006
Financial Services Act 2012
Companies Act 2006
Enterprise Act 2002
w: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 Part V sets out the specific criminal offences for insider dealing in the UK.

n.2: The Financial Services Act 2012 addresses misleading statements and impressions, not the core insider dealing offence.
n.3: The Companies Act 2006 governs corporate governance, not insider dealing offences.
n.1: The Fraud Act 2006 addresses general fraud, not insider trading.
n.4: The Enterprise Act 2002 concerns competition law, not market abuse.

q: A compliance trainee is asked where the civil regime for market abuse is set out in the FCA Handbook. Which provision should she point to?
o: FCA MAR 1.1.3
FCA PRIN 11
FCA DISP 1
FCA COBS 4
FCA SYSC 6
w: FCA MAR 1.1.3 outlines the civil framework for market abuse under FSMA 2000.

n.4: SYSC 6 covers compliance and internal systems, not the market abuse regime
n.3: COBS 4 governs financial promotions, not market abuse
n.2: DISP 1 sets complaint-handling rules, unrelated to market abuse
n.1: PRIN 11 is the principle on regulator dealings, not market abuse

q: Following an investigation, the FCA decides to act against an individual for market abuse using its civil powers rather than pursuing a criminal prosecution. Which sanction is available to it in that route?
o: Unlimited financial penalty
Maximum five years imprisonment
Community service order
Disqualification from being a company director
Revocation of UK citizenship
w: The FCA can impose unlimited financial penalties under its civil market abuse powers.

n.1: Imprisonment is a criminal sanction under the Criminal Justice Act, not a civil FCA penalty.
n.2: Community service orders are criminal penalties, not FCA civil remedies.
n.3: Director disqualification arises under the Companies Act, not FCA civil enforcement.
n.4: Citizenship revocation is unrelated to financial regulation.

q: A compliance officer is citing the section of the Financial Services Act 2012 that deals with creating misleading impressions of supply or demand. Which section is it?
o: Section 404
Section 62
Section 118
Section 92
Section 90
w: Section 92 of the Financial Services Act 2012 criminalises creating false or misleading impressions of supply, demand, or price of investments.

n.4: Section 90 relates to misleading statements in prospectuses, not supply and demand.
n.0: Section 404 deals with consumer redress schemes, not market abuse.
n.2: Section 118 was repealed when MAR replaced it, so it is not relevant under current law.
n.1: Section 62 does not address misleading market impressions.

q: A trainee is confirming the sentencing exposure for insider dealing under the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What is the maximum custodial sentence?
o: Ten years
Seven years
Five years
Two years
Life imprisonment
w: The Criminal Justice Act 1993 prescribes a maximum custodial sentence of seven years for insider dealing offences.

n.3: Two years is below the statutory maximum for insider dealing.
n.0: Ten years exceeds the maximum penalty under the Criminal Justice Act 1993.
n.2: Five years is less than the prescribed maximum sentence.
n.4: Life imprisonment is not applicable to insider dealing offences.

q: A compliance trainee researching how the FCA sets fines for market abuse needs the correct manual reference. Which FCA manual section outlines the penalties policy for market abuse?
o: COBS 12
ICOBS 7
DEPP 6
SYSC 3
MCOB 4
w: DEPP 6 sets out the FCA’s policy on imposing penalties for market abuse under FSMA.

n.0: COBS 12 relates to investment research and financial promotions, not penalties.
n.3: SYSC 3 covers systems and controls, not enforcement penalties.
n.4: MCOB 4 concerns mortgage sales, not market abuse sanctions.
n.1: ICOBS 7 deals with insurance communications, not enforcement policy.

q: A compliance officer is locating the FCA guidance describing how it uses its criminal prosecution powers for market abuse. Which reference is it?
o: DISP 3
CASS 7
COCON 2
SYSC 4
w: EG 12.3 in the Enforcement Guide sets out the FCA’s use of criminal prosecution for insider dealing and market abuse.

n.4: SYSC 4 covers organisational requirements, not prosecution policy
n.3: COCON 2 sets individual conduct rules, not prosecution guidance
n.0: DISP 3 concerns Ombudsman procedures, not FCA prosecutions
n.2: CASS 7 governs client money, unrelated to prosecution powers

q: The FCA has concluded an investigation and intends to impose a financial penalty on a firm for market abuse. Which FSMA provision empowers it to do so?
o: Section 402
Section 348
Section 137A
Section 1B
Section 166
w: Section 402 FSMA allows the FCA to impose financial penalties for breaches relating to market abuse.

n.2: Section 137A relates to rule-making powers, not penalty imposition.
n.1: Section 348 restricts disclosure of information, not market abuse penalties.
n.4: Section 166 allows skilled person reviews, not the imposition of penalties.
n.3: Section 1B defines the FCA’s objectives, not enforcement powers.

q: A firm is categorising the possible consequences of a market abuse finding. Which of the following is a civil, rather than criminal, outcome?
o: A community order imposed by a court
Imprisonment imposed in place of a fine
A conviction on indictment at Crown Court
A financial penalty imposed by the FCA
A custodial sentence of up to seven years
w: Civil outcomes include FCA-imposed financial penalties, unlike criminal outcomes such as imprisonment or conviction.

n.4: A custodial sentence is a criminal, not a civil, outcome
n.0: A community order is a criminal sentence handed down by a court
n.2: A conviction on indictment is a criminal outcome, not civil
n.1: Imprisonment is a criminal penalty, not a civil sanction

q: A compliance officer is confirming which body brings criminal market abuse prosecutions in the UK. Who prosecutes such cases?
o: Serious Fraud Office
Crown Prosecution Service
Bank of England
Financial Conduct Authority
Financial Ombudsman Service
w: The FCA itself prosecutes criminal cases of insider dealing and market abuse under FSMA and related statutes.

n.1: The CPS handles general crime; the FCA prosecutes insider dealing
n.0: The SFO handles serious or complex fraud, not FCA market abuse cases
n.2: The Bank of England is a prudential regulator; it does not prosecute
n.4: The Ombudsman resolves complaints and brings no criminal prosecutions

q: A surveillance analyst spots trading that looks like possible market abuse and prepares a STOR. What is the primary purpose of a Suspicious Transaction and Order Report?
o: To disclose conflicts of interest in research
To request guidance from the regulator on disclosure
To notify the FCA of suspected market abuse
To inform clients of unusual price movements
To confirm compliance with anti-money laundering obligations
w: A STOR is submitted to the FCA to alert them of suspected market abuse or insider dealing activity.

n.3: Client communications about price movements are separate from STOR obligations.
n.1: A STOR is a notification, not a request for guidance.
n.4: AML reports go to the NCA, not through a STOR.
n.0: Research conflicts must be disclosed, but not via a STOR.

q: A regulatory adviser is identifying which trading venues must run systems to detect suspicious transactions. Which venues carry that obligation?
o: Regulated markets and MTFs
Insurance brokers
Firms operating crowdfunding platforms
Credit reference agencies
Retail banks offering mortgages
w: Regulated markets and multilateral trading facilities must monitor and detect suspicious transactions and report them through STORs.

n.2: Crowdfunding platforms are not specifically mandated under MAR to detect and report STORs.
n.4: Retail banks monitor AML issues, not specifically MAR suspicious orders.
n.1: Insurance brokers have regulatory duties but not STOR reporting obligations.
n.3: Credit reference agencies do not operate trading venues under MAR.

q: A firm's surveillance team has just identified activity that looks suspicious. When must it submit a STOR to the FCA?
o: Without delay
At the next quarterly compliance review
Within seven business days
After internal audit sign-off
Only if FCA requests information
w: STORs must be submitted to the FCA without delay once suspicion of market abuse arises.

n.2: Seven business days would be too late for regulatory expectations.
n.1: Quarterly reviews are not an acceptable timeline for reporting suspicions.
n.3: Internal audit approval is not required before filing a STOR.
n.4: STORs are proactive obligations, not dependent on FCA requests.

q: A compliance officer is scoping who at the firm needs market abuse training. Which staff members require it?
o: Only employees who draft the firm's financial promotions
Only staff who deal directly with retail clients
All relevant employees involved in trading or handling orders
Only members of the firm's senior management team
Only the firm's designated compliance officers
w: All relevant employees handling orders or transactions must be trained to recognise and escalate suspicious behaviour.

n.3: Training extends to all relevant staff, not just senior management
n.4: Compliance staff are not the only ones needing this training
n.1: Order-handling staff need training regardless of client contact
n.0: Promotions drafters are not the only staff requiring training

q: A firm is preparing to file a suspicious transaction and order report. Which UK regulator is the recipient of STORs?
o: Bank of England
Serious Fraud Office
Financial Conduct Authority
Prudential Regulation Authority
Competition and Markets Authority
w: STORs must be submitted to the Financial Conduct Authority as the UK’s competent authority under MAR.

n.3: The PRA regulates prudential risk, not STOR reporting.
n.0: The Bank of England supervises monetary policy and stability, not STORs.
n.1: The SFO investigates fraud but does not administer STORs.
n.4: The CMA focuses on competition issues, not market abuse detection.

q: A compliance officer is explaining to management why the firm invests in trade surveillance systems. What is their role in preventing market abuse?
o: They calculate the firm's regulatory capital adequacy
They submit the firm's periodic tax returns to HMRC
They compile shareholder communication and voting packs
They record staff absence and annual leave for HR
They detect unusual trading patterns that may indicate abuse
w: Surveillance systems are designed to identify unusual trading activity that may indicate insider dealing or manipulation.

n.1: Tax reporting is a finance function, not the purpose of surveillance
n.0: Capital adequacy is a prudential calculation, unrelated to surveillance
n.2: Shareholder communications are unrelated to abuse-detection systems
n.3: Absence tracking is an HR matter, not a surveillance function

q: A dealer at the firm becomes aware of a series of client orders that look suspicious. What obligation does the firm have?
o: Submit a STOR to the FCA
File a SAR to the PRA
Cancel the order without explanation
Delay reporting until settlement
Request client clarification only
w: Firms must file a STOR with the FCA when suspicious transactions or orders are detected.

n.4: Asking the client for clarification does not replace the duty to report.
n.3: Delaying until settlement would breach the 'without delay' obligation.
n.2: Cancelling the order is not a substitute for reporting.
n.1: SARs relate to money laundering, not MAR market abuse.

q: A compliance officer is documenting why the firm keeps copies of every STOR it submits. What is the reason for retaining those records?
o: To calculate year-end bonuses for the trading staff
To support the planning of staff annual leave
To satisfy workplace health and safety requirements
To prepare forecasts of shareholder dividend payments
To evidence compliance with the firm's regulatory obligations
w: Retention of STOR records evidences regulatory compliance and allows inspection by the FCA if required.

n.1: Leave planning is unrelated to STOR record retention
n.0: Bonus calculation has no bearing on STOR record retention
n.3: Dividend forecasting is unrelated to STOR record-keeping
n.2: Health and safety rules do not drive STOR record retention

q: A surveillance analyst is scanning trading activity for signs of manipulation. Which of the following is a key indicator they must monitor for?
o: Wash trades creating false volume
Staff compliance training attendance
Correct completion of client forms
Quarterly publication of results
Timely settlement of trades
w: Wash trades, where no genuine risk transfer occurs, are a red flag for market manipulation and must be monitored.

n.4: Timely settlement is standard practice, not indicative of abuse.
n.2: Form completion relates to administration, not abuse.
n.3: Publishing results is disclosure, not manipulation.
n.1: Training attendance demonstrates compliance but is not an abuse indicator.

q: A junior trader spots what may be suspicious trading on the desk. What is the minimum expectation for internal escalation?
o: Only escalate if client confirms misconduct
Discuss with colleagues informally
Wait until the year-end compliance review
Escalate to auditors during annual audit
Prompt escalation to compliance or MLRO
w: Suspicious trades must be escalated promptly to compliance or the MLRO to ensure timely reporting obligations are met.

n.2: Year-end reviews are too late for timely escalation.
n.1: Informal discussions do not satisfy escalation requirements.
n.0: Client admissions are not required before escalation obligations apply.
n.3: Auditors review after the fact, not during live suspicious activity.

q: Which activity is expressly prohibited under UK MAR Article 14?
o: Reporting suspicious activity to the FCA as required
Dealing in financial instruments while holding inside information
Paying an approved final dividend to the shareholders
Publishing a company's duly authorised full annual report and accounts
Delivering compliance training to newly hired staff
w: UK MAR Article 14 prohibits dealing in financial instruments while in possession of inside information.

n.3: Publishing authorised accounts is a normal disclosure, not a breach
n.0: Reporting suspicions to the FCA is required conduct, not prohibited
n.4: Staff training is legitimate and not prohibited by Article 14
n.2: Paying dividends is ordinary corporate activity, not insider dealing

q: A compliance officer is training staff on Article 14 of UK MAR. Beyond insider dealing itself, what else does Article 14 prohibit?
o: Late filing of the company's annual confirmation statement
Failure to keep the statutory company registers up to date
Misclassifying a client's category under the COBS rules
Improper disclosure and recommending dealing on inside information
Poor record-keeping of client complaints under DISP
w: Article 14 prohibits insider dealing, improper disclosure of inside information, and recommending or inducing others to deal on it.

n.0: Late filings are company-law breaches, not Article 14 market abuse
n.1: Statutory register failures fall under company law, not MAR
n.4: Complaint record failures are DISP breaches, not Article 14
n.2: Client classification errors are COBS matters, unrelated to Article 14

q: An analyst passes price-sensitive information to a friend outside the ordinary course of their job. Under Article 14 UK MAR, what does this constitute?
o: Telling clients about publicly quoted current stock prices
Circulating published research notes to the firm's clients
Revealing inside information outside the normal course of duties
