Giving analysts the results after their official release
Explaining the financial promotion rules during training
w: Improper disclosure occurs when inside information is revealed outside the normal course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.1: Published research is public, so sharing it is not improper disclosure
n.0: Public price data is not inside information
n.3: Post-release results are public and lawful to discuss
n.4: Explaining rules in training involves no inside information

q: An adviser holding inside information is considering tipping a colleague to trade. Which type of recommendation is prohibited under Article 14 of UK MAR?
o: Encouraging a client to diversify into pooled investment funds
Recommending an investment based on public research reports
Advising a client on their annual ISA eligibility
Proposing a risk assessment under the SYSC rules
Suggesting another person deal on the basis of inside information
w: Article 14 prohibits recommending or inducing another person to engage in dealing while in possession of inside information.

n.0: Diversification advice involves no inside information and is permitted
n.1: Recommendations from public research are lawful, not prohibited
n.2: ISA eligibility advice is ordinary and uses public information
n.3: A SYSC risk assessment is a control, not a prohibited recommendation

q: A trainee asks a compliance officer to define 'inside information' under UK MAR. Which description is correct?
o: General market rumours circulating without any evidence
Past information that has already been published in reports
Any opinion publicly voiced by a market analyst
Precise, non-public information likely to affect a price
Acquisition plans that have already been publicly announced
w: Inside information is precise, non-public information that would likely have a significant effect on the price of financial instruments.

n.0: Rumours are not precise information and are not inside information
n.2: An analyst's public opinion is public, not inside information
n.1: Already-published information is public, not inside information
n.4: Publicly announced plans are, by definition, not non-public

q: An employee is unsure when passing on inside information becomes improper disclosure under Article 14. What is the key element that makes it improper?
o: It is not made in the normal course of the person's duties
It happens during routine periodic financial reporting
It is issued to the market through a regulatory news service
It appears within a formally published company prospectus
It is filed as a statutory return at Companies House
w: Improper disclosure arises when inside information is revealed outside the proper course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.1: Routine reporting is a normal disclosure, not improper
n.2: RNS releases make information public and are proper disclosure
n.3: A published prospectus is public disclosure, not improper
n.4: Companies House filings are lawful public disclosures

q: A compliance officer is illustrating insider dealing under Article 14 for a training session. Which of the following is an example?
o: Recommending a stock using widely available public research
Advising clients on the basis of an FCA press release
Selling shares just after a public trading update is issued
Buying shares before a takeover using confidential knowledge
Buying an ETF that tracks a published market index
w: Dealing on confidential, price-sensitive information such as a takeover announcement before it is public is insider dealing under Article 14.

n.2: Trading on already-public updates is not insider dealing
n.4: Buying an index ETF uses public data, not inside information
n.0: Using publicly available research is lawful, not insider dealing
n.1: Acting on public FCA releases involves no inside information

q: A trainee asks which people the Article 14 prohibition can apply to. Which category of persons does it cover?
o: Only the directors of a listed company
Only employees of a regulated market operator
Only firms that are authorised by the FCA
Only professional investment analysts
Any person who possesses inside information
w: Article 14 applies broadly to any person who possesses inside information, not just regulated firms or professionals.

n.2: Article 14 binds any person, not only FCA-authorised firms
n.0: It is not limited to directors; anyone holding inside information is caught
n.1: Market-operator employees are not the only persons covered
n.3: Analysts are not the only persons subject to Article 14

q: The FCA is pursuing a person for breaching Article 14 under the civil regime. What is the consequence?
o: Automatic imprisonment imposed by the FCA directly
Unlimited financial penalties and public censure by the FCA
Revocation of the person's British citizenship
A requirement to restate the firm's annual accounts
Loss of the person's shareholder voting rights
w: Civil breaches of Article 14 can result in unlimited fines, public censure, and prohibitions from the FCA.

n.0: The FCA imposes civil penalties; imprisonment is a criminal court outcome
n.4: Voting rights are unaffected by a civil market abuse penalty
n.2: Citizenship cannot be revoked as a market abuse sanction
n.3: Restating accounts is not a civil sanction for insider dealing

q: An adviser with inside information is thinking about nudging a client to trade. Which form of inducement is prohibited under Article 14?
o: Recommending diversification using publicly available data
Encouraging another person to trade while holding inside information
Offering colleagues training on the firm's compliance policies
Publishing regulated announcements through an RNS
Promoting a listed company's already public research reports
w: Article 14 prohibits inducing another person to trade while possessing inside information.

n.2: Compliance training is legitimate and involves no inside information
n.4: Promoting public research is lawful, not a prohibited inducement
n.3: RNS announcements are proper public disclosure
n.0: Advice from public data is not a prohibited inducement

q: A trader receives a tip and asks compliance whether it counts as inside information under UK MAR Article 7. Which feature would confirm that it does?
o: It is derived solely from rumours
It is always financial research
It is precise and not public
It is contained in press releases
It is based on speculation
w: Inside information must be precise, non-public, and likely to significantly affect the price of a financial instrument.

n.4: Speculation without precision does not meet the MAR definition.
n.3: Press releases are public and cannot constitute inside information.
n.1: Financial research is analysis, not non-public precise information.
n.0: Rumours are not precise and therefore fall outside Article 7.

q: A compliance officer is assessing whether some unpublished data amounts to inside information under Article 7 of UK MAR. Which element must the information have?
o: Automatic notification to the FCA upon its receipt
Publication within the company's next annual report
A likelihood of a significant effect on the price
Origination solely from a company's board minutes
A direct connection to the issuer's credit rating
w: Inside information must be likely to have a significant effect on the prices of relevant financial instruments.

n.0: Inside information need not be notified to the FCA automatically
n.3: It can arise from many sources, not only board minutes
n.1: Published information is public, not inside information
n.4: A credit-rating link is not a required element of inside information

q: A compliance officer is explaining Article 8 of UK MAR to a new dealer. What constitutes insider dealing under that article?
o: Buying shares after a public RNS announcement is made
Relying on analyst forecasts that are already published widely
Discussing quoted prices during a media interview
Selling a holding on the strength of general market rumours
Using inside information to acquire or dispose of instruments
w: Insider dealing involves using inside information to acquire or dispose of financial instruments, or attempting to do so.

n.1: Published forecasts are public; trading on them is not insider dealing
n.0: Trading after a public RNS uses public information
n.3: Rumours are not inside information under Article 8
n.2: Discussing public prices is not insider dealing

q: Which activity is prohibited under Article 10 UK MAR?
o: Publishing a company's audited financial statements
Delivering training sessions on the FCA's rules to staff
Unlawful disclosure of inside information to another person
Filing the required statutory documents at Companies House
Distributing the FCA's published consultation papers
w: Article 10 prohibits the unlawful disclosure of inside information outside the proper course of employment or duties.

n.1: Rule training discloses no inside information and is lawful
n.0: Publishing audited statements is proper public disclosure
n.3: Statutory filings are lawful public disclosures
n.4: Circulating public consultation papers is not unlawful disclosure

q: A trainee is asked to give an example of inside information under Article 7. Which of the following best illustrates it?
o: An analyst's forecast that is already published widely
A share price movement shown live on Bloomberg
Knowledge of an as-yet unannounced company merger
Minutes from an already-published company AGM
An unverified rumour spreading across social media
w: Information about an unannounced merger is precise, non-public, and likely to affect share prices, meeting the Article 7 definition.

n.0: A published forecast is public, not inside information
n.4: A rumour lacks the precision required for inside information
n.1: A visible price movement is public market data
n.3: Published AGM minutes are public information

q: A bond trader learns of an unpublished default risk and sells the holding. Under Article 8, which of the following is considered insider dealing?
o: Buying shares after a public takeover announcement
Trading on the basis of consensus analyst reports
Selling bonds while knowing of unpublished default risk
Investing regular sums into an index tracker fund
Rebalancing a portfolio after year-end results are public
w: Disposing of bonds using confidential knowledge of default risk constitutes insider dealing under Article 8.

n.0: Trading after a public announcement uses public information
n.3: Index-tracker investing relies on public data, not inside information
n.1: Consensus analyst reports are public, so trading on them is lawful
n.4: Rebalancing on published results involves public information

q: A compliance officer is defining when improper disclosure arises under Article 10. Improper disclosure occurs when:
o: Aggregate trading volume reports are published
A firm issues a prospectus approved by the regulator
Publicly available market data is discussed openly
Inside information is shared outside the person's normal duties
An FCA consultation paper is circulated among the firm's staff members
w: Improper disclosure occurs when inside information is shared outside the normal course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.2: Discussing public data involves no inside information
n.4: Circulating a public consultation is not improper disclosure
n.1: Issuing an approved prospectus is proper public disclosure
n.0: Published volume reports are public, not inside information

q: A trainee is sorting scenarios into inside information and not. Under Article 7, which of the following is NOT inside information?
o: Confidential and ongoing acquisition talks
A company's unpublished quarterly financial results
General opinions about overall market sentiment
A pending, unannounced change of key management
Non-public details of a currently pending takeover
w: General market opinions are not precise information and therefore do not meet the MAR definition of inside information.

n.4: Non-public takeover details are precise, price-sensitive inside information
n.1: Unpublished results are non-public, price-sensitive inside information
n.0: Confidential acquisition talks qualify as inside information
n.3: An unannounced management change can be inside information

q: A dealer trades on unpublished earnings figures. Which scenario breaches the Article 8 insider dealing prohibition?
o: Buying shares before earnings known only to insiders
Trading ETFs based purely on public index data
Following analyst recommendations printed in newspapers
Selling shares after the audited results are published
Hedging with derivatives after an FCA announcement
w: Using unpublished earnings results to trade shares is a breach of Article 8 insider dealing prohibition.

n.3: Trading after published results uses public information
n.1: ETF trades on public index data are not insider dealing
n.2: Newspaper recommendations are public information
n.4: Acting after a public FCA announcement is lawful

q: An employee shares takeover details with a personal friend. Which of the following is an unlawful disclosure under Article 10?
o: A listed company files its ordinary statutory returns
A firm publishes quarterly earnings through an RNS
A bank issues its legally required risk disclosures
An analyst cites data taken from a Bloomberg terminal
An employee leaks takeover details to a personal friend
w: Leaking takeover details to an unauthorised person constitutes unlawful disclosure under Article 10 UK MAR.

n.1: Publishing earnings via RNS is proper public disclosure
n.3: Citing public Bloomberg data is not unlawful disclosure
n.2: Required risk disclosures are lawful public statements
n.0: Filing statutory returns is lawful public disclosure

q: An analyst is unsure whether information about a possible corporate event counts as inside information. Under Article 7, when is information considered 'precise'?
o: When it is already freely available to the public
When it indicates circumstances that may reasonably occur
When it relates only to a company's past performance
When it is vague and entirely speculative in nature
When it rests solely on unverified market gossip
w: Information is precise if it indicates circumstances or events that exist or may reasonably occur and could influence prices.

n.3: Vague, speculative material is not precise information
n.4: Gossip is imprecise and does not meet the precision test
n.0: Publicly available information is not inside information at all
n.2: Past performance alone does not make information precise

q: A fund manager becomes aware of a not-yet-announced acquisition and considers how to act. Which of the following is an example of insider dealing under Article 8?
o: Trading derivatives after company accounts are published
Attempting to trade using non-public acquisition details
Selling securities after a public RNS announcement
Investing in a tracker fund linked to public indices
Buying shares using widely reported analyst forecasts
w: Article 8 prohibits dealing or attempting to deal while in possession of inside information, such as non-public acquisition details.

n.2: Selling after a public RNS uses public information
n.4: Widely reported forecasts are public, not inside information
n.0: Trading after published accounts relies on public data
n.3: Tracker-fund investment uses public index data

q: A compliance officer is explaining when passing on information is permitted. Which type of disclosure is considered lawful under Article 10?
o: Emailing draft earnings figures to close family members
Sharing takeover details with friends over lunch
Texting market-sensitive data to a financial journalist
Whispering a profit warning to a few selected investors
Disclosure made in the normal course of a person's employment
w: Lawful disclosure is permitted if made in the normal course of employment, profession, or duties.

n.1: Sharing takeover details socially is unlawful disclosure
n.3: Selective tipping of a profit warning is unlawful disclosure
n.0: Emailing inside information to family is unlawful disclosure
n.2: Passing market-sensitive data to a journalist is unlawful disclosure

q: A trainee asks how Articles 7 and 8 of UK MAR relate to each other. Which statement best describes the link?
o: Article 8 requires firms to publish all inside information
Article 7 sets the criminal penalties for dealing offences
Article 8 defines what counts as public information
Article 7 lists the sanctions for insider dealing convictions
Article 7 defines the inside information used in Article 8 offences
w: Article 7 defines inside information, which is the foundation for the insider dealing prohibition under Article 8.

n.1: Article 7 defines inside information; it does not set penalties
n.2: Article 8 sets the dealing prohibition, not a definition of public information
n.0: Prompt disclosure duties sit in Article 17, not Article 8
n.3: Article 7 is a definition, not a schedule of sanctions

q: An analyst becomes aware of several pieces of information about a listed firm. Under Article 7 of MAR, which of these would most likely amount to inside information?
o: An investor's general optimism about the wider markets
A consultation paper already published by the FCA
Rumours currently circulating on social media
Analysis that has been published in the financial press
Knowledge of a company's unpublished quarterly results
w: Unpublished financial results are precise, non-public, and price-sensitive, fitting the Article 7 definition of inside information.

n.0: General optimism is not precise, non-public information
n.3: Press analysis is public information
n.1: A published FCA paper is public, not inside information
n.2: Social-media rumours lack the required precision

q: A compliance officer is illustrating unlawful disclosure for staff. Which of the following constitutes unlawful disclosure under Article 10?
o: Discussing price movements on television after a public market release
Passing inside information to another person without any duty
Announcing a takeover to the market through an RNS
Providing market updates within an annual report
Publishing a prospectus to the wider market
w: Article 10 prohibits passing inside information to others unless in the normal course of duties.

n.2: An RNS takeover announcement is proper public disclosure
n.3: Annual-report updates are public disclosures
n.0: Post-release TV discussion involves public information
n.4: Publishing a prospectus is lawful public disclosure

q: A trainee is studying the market abuse regime and asks what Article 8 of MAR actually forbids. What is its central prohibition?
o: Dealing, or attempting to deal, using inside information
Failing to report a suspicious order to the FCA
Failing to keep proper staff training records
Publishing a company's audited accounts after the deadline
Withholding client complaint data from the FCA
w: Article 8 prohibits dealing or attempting to deal while in possession of inside information.

n.1: STOR reporting failures fall under the STOR rules, not Article 8
n.2: Training-record failures are systems breaches, not Article 8
n.4: Complaint-data failures are DISP matters, not Article 8
n.3: Late accounts are a company-law breach, not insider dealing

q: A compliance trainer lists several items and asks which would NOT count as inside information under Article 7. Which is it?
o: Unpublished product launch dates
Unannounced changes to board leadership
Draft annual financial figures
Published dividend announcements
Confidential negotiations for a merger
w: Published dividend announcements are already public and therefore not inside information under Article 7.

n.1: Board leadership changes can be precise and price-sensitive, fitting Article 7.
n.4: Merger negotiations are classic inside information.
n.0: Unpublished launch dates are precise and non-public.
n.2: Draft financial figures are confidential and price-sensitive.

q: A compliance officer is picking an example of unlawful disclosure for a case study. Which of these illustrates the offence under Article 10?
o: A listed company files accounts at Companies House
An analyst references public Bloomberg data
A company issues official financial results via RNS
An employee emails takeover details to a relative
A regulator publishes enforcement outcomes
w: Emailing takeover details to a relative constitutes unlawful disclosure of inside information under Article 10.

n.2: Official RNS disclosures are lawful and required, not improper.
n.1: Bloomberg data is public information and not unlawful disclosure.
n.4: Enforcement outcomes are published by regulators and not inside leaks.
n.0: Statutory filings are public and not unlawful disclosure.

q: A trainee compliance analyst is studying the market abuse regime and asks how Articles 7, 8 and 10 of MAR fit together. What is the correct description of the relationship between them?
o: All three articles require firms to submit STORs
Article 7 sets fines, Article 8 defines disclosure, Article 10 sets training duties
Articles 7 and 8 define training rules; Article 10 defines disclosure forms
Article 7 defines inside information; Articles 8 and 10 prohibit its misuse
Article 7 creates offences, Articles 8 and 10 define public announcements
w: Article 7 defines inside information, while Articles 8 and 10 prohibit dealing or disclosing it unlawfully.

n.1: Article 7 does not set fines; it defines inside information.
n.4: Offences arise from Articles 8 and 10, not Article 7.
n.0: STOR obligations arise separately under MAR, not directly from Articles 7–10.
n.2: These Articles regulate misuse of inside information, not training or disclosure templates.

q: A corporate finance team is preparing a market sounding under Article 11 of UK MAR. What is its purpose?
o: To gauge investor interest ahead of a possible transaction
To publish the issuer's annual financial statements
To provide the statutory audit disclosures required by law
To announce a confirmed corporate action to the market
To report a suspicious transaction to the FCA
w: A market sounding is the communication of information to assess investor interest before transactions such as placements or debt issues.

n.3: Soundings gauge interest before a deal, not public announcements
n.1: Publishing statements is a separate disclosure obligation
n.4: Suspicious-transaction reporting is the STOR process, not a sounding
n.2: Audit disclosures are unrelated to the purpose of a sounding

q: Before a disclosing party shares inside information in a market sounding, what must it obtain from the recipient?
o: A confirmation letter from the issuer's external auditor
A formal board resolution passed by the issuer
Prior written approval obtained from the FCA
The recipient's consent to receive the information
A signed copy of the issuer's latest annual report
w: The disclosing party must obtain the recipient’s consent to receive potentially inside information during a market sounding.

n.4: A sounding requires consent to receive information, not an annual report
n.2: No prior FCA approval is required to conduct a market sounding
n.0: Auditor confirmation is not a precondition for a sounding
n.1: A board resolution is not required before making a sounding

q: A firm that regularly conducts market soundings is reviewing its record-keeping. What retention requirement applies?
o: They must submit all records to Companies House
They must destroy notes after one month
They must store records only until settlement
They must rely on the counterparty’s records only
They must keep records for at least five years
w: Firms conducting market soundings must maintain detailed records of disclosures and consents for at least five years.

n.1: Records cannot be destroyed after one month under MAR obligations.
n.2: Retention is not limited to settlement periods.
n.0: Companies House does not administer market sounding records.
n.3: Each firm must maintain its own records, not rely solely on counterparties.

q: An analyst is contacted as part of a market sounding and told the disclosed information is inside information. Under Article 11, what duty does the recipient have?
o: To file the information promptly with the PRA
To treat the information as inside information if so identified
To ignore the information until its official release
To share the information freely with other analysts and colleagues
To disclose the information to the market immediately
w: Recipients must treat disclosed information as inside information if so identified, until it becomes public or ceases to be inside information.

n.4: The recipient must keep it confidential, not disclose it publicly
n.0: There is no duty to file sounding information with the PRA
n.2: The recipient must safeguard the information, not simply ignore it
n.3: Sharing it with analysts would be unlawful disclosure

q: A corporate finance team conducts a market sounding following the Article 11 conditions. What protection does compliance with Article 11 provide to the disclosing parties?
o: Immunity from all FCA enforcement
Right to delay disclosure indefinitely
Safe harbour against unlawful disclosure allegations
Exemption from capital adequacy requirements
Automatic exemption from insider dealing prohibitions
w: Article 11 provides a safe harbour for disclosing parties that follow the market sounding requirements, protecting them from unlawful disclosure allegations.

n.0: It does not grant immunity from all FCA enforcement actions.
n.4: It does not exempt insiders from Article 8 prohibitions.
n.1: Disclosure cannot be delayed indefinitely under MAR rules.
n.3: Capital adequacy is a prudential matter, not MAR Article 11.

q: A compliance officer is designing surveillance controls and reviews which practice Article 12 of UK MAR prohibits. Which practice is caught?
o: Submitting a STOR
Maintaining insider lists
Publishing audited financial reports
Market manipulation
Providing annual training
w: Article 12 prohibits engaging in or attempting market manipulation, including creating false or misleading signals about financial instruments.

n.1: Maintaining insider lists is required under MAR, not prohibited.
n.0: STORs are regulatory obligations, not prohibited actions.
n.2: Audited reports are lawful disclosures, not manipulation.
n.4: Training is a compliance requirement, not a manipulation offence.

q: A surveillance analyst is describing behaviour caught by Article 12. Which of the following is an example of market manipulation?
o: Entering wash trades to create artificial trading volume
Publishing a prospectus that is approved by the FCA
Providing tax planning advice to the firm's clients
Circulating research reports that are already public
Trading shares after an official public announcement
w: Wash trades designed to mislead by creating false volume are a classic form of market manipulation under Article 12.

n.1: Publishing an approved prospectus is legitimate disclosure
n.4: Trading after a public announcement uses public information
n.2: Tax advice is unrelated to market manipulation
n.3: Sharing public research is lawful, not manipulation

q: A market surveillance analyst is reviewing several activities to identify potential market abuse. Which behaviour could amount to market manipulation?
o: Training new staff on conduct rules
Submitting annual returns to Companies House
Filing statutory accounts on time
Holding client money in trust
Spreading false rumours to move prices
w: Spreading false rumours to influence market prices is market manipulation under Article 12.

n.2: Filing accounts is a legal duty, not manipulation.
n.3: Client money obligations are CASS rules, not MAR manipulation.
n.1: Annual returns are company law obligations, not MAR prohibitions.
n.0: Training staff is compliance, not manipulation.

q: A compliance officer is training trading staff on the conduct prohibited by UK MAR Article 12. What type of signal is prohibited under that article?
o: Risk warnings issued directly to firms by the FCA
False or misleading signals as to supply, demand or price
Accurate disclosures released to the market through an RNS
Verified results set out in the company's annual report
Announcements made within a published company prospectus
w: Article 12 prohibits creating false or misleading signals regarding supply, demand or price of financial instruments.

n.2: Accurate RNS disclosures are legitimate, not prohibited signals
n.3: Verified published results are lawful disclosures
n.0: FCA risk warnings are not misleading market signals
n.4: Prospectus announcements are proper public disclosures

q: A surveillance team spots a trader repeatedly entering large buy orders and cancelling them before they can execute. Which conduct could this be investigated as?
o: Submitting an insider list to the FCA on its request
Preparing the firm's annual FCA regulatory fee return
Running a training session on MAR compliance for staff
Recording client complaints within the firm's DISP logs
Placing large orders with no intention of executing them
w: Placing large orders without intent to execute, known as spoofing, is a form of attempted market manipulation.

n.0: Submitting an insider list is a compliance duty, not manipulation
n.3: Logging complaints is routine record-keeping, not manipulation
n.2: MAR training is legitimate and not manipulation
n.1: Preparing a fee return is administrative, not manipulation

q: A listed company's company secretary is reviewing the firm's disclosure duties. What is the general obligation on issuers under UK MAR Article 17?
o: Issuers must disclose all employee salaries
Issuers must file annual accounts within six months
Issuers must report quarterly tax payments to HMRC
Issuers must publicly disclose inside information as soon as possible
Issuers must notify only their largest shareholders of inside information
w: Article 17 requires issuers to disclose inside information to the public as soon as possible to ensure market transparency.

n.4: Disclosure must be to the entire market, not just shareholders.
n.1: Annual accounts are required by company law, not Article 17.
n.0: Employee salaries are not disclosure obligations under MAR.
n.2: Tax filings are not part of MAR disclosure rules.

q: An issuer needs to release price-sensitive information to the whole market at the same time. Which mechanism is typically used to disclose inside information under Article 17?
o: Internal staff bulletin
Private email to clients
Regulatory News Service announcement
Verbal announcement at a shareholder dinner
Annual general meeting minutes
w: Issuers use Regulatory News Service (RNS) or equivalent channels to ensure simultaneous public disclosure of inside information.

n.0: Staff bulletins are internal only and not public disclosure.
n.1: Private emails breach equal access rules under MAR.
n.3: Dinner announcements are selective disclosure, not compliant.
n.4: AGM minutes are retrospective and not immediate disclosure.

q: A listed issuer's advisers want to hold back an announcement of price-sensitive information for a short period. Under Article 17, on what condition may disclosure of inside information be delayed?
o: The shareholders have voted in favour of delaying disclosure
The market is currently experiencing a period of high volatility
The information is expected to leak into the market anyway
Immediate disclosure would prejudice the issuer's legitimate interests
The issuer has not yet notified its own members of staff
w: Disclosure may be delayed if it would prejudice legitimate interests, provided confidentiality is maintained and the market is not misled.

n.4: Not yet notifying staff is not a valid ground to delay disclosure
n.2: An expected leak undermines, rather than justifies, a delay
n.1: Market volatility is not a permitted ground for delay
n.0: A shareholder vote is not a condition for delaying disclosure

q: An issuer has been relying on a delay to public disclosure of inside information. What must it do once the information is finally disclosed?
o: File a report with HM Treasury
Disclose only to its largest creditors
Inform the FCA once disclosure occurs
Seek shareholder approval for the delay
Provide confidential notice to competitors
w: Issuers must inform the FCA when disclosure has been delayed, explaining how conditions for delay were satisfied.

n.3: Shareholders do not authorise delays; MAR governs this.
n.4: Competitors must not receive confidential inside information.
n.1: Creditors are not the disclosure audience under MAR.
n.0: HM Treasury is not the relevant regulator under MAR.

q: A trainee asks what principle sits behind the Article 17 disclosure obligations. Which key principle underpins them?
o: Equal access to information for all investors
Confidentiality of information at all times
Disclosure only to market makers
Priority access for institutional shareholders
Limiting disclosures to annual results
w: Article 17 aims to ensure equal access to inside information, preventing selective disclosure that advantages certain investors.

n.3: Institutional shareholders must not receive preferential access.
n.1: Confidentiality is important but disclosure must still occur publicly.
n.2: Market makers cannot be privileged with information.
n.4: Disclosure applies continuously, not only annually.

q: An issuer working on an unannounced deal must maintain an insider list under Article 18 of MAR. What is the purpose of that list?
o: To record board members' attendance at meetings
To disclose the salaries paid to the company's directors
To identify the individuals who have access to inside information
To track the company's historic dividend payments
To publish the names of the company's shareholders
w: Article 18 requires issuers and advisors to maintain insider lists to identify those with access to inside information.

n.4: Insider lists are not a public record of shareholders
n.0: They record access to inside information, not meeting attendance
n.1: Directors' pay disclosure is a separate reporting requirement
n.3: Dividend history is unrelated to the purpose of insider lists

q: A company preparing an announcement must maintain an insider list under Article 18 of MAR. What information must each entry on that list include?
o: Only the personal tax code of each person on the list
The identity, the reason for inclusion, and the date of access
The trading volumes attributed to each listed employee
The aggregate salary data for all the listed staff
The pension contribution history of each listed person
w: Insider lists must record the identity of individuals, reason for inclusion, and the date/time they gained access to inside information.

n.0: Tax codes are not part of the required insider-list content
n.3: Salary data is not required on an insider list
n.2: Trading volumes are not recorded on the insider list
n.4: Pension details are not part of an insider list

q: A corporate broker advising a listed company on a deal wonders whether it must keep an insider list under Article 18. Who is required to maintain such lists?
o: Only individual retail investors in the shares
Only the Financial Conduct Authority itself
Issuers and the persons acting on their behalf
Only the issuer's institutional shareholders
Only the market makers active in the instrument
w: Both issuers and anyone acting on their behalf (such as advisers) must maintain insider lists.

n.1: Issuers and their advisers keep the lists, not the FCA
n.0: Retail investors have no duty to maintain insider lists
n.4: Market makers are not the parties required to keep them
n.3: Institutional shareholders do not maintain insider lists

q: A company secretary is confirming the retention period for insider lists under Article 18. For how long must they be kept?
o: Three months
Until the insider leaves employment
One year
Ten business days
At least five years
w: Insider lists must be retained for at least five years after they are created or updated.

n.2: One year is below the minimum requirement.
n.0: Three months is far too short for retention under MAR.
n.1: Retention is required beyond employment termination.
n.3: Ten business days is not the statutory requirement.

q: A listed company maintains an insider list of everyone with access to a pending acquisition announcement. From the FCA's perspective, what is one purpose of requiring such lists?
o: To monitor the firm's ongoing tax compliance
To calculate each firm's regulatory capital ratio
To help set the Bank of England's interest rate policy
To calculate the company's dividend distributions
To help the FCA investigate potential market abuse
w: Insider lists assist the FCA in identifying who had access to inside information during investigations into possible market abuse.

n.1: Capital ratios are a prudential matter, unrelated to insider lists
n.0: Tax compliance is not the purpose of insider lists
n.2: Interest-rate policy has nothing to do with insider lists
n.3: Dividend calculations are unrelated to insider lists

q: A listed company's advisers are considering how to release price-sensitive news to the market under Article 17 of UK MAR. What is the overriding aim of that disclosure requirement?
o: To let shareholders vote on each announcement
To coordinate disclosures with the issuer's tax filings
To minimise the administrative costs for the issuers
To ensure transparency and prevent selective disclosure
To give the company's directors advance notice
w: Article 17 is designed to ensure transparency and equal access to inside information, preventing selective disclosure.

n.4: The aim is equal market access, not advance notice for directors
n.2: Article 17 is not designed to reduce issuers' costs
n.0: Shareholders do not vote on inside-information announcements
n.1: Disclosure timing is not tied to tax filings

q: An issuer is deciding whether it can lawfully delay disclosure under Article 17. What condition must always be met?
o: The firm must publish the information on its website first
The auditor must sign off on the decision
The board must notify all shareholders
Confidentiality of the information must be preserved
The FCA must pre-approve every delay
w: Delays are only valid if confidentiality is maintained and investors are not misled.

n.2: Shareholder notifications are not a requirement under Article 17.
n.4: The FCA does not pre-approve delays, though it must be informed after.
n.1: Auditor approval is not required for disclosure delays.
n.0: Website publication alone does not satisfy disclosure obligations.

q: After releasing inside information whose disclosure it had delayed, what must an issuer provide to the FCA?
o: A copy of the company's most recent annual report
An explanation of how the conditions for delay were met
A confirmation of the dividend payments that were made
A list of all the directors present at the decision
A summary of the relevant shareholder meeting minutes
w: Issuers must explain to the FCA how conditions for delaying disclosure were met once information is released.

n.3: The FCA requires the reasoning for delay, not an attendance list
n.0: The annual report is not what must be provided after a delay
n.4: Meeting minutes are not the required post-delay explanation
n.2: Dividend confirmations are unrelated to a delayed disclosure

q: A listed company is drawing up its insider list ahead of an unannounced acquisition. Under Article 18 of MAR, which individuals must appear on the list?
o: Anyone who has access to the inside information
Only the firm's designated compliance officers
Only the company's statutory external auditors
Only the company's external shareholders
Only the members of the company's board
w: Insider lists must include all individuals with access to inside information, regardless of role or seniority.

n.4: The list covers all with access, not only board members
n.3: External shareholders are not automatically insiders
n.1: Compliance officers are not the only people listed
n.2: Auditors are not the only individuals recorded

q: A listed company adds and removes staff who have access to a confidential deal. Why must its insider lists be updated promptly under Article 18?
o: To comply with the company's corporation tax rules
To reflect changes in who can access inside information
To keep track of the staff holiday schedules
To ensure the dividend calculations remain accurate
To monitor the outcome of staff performance reviews
w: Insider lists must be kept accurate and updated whenever new individuals gain or lose access to inside information.

n.3: Dividend accuracy has nothing to do with insider lists
n.2: Holiday tracking is an HR matter, not an insider-list purpose
n.0: Tax compliance is unrelated to updating insider lists
n.4: Performance reviews are not the reason for updating the list

q: A company secretary is explaining to the board why the firm keeps insider lists. What legal risk do they help mitigate?
o: Unpaid corporation tax
Market abuse investigations
Employment law disputes
Breach of health and safety law
Breach of data protection
w: Insider lists help regulators identify who had access to inside information, supporting market abuse investigations.

n.4: Data protection issues are not the purpose of insider lists.
n.0: Tax is unrelated to MAR insider lists.
n.2: Employment disputes are outside MAR obligations.
n.3: Health and safety is unrelated to insider list compliance.

q: An issuer is setting record-retention policy for its delayed disclosure decisions under Article 17. For how long must it keep the evidence?
o: At least five years
Ten business days
One year
Three months
Until the next shareholder meeting
w: Issuers must retain records of delayed disclosure decisions for at least five years to demonstrate compliance.

n.2: One year is shorter than MAR requires.
n.4: Shareholder meetings do not govern retention periods.
n.3: Three months is insufficient under Article 17.
n.1: Ten business days is far too short for MAR retention rules.

q: A listed company's company secretary is compiling its insider list ahead of a results announcement. For each person with access to the inside information, what detail must the list record?
o: Their voting record at the company's AGMs
The length of their current employment contract
Their full personal pension contribution history
Their current trading account cash balance
Their identity, their function, and their contact details
w: Insider lists must include identity, role or function, and contact details of individuals with access to inside information.

n.3: Account balances are not part of an insider list
n.1: Contract length is not required on an insider list
n.2: Pension history is not recorded on the list
n.0: AGM voting records are not insider-list content

q: A listed issuer is preparing an insider list ahead of a confidential deal. Under Article 18, which regulator must be able to request that list on demand?
o: Competition and Markets Authority
Financial Conduct Authority
Serious Fraud Office
Prudential Regulation Authority
Bank of England
w: The FCA, as the UK’s competent authority for MAR, must be able to request insider lists on demand.

n.0: The CMA handles competition law, not MAR insider lists.
n.2: The SFO investigates fraud, not insider list compliance.
n.3: The PRA supervises prudential issues, not insider lists.
n.4: The Bank of England handles monetary policy, not MAR lists.

q: A company secretary is explaining why each person added to the insider list must sign an acknowledgement. Why is that required?
o: To accept a permanent reduction in their statutory employment rights
To confirm they understand their duties over inside information
To confirm their personal trading account balances
To consent to the publication of their salary
To agree to disclose their personal tax history
w: Individuals must acknowledge their inclusion to confirm they understand their duties not to misuse inside information.

n.0: Acknowledgement confirms duties; it does not cut employment rights
n.2: It is about legal duties, not confirming account balances
n.4: Tax history disclosure is not part of the acknowledgement
n.3: Salary publication is unrelated to the acknowledgement

q: A compliance officer is confirming the principal offence created by Section 52 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What is it?
o: False accounting
Breach of directors’ duties
Insider dealing
Market manipulation
Money laundering
w: Section 52 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 makes insider dealing a criminal offence.

n.4: Money laundering is dealt with under POCA, not Section 52 CJA 1993.
n.3: Market manipulation is addressed separately under MAR, not CJA Section 52.
n.1: Directors’ duties are under the Companies Act, not CJA 1993.
n.0: False accounting falls under the Theft Act, not insider dealing legislation.

q: A trainee is checking which section of the CJA 1993 defines the term 'inside information'. Which section is it?
o: Section 58
Schedule 2
Section 56
Section 61
Section 52
w: Section 56 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 provides the definition of 'inside information'.

n.0: Section 58 addresses when information is treated as made public, not its definition
n.4: Section 52 creates the offence of insider dealing, not the definition
n.1: Schedule 2 lists the securities covered, not the definition
n.3: Section 61 deals with penalties and prosecution, not the definition

q: A compliance officer is confirming how an 'insider' is defined under the CJA 1993. Which description is correct?
o: Any person who simply buys shares in a listed company
A shareholder who attends a company's AGM
A journalist who reports on the financial markets
An employee who completes mandatory annual training
A person who has information through a position or access
w: An insider is someone who possesses inside information by virtue of their position, office, or access to information.

n.0: Merely buying shares does not make someone an insider
n.1: Attending an AGM does not confer insider status
n.2: A journalist reporting on markets is not, by that fact, an insider
n.3: Completing training does not make an employee an insider

q: A defence lawyer is locating the section of the CJA 1993 that sets out defences to insider dealing. Which section is it?
o: Section 57
Section 61
Section 56
Schedule 2
Section 52
w: Section 57 sets out the statutory defences available to insider dealing charges.

n.4: Section 52 creates the insider dealing offence, not the defences
n.2: Section 56 defines inside information, not the defences
n.1: Section 61 covers penalties and prosecution, not the defences
n.3: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the defences

q: A trader is convicted of insider dealing under the Criminal Justice Act 1993. Which section of the Act sets out the penalties for the offence?
o: Section 58
Section 60
Schedule 2
Section 52
Section 56
w: Section 58 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993 specifies the penalties for insider dealing offences.

n.3: Section 52 sets out the offence, not the penalties
n.4: Section 56 defines inside information, not the penalties
n.2: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the penalties
n.1: Section 60 contains supplementary provisions, not the penalties

q: A prosecutor is confirming which instruments fall within the insider dealing regime under the CJA 1993. What types of financial instruments are listed in Schedule 2?
o: Gold bullion and other physical commodities
Securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives
Real estate holdings and property title deeds
Insurance contracts and personal pensions only
Residential mortgages and personal bank loans
w: Schedule 2 lists securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives covered by the insider dealing provisions.

n.3: Insurance and pensions are not the securities listed in Schedule 2
n.4: Mortgages and loans are not covered by Schedule 2
n.2: Property deeds are not securities under Schedule 2
n.0: Physical commodities are not Schedule 2 securities

q: A dealer trades in price-affected securities while holding inside information. Which of the following is an offence under Section 52 of the CJA 1993?
o: Breaching the listing rules on timely disclosure
Issuing a misleading financial promotion to clients
Dealing in price-affected securities while holding inside information
Filing the company's annual accounts after the deadline
Failing to disclose a personal conflict of interest to the firm's clients
w: Section 52 makes it an offence to deal in securities that are price-affected by inside information possessed by the individual.

n.4: Conflict-of-interest failures are SYSC or COBS matters, not a s.52 offence
n.1: Misleading promotions breach COBS, not the s.52 dealing offence
n.0: Listing-rule breaches are separate from the s.52 offence
n.3: Late accounts are a company-law matter, not s.52 insider dealing

q: In an insider dealing case, the prosecution must establish that certain material amounted to 'inside information'. Under Section 56, what quality must such information possess?
o: It must be speculative and vague
It must relate only to government securities
It must always come from annual reports
It must be precise and price-sensitive
It must be based solely on market gossip
w: Inside information under Section 56 must be precise, non-public, and likely to affect security prices.

n.0: Speculative information does not qualify as inside information.
n.2: Annual reports are public, not inside information.
n.4: Market gossip is not precise or reliable under CJA definitions.
n.1: Inside information can relate to a wide range of securities, not just government ones.

q: A compliance officer is confirming the maximum custodial penalty for insider dealing under Section 58 of the CJA 1993. What is it?
o: Seven years' imprisonment
Life imprisonment
Ten years' imprisonment
Three years' imprisonment
Five years' imprisonment
w: Section 58 provides for a maximum penalty of seven years’ imprisonment for insider dealing offences.

n.3: The maximum custodial term is seven years, not three
n.4: The maximum is seven years, not five
n.2: Ten years exceeds the seven-year statutory maximum
n.1: Life imprisonment is not available for insider dealing

q: An individual is charged with insider dealing after trading in a listed company's shares. Which of the following would provide a defence under Section 57 of the CJA 1993?
o: The information was already generally available to the public
The insider disclosed the information only to close friends
The insider acted on the basis of general market rumours
The transaction ultimately turned out to be profitable
The individual was not a registered FCA-approved person
w: A key defence is that the information was already generally available to the public at the time of the transaction.

n.4: FCA registration status is irrelevant to an insider dealing defence
n.3: Making a profit is not a defence; it is closer to the harm targeted
n.1: Disclosing to friends is itself improper, not a defence
n.2: Acting on rumours is not a recognised statutory defence

q: A trainee asks what 'price-affected securities' means under Section 52 of the CJA 1993. Which description is best?
o: Shares that are held directly by the directors of the issuing company
Only bonds and other debt instruments issued by a national government
Any position taken in the foreign exchange or spot commodity markets
Securities whose price would be significantly moved by the inside information
Any security that is admitted to trading on a recognised regulated market
w: Price-affected securities are those whose price would likely change significantly if the inside information were made public.

n.4: Being traded on a market does not make a security price-affected in the statutory sense.
n.1: The concept is not limited to government bonds.
n.0: Directors' holdings are not the definition of price-affected securities.
n.2: FX and spot commodities are outside this definition.

q: According to Section 56 of the CJA 1993, a compliance officer is confirming what inside information must relate to. What is it?
o: Speculative commentary appearing in the media
Rumours about overall market confidence levels
Particular securities or a particular issuer
General macroeconomic conditions and trends
Long-term historic trading volume data only
w: Inside information must be specific to particular securities or issuers and not general or speculative data.

n.3: Inside information is issuer or security specific, not general economic data
n.1: General confidence rumours are not specific inside information
n.0: Speculative media commentary is not precise inside information
n.4: Historic volume data is public, not issuer-specific inside information

q: A defendant is preparing to rely on Section 57 of the CJA 1993. What is a key statutory defence it provides?
o: The person had consulted their own financial adviser
The person was an FCA-authorised insider at the time
The person did not directly profit from the trade
The person would have acted the same way without the information
The person had first obtained approval from the shareholders
w: It is a defence if the person would have acted in the same way even without the inside information.

n.4: Shareholder approval is not a statutory insider dealing defence
n.1: Being FCA-authorised is not a defence to insider dealing
n.0: Consulting an adviser does not provide a defence
n.2: Absence of direct profit is not by itself a statutory defence

q: A compliance officer is confirming the maximum fine available under Section 58 for insider dealing. What is it?
o: A fine capped at 100,000 pounds
A fine capped at 500,000 pounds
An unlimited fine
A fine of up to 1 million pounds
A fine of up to 50,000 pounds
w: Section 58 allows for an unlimited fine to be imposed alongside custodial penalties.

n.4: The fine is unlimited on indictment, not capped at 50,000 pounds
n.0: There is no 100,000-pound cap on the fine
n.1: The fine is not capped at 500,000 pounds
n.3: The fine is unlimited, not limited to 1 million pounds

q: A trainee is checking which instruments fall within Schedule 2 of the CJA 1993. Which type of instruments are included?
o: Consumer credit and personal loan agreements
Shares, bonds, options, and futures
Personal pension scheme entitlements
General insurance policies and annuities
Property deeds and land registrations
w: Schedule 2 specifies securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives including options and futures as covered instruments.

n.4: Property deeds are not Schedule 2 securities
n.2: Pension entitlements are not covered by Schedule 2
n.0: Consumer credit agreements are not Schedule 2 securities
n.3: Insurance policies are not covered by Schedule 2

q: A friend passes an analyst a tip and mentions it came from someone inside a listed company. Under the CJA 1993, who qualifies as a 'secondary insider'?
o: Any person authorised and regulated by the FCA to conduct investment business
Any retail investor who happens to hold shares in the relevant company
A director or other primary insider of the company whose securities are affected
A person who receives inside information indirectly and knows that it is inside information
An auditor carrying out the statutory audit of the company's accounts
w: A secondary insider is someone who receives inside information indirectly and knows, or ought to know, it is inside information.

n.2: That describes a primary insider, not a secondary one.
n.0: Being FCA-authorised does not make someone a secondary insider.
n.1: Merely holding shares does not make a retail investor a secondary insider.
n.4: An auditor is not a secondary insider by virtue of the audit.

q: A dealer receives inside information and is unsure which behaviours could expose him to prosecution. Which of the following actions is covered by the Section 52 insider dealing offence?
o: Dealing, encouraging another to deal, or disclosing inside information
Failing to attend a scheduled company board meeting
Failing to record and investigate the firm's client complaints properly
Publishing the company's annual accounts after the deadline
Not completing the required FCA-related staff training
w: Section 52 covers dealing, encouraging another to deal, and disclosing inside information unlawfully.

n.1: Missing a board meeting is not an insider dealing offence
n.3: Late accounts are a company-law breach, not s.52 conduct
n.4: Incomplete training is not an insider dealing offence
n.2: Poor complaint records are a DISP matter, not s.52

q: The FCA is building a case against an individual for insider dealing under Section 52 of the Criminal Justice Act 1993. What must prosecutors prove for the offence to be made out?
o: That the person disclosed the annual results late
That the person actually made a financial profit on the deal
That the person dealt while in possession of inside information
That the person was a shareholder of the issuer
That the person was a director of the relevant company
w: Prosecutors must show that the accused dealt in securities while in possession of inside information.

n.1: Profit need not be proved to establish the s.52 offence
n.4: Director status is not a required element of the offence
n.0: Late results disclosure is not an element of insider dealing
n.3: Being a shareholder is not what prosecutors must prove

q: A compliance officer is summarising the penalties under Section 58 of the CJA 1993. Which statement is correct?
o: They include imprisonment and unlimited fines
They apply only to companies, not to individuals
They are capped at a maximum of 50,000 pounds
They allow imprisonment of up to fifteen years
They require mandatory community service orders
w: Section 58 provides for custodial penalties up to seven years and unlimited fines for insider dealing offences.

n.1: The penalties apply to individuals, not only companies
n.2: The fine is unlimited, not capped at 50,000 pounds
n.3: The maximum custodial term is seven years, not fifteen
n.4: Community service is not a mandatory penalty for the offence

q: A trader is unsure whether a particular instrument falls within the insider dealing regime. Which best describes the scope of instruments covered by the CJA 1993 rules?
o: All pension schemes and life insurance policies
All everyday consumer banking and savings products offered by banks
All foreign currency spot exchange transactions
Securities listed in Schedule 2, including shares and derivatives
All tangible physical commodities and raw materials
w: CJA 1993 insider dealing applies to securities in Schedule 2, such as shares, bonds, and derivatives.

n.1: Consumer banking products are not Schedule 2 securities
n.2: Foreign-currency spot trades are not covered by Schedule 2
n.4: Physical commodities fall outside Schedule 2
n.0: Pensions and insurance policies are not Schedule 2 securities

q: An accused trader argues he would have made exactly the same trade even without the inside information he held. Which general defence under Section 53 CJA 1993 does this represent?
o: The person would have acted the same way without the information
The person made no profit at all from the trade
The person had been trading in these particular shares quite regularly
The person was not a director of the company
The person disclosed the information only to family
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the accused can show they would have acted the same way without the inside information.

n.1: Absence of profit is not the s.53 same-decision defence
n.3: Not being a director is not a statutory defence
n.4: Disclosing to family is improper, not a defence
n.2: A history of regular trading is not a statutory defence

q: A defendant wants to run the 'same decision defence' under Section 53. What must they prove?
o: That the information involved was merely speculative and unverified in nature
That the FCA had not prohibited the transaction
That the trade produced no financial gain at all
That the information came from public news outlets
That they would have traded regardless of the inside information
w: The same decision defence applies if the defendant can show they would have made the trade even without the inside information.

n.2: No-gain is not what the same-decision defence requires
n.0: Speculative-information claims are not this defence
n.3: Public-source claims relate to a different point, not this defence
n.1: Lack of an FCA prohibition is irrelevant to the defence

q: A defendant is relying on the defence of prior intent under Section 53. Which factor supports it?
o: Evidence the trade was ordered before the information was received
Evidence the person consulted a financial adviser first
Evidence the person traded through a nominee account
Evidence the person held a well-diversified portfolio
Evidence the person was completely unaware of any circulating market rumours
w: Prior intent is a defence if there is evidence that instructions to trade were given before the inside information was obtained.

n.2: Using a nominee account does not establish prior intent
n.1: Consulting an adviser does not evidence prior intent
n.3: Portfolio diversification is irrelevant to prior intent
n.4: Ignorance of rumours does not prove a pre-existing order

q: A trader accused of insider dealing is trying to establish a Section 53 defence with his solicitor. Which of the following is NOT a valid statutory defence?
o: That the trade was required under a prior agreement
That the person already had binding obligations to trade
That the person would have traded anyway without the information
That the person gained no profit from the trade
That the decision to trade was made before receiving inside information
w: Absence of profit is not a statutory defence; liability depends on dealing while in possession of inside information.

n.4: Prior decisions before receipt of inside information can be a defence.
n.2: Trading regardless of the information is a valid statutory defence.
n.1: Pre-existing binding obligations may provide a defence under Section 53.
n.0: Trading under a prior agreement is a recognised statutory defence.

q: A trader executed a deal under a binding obligation entered before receiving inside information. How does Section 53 treat such trades?
o: They are permitted only with the shareholders' approval
They are always prohibited whatever the circumstances
They may be defended if entered before the information was received
They are excused only if the FCA specifically authorises them
They are valid only if executed by an external broker
w: Trades under binding obligations entered into before receipt of inside information can be defended under Section 53.

n.1: Such trades are not always prohibited; a defence can apply
n.3: No FCA authorisation is needed for this defence
n.0: Shareholder approval is not the relevant condition
n.4: Using an external broker is not what validates the trade

q: An individual with inside information completes a share sale, but the trade fulfilled a contract entered into before he received that information. Which statutory defence may apply?
o: The shareholder vote approval defence
The nominee account trading defence
The transaction profitability defence
The prior contractual obligation defence
The director independence defence
w: Section 53 provides a defence if the trade occurred under a binding legal obligation existing before receipt of inside information.

n.2: There is no profitability defence to insider dealing
n.0: A shareholder vote does not create a statutory defence
n.4: Director independence is not a recognised defence
n.1: Using a nominee account is not a statutory defence

q: A defendant in an insider dealing case relies on the 'same decision regardless' defence. What must they demonstrate to succeed?
o: That the FCA had been notified of the trade in advance
That the decision to trade was not influenced by the information
That the trade had been recommended by an analyst
That the securities were very widely held in the market
That the transaction ultimately produced no net profit
w: The defendant must show that the decision was not influenced by inside information and would have been taken in any case.

n.4: No-profit is not what this defence requires
n.0: Advance FCA notification is not part of the defence
n.2: An analyst recommendation does not establish the defence
n.3: Wide ownership of the securities is irrelevant to the defence

q: A defendant is raising a statutory defence under Section 53. Which burden of proof applies to it?
o: The court must simply assume the defendant's honesty
The FCA must prove beyond reasonable doubt that no such defence exists
The defendant must prove the defence on the balance of probabilities
The firm's auditor must certify that the defence applies
The burden rests automatically on the regulator alone
w: Defendants must prove statutory defences on the balance of probabilities, unlike the prosecution’s burden of proof for offences.

n.1: The defendant bears the defence burden; the FCA need not disprove it
n.0: The court does not presume the defendant's honesty
n.4: The burden for the defence rests on the defendant, not the regulator
n.3: No auditor certification is involved in proving a defence

q: A defence lawyer is choosing an example of the prior intent defence. Which best illustrates it?
o: Trading based on analyst speculation printed in a newspaper
Selling bonds following the release of an FCA press statement
A dividend reinvestment instruction set before the information was received
Buying shares after a public company results announcement
A spontaneous share trade placed after overhearing confidential boardroom news
w: Automatic reinvestment instructions set prior to receiving inside information are an example of the prior intent defence.

n.4: A spontaneous trade after learning inside news shows no prior intent
n.0: Acting on newspaper speculation is not the prior-intent defence
n.3: Buying after a public announcement involves public information
n.1: Selling after an FCA release involves public information

q: A compliance trainer is explaining the significance of Section 53 in insider dealing prosecutions. Why is it important?
o: It removes all penalties for insider dealing offences
It provides statutory defences balancing the offence's strict liability
It allows the regulators to bring only civil enforcement actions, never criminal
It exempts institutional investors from their MAR duties
It prevents the FCA from prosecuting company directors
w: Section 53 is important as it provides statutory defences, ensuring individuals are not convicted where trades were independent of inside information.

n.0: Section 53 provides defences; it does not remove penalties
n.2: It does not restrict enforcement to civil actions only
n.4: It does not shield directors from prosecution
n.3: It does not exempt institutions from MAR obligations

q: A market maker is checking which special defence under the CJA 1993 protects its activity. Which one applies?
o: They may pass inside information on to research analysts
They may trade in good faith in their legitimate market-making role
They may trade using information shared with their family members
They may ignore their reporting obligations to the FCA
They may delay disclosure until after a profit has been made
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence for market makers who act in good faith while carrying out their legitimate market-making role.

n.2: Trading on family-shared inside information is not a defence
n.4: Delaying disclosure to secure profit is not a market-maker defence
n.0: Passing inside information to analysts is unlawful disclosure
n.3: Market makers are not exempt from FCA reporting obligations

q: A trainee asks why the CJA 1993 gives market makers a special defence. What is its purpose?
o: To permit the disclosure of confidential inside information
To exempt them from the market abuse laws altogether
To let market makers provide liquidity without fear of prosecution
To exempt market makers entirely from all FCA oversight
To remove their record-keeping requirements altogether
w: The market-maker defence exists to protect legitimate liquidity provision activities from being classed as insider dealing.

n.3: The defence is narrow; it does not remove all FCA oversight
n.0: It does not permit disclosing confidential inside information
n.4: Record-keeping duties are not removed by the defence
n.1: Market makers remain subject to the market abuse laws

q: A dealer trades using information legitimately available in the market. Which special defence under Schedule 1 applies?
o: Where the trade is based on leaked company board minutes
Where the trade uses information legitimately available in the market
Where the trade relies on private family knowledge
Where the trade uses unpublished company earnings figures
Where the trade rests solely on unverified and speculative market rumours
w: Schedule 1 provides a defence when trades are based on information that is legitimately part of the market itself.

n.4: Trading on rumours is not the market-information defence
n.0: Using leaked board minutes is insider dealing, not a defence
n.2: Private family knowledge is not legitimate market information
n.3: Unpublished earnings are inside information, not a defence

q: A compliance officer is explaining why the 'market information' defence exists. Why is it important?
o: It exempts company directors from any liability for their own trading decisions
It excuses trading that is based on information obtained through a deliberate leak
It allows an insider to deal on inside information for their own personal gain
It protects traders acting on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand or price
It permits dealing on data that has been stolen from another market participant
w: This defence ensures that genuine market activity based on legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or pricing is not treated as insider dealing.

n.4: The defence does not cover stolen data.
n.1: It does not excuse trading on deliberate leaks.
n.2: It does not permit insider dealing for personal gain.
n.0: It does not give directors blanket immunity.

q: An underwriter is confirming what the price stabilisation defence under Schedule 1 covers. What is it?
o: A defence for permitted stabilisation after a new securities issue
A defence for journalists who publish inside information
A defence for shareholders who delay required disclosures
A defence letting market makers withhold required disclosures
A defence for trading on the basis of insider leaks
w: The price stabilisation defence permits stabilisation activity following new issues of securities when carried out under proper rules.

n.4: Trading on insider leaks is never a defence
n.3: There is no defence for market makers withholding disclosures
n.1: Publishing inside information is not a stabilisation defence
n.2: Delaying required disclosures is not the stabilisation defence

q: An underwriter supporting a new share issue engages in price stabilisation during the offer. Why does the law provide a defence for this activity?
o: To allow controlled activity that keeps markets orderly during issues
To exempt underwriters from all of their disclosure rules
To place underwriters beyond the FCA's enforcement powers
To let insiders profit without any regulatory oversight at all
To override the market abuse prohibitions entirely
w: Price stabilisation helps maintain orderly markets during securities issuance and is recognised as a legitimate activity under CJA defences.

n.3: The defence supports orderly markets, not unchecked insider profit
n.1: It does not exempt underwriters from disclosure rules
n.2: Underwriters remain within the FCA's enforcement reach
n.4: It does not override the market abuse prohibitions generally

q: A trainee asks which party most often relies on the price stabilisation defence. Which is it?
o: Ordinary retail shareholders in the company
Financial journalists reporting on the issue
Government financial regulators and agencies
Underwriters of a new securities issue
The external auditors of the listed company
w: Underwriters conducting stabilisation after a new issue may rely on the statutory defence if rules are followed.

n.0: Retail shareholders do not rely on the stabilisation defence
n.1: Journalists are not the party conducting stabilisation
n.4: Auditors do not carry out stabilisation activity
n.2: Regulators supervise; they do not rely on the defence

q: A compliance officer is briefing traders on the special defences to insider dealing set out in Schedule 1 of the Criminal Justice Act. Which of the following would NOT count as a recognised defence?
o: Trading based on legitimate market information
Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks
Trading to provide liquidity in a regulated market
Price stabilisation following a new issue
Trading in good faith as a market maker
w: Trading for personal enrichment using inside leaks is never a defence; it constitutes insider dealing.

n.4: Good-faith market making is a recognised Schedule 1 defence
n.3: Price stabilisation after a new issue is a recognised defence
n.0: Trading on legitimate market information is a recognised defence
n.2: Providing liquidity is part of the market-making defence

q: A compliance officer is locating where the special defences to insider dealing are set out. Which statutory document contains them?
o: FCA Handbook rule MAR 1.1.3
Schedule 1 to the CJA 1993
Part VIII of the FSMA 2000
Section 52 of the CJA 1993
Schedule 2 to the CJA 1993
w: Special defences such as market making, market information, and price stabilisation are set out in Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993.

n.4: Schedule 2 lists the covered securities, not the special defences
n.3: Section 52 creates the offence, not the special defences
n.2: FSMA Part VIII concerns the civil market abuse regime, not CJA defences
n.0: MAR 1.1.3 is FCA guidance, not the CJA special defences

q: A market maker wants to rely on its special defence. How must it demonstrate good faith?
o: By showing the trades produced no gain for the firm
By showing the trades were pre-cleared by the market operator
By showing it acted only on instructions from its clients
By showing the trades were part of its normal market-making activity
By showing it held no inside information when it dealt
w: The market maker must show that trades were carried out in good faith and as part of their normal role of providing liquidity.

n.4: The defence exists precisely for dealing while holding inside information; absence of it is not the test.
n.1: There is no pre-clearance-by-operator requirement for the market-maker defence.
n.2: Acting on client instructions is not the basis of the market-maker defence.
n.0: Whether a profit was made is irrelevant to establishing the defence.

q: A trainee asks what the 'good faith' requirement means for a market maker under Schedule 1. What does it mean?
o: Trades must be part of a genuine market-making liquidity function
Trades must be limited to the firm's own proprietary book
Trades must be reported to the FCA before they are executed
Trades must be matched against a client order each time
Trades must avoid any instrument the firm has researched
w: Good faith means market makers must trade genuinely to provide liquidity rather than exploit inside information.

n.2: There is no pre-trade FCA reporting condition for the defence.
n.1: The defence is not confined to proprietary-book trades.
n.3: No requirement to match each trade against a client order.
n.4: Good faith is about liquidity provision, not avoiding researched instruments.

q: Which activity is covered by the 'market information' defence?
o: Dealing on the basis of a merger announcement that has been leaked before release
Trading ahead of confidential earnings figures obtained from within the issuer
Dealing on a tip received in confidence from a family member who is an insider
Using legitimate knowledge of market supply, demand or price movements
Acting on the contents of a private boardroom discussion one was told about
w: The market information defence protects trades made using legitimate knowledge of supply, demand, or price available within the market system.

n.0: Trading on leaked merger information is not the market-information defence.
n.1: Confidential earnings figures are inside information, not market information.
n.4: Private boardroom discussions are inside information.
n.2: A confidential insider tip is not legitimate market information.

q: A trainee asks which situations typically involve price stabilisation activity. Which instrument issues are these?
o: New issues of shares or bonds
Money-market repo transactions
Routine foreign exchange dealing
Secondary trading in listed gilts
Exchange-traded fund redemptions
w: Price stabilisation activities are associated with new issues of securities such as shares or bonds to ensure orderly markets.

n.3: Stabilisation attaches to new issues, not ordinary secondary gilt trading.
n.2: FX dealing is not the context for price stabilisation.
n.4: ETF redemptions are not price-stabilisation activity.
n.1: Repo transactions are not stabilisation of a new issue.

q: A market maker must continue quoting and dealing in a stock despite holding confidential client order-flow information. Why is the market-maker defence necessary under the CJA?
o: Because they trade solely as agents for the issuing company
Because they must often deal while holding confidential order-flow information
Because they are supervised directly by the Bank of England
Because they must publish every quote they receive from clients
Because they are barred from ever holding any inside information
w: Market makers may hold confidential order flow and still need to trade; the defence ensures legitimate activity is protected from prosecution.

n.4: Market makers are not barred from holding inside information; the defence assumes they may.
n.3: There is no rule requiring publication of every client quote.
n.0: Market makers act as principals providing liquidity, not solely as issuer agents.
n.2: Market makers are supervised by the FCA, not directly by the Bank of England.

q: An investment bank running a book-build wants to rely on price stabilisation as a defence to a market abuse allegation. What condition must be satisfied for that defence to be valid?
o: It must be disclosed to the issuer's shareholders after each trade
It must be approved in advance by the issuer's external auditors
It must be carried out only on a recognised regulated exchange
It must be confined to trades below the daily average traded volume
It must follow the relevant rules and stay within permitted time periods
w: Price stabilisation is only a defence when carried out under proper rules and within specific permitted time periods.

n.1: Auditor approval is not a condition of the stabilisation defence.
n.3: There is no daily-average-volume cap governing the defence.
n.2: Stabilisation is not restricted to regulated-exchange trades only.
n.0: Per-trade shareholder disclosure is not required for the defence.

q: A compliance officer is describing the underwriters' function in the price stabilisation defence. What role do they play?
o: They may delay publishing the issue's results for a period
They may buy unlimited stock at any price after listing
They may set the final offer price without the issuer's agreement
They may make stabilising trades to support orderly markets in new issues
They may allocate shares only to their own client accounts
w: Underwriters may rely on the defence when stabilising transactions are necessary to support orderly markets in new issues.

n.2: Underwriters do not set the offer price without issuer agreement under the defence.
n.0: The defence does not allow delaying publication of results.
