n.1: Stabilisation is capped, not unlimited buying at any price.
n.4: The defence is about orderly markets, not self-favouring allocation.

q: A dealer intends to rely on the market information defence after a trade. What is a key limitation of that defence he needs to understand?
o: It requires the trades to be approved by the market operator
It applies only to trades executed on a regulated market
It does not apply where the information is in fact inside information
It covers only transactions made by authorised persons
It protects only trades below a set monetary threshold
w: The market information defence does not apply if the information used is inside information rather than legitimate market data.

n.1: The defence is not limited to regulated-market execution.
n.0: No market-operator approval is required for the defence.
n.3: The defence is not confined to authorised persons.
n.4: There is no monetary threshold limiting the market-information defence.

q: A trader relies on observed order-book supply and demand. Which example would qualify under the market information defence?
o: Trading on an unannounced change of chief executive
Trading on observed order-book supply and demand
Trading on confidential merger negotiations
Trading on a leaked draft of the annual results
Trading on advance notice of a rights issue
w: Using legitimate order book data relating to supply and demand is covered under the market information defence.

n.3: Leaked unpublished results are inside information, outside the market-information defence.
n.0: An unannounced CEO change is inside information, not legitimate market data.
n.4: Advance notice of a rights issue is inside information.
n.2: Confidential merger talks are inside information, not order-book data.

q: During a new share issue, an underwriter engages in activity aimed at supporting an orderly market. What is the purpose of recognising price stabilisation as a statutory defence?
o: To support orderly securities markets during new issues
To guarantee the issue is fully subscribed at launch
To let underwriters recover their full fees quickly
To exempt the issue from prospectus disclosure rules
To fix the secondary market price for twelve months
w: Price stabilisation is recognised to ensure new issues of securities are not destabilised by short-term volatility.

n.2: The defence is about market order, not helping underwriters recover fees.
n.1: Stabilisation does not guarantee full subscription.
n.4: It does not fix a price for a year; it operates only briefly.
n.3: It has no bearing on prospectus disclosure obligations.

q: Which statute contains the specific special defences to insider dealing?
o: FSMA 2000 Part VIII
Companies Act 2006
FCA Handbook MAR 1
CJA 1993 Schedule 1
CJA 1993 Schedule 2
w: Schedule 1 of the CJA 1993 sets out the special defences including market making, market information, and price stabilisation.

n.4: Schedule 2 lists regulated markets and securities, not the special defences.
n.0: FSMA Part VIII deals with market abuse penalties, not CJA insider-dealing defences.
n.2: MAR 1 is FCA guidance on market abuse, not the statutory special defences.
n.1: The Companies Act 2006 does not contain the insider-dealing special defences.

q: A compliance officer is briefing staff on the operative prohibition under UK MAR. What is the effect of Article 15 in relation to market manipulation?
o: It defines the four categories of market manipulation
It permits manipulation below a de minimis threshold if promptly disclosed
It applies only to behaviour on regulated markets, not MTFs or OTFs
It requires proof of intent for any enforcement action to proceed
It prohibits engaging in or attempting to engage in market manipulation
w: Article 15 is the operative prohibition: a person must not engage in, or attempt to engage in, market manipulation. The definitional detail of what constitutes manipulation sits primarily in Article 12, but Article 15 is the rule that outlaws both completed and attempted conduct. The prohibition is technology- and venue-neutral within the scope of UK MAR, reflecting an outcomes-based approach focused on market integrity.

n.0: Article 12, not Article 15, sets out examples and forms of market manipulation. Article 15 contains the ban itself.
n.1: There is no de minimis safe harbour for manipulation under Article 15; conduct within scope is prohibited regardless of size.
n.3: The civil prohibition does not hinge on proving subjective intent where behaviour is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead the market.
n.2: UK MAR applies across instruments within scope of trading venues (including MTFs and OTFs) and related instruments, not just regulated markets.

q: A compliance officer is explaining the reach of the Article 15 prohibition. Which statement best captures its scope?
o: It applies only to on-venue trades and never to OTC dealing
It applies only to authorised firms and their approved persons
It binds any person within UK MAR's scope and also captures attempts
It applies only to shares admitted to a UK regulated market
It applies only once a profit has been made from the conduct
w: Article 15 binds “any person”, covering both natural and legal persons, and captures attempts as well as completed behaviour. The scope of UK MAR then determines which instruments and venues are in play; within that scope, the prohibition is broad and does not depend on the status of the actor or on whether a profit was achieved.

n.3: UK MAR covers more instruments and venues than shares on a regulated market.
n.1: Article 15 binds any person, not just authorised firms.
n.4: No realised profit is required for the prohibition to bite.
n.0: Within scope it can reach OTC as well as on-venue conduct.

q: A trainee is trying to understand how Articles 12 and 15 of UK MAR fit together. Which pairing correctly distinguishes the two?
o: Article 12 sets disclosure rules; Article 15 sets stabilisation rules
Article 12 covers PDMRs; Article 15 covers investment analysts
Article 12 prohibits manipulation; Article 15 defines the offences
Article 12 defines manipulation; Article 15 prohibits it and attempts
Article 12 imposes fines; Article 15 sets out criminal penalties
w: Article 12 contains the taxonomy and examples of behaviours that amount to market manipulation, while Article 15 is the operative ban that outlaws both engaging in and attempting such behaviour. This structure separates the definitional guidance from the prohibition itself.

n.2: The roles are reversed: Article 12 defines, Article 15 prohibits.
n.0: Neither article is about disclosure or stabilisation rules.
n.4: Neither article fixes fines or criminal penalties in this way.
n.1: PDMRs and analysts are dealt with under Articles 19 and 20.

q: A surveillance analyst is deciding what the Article 15 prohibition actually captures. Which of the following is caught?
o: Considering a strategy without placing or changing any orders
Publishing balanced research with all conflicts disclosed
Running a stabilisation trade under an applicable safe harbour
Holding inside information without carrying out any trade
Attempting to create a false impression of supply or demand
w: Article 15 extends to attempts to manipulate the market, which includes endeavouring to mislead the market about supply, demand or price. Contemplation alone is not captured, and separate regimes apply to research, stabilisation safe harbours and inside information duties.

n.0: Mere contemplation without any order or trade is not caught.
n.1: Balanced, conflict-disclosed research is legitimate, not manipulation.
n.2: Stabilisation within a safe harbour is permitted behaviour.
n.3: Passive holding of inside information falls under the insider-dealing regime.

q: A trader argues that his benchmark submissions cannot breach Article 15 of MAR because prosecutors could not prove he meant to mislead anyone. Which statement about intent in relation to Article 15 is most accurate?
o: Intent is irrelevant since only realised outcomes are assessed
Subjective intent to mislead must always be proven to establish a breach
Only deliberate benchmark submissions fall within its scope
Conduct likely to mislead can breach the ban even without proven intent
Recklessness is the minimum standard and negligence never suffices
w: The definitional test for manipulation (Article 12) captures behaviour that is false or misleading or likely to mislead. Article 15 then prohibits that behaviour. The regime is effects-focused, and the absence of proven subjective intent does not automatically take behaviour outside the prohibition where it is of a kind that misleads or is likely to mislead.

n.1: Proven subjective intent is not always required; the test is effects-focused.
n.4: There is no fixed recklessness-minimum rule under the definition.
n.2: The prohibition is far wider than deliberate benchmark submissions.
n.0: The regime looks at likely-to-mislead conduct, not only realised outcomes.

q: A trainee asks who falls within the personal scope of the Article 15 prohibition. Who is caught?
o: Only individuals directly employed by FCA-authorised firms
Only UK-resident persons dealing on recognised UK venues
Any person, natural or legal, within UK MAR's scope
Only directors and PDMRs of UK-listed corporate issuers
Only registered market makers and appointed primary dealers
w: Article 15 applies to "any person" and is not limited by employment status, role or domicile. The perimeter question is determined by UK MAR’s instrument and venue scope; within that perimeter, the prohibition is actor-neutral.

n.0: Article 15 is not limited to employees of authorised firms.
n.4: It is not confined to market makers or primary dealers.
n.3: It is not limited to directors and PDMRs.
n.1: Domicile does not define scope; the perimeter is the instruments and venues.

q: A compliance officer is confirming how attempts are treated under Article 15. Which statement is correct?
o: Attempted manipulation is outside UK MAR unless a trade executes
Only benchmark manipulation can be attempted under UK MAR
An attempt is caught only during the primary auction window
An attempt is prohibited only where it yields a profit
Attempted manipulation is banned even if no trade or price move results
w: Article 15 expressly captures attempts. The rule targets conduct designed to manipulate, regardless of whether an order executes, a price moves, or any profit is made. This ensures enforcement can address preparatory or abortive behaviours that threaten market integrity.

n.0: Attempts are prohibited whether or not a trade executes.
n.1: Attempts are not confined to benchmark manipulation.
n.2: There is no auction-window limitation on attempts.
n.3: An attempt is caught regardless of whether any profit arises.

q: A trader is investigated for conduct suspected of breaching the Article 15 prohibition under UK MAR. Which UK authority is primarily responsible for enforcing that prohibition?
o: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC)
Takeover Panel
Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS)
Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA)
w: The FCA is the UK’s competent authority for market abuse. It investigates and can impose civil sanctions and prohibitions for contraventions of UK MAR, including the Article 15 prohibition on market manipulation, using domestic enforcement powers.

n.4: The PRA focuses on prudential supervision; it is not the competent authority for market abuse enforcement.
n.2: The Takeover Panel administers the Takeover Code; it does not enforce UK MAR Article 15.
n.3: FOS handles individual customer complaints, not market-abuse enforcement.
n.1: HMRC is responsible for taxation, not UK MAR enforcement.

q: A trader argues their transactions should be exempt from the Article 15 manipulation ban because they conform to an accepted market practice. Which statement best reflects how Article 15 interacts with AMPs?
o: AMPs apply only to benchmark submissions and never to trading
AMPs excuse any conduct provided that it ultimately turns a profit
AMPs turn criminal manipulation into merely civil manipulation
No conduct within Article 12(1)(a) can ever escape Article 15
Conduct meeting an accepted market practice may fall outside the ban
w: Under Article 13, activity falling under Article 12(1)(a) may be outside the Article 15 prohibition where it conforms to an accepted market practice and the person can establish legitimate reasons for entering the transaction. AMPs are narrow, criteria-based carve-outs overseen by the competent authority.

n.3: Article 13 does allow AMP-conforming Article 12(1)(a) conduct to escape the ban.
n.0: AMPs are not restricted to benchmark submissions.
n.1: Profitability does not trigger an AMP; strict criteria must be met.
n.2: AMPs are carve-outs, not a device converting criminal to civil manipulation.

q: A compliance officer is defining which instruments fall within the market manipulation prohibition in Article 15 of UK MAR. Which statement correctly states the venue and instrument perimeter?
o: Only instruments where a request for admission to trading has been formally granted are within scope
Instruments admitted only to an EU regulated market fall within Article 15 scope in the UK
Only financial instruments admitted to a UK regulated market, and not those on an MTF or OTF, are within scope
Instruments are within scope only once actual trading in them has commenced on a UK venue
Instruments admitted, or requested to be admitted, to trading on UK venues, plus related instruments
w: The Article 15 prohibition applies across the UK MAR perimeter, which covers financial instruments admitted to trading or for which admission has been requested on UK venues (regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs) and certain related instruments, with additional reach to benchmarks and emission-allowance products under the regulation.

n.1: UK MAR applies to UK venues and instruments, not by reference to EU regulated markets post-onshoring.
n.2: Scope extends to instruments traded on MTFs and OTFs, not just regulated markets.
n.0: A request for admission to trading is sufficient; formal admission is not required.
n.3: Scope is triggered by admission or a request for admission, not by trading actually starting.

q: A regulatory adviser is confirming which UK instrument gives the FCA its prohibition and sanction powers where Article 15 is breached. Which is it?
o: The MiFID Organisational Regulation 2017/565
The Criminal Justice Act 1993, Part V
The FSMA 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016
The Money Laundering Regulations 2017, as amended
The Financial Services Act 2012 enforcement provisions
w: Domestic enforcement mechanics sit in UK legislation. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Market Abuse) Regulations 2016 implement and supplement UK MAR, empowering the FCA, for example, to impose prohibition orders and other sanctions for contraventions including Article 15.

n.4: The FS Act 2012 restructured the regulators; it is not the MAR enforcement instrument.
n.3: The MLR 2017 govern anti-money-laundering, not market abuse sanctions.
n.0: The MiFID Org Regulation covers firm organisation, not MAR sanctions.
n.1: CJA 1993 Part V is criminal insider dealing, not FCA MAR enforcement.

q: A compliance officer is training staff on the behaviours caught by UK MAR. What is the effect of Article 12 of UK MAR?
o: It defines forms of market manipulation
It prohibits all insider dealing
It sets penalties for criminal offences
It regulates client money protection
It establishes disclosure rules for issuers
w: Article 12 defines and illustrates the forms of behaviour that constitute market manipulation.

n.1: Insider dealing is addressed separately in UK MAR and the Criminal Justice Act, not in Article 12.
n.2: Penalties are provided through national law, not defined by Article 12 itself.
n.4: Disclosure requirements are set out in Article 17 and related provisions, not Article 12.
n.3: Client money rules are in the FCA's CASS sourcebook, not UK MAR Article 12.

q: Which activity best illustrates 'manipulating transactions' under Article 12?
o: Submitting false data to a financial benchmark
Issuing an unbalanced investment recommendation
Publishing a research report with misleading conclusions
Entering trades to give a false impression of demand
Failing to notify the market of a PDMR's dealing
w: Manipulating transactions involve placing orders or trades that create a false or misleading impression of supply, demand or price.

n.2: Misleading research is dissemination, not manipulating transactions.
n.0: False benchmark data is benchmark manipulation, a separate limb.
n.4: A missed PDMR notification is an Article 19 breach, not a manipulating transaction.
n.1: Unbalanced recommendations engage Article 20, not manipulating transactions.

q: A surveillance analyst is identifying a 'manipulating device' under Article 12. Which behaviour would qualify?
o: Using a fictitious device or contrivance to move a price
Publishing generic research without a disclaimer
Submitting false rate inputs to a benchmark like LIBOR
Failing to disclose a director's share transaction
Selectively releasing inside information to some investors
w: Manipulating devices are artificial schemes or contrivances designed to mislead the market or distort pricing.

n.4: Selective disclosure is unlawful disclosure, not a manipulating device.
n.2: False benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, a distinct limb.
n.3: Non-disclosure of a director's trade is an Article 19 breach.
n.1: Missing a research disclaimer is an Article 20 matter, not a device.

q: A trader spreads misleading rumours about a stock. Which form of manipulation under Article 12 does this fall under?
o: Manipulating transactions
Benchmark manipulation
Manipulating devices
Legitimate stabilisation measures
Dissemination
w: Dissemination covers spreading false or misleading information likely to influence prices.

n.2: Manipulating devices involve artificial schemes, not the spreading of rumours.
n.1: Benchmark manipulation involves submissions to a benchmark, not market rumours.
n.0: Manipulating transactions require actual trading activity, not information dissemination.
n.3: Legitimate stabilisation is a recognised safe harbour, not unlawful dissemination.

q: Which action best illustrates benchmark manipulation?
o: Providing false submissions to LIBOR
Spreading rumours about a takeover
Cross-trading between accounts
Publishing an unbalanced analyst report
Withholding disclosure of director trades
w: Benchmark manipulation arises when false or misleading inputs are submitted to a benchmark-setting process.

n.1: Rumours about a takeover fall under dissemination, not benchmark manipulation.
n.2: Cross-trading to mislead demand is manipulating transactions, not benchmarks.
n.4: Director trade disclosures are Article 19 duties, not benchmark manipulation.
n.3: Unbalanced analyst reports breach Article 20, not benchmark manipulation rules.

q: A listed company repurchases its own shares within a recognised safe harbour and asks whether this risks a manipulation finding. Under Article 9, which behaviour is treated as legitimate?
o: Releasing false takeover announcements to the market
Withholding notice of a PDMR's transactions
Submitting incorrect data to a pricing benchmark
Placing wash trades to move a share price
Carrying out share buy-backs under a safe harbour
w: Article 9 allows recognised legitimate behaviour such as buy-backs conducted under safe harbour conditions.

n.0: False takeover announcements are manipulation, not legitimate behaviour.
n.2: Incorrect benchmark data is manipulation, not permitted conduct.
n.1: Withholding PDMR notice breaches Article 19.
n.3: Wash trades are a classic manipulating transaction.

q: A compliance officer is explaining the point of accepted market practices under Article 13. What is their purpose?
o: To set out where conduct is not treated as manipulation
To fix the penalties imposed for insider dealing
To exempt firms from prudential capital requirements
To set the reporting deadlines for PDMR dealings
To require conflict disclosures in investment research
w: Article 13 defines accepted market practices that allow certain conduct to fall outside the prohibition when conditions are met.

n.1: Article 13 does not set insider-dealing penalties.
n.3: PDMR deadlines are set by Article 19, not Article 13.
n.4: Research conflict disclosure is governed by Article 20.
n.2: Article 13 has nothing to do with capital requirements.

q: A director who is a PDMR is reviewing their duties under Article 19. Which obligation does it impose on them?
o: Report their transactions promptly
Publish investment research annually
Disclose client orders transparently
Avoid benchmark submissions
Approve corporate buy-back programmes
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify the issuer and competent authority of their own transactions promptly.

n.3: Benchmark submissions are not covered by Article 19, which focuses on PDMR disclosures.
n.1: Investment research is governed by Article 20, not Article 19.
n.4: Buy-back programmes are addressed by stabilisation provisions, not PDMR obligations.
n.2: Client order disclosures are covered under COBS, not Article 19.

q: A PDMR has just dealt in the issuer's shares. Under Article 19, who must they notify of the transaction?
o: Only the company's legal department
Both the issuer and the FCA
Both the PRA and HM Treasury
Only the firm's auditors
Only their immediate line manager
w: PDMRs must notify both the issuer and the FCA of transactions in the issuer's shares or related instruments.

n.3: Auditors are not the recipients of PDMR notifications under Article 19.
n.4: Line managers are not designated recipients under Article 19.
n.0: The legal department is not the competent authority specified under Article 19.
n.2: The PRA and Treasury are not the required authorities for Article 19 notifications.

q: An analyst is publishing an investment recommendation subject to Article 20 of MAR. What does that article require?
o: Report stabilisation trades weekly
Publish PDMR dealings
Register safe harbours with FCA
Submit benchmark contributions
Disclose conflicts of interest
w: Article 20 requires those providing investment recommendations to disclose any conflicts of interest clearly.

n.3: Benchmark contributions are covered by Article 12 and 15, not Article 20.
n.1: PDMR dealings are Article 19 duties, not Article 20.
n.2: Safe harbours apply under Article 5, not Article 20 recommendations.
n.0: Reporting stabilisation trades is separate and not an Article 20 obligation.

q: A trading desk is reviewing several activities against the market manipulation prohibition. Which conduct is least likely to breach Article 15 when carried out strictly within a published safe harbour?
o: Price stabilisation meeting all the Article 5 conditions
Spreading takeover rumours across social media
Cross trades arranged to fix the closing price
Layering large visible orders and then cancelling
Feeding false inputs into a market benchmark
w: Stabilisation within the Article 5 safe harbour is legitimate behaviour and therefore outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.2: Fixing closing prices via cross trades is manipulation.
n.3: Layering and cancelling is a manipulating transaction.
n.1: Spreading rumours is dissemination-based manipulation.
n.4: False benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation.

q: The FCA is deciding whether a particular trading behaviour should be recognised as an Accepted Market Practice. Under Article 13, how are such practices established?
o: By issuers through their market disclosures
By investment banks under syndicate agreements
By the competent authority applying the Article 13 criteria
By industry trade bodies through voluntary codes
By trading venues within their membership rules
w: Accepted Market Practices must be established by the competent authority against the specific criteria in Article 13.

n.3: AMPs are set by the competent authority, not voluntary trade codes.
n.0: Issuer disclosures do not establish AMPs.
n.4: Venue membership rules do not establish AMPs.
n.1: Syndicate agreements cannot create an AMP.

q: Surveillance flags a trader who repeatedly posts large visible buy orders and then pulls them just before execution. Which Article 12 behaviour does this best describe?
o: Crossing orders internally to cut trading fees
Placing visible orders to mislead, then cancelling them
Failing to report a director's share dealing
Feeding incorrect inputs into a benchmark
Publishing an over-optimistic research note
w: Layering involves placing orders to create a false impression of depth or demand and then cancelling to move price.

n.4: An optimistic research note is not layering.
n.3: Incorrect benchmark inputs are benchmark manipulation, not layering.
n.0: Internal crossing to cut fees is not layering.
n.2: A missed director-dealing report is an Article 19 breach.

q: A director's spouse buys shares in the company where the director serves as a PDMR. Under Article 19 of MAR, which statement about the notification obligations is correct?
o: Notifications are due only after the financial year-end
Persons closely associated with PDMRs must also notify dealings
The issuer automatically reports on the PDMR's behalf
Only shares held directly by a PDMR are reportable
Notifications are needed only where a profit arises
w: Article 19 extends notification duties to persons closely associated with PDMRs as well as the PDMRs themselves.

n.3: Reporting is not limited to directly held shares.
n.0: Notifications are due promptly, not only after year-end.
n.2: PDMRs must notify themselves; the issuer does not do it automatically.
n.4: Notification duty does not depend on a profit arising.

q: A trader posts false information likely to move prices. How does Article 12 treat such dissemination?
o: As legitimate where it comes from anonymous posts
As acceptable if it carries a written disclaimer
As acceptable if no trade follows the statement
As market manipulation where it is likely to affect prices
As acceptable if it is retracted within 24 hours
w: Dissemination of false or misleading information that is likely to influence prices constitutes market manipulation.

n.4: A later retraction does not cure the dissemination offence.
n.1: A disclaimer does not make misleading dissemination lawful.
n.0: An anonymous source does not legitimise misleading information.
n.2: Manipulation does not require a following trade.

q: A market surveillance analyst is classifying suspected abuse and must separate 'manipulating devices' from 'manipulating transactions'. Which statement best distinguishes the two?
o: Devices need benchmarks; transactions need spread rumours
Devices need issuer consent; transactions need venue consent
Devices require a profit; transactions require a loss
Devices are lawful while transactions are always unlawful
Devices use artifices; transactions rely on orders or trades
w: Manipulating devices involve artifices or contrivances, whereas manipulating transactions involve orders or trades that mislead supply, demand, or price.

n.0: Neither limb is defined by benchmarks or rumours in that way.
n.3: Manipulating devices are not lawful; both limbs are prohibited.
n.1: Neither limb turns on issuer or venue consent.
n.2: Neither limb requires a specific profit or loss.

q: An issuer enters a liquidity contract with a broker to support trading in its own shares. In which situation might this fall outside the Article 15 market manipulation prohibition?
o: When carried out under an accepted market practice
When performed by a broker outside the UK
When executed off-venue outside market hours
When any profits are donated to charity
When disclosed only to professional clients
w: Execution under a competent authority-recognised accepted market practice can place a liquidity contract outside the Article 15 prohibition.

n.1: A foreign broker does not place a contract outside Article 15.
n.3: Donating profits does not legitimise the conduct.
n.4: Limiting disclosure to professionals is irrelevant.
n.2: Off-venue after-hours execution does not create an exemption.

q: A research analyst is preparing an investment recommendation for publication. Under Article 20 of MAR, what obligation applies to the producer?
o: Guarantee they are free of any conflict of interest
Keep records that support the basis of the recommendation
Disclose the names of all clients consulted
Publish only recommendations with a positive rating
Submit each draft to the issuer for review
w: Producers must keep adequate records supporting the recommendation and comply with fair presentation and conflict disclosure duties.

n.2: There is no duty to name all clients consulted.
n.4: Drafts need not be submitted to the issuer for review.
n.0: Conflicts must be disclosed, not guaranteed absent.
n.3: Recommendations need not be limited to positive ratings.

q: A firm arranges OTC trades designed to mislead prices on a venue. Which off-venue behaviour can still breach Article 15?
o: Holding issuer shares for the long term
Silent observation of order-book movements
Internal model back-testing with historical data
OTC trades designed to mislead prices on a venue
Private investment club discussions about macroeconomics
w: OTC conduct intended to mislead venue pricing may constitute manipulation because UK MAR focuses on effects on in-scope instruments.

n.4: General macro discussions are not manipulative, whereas misleading OTC trades can be.
n.2: Back-testing is internal analysis, while misleading trading behaviour targets market perception.
n.1: Observation alone is not manipulative, whereas deceptive OTC trading is.
n.0: Passive holding is not manipulative, whereas deceptive trading is.

q: Which activity is recognised as legitimate behaviour under Article 9 of UK MAR?
o: Publishing biased research without disclosing conflicts
Running a stabilisation programme within the set conditions
Failing to notify a director's share dealing
Submitting inaccurate interest-rate benchmark data
Spreading misleading takeover rumours to lift trading
w: Article 9 recognises stabilisation conducted within specified conditions as legitimate behaviour outside the scope of manipulation.

n.4: Spreading misleading rumours is manipulation.
n.3: Inaccurate benchmark data is benchmark manipulation.
n.2: A missed director-dealing notification breaches Article 19.
n.0: Biased, non-disclosed research breaches Article 20.

q: A compliance officer is explaining why Article 9 permits stabilisation activities when conditions are met. Why are they allowed?
o: They exempt issuers from the insider dealing rules
They guarantee a trading profit for market makers
They remove the issuer's disclosure obligations
They lower the firm's regulatory capital requirements
They support orderly markets without misleading investors
w: Stabilisation is permitted because it supports orderly markets without misleading investors when carried out under Article 9 conditions.

n.1: Stabilisation guarantees no profit to market makers.
n.2: It does not remove disclosure obligations.
n.0: It gives no relief from insider-dealing rules.
n.3: It has no bearing on capital requirements.

q: The FCA is considering whether to approve an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13. Which factor must it consider?
o: The firm’s marketing strategies
The impact on market integrity
The firm’s profitability targets
The political views of the issuer
The nationality of shareholders
w: Article 13 requires the authority to consider whether the practice upholds market integrity before recognition as accepted.

n.2: Profitability targets are irrelevant, while market integrity is central.
n.3: Political views are not relevant criteria for AMPs.
n.4: Shareholder nationality is not considered in approving AMPs.
n.0: Marketing strategies are not a recognised criterion for AMPs.

q: A trading desk asks its compliance officer which of its activities could still be lawful under an Accepted Market Practice even though it influences price. Which is an example of such permitted conduct?
o: Disseminating false information about an issuer
Directors concealing their share purchases
Submitting fabricated commodity benchmark data
Liquidity-provision arrangements accepted by the FCA as an AMP
Publishing recommendations without stating conflicts
w: Liquidity provision arrangements recognised as AMPs can be lawful even if they influence price, as long as conditions are met.

n.0: Disseminating false information is manipulation, not an AMP.
n.2: Fabricated benchmark data is manipulation.
n.1: Concealing share purchases breaches Article 19.
n.4: Undisclosed-conflict recommendations breach Article 20.

q: A trader relies on an Accepted Market Practice to justify a pattern of trading questioned by the regulator. How must the participant demonstrate compliance when relying on an AMP?
o: By evidencing the trades were entered for legitimate reasons
By ensuring every trade produces a profit
By recording the nationality of all its clients
By filing daily trade reports to HM Treasury
By securing the issuer's consent before every trade
w: To rely on an AMP, the participant must show transactions were for legitimate purposes consistent with the approved practice.

n.4: Issuer consent is not the test for relying on an AMP.
n.3: No daily HM Treasury reporting is required.
n.1: Producing a profit is not a condition of the AMP.
n.2: Recording client nationality is not the AMP requirement.

q: A trading venue is assessing whether a practice can be recognised as an Accepted Market Practice under Article 13. Which of the following is NOT a recognition criterion?
o: Potential to damage market confidence
Consistency with trading venue rules
Profitability of market participants
Degree of impact on market liquidity
Degree of transparency provided to the market
w: Profitability is not a recognition criterion, whereas transparency, liquidity, and confidence are factors under Article 13.

n.0: Potential damage to market confidence is explicitly assessed under Article 13.
n.4: Transparency is a required factor in recognising AMPs.
n.1: Consistency with venue rules is considered when approving AMPs.
n.3: Impact on liquidity is considered when assessing AMPs.

q: A compliance analyst is briefing colleagues on why the FCA publishes each Accepted Market Practice it recognises under Article 13. What is the main reason for publication?
o: So auditors can verify benchmark submissions
So issuers may avoid disclosing PDMR transactions
So firms can lower their capital requirements
So participants know the conditions for permitted conduct
So employees can bypass the insider dealing rules
w: Publication ensures transparency, allowing market participants to understand which behaviours are permitted under Article 13.

n.1: Publication does not let issuers avoid PDMR disclosure.
n.0: It is not about auditors verifying benchmarks.
n.2: It has no effect on capital requirements.
n.4: It does not allow bypassing insider-dealing rules.

q: A listed company plans a share buy-back and its adviser checks whether the trades count as legitimate behaviour under Article 9. Which of the following would qualify?
o: Submitting fictitious commodity data to move prices
Concealing director dealings from the regulator
Issuing investment advice without disclosing conflicts
Executing buy-backs in line with the safe harbour rules
Spreading false rumours about a planned merger
w: Buy-backs executed within the Article 5 safe harbour are recognised by Article 9 as legitimate behaviour.

n.4: Spreading false merger rumours is manipulation.
n.0: Fictitious commodity data is benchmark/price manipulation.
n.1: Concealing director dealings breaches Article 19.
n.2: Undisclosed-conflict advice breaches Article 20.

q: A compliance trainer is contrasting Article 9 legitimate behaviour with Article 13 accepted market practices for new staff. What is the main distinction between them?
o: Article 9 exempts all trades; Article 13 exempts only dividends
Article 9 sets the penalties; Article 13 defines insider dealing
Article 9 needs FCA approval; Article 13 needs issuer approval
Article 9 applies only to benchmarks; Article 13 only to PDMRs
Article 9 sets specific safe harbours; Article 13 needs authority recognition
w: Article 9 defines specific safe harbours, while Article 13 requires the competent authority to recognise practices as accepted.

n.1: Article 9 does not set penalties, nor does Article 13 define insider dealing.
n.2: Article 9 safe harbours need no FCA case-by-case approval; issuer approval is irrelevant.
n.3: Neither article is limited to benchmarks or PDMRs.
n.0: Neither article gives a blanket exemption for all trades or dividends.

q: An MLRO reviewing MAR notes that regulators keep Accepted Market Practices confined to narrow circumstances. What is a key reason for this restriction?
o: To maximise the profitability of regulated firms
To replace national prudential capital rules
To encourage more frequent insider trading
To remove the need to disclose PDMR dealings
To avoid undermining the prohibition on manipulation
w: AMPs are narrowly defined to ensure they do not undermine the broad prohibition against market manipulation.

n.0: AMPs are not designed to boost firm profitability.
n.3: They do not remove PDMR disclosure duties.
n.2: They are not intended to facilitate insider trading.
n.1: They do not replace prudential capital rules.

q: A director of a listed issuer buys shares in the company and asks compliance whom they must notify under Article 19 of MAR. Who must be told?
o: Both the issuer and the FCA
Only the Prudential Regulation Authority
Only the company's auditors
Only the company’s legal counsel
Only their immediate manager
w: Article 19 requires PDMRs to notify both the issuer and the FCA of their transactions in issuer securities.

n.2: Auditors are not the designated recipients under Article 19; the issuer and FCA are.
n.4: Immediate managers are not notified under Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.3: Company legal counsel is not specified in Article 19, unlike the issuer and FCA.
n.1: The PRA is not the competent authority for MAR disclosures; the FCA is.

q: A director of a listed company buys shares in her own firm and must report it under Article 19 of UK MAR. Within what timeframe must this PDMR notify the transaction?
o: Within one month
Only after profits are realised
By the next annual report
By the end of the quarter
Within three business days
w: Article 19 requires notifications to be made within three business days of the transaction.

n.0: One month exceeds the three-day requirement under Article 19.
n.3: Quarterly reporting would be too late; Article 19 requires three days.
n.2: Annual report timing is far beyond the prescribed three-day deadline.
n.1: Profit realisation is irrelevant; notification is based on transaction timing.

q: A director's dealings in her employer's listed shares are being tracked for notification purposes. Which threshold triggers the requirement for PDMRs to notify their transactions?
o: Exceeding €50,000 in a single trade
Exceeding €1 million in total holdings
Exceeding €5,000 in a calendar year
Exceeding €500 per transaction
Exceeding 5% shareholding in the issuer
w: Article 19 sets a de minimis threshold of €5,000 per calendar year before PDMRs must notify transactions.

n.0: The threshold is not €50,000 per trade; Article 19 specifies €5,000 per year.
n.3: €500 is too low; Article 19 sets the threshold at €5,000 annually.
n.1: Total holdings are not the basis; it is annual transaction value.
n.4: Shareholding percentage is unrelated; the rule is based on transaction value.

q: A listed issuer's company secretary is briefing directors on who else must notify their dealings in the company's shares. Under Article 19, which category of persons must also notify?
o: Persons closely associated with PDMRs
Only investment analysts covering the issuer
Only major shareholders above 3%
Only external auditors of the issuer
Only FCA-approved senior managers
w: Article 19 extends the notification requirement to persons closely associated with PDMRs.

n.3: Auditors are not covered; Article 19 refers to PDMRs and their closely associated persons.
n.1: Analysts are not obligated under Article 19, unlike PCAs.
n.2: Shareholding thresholds do not trigger Article 19 duties; transaction value does.
n.4: Senior managers are covered only if they are PDMRs or PCAs.

q: A director at a listed issuer buys shares in the company and asks compliance which of their dealings must be reported under Article 19 of UK MAR. Which transactions are reportable?
o: Dealings only in the issuer's debt securities
Dealings in commodities unrelated to the issuer
Dealings in the shares of competitor companies
Dealings in the issuer's shares, debt and related derivatives
Dealings in any securities anywhere in the world
w: Article 19 requires reporting of transactions in issuer shares, debt, and related derivatives.

n.4: Reporting is confined to the issuer's own instruments, not all securities.
n.0: It covers shares and derivatives too, not debt alone.
n.2: Competitor shares are not within the issuer's PDMR reporting.
n.1: Unrelated commodities are outside Article 19.

q: A compliance officer is explaining to the board why PDMR disclosures under Article 19 matter. What is their main purpose?
o: They exempt issuers from other disclosure duties
They boost transparency and deter abuse by senior insiders
They reduce the firm's FCA capital requirements
They replace duties under the Prospectus Regulation
They guarantee the issuer meets its profit targets
w: PDMR disclosures enhance transparency and help deter insider abuse by showing transactions of senior insiders.

n.0: PDMR disclosure does not relieve other disclosure duties.
n.2: It has no effect on capital requirements.
n.4: It cannot guarantee profit targets.
n.3: It does not replace Prospectus Regulation duties.

q: An issuer's company secretary receives a PDMR transaction notification and asks what the firm must now do under Article 19. What is required?
o: Publicly disclose the information within the set deadline
Forward it to the PRA for a prudential review
Record it only in the internal board minutes
Send it solely to the company's registrar
Report it once a year in the issuer's accounts
w: Issuers must publish PDMR transaction information promptly within the deadline to maintain market transparency.

n.1: The issuer must publish it, not send it to the PRA for review.
n.2: Internal minutes do not satisfy the public-disclosure duty.
n.3: Sending it only to the registrar is not public disclosure.
n.4: It must be published promptly, not annually in the accounts.

q: A firm is deciding which of its people count as PDMRs for MAR purposes. How does Article 19 define a Person Discharging Managerial Responsibilities?
o: Those with regular access to inside information and power to take management decisions
External consultants engaged to provide advice to the board
The external auditors appointed to sign off the annual accounts
All registered shareholders holding stock in the company
Any employee of the issuer, irrespective of their seniority or role
w: Article 19 defines PDMRs as those with regular access to inside information and decision-making power.

n.4: A PDMR is defined by managerial responsibility, not by being any employee.
n.3: Ordinary shareholders are not PDMRs by virtue of their holding.
n.1: Advisory consultants are not PDMRs unless they meet the managerial test.
n.2: Auditors are not PDMRs of the issuer.

q: A director of a listed issuer enters a derivative transaction and the firm must assess PDMR reporting obligations. Which type of derivative transaction must be reported?
o: Interest-rate swaps not referencing the issuer
Options or swaps linked to the issuer's shares
Currency derivatives unrelated to the issuer
Derivatives written on a competitor's shares
Commodity futures with no link to the issuer
w: Derivatives linked to issuer securities fall within Article 19 and must be reported.

n.2: Unrelated currency derivatives are outside Article 19.
n.4: Commodity futures with no issuer link are not reportable.
n.3: Derivatives on a competitor's shares are outside scope.
n.0: Swaps not referencing the issuer are not reportable.

q: A senior manager at an issuer forgets to report a share purchase within the Article 19 deadline. What consequence may follow?
o: Automatic cancellation of all their shareholdings
Regulatory sanctions for breaching disclosure obligations
Automatic removal of the PDMR from the board
Automatic exemption from insider dealing liability
Loss of the firm's capital requirement reliefs
w: Non-compliance with Article 19 may result in regulatory sanctions for breaching disclosure obligations.

n.0: Non-compliance does not cancel shareholdings automatically.
n.3: It does not grant any insider-dealing exemption.
n.4: It does not trigger loss of capital reliefs.
n.2: There is no automatic board removal for a breach.

q: A research analyst is preparing an investment recommendation for publication and checks the Article 20 requirements. What is a primary obligation when issuing it?
o: Ensure only positive recommendations are released
Submit drafts to the issuer for approval
Guarantee accuracy of future price movements
Report recommendations directly to HM Treasury
Disclose any material interests or conflicts
w: Article 20 requires disclosure of material interests or conflicts when investment recommendations are issued.

n.2: Future accuracy cannot be guaranteed; Article 20 requires disclosure of conflicts instead.
n.1: Issuer approval is not required; independence and disclosure are essential.
n.0: Recommendations must be fair and balanced, not only positive.
n.3: Article 20 does not require reporting recommendations to HM Treasury.

q: A compliance reviewer is checking that a firm's research note is fairly presented under Article 20. Which requirement helps ensure this?
o: Distinguishing clearly between fact and opinion
Providing issuer pre-clearance before publication
Guaranteeing profit for all investors
Reporting directly to the FCA before release
Excluding any negative analysis
w: Article 20 requires recommendations to clearly separate fact from opinion to ensure fairness.

n.2: Guaranteeing profit is impossible and not required; clarity is required instead.
n.4: Excluding negatives would bias the analysis; fairness requires balance.
n.1: Issuer pre-clearance is not mandated; independence is required.
n.3: Pre-release submission to the FCA is not required; fair presentation is.

q: A firm publishes investment recommendations to clients and must comply with the disclosure rules. Why must it disclose the methodologies it used?
o: To meet the firm's capital adequacy requirements
To exempt the firm from its Article 19 duties
To satisfy shareholders' profitability targets
To reduce the need for a statutory audit
To let readers assess the basis of the recommendation
w: Article 20 requires methodology disclosure so readers can assess how the recommendation was formed.

n.0: Methodology disclosure is unrelated to capital adequacy.
n.2: It is not about shareholder profitability targets.
n.1: It gives no relief from Article 19 duties.
n.3: It does not reduce statutory audit requirements.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing analysts' conduct for possible Article 20 breaches. Which of the following would breach the obligations?
o: Keeping records that substantiate the recommendation made
Openly disclosing every conflict of interest in the report
Publishing research without disclosing the analyst's holding in the issuer
Clearly separating statements of fact from opinion in a note
Using transparent, disclosed methods to reach the conclusion
w: Failure to disclose analyst shareholdings is a breach of Article 20 disclosure obligations.

n.3: Separating fact from opinion is required good practice, not a breach.
n.1: Openly disclosing conflicts complies with Article 20.
n.0: Keeping substantiating records complies with Article 20.
n.4: Using transparent, disclosed methods complies, it is not a breach.

q: A firm that produces investment recommendations is setting its record-keeping policy under Article 20. Which duty applies?
o: Keep sufficient records to substantiate the recommendation
Destroy the supporting documents once published
Keep only oral explanations given to clients
Rely solely on issuer data without any notes
Send all records quarterly to HM Treasury
w: Article 20 requires keeping adequate records to substantiate the recommendation and demonstrate fair presentation.

n.2: Oral explanations alone do not meet the record-keeping duty.
n.3: Relying on issuer data without notes fails the duty.
n.1: Records must be retained, not destroyed after publication.
n.4: There is no quarterly HM Treasury filing requirement.

q: A paraplanner is asked how Article 20 promotes transparency in the research notes their firm publishes. How is this achieved?
o: By requiring disclosure of conflicts, interests and methodology
By guaranteeing the issuer's future performance
By requiring FCA pre-approval of every research note
By requiring disclosure of every shareholder's identity
By restricting recommendations to authorised firms only
w: Transparency is achieved by requiring disclosure of conflicts, interests, and methodologies behind recommendations.

n.2: No FCA pre-approval of each research note is required.
n.4: Article 20 is not limited to authorised firms.
n.1: It cannot guarantee future issuer performance.
n.3: It does not require disclosing every shareholder's identity.

q: A firm's in-house analyst is about to have an investment recommendation published through a national newspaper. Which obligation applies when investment recommendations are disseminated via the media in this way?
o: They require the issuer's clearance before broadcast
They need disclosures only where they are positive
They must guarantee a profit if widely shared
They must carry the same disclosures as formal reports
They fall outside the Article 20 requirements entirely
w: Media-distributed recommendations must meet the same disclosure and fair presentation requirements as formal reports.

n.4: Media recommendations are not outside Article 20.
n.1: Disclosure is required regardless of a positive rating.
n.2: No profit can or need be guaranteed.
n.0: Issuer clearance before broadcast is not required.

q: An adviser wonders why analysts must disclose conflicts when issuing recommendations under Article 20. Why are these disclosures essential?
o: They shield analysts from insider dealing liability
They help investors judge potential bias in the analysis
They guarantee the accuracy of the predictions
They remove the need for market disclosures
They meet the firm's capital adequacy standards
w: Conflict disclosures allow investors to understand potential bias and make informed decisions.

n.0: Conflict disclosure gives no shield from insider-dealing liability.
n.2: It cannot guarantee the accuracy of predictions.
n.4: It is unrelated to capital adequacy standards.
n.3: It does not remove other market disclosure duties.

q: An analyst is writing an investment recommendation for publication to clients. Under Article 20, what must be avoided when issuing it?
o: Balanced analysis covering risks and benefits
Selective presentation designed to mislead
Clear disclosure of methodologies used
Open declaration of analyst shareholdings
Separation of fact and opinion in reports
w: Selective or misleading presentation violates Article 20, which requires fair and balanced analysis.

n.2: Disclosure of methodologies supports transparency and is required.
n.3: Declaration of shareholdings is mandatory for conflict transparency.
n.0: Balanced analysis is the goal of Article 20, not a breach.
n.4: Separation of fact and opinion ensures clarity, not a violation.

q: A freelance market commentator, not employed by any authorised firm, regularly posts buy and sell recommendations online and asks whether Article 20 of MAR applies to him. Which statement best reflects the scope of Article 20 obligations?
o: They apply only to sell-side analysts at investment banks
They apply only to formally published equity research notes
They apply to anyone producing or disseminating recommendations
They apply only to firms authorised and regulated by the FCA
They apply only where the recommendation carries a positive rating
w: Article 20 applies to any person producing or disseminating investment recommendations, not just authorised firms or analysts.

n.3: Article 20 is not confined to authorised firms.
n.0: It is not limited to sell-side analysts.
n.4: It applies regardless of a positive rating.
n.1: It is not restricted to equity research.

q: An MLRO is training staff on the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and asks how the Act defines criminal property. Which is correct?
o: Any property used in financial markets
Any benefit derived from criminal conduct
Property owned by a convicted individual
Property transferred between family members
Assets disclosed to the National Crime Agency
w: Criminal property is defined as any benefit derived from criminal conduct, regardless of who holds it.

n.0: Property used in financial markets is not automatically criminal without connection to crime, unlike benefits from criminal conduct.
n.2: Property owned by a convicted individual is not necessarily criminal unless it results from crime.
n.3: Transfers between family members are not criminal unless sourced from criminal conduct.
n.4: Assets disclosed to the NCA are not criminal by definition; they must originate from crime.

q: A compliance officer is checking who has the power to specify what amounts to 'relevant criminal conduct' under POCA 2002. Who holds this power?
o: The Crown Prosecution Service
The High Court
The Secretary of State
The Financial Conduct Authority
The Serious Fraud Office
w: The Secretary of State has statutory authority to specify what conduct is relevant for money laundering purposes.

n.0: The CPS prosecutes but does not define what constitutes relevant criminal conduct.
n.3: The FCA regulates financial firms but cannot determine statutory definitions of criminal conduct.
n.4: The SFO investigates serious fraud but does not define relevant criminal conduct.
n.1: The High Court interprets law but does not hold power to define relevant criminal conduct.

q: A new adviser asks their MLRO how money laundering is best described under POCA 2002. Which statement is correct?
o: Concealing or disguising the origins of criminal property
Moving money legitimately across UK borders
Any cash transaction above ten thousand pounds
Buying real estate through a licensed broker
Investing company profits into overseas markets
w: Money laundering involves concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removing criminal property to obscure its illicit origin.

n.4: Investing legitimate profits abroad is not money laundering.
n.1: Lawfully moving money across borders is not laundering.
n.2: A large cash transaction is not laundering by itself.
n.3: Buying property through a broker is not inherently laundering.

q: During induction training, a new analyst asks the MLRO how broadly the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 reaches in terms of the offences it covers. What is the correct explanation of its scope?
o: It applies only to organised crime groups
It applies only to cross-border money movements
It applies only to drug-trafficking offences
It applies only to financial services offences
It applies to all crimes that generate criminal property
w: POCA applies to all crimes that generate criminal property, not just specific categories like drugs or fraud.

n.2: POCA is an all-crimes regime, not just drug trafficking.
n.3: It is not confined to financial services offences.
n.0: It is not limited to organised crime groups.
n.1: It is not limited to cross-border money movements.

q: A compliance analyst is defining terms for an AML policy and needs the label for conduct that is an offence in the UK, or would be if committed here. Which term applies?
o: Relevant criminal conduct
Criminal transaction
Suspicious financial activity
Predicate offence
Unlawful benefit conduct
w: Relevant criminal conduct is behaviour that is an offence in the UK or would be if carried out there.

n.4: Unlawful benefit conduct is not a statutory term within POCA.
n.2: Suspicious activity is a reporting trigger, not the legal definition.
n.3: Predicate offence is used internationally but POCA uses 'relevant criminal conduct'.
n.1: Criminal transaction is descriptive but not the statutory term under POCA.

q: An MLRO is assessing whether funds moved through several conversions still fall within POCA. What must the property retain to remain within POCA's definition of criminal property?
o: It must have crossed a national border
It must be held in the form of cash
It must be deposited in a UK bank account
It must be worth more than one thousand pounds
It must still represent a benefit from crime
w: Property remains criminal if it continues to represent the benefit of criminal conduct, regardless of form or value.

n.1: Criminal property need not be cash; any form counts.
n.0: It need not have crossed a border.
n.3: There is no minimum value for criminal property.
n.2: It need not be held in a UK bank.

q: An MLRO reviews a client's affairs and considers which activity would be criminal conduct under POCA 2002. Which of the following qualifies?
o: Investing in a regulated pension fund
Receiving a lawful inheritance
Tax evasion by a UK resident
Holding cash savings in a bank account
Purchasing listed shares on the LSE
w: Tax evasion is an offence and therefore constitutes criminal conduct under POCA 2002.

n.0: Pension investments are lawful and not criminal conduct.
n.1: Inheritance is legitimate property unless obtained by fraud.
n.3: Holding cash savings is lawful unless funds are from crime.
n.4: Buying listed shares is lawful unless connected to criminal funds.

q: During a POCA training session, an adviser asks the MLRO how widely the phrase 'benefit from criminal conduct' should be understood when identifying proceeds. Which description is correct?
o: It is limited to direct cash gains
It covers all forms of property obtained
It is limited to corporate crime proceeds
It applies solely to tangible assets
It refers only to profits hidden offshore
w: Benefit from criminal conduct covers all forms of property obtained, whether direct or indirect, tangible or intangible.

n.0: Cash is included, but the definition covers all property types.
n.4: Offshore concealment is laundering but not the definition itself.
n.3: Intangible benefits like rights or claims also qualify as property.
n.2: Corporate proceeds are included, but the scope extends to all crime.

q: A prosecutor is considering a money laundering charge against a firm's employee under POCA 2002. Which element is essential to establish the offence?
o: The involvement of two or more offenders
A suspicion that the property is criminal
A single transaction above five thousand pounds
A prior FCA enforcement notice against the firm
The use of an overseas bank account
w: A suspicion that property is criminal is sufficient to establish the offence under POCA 2002.

n.2: No monetary threshold is needed to establish the offence.
n.3: A prior FCA notice is not an element of the offence.
n.4: Use of an overseas account is not a required element.
n.0: Multiple offenders are not needed for the offence.

q: A trainee compliance officer asks how 'criminal conduct' is defined under POCA 2002. Which statement is correct?
o: Conduct reported to the National Crime Agency
Conduct resulting in imprisonment over six months
Conduct committed only outside the UK
Conduct restricted to financial services offences
Conduct constituting an offence in the UK
w: Criminal conduct includes any conduct that constitutes an offence in the UK, regardless of severity.

n.1: There is no minimum sentence threshold in the definition.
n.2: Conduct outside the UK is relevant only if it would be an offence in the UK.
n.3: Financial services offences are included, but definition is broader.
n.0: Reports to the NCA are separate obligations, not the definition of criminal conduct.

q: A firm's AML induction asks staff to name the act of disguising the origin of criminally obtained assets. Which phrase describes it?
o: Market manipulation
Regulatory arbitrage
Capital gains
Money laundering
Tax avoidance
w: Money laundering involves disguising the origin of assets derived from criminal conduct to make them appear legitimate.

n.4: Tax avoidance is legal planning, unlike laundering which conceals criminal origins.
n.0: Market manipulation distorts prices but is not the concealment of criminal assets.
n.2: Capital gains are lawful profits, not criminal property concealment.
n.1: Regulatory arbitrage exploits rules but is not concealment of criminal property.

q: An adviser asks whether a small benefit from crime falls outside POCA 2002. How does the Act treat low-value benefits?
o: They must involve cross-border transfer
They qualify as criminal property
They are excluded unless repeated
They are excluded if under £500
They must be cash-based to qualify
w: Any benefit from criminal conduct, regardless of value, qualifies as criminal property under POCA 2002.

n.3: No monetary threshold excludes benefits from being criminal property.
n.2: Single low-value acts can still create criminal property.
n.0: Cross-border transfer is not required for property to be criminal.
n.4: Cash is not necessary; any form of property can qualify.

q: A compliance officer is applying the test for whether an asset is 'criminal property' under POCA. What is the primary legal test?
o: Whether the property is registered with authorities
Whether the property is a benefit from criminal conduct
Whether the property is tangible and movable
Whether the property is traded internationally
Whether the property has a market value
w: Criminal property is defined by its connection to crime, being a benefit obtained through criminal conduct.

n.4: Having market value does not make property criminal.
n.0: Registration status is irrelevant to the test.
n.2: Being tangible or movable is not the test.
n.3: International trading is not the defining test.

q: An MLRO submits a suspicious activity report under POCA 2002 about a client's transactions. Which authority is responsible for investigating that report?
o: Financial Conduct Authority
Bank of England
Serious Fraud Office
National Crime Agency
Prudential Regulation Authority
w: Suspicious activity reports under POCA 2002 are investigated by the National Crime Agency.

n.0: The FCA regulates firms but does not investigate laundering suspicions.
n.4: The PRA oversees prudential issues, not laundering cases.
n.2: The SFO investigates fraud, but laundering reports go to the NCA.
n.1: The Bank of England has no investigative role under POCA.

q: An MLRO is explaining to new staff why 'relevant criminal conduct' is central to money laundering law. Why is the concept important?
o: It lays out the required audit procedures
It sets the transaction reporting thresholds
It limits cross-border cooperation between states
It specifies the maximum penalties available
It defines which criminal conduct is covered
w: Relevant criminal conduct defines which offences generate criminal property subject to laundering controls.

n.1: POCA has no monetary reporting threshold set by this concept.
n.0: It is not about audit procedures.
n.3: It does not specify maximum penalties.
n.2: It does not limit cross-border cooperation.

q: An MLRO is deciding whether an asset held by a client counts as criminal property under POCA 2002. What does the Act require to establish the link between that property and criminal conduct?
o: The property must be physically marked or tagged
The property must be kept within the UK
The property must still represent a benefit from crime
The property must be hidden in an offshore account
The property must be worth over ten thousand pounds
w: Criminal property must represent the benefit of criminal conduct, regardless of form, location or value.

n.0: Property need not be physically marked to be criminal.
n.1: It need not be kept in the UK.
n.4: There is no minimum value requirement.
n.3: It need not be hidden offshore.

q: An MLRO is training staff on what counts as criminal property under POCA 2002. Which of the following would NOT be criminal property?
o: Cash obtained through tax evasion
A lawful inheritance from a deceased relative
Assets gained from insider dealing
Money obtained through fraud
Profits made from drug trafficking
w: A lawful inheritance is not criminal property, as it does not derive from criminal conduct.

n.0: Cash from tax evasion is criminal property, so it does not answer 'not'.
n.4: Drug-trafficking profits are criminal property.
n.2: Insider-dealing gains are criminal property.
n.3: Proceeds of fraud are criminal property.

q: An MLRO is explaining to staff what qualifies as 'criminal conduct' under POCA. What is the key defining feature?
o: It must involve corporate entities
It must exceed £1 million
It must be an offence in UK law
It must be indictable only
It requires international conspiracy
w: Criminal conduct is defined as any conduct that constitutes an offence under UK law, regardless of severity.

n.4: International conspiracy is not required; any offence suffices.
n.3: It includes summary and indictable offences alike.
n.0: It applies to individuals as well as companies.
n.1: There is no financial threshold for criminal conduct.

q: A compliance officer is briefing the board on how the scope of money laundering offences can change. How may the Secretary of State alter that scope?
o: By publishing binding case-law precedents
By amending the FCA's published guidance
By determining what counts as relevant criminal conduct
By granting exemptions to individual firms
By setting monetary reporting thresholds
w: The Secretary of State has authority to determine relevant criminal conduct, shaping the scope of laundering offences.

n.1: The scope is not altered by amending FCA guidance.
n.0: Case law is made by courts, not by the Secretary of State.
n.4: Scope is not changed by setting monetary thresholds.
n.3: Individual firm exemptions do not shape the offence's scope.

q: An MLRO is giving examples of the three stages of money laundering to new staff. Which of the following best illustrates money laundering under POCA?
o: Paying declared dividends to shareholders
Withdrawing cash for lawful purchases
Saving wages in a deposit account
Placing criminal funds into banks
Delaying tax payments by two months
w: Money laundering often begins by placing criminally derived funds into the banking system to disguise their origin.

n.4: Late tax payments may be unlawful but do not conceal criminal proceeds.
n.1: Withdrawing cash for lawful purchases is not laundering.
n.2: Legitimate savings are not laundering, as their origin is legal.
n.0: Declared dividends are lawful distributions, not concealment of criminal proceeds.

q: Which legislation provides the primary framework for criminal offences of money laundering in the UK?
o: Money Laundering Regulations 2017
Financial Services Act 2012
Senior Managers and Certification Regime
Companies Act 2006
Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
w: The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 is the main statute creating money laundering offences in the UK.

n.1: The Financial Services Act 2012 focuses on regulatory structure, not primary laundering offences.
n.0: MLR 2017 sets preventive measures but POCA defines laundering crimes.
n.2: SMCR regulates conduct and accountability, not laundering offences.
n.3: The Companies Act 2006 governs corporate law, not laundering offences.

q: Which Act amended POCA to strengthen investigative powers for tackling organised crime?
o: The Financial Services Act 2012 reforms
The Criminal Justice Act 1993, Part V
The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 itself
Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005
The Terrorism Act 2000 provisions
w: The Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005 expanded investigative and confiscation powers under POCA.

n.0: The FS Act 2012 restructured the regulators; it did not expand POCA powers.
n.1: CJA 1993 concerns insider dealing, not POCA investigative powers.
n.2: POCA cannot be the Act that amended POCA.
n.4: The Terrorism Act 2000 addresses terrorist finance, not POCA amendments.

q: A firm is documenting which rules govern its customer due diligence and fund-transfer duties. Which UK regulations implement the EU requirements in this area?
o: Money Laundering Regulations 2017
Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls
Financial Services Compensation Scheme
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group Guidance
Banking Act 2009
w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 implement EU directives on due diligence and fund transfer requirements.

n.3: The JMLSG Guidance interprets obligations but is not law itself.
n.1: SYSC covers management systems, not EU fund transfer rules.
n.2: The FSCS covers compensation for customers, not laundering rules.
n.4: The Banking Act 2009 focuses on bank stability, not laundering regulations.

q: A newly appointed MLRO wants to know which FCA sourcebook makes senior management responsible for AML systems. Which sourcebook is it?
o: The Prudential sourcebook for investment firms
The Supervision manual's reporting provisions
The Training and Competence sourcebook (TC)
Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls
The Conduct of Business sourcebook (COBS)
w: SYSC sets requirements for senior management to establish and maintain effective systems to prevent financial crime.

n.2: TC covers competence of staff, not AML systems responsibility.
n.0: The prudential sourcebook covers capital, not AML systems.
n.4: COBS covers dealing with customers, not AML senior-management duties.
n.1: SUP covers supervision processes, not the AML systems requirement.

q: A firm updating its AML procedures wants the industry guidance it should follow when interpreting money laundering obligations in practice. Which body issues that guidance?
o: The House of Commons Treasury Committee
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group
The Financial Ombudsman Service
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Serious Fraud Office
w: The Joint Money Laundering Steering Group provides industry guidance on how firms should apply AML laws and regulations.

n.2: The Ombudsman resolves disputes; it does not issue AML interpretive guidance.
n.3: The PRA sets prudential rules, not the industry AML guidance firms follow.
n.0: A parliamentary committee does not issue firms' AML guidance.
n.4: The SFO investigates fraud; it does not issue the JMLSG-style guidance.

q: A compliance officer is mapping how the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 sit alongside POCA. How do the two interact?
o: They create a parallel set of criminal offences
They apply only to overseas transactions
They replace POCA's offences completely
They shield senior managers from all liability
They impose preventive obligations on firms
w: MLR 2017 impose preventive requirements such as customer due diligence, complementing POCA’s criminal offences.

n.2: MLR 2017 supplement POCA; they do not replace its offences.
n.0: They set preventive duties rather than parallel criminal offences.
n.1: They are not confined to overseas transactions.
n.3: They do not shield senior managers from liability.

q: A new compliance analyst at an investment firm asks how the FCA Financial Crime Guide fits into the wider AML regime. What is the main role of that Guide?
o: To issue asset confiscation orders
To set out practical AML expectations for firms
To amend retained EU directives directly
To define the statutory criminal offences
To enforce criminal convictions in court
w: The Financial Crime Guide sets FCA expectations and good practice examples for firms to combat money laundering and related crime.

n.3: Offences are defined by POCA, not the Financial Crime Guide.
n.4: The Guide does not enforce convictions; courts do.
n.2: It does not amend directives.
n.0: It does not issue confiscation orders.

q: A compliance analyst is reviewing the AML legislative timeline and asks what the Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005 introduced. What did it bring in?
o: Transaction reporting duties
Customer due diligence requirements
Civil recovery powers
Regulated activity definitions
Senior management accountability
w: SOCPA 2005 introduced civil recovery powers, allowing confiscation of criminal property without conviction.

n.1: Due diligence duties were set out in later regulations, not SOCPA.
n.4: Senior management accountability is defined under SYSC, not SOCPA.
n.0: Transaction reporting arises under other FCA rules, not SOCPA.
n.3: Definitions of regulated activities come from FSMA, not SOCPA.

q: A firm's AML manual references both SYSC and the JMLSG Guidance, and a trainee asks what links them. Which element connects the two?
o: Both set out confiscation procedures
Both require court approval
Both are legally binding criminal statutes
Both deal exclusively with terrorist financing
Both provide expectations for AML systems
w: SYSC imposes management obligations and JMLSG Guidance provides interpretation, both guiding firms on AML systems.

n.2: Only POCA is a statute; SYSC and JMLSG are not criminal laws.
n.0: Confiscation is handled under POCA, not SYSC or JMLSG.
n.1: Neither requires court approval to apply to firms.
n.3: Both cover money laundering broadly, not only terrorist financing.

q: A compliance officer is summarising how POCA, MLR 2017 and SYSC fit together for the board. Which statement best describes their interaction?
o: All three impose identical customer due diligence rules
POCA sets offences, MLR the preventive duties, SYSC governance
POCA becomes optional wherever SYSC governance applies
MLR 2017 replaces both the POCA offences and SYSC
SYSC sets the penalties while MLR and POCA only give guidance
w: POCA establishes laundering offences, MLR 2017 sets preventive compliance duties, and SYSC allocates responsibility to senior management.

n.0: The three instruments have distinct roles, not identical due-diligence rules.
n.4: SYSC does not set penalties; POCA sets offences, not mere guidance.
n.3: MLR 2017 does not replace POCA or SYSC.
n.2: POCA offences are never optional.

q: Which legislation requires firms to apply customer due diligence and maintain records to prevent money laundering?
o: Companies Act 2006
Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005
Money Laundering Regulations 2017
Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
Senior Managers and Certification Regime
w: The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 require customer due diligence, ongoing monitoring, and record-keeping by regulated firms.

n.3: POCA creates criminal offences but does not prescribe CDD procedures.
n.1: SOCPA extends investigative powers, not CDD obligations.
n.4: SMCR governs accountability but not CDD rules.
n.0: The Companies Act 2006 relates to company law, not AML requirements.

q: An MLRO wants the source that gives practical industry interpretation of AML laws and regulations. Which document provides this?
o: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group Guidance
Money Laundering Regulations 2017
Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls
Financial Crime Guide
w: The JMLSG Guidance helps firms apply AML laws effectively in practice through industry interpretation.

n.4: The Financial Crime Guide provides FCA expectations, but JMLSG is the main industry interpretation.
n.0: POCA is legislation, not guidance.
n.2: MLR 2017 impose obligations but do not interpret them.
n.3: SYSC sets governance requirements but not industry guidance.

q: A newly appointed MLRO wants FCA material giving worked examples of good practice to strengthen the firm's anti-money-laundering controls. Which FCA publication provides this?
o: Companies Act Guidance
Basel Principles
Financial Crime Guide
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group Guidance
UK Corporate Governance Code
w: The FCA Financial Crime Guide gives examples of good practice to help firms prevent financial crime.

n.0: The Companies Act Guidance relates to company law, not AML practice.
n.3: The JMLSG Guidance interprets AML law, not FCA good practice examples.
n.4: The UK Corporate Governance Code relates to board structures, not AML.
n.1: The Basel Principles are international standards, not FCA good practice.

q: A compliance trainer explains how SOCPA 2005 fits into the UK's money laundering framework. What did that Act add?
o: Civil recovery powers and enhanced disclosure duties
The risk-based approach requirements
Client money segregation requirements
Cross-border payment reporting rules
Customer due diligence monetary thresholds
w: SOCPA 2005 introduced civil recovery powers and enhanced disclosure obligations within the AML framework.

n.4: CDD thresholds sit in the MLR, not SOCPA 2005.
n.2: Client-money segregation is a CASS matter, not SOCPA.
n.1: The risk-based approach is an MLR feature.
n.3: Payment reporting rules are not what SOCPA added.

q: A trainee at a compliance consultancy asks how POCA and the MLR 2017 fit together in the UK AML framework. Which of these best describes the relationship between them?
o: Both set identical reporting standards
POCA sets the offences; MLR impose compliance duties
POCA gives guidance while MLR enforce it
MLR 2017 repealed POCA in its entirety
Both are simply FCA guidance documents
w: POCA establishes criminal offences, while MLR 2017 impose compliance obligations to prevent laundering.

n.0: They do not set identical reporting standards.
n.2: POCA sets offences, not guidance; MLR do not enforce POCA.
n.4: Both are legislation, not FCA guidance documents.
n.3: MLR 2017 did not repeal POCA.

q: A compliance officer is explaining how SYSC supports the firm's AML regime. What is SYSC's main AML function within the FCA Handbook?
o: It defines the money laundering offences
It sets customer due diligence standards
It issues asset confiscation orders
It imposes governance and systems responsibilities
It provides the industry AML guidance
w: SYSC requires firms to allocate responsibility, establish controls, and ensure governance for AML compliance.

n.0: Offences are defined by POCA, not SYSC.
n.1: CDD standards are set by the MLR, not SYSC.
n.4: Industry AML guidance is the JMLSG's role.
n.2: SYSC does not issue confiscation orders.

q: A firm is embedding a risk-based approach to customer due diligence and asks which regulation mandates it. Which one applies?
o: SYSC
SOCPA 2005
MLR 2017
Bribery Act 2010
POCA 2002
w: MLR 2017 require firms to adopt a risk-based approach to due diligence and monitoring of clients.

n.4: POCA defines offences but does not mandate risk-based CDD.
n.1: SOCPA extended investigative powers, not risk-based CDD duties.
n.0: SYSC requires governance, not detailed CDD rules.
n.3: The Bribery Act deals with corruption, not AML due diligence.

q: A new compliance analyst is mapping the UK AML framework and asks which source is influential but not legally binding. Which is it?
o: The Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
The Serious Organised Crime and Police Act 2005
The Money Laundering Regulations 2017
The SYSC sourcebook rules
Joint Money Laundering Steering Group Guidance
w: The JMLSG Guidance is non-binding but influential in demonstrating compliance with AML obligations.
