n.1: It does not exist to help boards frustrate bids.

Owning an employee identity card for the firm
Holding call options that may deliver voting rights

n.0: Advisory panel membership is not an interest in shares.
n.3: An employee ID card confers no interest in shares.

n.4: Options over target shares are relevant securities.

q: In a single purchase, a shareholder passes through several DTR thresholds at once. How must disclosure be made?
o: Only the highest threshold crossed needs to be disclosed
The shareholder may wait until reaching the 10% level
All thresholds crossed must be disclosed in a single notification
Only the initial 3% threshold needs to be reported
Disclosure is needed only if the issuer requests it
w: All thresholds crossed must be reported to ensure the market receives a full picture of holdings after the transaction.

n.0: Disclosing only the highest threshold is insufficient.
n.3: Reporting only the 3% level is insufficient.
n.1: The shareholder cannot wait until 10%.
n.4: Disclosure is mandatory, not dependent on issuer request.

q: A major shareholder crosses a notifiable threshold but does not disclose it on time. What is the consequence of this failure to make timely disclosure?
o: The FCA may impose sanctions and the market may be misled
The issuer's financial statements become invalid
The company secretary is personally fined instead
The shareholder is automatically barred from voting
The shareholder must pay tax on the holding twice
w: Failure to disclose can mislead the market, and the FCA has the power to impose sanctions or penalties.

n.3: There is no automatic voting bar for late disclosure.
n.1: Financial statements are not invalidated by this.
n.4: There is no double taxation consequence.
n.2: The company secretary is not fined in the shareholder's place.

q: A shareholder crossing a DTR threshold must notify both the issuer and the FCA. Why are both required to be informed?
o: To let HR oversee employee shareholdings
To reduce duplication in the firm's tax reporting
So both the company and the regulator can act promptly
To give auditors extra evidence for the accounts
To meet marketing requirements towards investors
w: Informing both ensures transparency: the company alerts the market and the FCA monitors compliance.

n.1: It is not about reducing tax reporting duplication.
n.3: It is not to supply auditors with evidence.
n.0: It is not for HR oversight of shareholdings.
n.4: It is not a marketing requirement.

q: A listed company receives a notification of a major shareholding from an investor. What does the issuer typically do after receiving the disclosure?
o: Record it solely within the annual accounts
Keep it private until a regulator requests it
Ignore it unless the holding exceeds 25%
Send it only to the internal HR department
Issue a public regulatory announcement to the market
w: Issuers must publish a regulatory announcement so that all market participants are informed of the disclosure.

n.3: HR is not the recipient of such disclosures.
n.0: It must be announced, not merely put in the accounts.
n.1: It must be made public, not kept private.
n.2: It cannot be ignored below 25%.

q: A multinational investor is comparing UK major-shareholding thresholds with those in Europe. How do UK disclosure thresholds compare with most EU member states?
o: UK requires disclosure at 3%, EU often at 5%
UK requires disclosure at 10%, EU at 3%
UK and EU both require disclosure at 1%
UK has no formal disclosure threshold, unlike the EU
UK requires disclosure only for majority shareholders
w: The UK requires disclosure at 3%, whereas many EU jurisdictions set the initial threshold at 5%.

n.2: Neither the UK nor EU uses 1% as the standard threshold.
n.3: The UK does have a disclosure regime under DTR.
n.1: The UK requires disclosure at 3%, not 10%.
n.4: Disclosure applies well before majority ownership is reached.

q: An analyst comparing shareholding disclosure thresholds internationally asks which jurisdiction typically requires disclosure once 5% of voting rights is reached. Which one is it?
o: United Kingdom
United States
Japan
Australia
Switzerland
w: In the US, beneficial ownership of more than 5% must be disclosed through SEC filings.

n.0: The UK uses a 3% disclosure threshold, not 5%.
n.2: Japan’s disclosure rules differ and are generally higher.
n.4: Switzerland has a sliding scale, starting at 3%.
n.3: Australia uses different disclosure regimes under ASIC rules.

q: A compliance officer is comparing substantial shareholding disclosure thresholds across jurisdictions for a global equity fund. Which country applies a 10% disclosure threshold?
o: United Kingdom
United States
Australia
Germany
France
w: Australia requires disclosure at 10% for substantial shareholdings under its Corporations Act.

n.0: The UK threshold is 3%, not 10%.
n.4: France applies EU-based 5% disclosure rules.
n.3: Germany also follows EU directives with a 5% base.
n.1: The US requires disclosure at 5%, not 10%.

q: A firm building a US position asks which regulator requires a filing once beneficial ownership passes 5%. Which global regulator requires Schedule 13D filings at that level?
o: US Securities and Exchange Commission
Japanese Financial Services Agency
UK Financial Conduct Authority
Australian Securities and Investments Commission
Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority
w: The SEC requires Schedule 13D filings when beneficial ownership exceeds 5% in a US-listed company.

n.2: The FCA enforces DTR in the UK, not SEC rules.
n.3: ASIC operates in Australia, not the US.
n.1: Japan’s FSA sets domestic thresholds, not SEC filings.
n.4: FINMA supervises Switzerland, not US disclosure.

q: An investor building a stake in a Swiss-listed company reviews the local regime. How does Switzerland differ in its disclosure requirements?
o: It requires disclosure starting at 3% with several higher thresholds
It requires disclosure only from foreign investors
It exempts any shareholder holding below 25%
It requires disclosure only for state-owned entities
It permits holdings up to 20% without any disclosure
w: Switzerland requires disclosure beginning at 3%, with additional thresholds at 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 33%.

n.2: Switzerland does not exempt all holdings below 25%.
n.3: Disclosure is not limited to state-owned entities.
n.4: Holdings well below 20% must be disclosed.
n.1: Disclosure applies to domestic investors too.

q: A global asset manager is drafting a disclosure policy spanning several markets. Why must multinational investors be cautious about global transparency rules?
o: Because disclosure is optional everywhere outside the UK
Because disclosure rules apply only to banks
Because thresholds and timelines vary from one jurisdiction to another
Because every country applies exactly identical rules
Because auditors file the disclosures automatically
w: Multinational investors must track local laws since thresholds and deadlines differ across markets.

n.3: Countries do not apply identical rules.
n.0: Disclosure is not optional outside the UK.
n.4: Auditors do not file these disclosures automatically.
n.1: The rules are not limited to banks.

q: An analyst comparing disclosure regimes across several countries wants to identify the principle they all share. Which key principle is common across global disclosure regimes?
o: Reducing the accounting fees paid by firms
Standardising corporate tax rates across the world
Ensuring transparency of significant influence over companies
Guaranteeing that shareholders receive dividends
Limiting how many companies may list each year
w: Despite differences, all regimes aim to provide transparency on significant holdings that may influence corporate control.

n.3: Disclosure regimes do not guarantee dividends.
n.0: They do not exist to reduce accounting fees.
n.4: They do not cap the number of listings.
n.1: They do not standardise global tax rates.

q: A global asset manager is comparing major-shareholding disclosure thresholds across markets. How does Japan's disclosure requirement differ from the UK's?
o: Japan does not recognise derivative exposures
Japan typically requires disclosure at 5% rather than 3%
Japan exempts domestic investors from any disclosure
Japan requires disclosure only for government bond holdings
Japan sets its threshold at 1% of voting rights
w: Japan requires disclosure at 5%, compared to the UK’s lower 3% trigger.

n.2: Domestic investors are still required to disclose holdings.
n.4: 1% is not the Japanese disclosure threshold.
n.3: Bond holdings are not the focus of Japan’s disclosure regime.
n.0: Derivative exposures are recognised in Japanese disclosure law.

q: A fund crossing thresholds in both London and New York checks its filing deadlines. How do US disclosure timelines differ from the UK's?
o: The US requires filing immediately, the UK allows 30 days
The US requires no disclosure at all, unlike the UK
The US requires a filing at every 0.5% increment
The US allows 10 days to file, the UK requires 2 trading days
The US requires disclosure only above 25% ownership
w: US investors must file Schedule 13D within 10 days, whereas the UK requires disclosure within 2 trading days.

n.0: The US does not require immediate filing with a 30-day UK window.
n.1: The US does require disclosure, contrary to this claim.
n.4: US disclosure does not begin only at 25%.
n.2: The US does not require filing at every 0.5% increment.

q: A compliance head at a cross-border firm reviews its disclosure obligations worldwide. What is a major challenge for global firms given differing transparency rules?
o: Preparing detailed environmental impact reports
Ensuring faster processing of the company payroll
Setting appropriate bonus targets for directors
Avoiding the payment of any corporation tax
Maintaining systems that track multiple disclosure regimes
w: Firms must build systems to monitor global thresholds and timescales to stay compliant in multiple jurisdictions.

n.3: The challenge is not about avoiding corporation tax.
n.1: It is not about payroll processing speed.
n.0: It is not about environmental impact reports.
n.2: It is not about setting director bonus targets.

q: The company secretary of a listed firm suspects an undisclosed party is building a stake through nominees. Which power under Section 793 of the Companies Act 2006 could the company use to address this?
o: To require disclosure of who is interested in the company's shares
To cancel existing shareholder agreements at will
To amend the Articles without any resolution
To remove directors without shareholder approval
To block dividends payable to minority shareholders
w: Section 793 allows companies to demand information about persons with an interest in their shares, aiding transparency.

n.1: Section 793 does not let a company cancel shareholder agreements.
n.2: It does not permit amending the Articles without a resolution.
n.3: It does not allow removing directors without approval.
n.4: It does not authorise blocking minority dividends.

q: A shareholder in a listed company receives a formal notice from the company under Section 793 and asks his adviser what he is now obliged to do. What must a shareholder do if served with a Section 793 notice?
o: Provide details of interests in the shares within the specified period
File a petition with the High Court in response
Attend a compulsory general meeting of members
Disclose their personal annual tax return
Transfer the shares back to the company
w: A Section 793 notice compels the shareholder to provide details of interests in shares within the required timeframe.

n.1: No court petition is required in response to the notice.
n.3: The notice does not require a personal tax return.
n.4: It does not require transferring shares back.
n.2: It does not compel attendance at a meeting.

q: A listed company's board suspects an undisclosed party is building a stake through nominees and wants to use its Companies Act powers to investigate. Under Section 793 of the Companies Act 2006, who may be investigated?
o: Only the company's serving directors
Only retail shareholders holding over 10%
Only shareholders resident outside the UK
Only institutional investors in the company
Any person reasonably believed to hold an interest in the shares
w: Section 793 applies broadly to anyone reasonably suspected of holding or having an interest in shares.

n.0: Section 793 is not limited to directors.
n.3: It is not limited to institutional investors.
n.1: It is not limited to holders above 10%.
n.2: It is not limited to overseas shareholders.

q: A shareholder ignores a company's Section 793 notice requesting details of their interest. What enforcement action can the company take?
o: Strike the shareholder off the register without process
Levy capital gains tax penalties on the holding
Impose a criminal fine on the shareholder directly
Restrict the shares' rights, such as voting or dividend rights
Terminate the shareholder's employment contract
w: Companies can impose restrictions on shares, including suspending voting rights and withholding dividends, until compliance.

n.2: The company itself cannot impose a criminal fine.
n.4: It cannot terminate an employment contract for this.
n.0: It cannot remove a member from the register without due process.
n.1: It cannot levy capital gains tax penalties.

q: A director asks the company secretary why the firm has powers under Section 793 of the Companies Act 2006. What is the rationale behind them?
o: To let small companies avoid shareholder meetings
To simplify the company's annual audit requirements
To allow boards to raise executive pay levels
To harmonise accounting standards across the world
To promote transparency and prevent hidden control of companies
w: The aim is to prevent undisclosed control or concert parties by requiring disclosure of share interests.

n.1: The power is not about simplifying audits.
n.2: It does not exist to raise executive pay.
n.3: It is unrelated to harmonising accounting standards.
n.0: It does not let companies avoid meetings.

q: A listed company serves a Section 793 notice on a shareholder to establish who has an interest in its shares. How quickly must the shareholder normally respond?
o: By the end of the company's next financial year
Within the period the company specifies, typically a few days
Within six months of receiving the request
Only when the annual accounts are being prepared
Only after a dividend has been declared
w: The company sets the response time, often a few days, and the shareholder must comply within that period.

n.0: The response is not tied to the next financial year end.
n.2: Six months is far longer than the notice usually allows.
n.3: It is not tied to accounts preparation.
n.4: It is not conditional on a dividend being declared.

q: A listed company suspects shares are being held on its behalf through nominees. What can it seek to uncover by issuing a Section 793 notice?
o: The ultimate beneficial owners of shares held via nominees
The tax residency of institutional investors
The insurance cover held by each shareholder
The personal bank account details of the directors
The employment contracts held by shareholders
w: Section 793 powers are often used to identify beneficial owners behind nominee holdings.

n.3: It does not reveal directors' personal bank details.
n.1: It is not aimed at investors' tax residency.
n.2: It does not uncover shareholders' insurance cover.
n.4: It does not reveal shareholders' employment contracts.

q: A shareholder repeatedly refuses to respond to Section 793 notices. Which sanction is commonly applied for that persistent non-compliance?
o: Automatic criminal conviction
Termination of the shareholder’s board seat
Suspension of voting and dividend rights
Exemption from takeover regulation
Deregistration of the company
w: If a shareholder fails to comply, companies may restrict rights such as voting and dividend entitlements until information is provided.

n.0: Criminal convictions are not imposed directly by companies.
n.4: Deregistration of a company is unrelated to Section 793.
n.1: Board seats cannot be terminated through Section 793 notices.
n.3: Takeover regulations remain in force regardless of Section 793.

q: During a bid, a company uses Section 793 to investigate its share register. How does Section 793 support the operation of the Takeover Code?
o: By enforcing bank capital adequacy standards
By setting the corporate governance codes
By regulating the directors' remuneration policies
By prescribing the format of accounting disclosures
By revealing hidden parties acting in concert through shareholdings
w: The power to investigate share interests helps identify parties acting in concert, supporting transparency in takeovers.

n.2: It does not regulate directors' remuneration.
n.0: It does not enforce capital adequacy standards.
n.1: It does not set corporate governance codes.
n.3: It does not prescribe accounting disclosure formats.

q: A compliance officer explains to a client why Section 793 powers exist for the benefit of shareholders. What is the key investor protection purpose?
o: Guaranteeing dividends are paid regardless of profits
Allowing directors to bypass shareholder approval
Ensuring shareholders know who holds significant influence in the company
Requiring the company to subsidise shareholders' tax bills
Exempting institutional investors from disclosure rules
w: Section 793 helps ensure shareholders and the market know who exercises influence, protecting against hidden control.

n.0: Section 793 does not guarantee dividends.
n.3: It does not require subsidising shareholders' tax.
n.1: It does not let directors bypass approval.
n.4: It does not exempt institutional investors.

q: A firm's operations team is checking whether a completed trade must be reported. Under UK MiFIR, what is a reportable transaction?
o: Only trades made between retail clients and their banks
Any informal verbal agreement to trade at a later date
Any executed trade in an instrument admitted to a UK trading venue
Only transactions carried out in government bonds
Only trades settled through overseas clearing houses
w: A reportable transaction includes any executed trade in a financial instrument admitted to trading on a UK trading venue.

n.0: Reportable transactions are not limited to retail-bank trades.
n.4: It is not limited to overseas-settled trades.
n.1: An informal verbal agreement is not an executed trade.
n.3: Reporting is not limited to government bonds.

q: A broker executes a share deal on behalf of a retail client. Under UK MiFIR, which entity is primarily responsible for submitting the transaction report?
o: The FCA, which receives the reports
The company registrar of the issuer
The retail client who places the order
The issuer of the security being traded
The investment firm that executes the transaction
w: The executing investment firm is responsible for submitting transaction reports to the FCA under MiFIR requirements.

n.2: The retail client is not responsible for reporting.
n.3: The issuer does not submit transaction reports.
n.1: The registrar has no reporting duty here.
n.0: The FCA receives, but does not submit, the reports.

q: A compliance officer is scoping which instruments generate transaction reports at the firm. Which financial instruments are typically in scope?
o: Only shares in the FTSE 100 constituent companies
Only unlisted private equity investments
Equities, bonds, derivatives and other instruments admitted to trading
Only bonds issued by the UK government
Only structured products sold to retail clients
w: Equities, bonds, derivatives, and other instruments admitted to trading on regulated venues are reportable under UK MiFIR.

n.0: Scope is not limited to FTSE 100 shares.
n.3: It is not limited to UK government bonds.
n.4: It is not limited to retail structured products.
n.1: Unlisted private equity is generally not the focus of scope.

q: A trainee asks why the firm submits transaction reports to the FCA at all. Under FCA and MiFIR rules, what is the primary purpose of transaction reporting?
o: To produce newsletters for the firm's shareholders
To calculate the corporation tax that firms owe
To give regulators data with which to detect market abuse
To generate marketing insights for the firm
To replace disclosures in the financial statements
w: Transaction reporting provides regulators with granular data to monitor markets and detect market abuse.

n.1: Reporting is not for calculating corporation tax.
n.3: It is not a source of marketing insight.
n.0: It is not for shareholder newsletters.
n.4: It does not replace financial statement disclosures.

q: A firm is building the data fields for its MiFIR transaction reports. Which of the following details is NOT normally required in such a report?
o: Date and time of execution
Identity of buyer and seller (where required)
Marketing expenses linked to the transaction
Instrument identification (ISIN)
Price and quantity of the trade
w: Reports must include ISIN, price, quantity, time, and counterparties, but marketing costs are irrelevant.

n.3: ISINs are mandatory identifiers in MiFIR reporting.
n.4: Price and quantity are core reporting fields.
n.0: Execution date and time must be reported.
n.1: Counterparty details are required in many cases.

q: A trading desk manager is explaining the two distinct reporting duties under UK MiFIR to a graduate. How does trade reporting differ from transaction reporting?
o: Trade reporting covers tax; transaction reporting covers dividends
Trade reporting fully replaces the firm's financial accounting
Trade reporting is for retail clients; transaction reporting for institutions
Trade reporting is annual; transaction reporting is quarterly
Trade reporting informs the market; transaction reporting informs regulators
w: Trade reporting is market-facing for transparency, while transaction reporting is regulatory-facing for oversight.

n.2: The split is not by retail versus institutional clients.
n.3: Neither is filed on an annual or quarterly cycle in that way.
n.0: Neither reporting type is about tax or dividends.
n.1: Trade reporting does not replace financial accounting.

q: A broker-dealer's operations team is finalising where its daily MiFIR transaction reports must be sent. To which UK regulator should these reports be submitted?
o: The Prudential Regulation Authority
HM Treasury
The Bank of England
The Competition and Markets Authority
The Financial Conduct Authority
w: The FCA is the UK regulator that receives MiFIR transaction reports for monitoring markets and detecting abuse.

n.0: The PRA focuses on prudential supervision, not transaction reporting.
n.2: The Bank of England oversees monetary policy, not MiFIR reports.
n.3: The CMA enforces competition law, not transaction reporting.
n.1: HM Treasury sets policy but does not receive reports.

q: A brokerage executes a large equity trade for a client on Tuesday afternoon. Under MiFIR, by when must the firm generally submit the transaction report?
o: By the close of business on the same trading day
No later than the close of the next working day
Within fifteen minutes of the trade being executed
By the end of the month the trade occurred in
Within five working days of the transaction date
w: Firms must report transactions no later than the close of the next working day to ensure timely regulatory oversight.

n.0: T+1 applies, not same-day; reports are due by close of the next working day.
n.2: Near-real-time (minutes) is trade (public) reporting, not transaction reporting.
n.3: Monthly reporting is not permitted; the deadline is the next working day.
n.4: Five days is too long; the deadline is the following working day.

q: A trading desk is deciding which of its recent deals must be transaction reported to the FCA. Which of the following is a reportable transaction?
o: A physical commodity bought for immediate spot delivery
A cash deposit placed into a client savings account
A retail mortgage advance made to a banking customer
A derivative trade executed on a UK regulated market
A spot FX deal settled purely for commercial purposes
w: Derivative trades executed on regulated markets are reportable under FCA and MiFIR rules.

n.4: Spot FX is not a MiFID financial instrument, so it is not reportable.
n.1: A bank deposit is not a financial-instrument transaction under MiFIR.
n.0: Spot physical commodity purchases fall outside MiFIR transaction reporting.
n.2: Mortgage lending is not a reportable financial-instrument transaction.

q: A firm's reporting system has been submitting inaccurate transaction reports for several weeks before anyone noticed. What is the regulatory risk of this failure?
o: A statutory increase in the firm's corporation tax rate
Personal criminal liability imposed on every one of the firm's shareholders
Immediate loss of the firm's FCA authorisation to operate
Regulatory fines and a greater risk of undetected market abuse
Automatic suspension of the firm's stock exchange listing
w: Failure to report accurately risks sanctions and undermines regulators’ ability to detect and prevent market abuse.

n.4: Reporting failures do not automatically suspend a listing; they draw FCA fines.
n.2: Authorisation is not lost immediately; the FCA imposes sanctions and fines.
n.0: Reporting breaches do not change a firm's corporation tax rate.
n.1: Shareholders are not personally criminally liable for the firm's reporting.

q: A compliance officer explains to a graduate why the firm must submit transaction reports under UK MiFIR. What is the main purpose of that reporting?
o: To calculate the stamp duty owed on each securities trade
To supply the market with real-time pre-trade price quotes
To publish executed prices to all participants in the market
To give regulators data to detect and monitor market abuse
To register beneficial share ownership at Companies House
w: Transaction reporting gives regulators granular data to detect market abuse and insider dealing.

n.1: Pre-trade quotes are a transparency duty, not the purpose of transaction reporting.
n.0: Transaction reporting is not used to compute stamp duty.
n.2: Publishing executed prices is trade reporting to the market, not to regulators.
n.4: Beneficial ownership registration is separate from MiFIR transaction reporting.

q: A broker executes a client order in a MiFIR-reportable instrument on a trading venue, with a custodian settling the trade. Which entity must submit the transaction report to the FCA?
o: The investment firm that executes the transaction
The issuer of the financial instrument traded
The retail client who initiated the original order
The custodian bank that settles the transaction
The trading venue on which the order was matched
w: The executing firm has the obligation to submit reports to the FCA under MiFIR.

n.2: Clients do not submit transaction reports; the executing firm does.
n.4: The venue reports only for non-MiFIR members; the executing firm is responsible.
n.3: Settlement custodians have no transaction-reporting duty under MiFIR.
n.1: The instrument's issuer has no obligation to report others' trades.

q: An operations analyst is building a MiFIR transaction report for an executed trade. Which information must it contain?
o: The firm's projected profit and loss on the position
The settlement bank's fees and custody charges applied
The instrument's expected dividend, coupon and future redemption schedule
The client's credit score, income and employment status
Instrument identifier, price, quantity, date and the counterparties
w: Reports must include ISIN, trade details, and counterparties to give regulators oversight of market activity.

n.3: Credit scores and employment details are not transaction-report fields.
n.0: Projected profit and loss is not part of a transaction report.
n.1: Custody fees and charges are not reported in transaction reports.
n.2: Expected dividends or coupons are not required transaction-report data.

q: A firm executes a reportable trade and must file its MiFIR transaction report. By when must the report be submitted?
o: By the close of the next working day
Within 30 days of the trade
At the end of the financial year
Immediately after dividend declaration
At the next AGM
w: MiFIR requires transaction reports to be submitted by the close of the following working day.

n.2: Year-end reporting is far too late for oversight.
n.1: 30 days would not meet timely regulatory needs.
n.4: AGMs are unrelated to reporting obligations.
n.3: Dividend declarations are not linked to MiFIR reporting.

q: A trading firm has executed a batch of equity transactions and must submit its MiFIR transaction reports to the correct UK authority. Which regulator receives UK MiFIR transaction reports?
o: Companies House
The Financial Conduct Authority
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Bank of England
The Competition and Markets Authority
w: The FCA is the designated UK regulator for MiFIR transaction reports.

n.2: The PRA supervises prudential issues, not MiFIR reporting.
n.0: Companies House records company data, not trade data.
n.3: The Bank of England focuses on monetary policy, not transaction reports.
n.4: The CMA enforces competition law, not MiFIR reporting.

q: A firm discovers its transaction reports contain persistent inaccuracies. What is the regulatory risk of failing to report transactions accurately?
o: Automatic delisting of the firm from the stock exchange
Forfeiture of the firm's entire regulatory capital buffer
A mandatory rise in both the firm's corporation tax and VAT bills
FCA sanctions and a weakened ability to detect market abuse
Loss of limited liability protection for the firm's board
w: Failure to report accurately undermines market surveillance and exposes firms to fines and sanctions.

n.0: Reporting failures do not automatically delist a firm; the FCA fines it.
n.2: Tax bills are unaffected by transaction-reporting breaches.
n.1: Capital buffers are not forfeited for reporting failures.
n.4: Limited liability is unaffected by a firm's reporting breaches.

q: A compliance officer is determining which of the desk's trades are caught by the reporting rules. Which trades are reportable under MiFIR?
o: Only trades cleared and settled through a UK central counterparty
Any trade in an instrument admitted to trading on a UK venue
Only trades executed between two UK-authorised banks
Only trades in shares above one million pounds in value
Only trades placed by professional, non-retail clients
w: Any trade in a financial instrument admitted to trading on a UK venue must be reported, regardless of value or counterparty.

n.3: Reportability does not depend on trade value; no monetary threshold applies.
n.2: Counterparty type is irrelevant; retail and non-bank trades are reportable too.
n.4: Retail-client trades are reportable; classification does not exempt them.
n.0: Reportability turns on admission to trading, not the settlement route.

q: An operations analyst must uniquely identify the instrument on a MiFIR transaction report. Which detail must be included for that purpose?
o: The ISIN, the International Securities Identification Number
The BIC code of the executing broker's own bank
The LEI of the firm executing the transaction
The sort code of the client's nominated bank account
The IBAN of the client's nominated securities settlement account
w: The ISIN uniquely identifies financial instruments in transaction reports.

n.2: The LEI identifies legal entities, not the financial instrument traded.
n.4: An IBAN identifies a bank account, not a security.
n.1: A BIC identifies a bank, not the instrument in the report.
n.3: A sort code identifies a bank branch, not a financial instrument.

q: An FCA surveillance team is using transaction data to spot suspicious activity. How does MiFIR transaction reporting help regulators detect insider trading?
o: By giving detailed data on trade timing, size and counterparties
By strictly capping the number of trades that any insider may execute
By forcing clients to disclose their reasons for trading
By ranking firms according to their annual trading volume
By requiring firms to publish directors' dealings each week
w: Trade data allows regulators to analyse suspicious activity patterns and detect insider trading.

n.4: Transaction reports go to the FCA, not published; that describes PDMR rules.
n.1: MiFIR sets no cap on the number of trades a person may make.
n.2: Clients are not required to state their motives for trading.
n.3: Reporting is not used to rank firms by trading volume.

q: A firm's operations team is populating the fields of a MiFIR transaction report. Which field identifies the firm responsible for executing the trade?
o: The company’s VAT number
The firm’s payroll code
The bank sort code
The director’s national insurance number
The LEI (Legal Entity Identifier)
w: The LEI uniquely identifies the firm responsible for the trade in a MiFIR transaction report.

n.0: VAT numbers are unrelated to MiFIR reports.
n.3: Directors’ personal details are not reported.
n.1: Payroll codes are internal, not regulatory identifiers.
n.2: Sort codes are for payments, not trade reports.

q: An operations analyst is asked why executed trades must be published to the market. Under UK MiFIR, what is the primary role of trade reporting?
o: To give the market pre-trade transparency on quotes
To supply regulators with confidential surveillance data
To set the official closing price of each instrument
To provide the market with post-trade transparency
To confirm settlement of trades at the central depository
w: Trade reporting ensures that the market has timely post-trade transparency, publishing price, volume, and time of execution.

n.0: Pre-trade transparency is a separate obligation; trade reporting is post-trade.
n.1: Confidential regulator surveillance is transaction reporting, not trade reporting.
n.4: Trade reporting publishes executions; it does not confirm settlement.
n.2: Trade reporting does not set official closing prices.

q: A firm's reporting team is confirming the scope of its post-trade obligations under UK MiFIR. Which types of financial instruments require trade reporting?
o: Only sterling-denominated UK government gilts and bonds
Only equities listed on the FTSE 100 and FTSE 250 indices
Equities, bonds, derivatives and other instruments traded on venues
Only instruments held by professional or institutional, non-retail investors
Only exchange-traded funds and their underlying assets
w: Trade reporting applies to all financial instruments admitted to trading on a UK venue, not just equities.

n.1: Scope is not limited to FTSE index constituents; many instruments qualify.
n.0: Reporting is not restricted to gilts; equities and derivatives are included.
n.4: Scope is far broader than ETFs; bonds and derivatives are covered.
n.3: Investor classification does not determine which instruments are reportable.

q: A dealer relies on published post-trade information before quoting a price to a client. Who benefits directly from trade reporting obligations in this way?
o: Shareholders voting at the annual general meeting
Auditors preparing the firm's statutory annual accounts
Company payroll teams processing employee wages
Market participants who rely on transparent pricing
Tax authorities collecting stamp duty on share deals
w: Market participants benefit from knowing executed trade details, ensuring fair pricing and transparency.

n.2: Payroll teams gain nothing from post-trade market data.
n.4: Stamp duty collection does not depend on trade reporting.
n.1: Statutory audits do not rely on published trade data.
n.0: AGM voting is unrelated to post-trade transparency.

q: An investment firm is setting the timing of its post-trade publication obligations. Under MiFIR, when must trades be reported to the market?
o: Only once the trade has completely settled
At the end of the calendar month of execution
As close to real time as technically possible
By the close of the next working day at the latest
Within one hour of the market's daily closing time
w: MiFIR requires trades to be reported to the market as close to real time as possible.

n.3: Next-working-day is the transaction-reporting deadline, not trade reporting.
n.4: Trade reporting is near real time, not within an hour of close.
n.1: Monthly reporting is not permitted for post-trade transparency.
n.0: Publication cannot wait for settlement; it is near real time.

q: A trader checks what information becomes public when the firm publishes a trade report under MiFIR. What detail is published?
o: The firm's inventory position after the trade
The client's classification and risk profile
The commission and fees charged to the client
The names and addresses of both counterparties
The price, volume and time of the execution
w: Trade reports publish price, volume, and execution time to inform market participants.

n.3: Counterparty identities are not published in post-trade transparency reports.
n.2: Commissions and fees are not part of a published trade report.
n.1: Client classification is not disclosed in trade reports.
n.0: A firm's inventory position is not published in trade reports.

q: A UK trading venue is unsure which body oversees its trade reporting obligations. Which regulator enforces trade reporting requirements in the UK?
o: Companies House
The Competition and Markets Authority
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Financial Conduct Authority
The Bank of England
w: The FCA enforces trade reporting obligations under MiFIR in the UK.

n.4: The Bank of England oversees monetary policy, not trade reporting.
n.2: The PRA supervises prudential standards, not trade reports.
n.0: Companies House is not responsible for market transparency.
n.1: The CMA enforces competition law, not MiFIR.

q: A compliance officer explains to new staff how post-trade publication benefits the wider market. How does trade reporting support market integrity?
o: By guaranteeing every investor a minimum trading profit
By giving all participants equal access to post-trade data
By fixing the spread allowed between the bid and offer prices
By granting large firms priority access to price data
By keeping execution prices confidential from the public
w: Trade reporting ensures fairness by giving all market participants equal access to executed trade information.

n.0: Reporting provides transparency, not guaranteed profits.
n.3: It gives equal, not priority, access; favouring large firms is the opposite aim.
n.4: Trade reporting publishes prices rather than keeping them confidential.
n.2: Reporting does not set or fix bid-offer spreads.

q: An investment firm repeatedly misses its trade reporting deadlines. What happens as a result?
o: Shareholders are stripped of voting rights
The company is deregistered at Companies House
Directors lose their pensions
The FCA may impose fines or sanctions
The firm automatically loses its listing
w: Non-compliance with trade reporting obligations can result in FCA fines and sanctions.

n.4: Listing is not automatically lost due to trade reporting breaches.
n.0: Shareholder voting rights are not revoked under MiFIR.
n.1: Companies House deregistration is unrelated to MiFIR reporting.
n.2: Director pensions are not tied to trade reporting compliance.

q: A new analyst is confused about the difference between transaction reporting and trade reporting. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
o: Transaction reports are annual; trade reports are filed monthly
Transaction reports go to the regulator; trade reports go to the market
Transaction reports are entirely optional, while trade reports remain mandatory
Transaction reports are public; trade reports stay confidential
Transaction reports cover only bonds; trade reports only shares
w: Transaction reporting is regulatory, while trade reporting is public and market-facing.

n.0: Both are near-term duties, not annual or monthly filings.
n.4: Neither is restricted by instrument type in that way.
n.2: Both transaction and trade reporting are mandatory, not optional.
n.3: This is reversed: transaction reports go to the regulator, trade reports are public.

q: An investment firm needs to make an executed OTC trade public. Which post-trade transparency obligation applies specifically to it?
o: Publishing trade details through an Approved Publication Arrangement
Sending trade details directly to Companies House
Posting trade details on the firm's own public website
Submitting trade details to a registered trade repository
Filing the trade details with an Approved Reporting Mechanism, not an APA
w: Investment firms must use Approved Publication Arrangements to publish trades for transparency.

n.4: An ARM transmits transaction reports to the FCA, not public post-trade data.
n.3: Trade repositories handle EMIR/SFTR data, not MiFIR post-trade transparency.
n.2: Post-trade data must go via an APA, not just a firm's own website.
n.1: Companies House does not receive MiFIR trade reports.

q: A regulator relies on UK EMIR data to oversee the derivatives market. What is the primary purpose of that reporting?
o: To provide pre-trade price quotes for equity markets
To set margin rates for retail spread-betting accounts
To register changes in share ownership directly with the issuer
To publish daily net asset values for investment funds
To monitor systemic risk arising in derivatives markets
w: UK EMIR reporting ensures regulators have data to monitor systemic risk arising from derivatives markets.

n.0: EMIR concerns derivatives risk, not equity pre-trade quotes.
n.1: EMIR does not set retail margin rates.
n.3: Publishing fund NAVs is unrelated to EMIR reporting.
n.2: Share ownership registration is not an EMIR function.

q: Two firms enter an OTC derivative and must comply with UK EMIR. Who must report the trade?
o: Only the financial counterparty, not the non-financial one
Both counterparties to the derivatives contract
Only the counterparty that sells the derivative
Only the party with the larger notional exposure
Only the clearing house that handles the contract
w: EMIR requires both parties to a derivative to report, ensuring accuracy and completeness of data.

n.2: Both parties report under EMIR, not only the seller.
n.4: The clearing house does not report on the parties' behalf under EMIR.
n.3: Both parties report regardless of the size of exposure.
n.0: Both financial and non-financial counterparties must report.

q: A firm has entered into a derivatives contract that falls under EMIR. Where must the resulting trade report be submitted?
o: To an Approved Publication Arrangement, or APA
To the Bank of England's markets division
To an Approved Reporting Mechanism, or ARM
To a trade repository registered with the FCA
To the London Clearing House directly
w: EMIR reports are sent to trade repositories, which are authorised to collect and maintain derivatives data.

n.0: APAs publish MiFIR trade data; EMIR reports go to trade repositories.
n.2: ARMs handle MiFIR transaction reports, not EMIR derivatives data.
n.4: A clearing house is not the EMIR reporting destination.
n.1: EMIR reports go to trade repositories, not the Bank of England.

q: Two counterparties enter a derivative contract and each submits a report to a trade repository under EMIR. Why are both parties required to report the same contract?
o: To split the reporting cost equally between them
To ensure accuracy and allow reconciliation of both sides
To double the fees earned by the trade repository
To let each party report a different set of terms
To create a data backup should either counterparty later default
w: Dual reporting enables regulators to reconcile exposures and validate data accuracy across counterparties.

n.2: Dual reporting improves data quality; it is not about repository fees.
n.3: Both must report matching terms, not differing ones.
n.0: The aim is reconciliation, not cost-sharing.
n.4: The purpose is reconciliation of data, not a default backup.

q: A firm's operations team is scoping which of its derivative trades must be reported under EMIR. Which types of contracts fall within scope?
o: Only derivatives with a UK-based counterparty
Only interest-rate and credit derivative contracts
Only centrally cleared derivative contracts
Only over-the-counter derivatives, not exchange-traded ones
Both OTC and exchange-traded derivative contracts
w: Both over-the-counter and exchange-traded derivatives are reportable under EMIR.

n.3: Exchange-traded derivatives are also in scope, not only OTC.
n.1: All asset classes of derivatives are covered, not just rates and credit.
n.0: Scope is not limited to UK-based counterparties.
n.2: Both cleared and uncleared derivatives are reportable.

q: A risk officer explains what danger EMIR reporting is chiefly designed to contain in derivatives markets. What systemic risk does it aim to reduce?
o: Counterparty credit risk within derivatives markets
Operational risk within firms' payroll systems
Liquidity risk in the government bond market
Interest-rate risk on long-term residential mortgages
Currency inflation risk faced by retail savers
w: By reporting trades, regulators can monitor and mitigate counterparty credit risk across derivatives markets.

n.4: EMIR targets counterparty risk, not consumer inflation.
n.2: EMIR addresses derivatives counterparty risk, not gilt liquidity.
n.1: Payroll operational risk is outside EMIR's purpose.
n.3: Mortgage interest-rate risk is not what EMIR addresses.

q: An operations analyst is completing an EMIR report and must identify each counterparty. Which field is crucial for that purpose?
o: The SWIFT BIC of the counterparty's custodian bank
The Companies House registration number of each firm
The VAT registration number of each party
The ISIN of the derivative being reported
The Legal Entity Identifier, or LEI, of each party
w: The LEI uniquely identifies counterparties in derivatives reporting under EMIR.

n.3: The ISIN identifies the instrument, not the counterparty.
n.0: A BIC identifies a bank, and EMIR uses the LEI for counterparties.
n.2: VAT numbers are not used to identify EMIR counterparties.
n.1: Company registration numbers are not the EMIR counterparty identifier.

q: A firm neglects its UK EMIR derivatives reporting obligations. What is the consequence?
o: The directors must resign by law
The firm is exempted from MiFIR reporting
The FCA can impose fines and sanctions
The board is dissolved immediately
The firm loses its listing automatically
w: The FCA can fine or sanction firms that fail to comply with EMIR reporting rules.

n.4: Listing is not automatically removed for EMIR failures.
n.3: Boards are not dissolved by EMIR breaches.
n.1: MiFIR reporting obligations still apply separately.
n.0: Directors are not forced to resign automatically.

q: A regulator wants a complete picture of a firm's trading by combining EMIR and MiFIR data. How does EMIR reporting complement MiFIR transaction reporting?
o: EMIR captures derivatives; MiFIR captures instruments admitted to trading
EMIR covers equities, while MiFIR covers only derivatives
EMIR applies only pre-trade, while MiFIR applies post-trade
EMIR covers retail loans, while MiFIR covers bank deposits
EMIR is purely a tax regime, whereas MiFIR is only a market-conduct regime for firms
w: EMIR focuses on derivatives reporting while MiFIR covers securities admitted to trading, giving regulators a full view of market activity.

n.1: This is reversed: EMIR covers derivatives, not equities.
n.4: Neither EMIR nor MiFIR is a tax regime.
n.2: Both regimes concern reporting, not a pre/post-trade split like this.
n.3: Neither covers retail loans or deposits.

q: A trainee asks which 2008 event exposed the opacity of derivatives markets and drove EMIR-style reporting. Which risk event was it?
o: The 2008 collapse of Lehman Brothers over opaque derivatives
The 2012 mis-selling of payment protection insurance
The 2020 market disruption caused by the global COVID-19 pandemic
The 1995 failure of Barings Bank through rogue trading
The 2001 bursting of the dot-com technology bubble
w: Lehman Brothers’ collapse revealed systemic opacity in derivatives, leading to EMIR’s reporting requirements.

n.3: Barings failed from rogue futures trading, not the derivatives opacity EMIR addresses.
n.1: PPI mis-selling was a conduct issue, not the trigger for EMIR.
n.4: The dot-com crash was an equity bubble, unrelated to derivatives reform.
n.2: EMIR predates COVID-19; the 2008 crisis prompted it.

q: A hedge fund builds a large net short position in a UK-listed company and must comply with short selling reporting rules. What is the primary purpose of that reporting?
o: To ban the short selling of all UK-listed shares
To guarantee a minimum share price for issuers
To allocate short positions fairly among competing brokers and dealers
To collect a levy on every short sale executed
To give transparency over significant net short positions
w: Short selling reporting aims to ensure transparency and prevent market abuse by disclosing large net short positions.

n.0: The regime requires disclosure, not an outright ban on short selling.
n.1: It does not guarantee any share price.
n.3: No levy is charged on short sales under the regime.
n.2: It provides transparency, not allocation of positions.

q: A hedge fund is tracking when it must first notify the FCA of a net short position in a UK share. At what threshold must it be reported to the FCA?
o: A net short position of 3.0% of issued share capital
A net short position of 1.0% of issued share capital
A net short position of 0.2% of issued share capital
A net short position of 0.1% of issued share capital
A net short position of 0.5% of issued share capital
w: Net short positions of 0.2% or more must be reported to the FCA.

n.3: 0.1% is below the notification trigger; the threshold is 0.2%.
n.4: 0.5% triggers public disclosure, not the initial report to the FCA.
n.1: 1% is not the short-position reporting threshold.
n.0: 3% relates to major shareholding notifications, not short selling.

q: A fund's net short position in a UK share grows to 0.5% of issued share capital. What happens at that level?
o: It requires the position to be closed within a day
It triggers a mandatory share buy-back by the issuer
It must be publicly disclosed to the market
It must be reported privately to the FCA only
It is reported just once each year to the FCA
w: At 0.5% and above, short positions must be made public to enhance market transparency.

n.3: Private FCA reporting applies at 0.2%; 0.5% requires public disclosure.
n.1: A 0.5% position does not force the issuer to buy back shares.
n.0: There is no requirement to close the position within a day.
n.4: Disclosure is triggered by the position, not made annually.

q: A regulator requires large short positions to be reported publicly. Why is transparency of short positions important?
o: It permanently fixes the borrowing cost of shorting a listed stock
It lets firms avoid paying dividends to holders
It helps deter abusive short selling that could distort markets
It removes the need for any market supervision
It guarantees that listed share prices keep rising
w: Transparency deters abusive trading practices and maintains market confidence.

n.4: Transparency deters abuse; it cannot guarantee rising prices.
n.1: It is unrelated to dividend payments.
n.3: It supports supervision rather than removing it.
n.0: It does not set stock-borrowing costs.

q: A trading desk needs to confirm which UK body oversees compliance with the rules on short selling. Which regulator administers those rules?
o: The Prudential Regulation Authority
Companies House
The Financial Conduct Authority
The Competition and Markets Authority
The Bank of England
w: The FCA enforces the Short Selling Regulation in the UK.

n.4: The Bank of England focuses on monetary policy, not short selling.
n.0: The PRA oversees prudential standards, not short positions.
n.1: Companies House does not regulate market trading.
n.3: The CMA enforces competition law, not financial market rules.

q: A firm is checking whether it must disclose a net short position it has built up. Which positions are exempt from UK short selling disclosure requirements?
o: Certain market making activities
Retail shareholder positions under 1%
All foreign-listed company shares
All government bond transactions
All positions in FTSE 100 shares
w: Market makers engaged in genuine liquidity provision are exempt from disclosure rules.

n.1: Thresholds apply below 1% if the 0.2% trigger is crossed.
n.4: FTSE 100 shares are not exempt from short selling rules.
n.3: Government bonds may have different treatment, but not blanket exemption.
n.2: Foreign-listed shares admitted to UK venues are still covered.

q: A hedge fund fails to disclose a reportable net short position within the required timeframe. What is the consequence?
o: The London Stock Exchange revokes the firm's licence
The issuer must cancel the trader's short position
HMRC applies a surcharge on the trader's profits
The trader's shares are seized by the stock exchange
The FCA may impose fines and other sanctions
w: Failure to comply with short selling rules may result in FCA sanctions, including fines.

n.1: Issuers do not cancel positions; the FCA enforces the rules.
n.3: The exchange does not seize a trader's shares for non-disclosure.
n.0: The FCA, not the exchange, enforces short-selling disclosure.
n.2: HMRC has no role in short-selling disclosure penalties.

q: A regulatory analyst is preparing a briefing on the origins of the short selling restrictions now in force. Which event most clearly highlighted the need for stricter short selling regulation?
o: The Enron accounting scandal
The dot-com bubble collapse
The UK exit from the ERM
The 2008 financial crisis
The COVID-19 vaccination rollout
w: The 2008 crisis demonstrated risks from opaque short selling practices, leading to enhanced regulation.

n.1: The dot-com crash related to overvalued equities, not shorting practices.
n.0: Enron was an accounting scandal, not primarily about short selling.
n.2: ERM exit was a currency event, unrelated to short selling regulation.
n.4: COVID-19 health policy was unrelated to short selling rules.

q: A hedge fund builds a net short position in a listed company that crosses the 0.5% public disclosure threshold. Why must this be disclosed publicly?
o: To force the short seller to close out immediately
To let the issuer identify and block the short seller
To keep market confidence by revealing large bearish positions
To calculate the capital gains tax on the position
To set a strict daily short-selling limit for the individual stock
w: Public disclosure above 0.5% increases transparency and helps maintain orderly markets.

n.1: Disclosure informs the market; it does not let issuers block sellers.
n.3: It is not used to compute capital gains tax.
n.0: Public disclosure does not force closing the position.
n.4: It does not set daily short-selling limits.

q: A compliance officer is explaining to new traders why the UK regulates short selling at all. What is the broader purpose of that regulation?
o: To harmonise accounting standards across all firms
To boost the UK's gross domestic product growth
To standardise directors' employment contracts
To reduce firms' long-term pension scheme liabilities significantly
To prevent disorderly markets and improve transparency
w: Short selling regulation prevents disorderly markets and promotes transparency, protecting market stability.

n.0: Short-selling rules are not about accounting standards.
n.1: They do not target GDP growth.
n.2: They do not standardise director contracts.
n.3: They are unrelated to pension liabilities.

q: A compliance team is briefing staff on UK SFTR obligations for the firm's repo book. What is the primary purpose of SFTR reporting?
o: To set interest rates for interbank lending markets
To publish the credit ratings of listed issuers
To disclose the fees charged on consumer mortgages and personal loans
To increase transparency of securities financing transactions
To increase transparency of retail deposit accounts
w: UK SFTR reporting increases transparency of repos, securities lending, and other financing transactions to monitor systemic risk.

n.4: SFTR covers securities financing, not retail deposits.
n.1: SFTR does not publish issuer credit ratings.
n.0: SFTR does not set interbank interest rates.
n.2: SFTR is unrelated to consumer mortgage fees.

q: An operations analyst is identifying which of the firm's activities fall within UK SFTR. Which types of transactions are in scope?
o: Spot equity purchases and retail savings accounts
Exchange-traded futures and listed equity options
Corporate dividend payments and share buy-backs
Repos, securities lending and margin lending arrangements
Consumer mortgages, personal overdrafts and credit card facilities
w: UK SFTR covers securities financing transactions such as repos, stock lending, and margin lending arrangements.

n.0: Spot equity buys and savings accounts are not securities financing transactions.
n.2: Dividends and buy-backs are not in SFTR scope.
n.4: Consumer lending is outside SFTR.
n.1: Listed derivatives fall under EMIR/MiFIR, not SFTR.

q: A compliance officer at a UK investment firm is drafting its securities financing reporting policy under SFTR and needs to confirm which authority supervises the firm's compliance. Which regulator is it?
o: The Financial Conduct Authority
The Bank of England
Companies House
The Prudential Regulation Authority
The Competition and Markets Authority
w: The FCA supervises UK SFTR compliance and enforces reporting obligations.

n.1: The Bank of England supervises monetary policy, not SFTR reporting.
n.2: Companies House registers companies, not financing transactions.
n.3: The PRA handles prudential standards, not SFTR reports.
n.4: The CMA enforces competition law, not SFTR.

q: A risk analyst is explaining to the board why SFTR reporting exists. Which systemic risk is the regime primarily designed to make visible and address?
o: Excessive operational risk in payroll processing
Excessive foreign-exchange risk in retail banking
Excessive concentration risk within large equity index tracker funds
Excessive interest-rate risk on fixed mortgages
Excessive leverage built up through securities financing
w: SFTR reporting aims to capture leverage and interconnectedness created by securities financing, reducing systemic risk.

n.1: SFTR targets leverage in securities financing, not FX risk.
n.2: Fund concentration risk is not the focus of SFTR.
n.0: Payroll operational risk is outside SFTR.
n.3: Mortgage interest-rate risk is not what SFTR addresses.

q: A UK firm entering repo and securities lending transactions must file SFTR reports. To which type of entity does it submit those reports in the UK?
o: The Prudential Regulation Authority at the Bank of England
Trade repositories registered with the FCA
The Competition and Markets Authority
The Financial Ombudsman Service based in London
Approved Publication Arrangements overseen by the FCA
w: SFTR reports are submitted to FCA-registered trade repositories for collection and monitoring.

n.4: APAs publish MiFIR trade data; SFTR reports go to trade repositories.
n.0: The PRA does not receive SFTR reports.
n.3: The Ombudsman handles complaints, not SFTR reporting.
n.2: The CMA has no role in SFTR reporting.

q: A firm is configuring its SFTR reporting fields for a new repo book. Which set of details must each report contain?
o: The tax residency and VAT status of each party
The directors' remuneration and bonus arrangements
The marketing budget linked to the financing deal
The counterparties' external credit ratings and full audit reports
Counterparty identity, instrument details, value and collateral
w: SFTR requires reporting of counterparties, instruments, value, and collateral details to assess systemic exposures.

n.3: Credit ratings and audit reports are not SFTR report fields.
n.1: Director pay is not reported under SFTR.
n.0: Tax residency and VAT status are not SFTR data.
n.2: Marketing budgets are not part of SFTR reports.

q: A supervisor reviewing a firm's SFTR submissions places particular weight on the collateral fields. Why is collateral information so important in these reports?
o: It fixes the interest rate charged on the underlying repo transaction
It determines the corporation tax due on the deal
It identifies the retail clients involved in the deal
It sets the dividend payable to the securities lender
It shows the quality of collateral mitigating financing risk
w: Collateral information shows the type and quality of securities pledged, essential for assessing systemic risk exposures.

n.1: Collateral data assesses risk, not corporation tax.
n.3: It does not set any dividend.
n.0: It does not fix the repo interest rate.
n.2: SFTR collateral fields are not about identifying retail clients.

q: During a training session, a compliance analyst is asked which market event exposed the dangers of opaque securities financing and prompted regimes like SFTR. Which event was it?
o: The UK leaving the ERM
The COVID-19 vaccine rollout
The 2008 financial crisis
The Enron scandal
The dot-com bubble
w: The 2008 crisis highlighted how opaque repo and securities lending exposures created systemic risk, leading to SFTR rules.

n.4: The dot-com crash involved equity valuations, not repos.
n.3: Enron was an accounting fraud issue, not repo opacity.
n.0: ERM exit was currency-related, not securities financing.
n.1: COVID-19 health policy did not create SFTR.

q: A firm's operations team is scheduling submission of its securities financing transaction reports. How often must SFTR reports be submitted?
o: Annually, with the firm's audited accounts
Quarterly, with the firm's financial statements
Daily, by the close of the next business day
Weekly, by the close of the following Friday
Monthly, alongside the firm's management accounts
w: SFTR requires daily reporting to trade repositories, ensuring timely systemic risk monitoring.

n.3: SFTR reporting is daily (T+1), not weekly.
n.4: SFTR is not reported monthly with accounts.
n.1: SFTR is not a quarterly filing.
n.0: SFTR is not an annual submission.

q: A policy adviser is summarising the wider role SFTR plays in the UK framework. What is its broader purpose?
o: To regulate directors' service contracts and pay
To guarantee dividend payments to fund investors
To set minimum capital requirements for the largest retail banks
To harmonise consumer mortgage interest rates
To monitor shadow-banking activity and reduce systemic risk
w: SFTR targets shadow banking activities like repos, ensuring systemic risks are monitored and reduced.

n.1: SFTR does not guarantee dividends.
n.0: It does not regulate director contracts.
n.3: It is unrelated to mortgage rates.
n.2: Bank capital requirements are set under separate prudential rules.

q: An investment firm executes an equity order for a retail client on a trading venue. Under UK MiFIR, who is primarily responsible for submitting the transaction report to the FCA?
o: The investment firm that executes the transaction
The retail client who placed the original order
The company registrar maintaining the share register
The issuer of the security being traded
The trading venue where the order was executed
w: The executing investment firm is responsible for submitting the report to the FCA.

n.1: Clients do not report; the executing firm carries the obligation.
n.3: The issuer does not report others' transactions.
n.2: A registrar has no MiFIR transaction-reporting duty.
n.4: The executing firm reports; the venue reports only for non-members.

q: Two UK-authorised firms execute a securities financing transaction with each other. Who carries the reporting obligation for that trade?
o: Only the firm that acted as the buyer in the trade
Only the firm with the larger balance sheet
Both firms, unless one has delegated the obligation
Neither firm, because the venue reports it
Only whichever firm is acting as the designated market maker
w: Both firms are responsible, although they may delegate reporting to one party under agreement.

n.0: Both firms report; it is not limited to the buyer.
n.1: Balance-sheet size does not decide who reports.
n.4: Market-maker status does not remove the other firm's duty.
n.3: The venue does not report on behalf of MiFIR investment firms.

q: A UK-authorised firm executes and books a trade through its branch located overseas. Who must report that transaction?
o: Only the overseas branch, not the UK head office
The client, because the branch sits outside the UK
Neither, as overseas branches are not covered
The UK firm, even when the trade is booked abroad
Only the regulator in the branch's host country
w: UK firms must report all trades executed by overseas branches to the FCA to maintain transparency.

n.4: Foreign regulators do not report for the UK firm; the firm reports to the FCA.
n.0: The UK firm remains responsible, including its overseas branch.
n.1: Clients never carry the reporting obligation.
n.2: Overseas branches of UK firms are still within reporting scope.

q: When a non-UK firm trades on a UK trading venue, who is responsible for reporting?
o: No transaction report is needed at all for a non-UK firm
Only the firm's home-state regulator reports it
The UK counterparty reports for both parties
Only the UK trading venue reports the trade
The non-UK firm must report the trade to the FCA
w: Any firm trading on a UK venue must report transactions to the FCA, even if domiciled abroad.

n.3: The venue does not report for a firm trading on it under MiFIR.
n.1: The home-state regulator does not file the report.
n.2: The counterparty does not report on the other firm's behalf.
n.0: Trading on a UK venue triggers a reporting duty regardless of domicile.

q: An investment firm outsources its transaction reporting to a specialist third-party provider. If a reporting failure occurs, who holds ultimate responsibility for compliance?
o: The FCA assumes liability
The London Stock Exchange assumes liability
The delegated third party assumes full liability
Responsibility is waived if delegated
The executing firm remains responsible
w: Even if delegated, the executing firm remains ultimately responsible for compliance with reporting obligations.

n.2: Delegation does not transfer liability fully to third parties.
n.0: The FCA supervises but does not assume liability.
n.1: Exchanges are not liable for firm reporting.
n.3: Obligations cannot be waived under MiFIR.

q: A UK investment firm delegates its reporting to an overseas group affiliate. What condition continues to apply to the UK firm?
o: The affiliate assumes all legal liability
The report must be filed through Companies House
The trade is exempt from reporting
The overseas regulator must pre-approve
The UK firm remains responsible for accuracy
w: UK firms may delegate reporting abroad but remain accountable for accuracy under FCA rules.

n.0: Legal liability cannot be shifted away from the UK firm.
n.3: Pre-approval by overseas regulators is not required.
n.1: Companies House does not handle transaction reports.
n.2: Trades remain reportable regardless of delegation.

q: A US bank's London branch executes a trade in the UK market and the desk head asks who bears the reporting duty. Who must report the trade?
o: The UK branch must report the trade to the FCA
The US head office reports the trade to the FCA
The client involved must report the trade itself
No report is required for a UK branch trade
The US regulator reports it on the bank's behalf
w: UK branches of overseas banks must report trades executed in the UK to the FCA.

n.1: The UK branch, not the US head office, reports the London trade.
n.4: The US regulator does not file UK reports.
n.2: Clients do not carry the reporting obligation.
n.3: A UK branch's trade is reportable to the FCA.

q: A UK-authorised firm executes a trade with a non-UK counterparty on an overseas venue. Who must report that transaction?
o: The client's custodian must report the trade
No reporting obligation applies in this case
Only the overseas venue reports the trade
Only the non-UK counterparty must report it
The UK firm must report the trade to the FCA
w: The UK firm must report trades to the FCA even if executed abroad.

n.3: The UK firm has its own duty regardless of the counterparty.
n.2: An overseas venue does not report for the UK firm.
n.0: Custodians do not carry the reporting obligation.
n.1: The UK firm must report even trades executed abroad.

q: A compliance officer is briefing staff on how MiFIR allocates responsibility when a firm outsources its transaction reporting. Which principle governs that responsibility?
o: The executing firm stays responsible even if reporting is delegated
Responsibility passes to whichever party is larger
Responsibility alternates between the two counterparties
The FCA itself becomes liable the moment a trade is misreported to it
Responsibility rests solely with the trading venue
w: MiFIR makes the executing firm accountable for compliance, even if reporting is delegated.

n.3: The FCA never assumes the firm's reporting liability.
n.1: Responsibility does not shift to the larger party.
n.4: The venue is not solely responsible for a firm's reports.
n.2: Responsibility does not alternate; the executing firm remains accountable.

q: A firm's delegated reporting agent files inaccurate transaction data because the delegation was set up incorrectly. Who remains liable to the FCA?
o: The FCA takes responsibility
The executing firm remains liable to the FCA
The trading venue takes responsibility
The third-party delegate assumes sole liability
The client who initiated the trade
w: Regardless of delegation, the executing firm is liable for inaccurate reporting.

n.3: Delegates may assist but ultimate liability remains with the firm.
n.0: The FCA regulates but does not assume liability.
n.2: Venues publish trades but do not assume reporting responsibility.
n.4: Clients are not reporting entities under MiFIR.

q: A firm is selecting a channel to submit its MiFIR transaction reports to the FCA. Which type of system do firms typically use for this?
o: A trade repository registered under EMIR rules
A systematic internaliser's matching engine
An Approved Reporting Mechanism, known as an ARM
The FCA's own Companies House filing portal
An Approved Publication Arrangement, known as an APA
w: Firms use ARMs, which are authorised intermediaries, to submit transaction reports to the FCA.

n.4: APAs publish trade data to the market; transaction reports go via an ARM.
n.0: Trade repositories receive EMIR data, not MiFIR transaction reports.
n.3: Companies House does not receive transaction reports.
n.1: A systematic internaliser is a trading capacity, not a reporting channel.

q: A paraplanner is documenting how the firm's transaction reports reach the regulator. What is the function of an ARM in the reporting chain?
o: To calculate the capital a firm is required to hold
To settle and clear the firm's executed trades
To publish executed trade prices to the public market
To maintain the firm's statutory register of its shareholders
To transmit firms' transaction reports securely to the FCA
w: ARMs act as authorised intermediaries that send transaction reports securely to the FCA.

n.2: Publishing prices to the public is an APA function, not an ARM's.
n.0: ARMs do not calculate capital requirements.
n.1: ARMs do not settle or clear trades.
n.3: ARMs do not maintain shareholder registers.

q: A firm dealing in derivatives and securities financing transactions must submit its EMIR and SFTR reports. Which system does it use?
o: Companies House filings
The Competition and Markets Authority platform
Approved Reporting Mechanisms
Trade repositories authorised by the FCA
HMRC’s tax return system
w: EMIR and SFTR reports are submitted to trade repositories registered with the FCA.

n.2: ARMs are for MiFIR transaction reports, not EMIR/SFTR.
n.0: Companies House is unrelated to derivatives or repo reporting.
n.4: Tax return systems are unrelated to trade reporting.
n.1: The CMA enforces competition law, not financial reporting.

q: A firm needs to make the details of an executed equity trade public under MiFIR. Which system ensures post-trade transparency for equity trades?
o: A registered trade repository authorised under the EMIR regime
A systematic internaliser's internal order book
An Approved Publication Arrangement, known as an APA
A central securities depository handling settlement
An Approved Reporting Mechanism, known as an ARM
w: APAs publish trade data publicly to ensure post-trade transparency under MiFIR.

n.4: An ARM reports to the FCA; public post-trade data is published via an APA.
n.0: EMIR trade repositories do not provide MiFIR post-trade transparency.
n.3: A CSD handles settlement, not trade publication.
n.1: An internal order book is not a publication channel.

q: A compliance team is confirming the acceptable method for filing MiFIR transaction reports. Which channel is mandatory for firms to use?
o: Publication in a national newspaper of record
Electronic submission via an ARM or direct to the FCA
Posted paper records physically delivered to the FCA offices
Announcements made at the firm's annual meeting
Faxed report copies sent to the FCA each day
w: Reports must be submitted electronically through an ARM or directly to the FCA.

n.4: Reporting must be electronic, not by fax.
n.2: Paper submissions are not an accepted reporting channel.
n.3: AGM announcements are not a reporting channel.
n.0: Newspaper publication is not how transaction reports are made.

q: An operations analyst is completing an electronic transaction report and checks which identifier for the reporting firm is mandatory. Which is it?
o: The firm's Companies House registration number
The firm's FCA reference number alone
The Legal Entity Identifier, or LEI, of the firm
The firm's VAT registration number
The firm's SWIFT BIC code used for international banking
w: The LEI is required to identify firms consistently in transaction reports.

n.3: VAT numbers are not used to identify firms in transaction reports.
n.0: The Companies House number is not the required identifier.
n.4: A SWIFT BIC identifies a bank, not the reporting entity here.
n.1: The FRN alone is not the mandatory identifier; the LEI is required.

q: An operations manager wants to ensure the firm's transaction reports are submitted securely. How do firms achieve secure submission?
o: By posting sealed paper records to the FCA
By publishing the reports on the firm's website
By emailing spreadsheets from a personal account
By using encrypted electronic reporting systems
By circulating the reports to all shareholders
w: Encrypted electronic submissions via ARMs or repositories ensure confidentiality and security.

n.0: Paper posting is not a secure reporting method under the rules.
n.2: Personal-email spreadsheets are not a secure or approved channel.
n.1: Reports are not published on the firm's website.
n.4: Reports are confidential and not sent to shareholders.

q: The FCA needs visibility of firms' derivative exposures across the market. Which system provides regulators with that oversight?
o: The Bank of England Prudential Gateway
Companies House database
Trade repositories under EMIR
Approved Publication Arrangements
HMRC tax filing portal
w: Trade repositories collect derivatives data under EMIR and provide regulators with oversight of exposures.

n.3: APAs publish trades publicly, but do not capture derivatives exposures.
n.1: Companies House does not collect derivatives data.
n.4: HMRC handles tax, not EMIR reporting.
n.0: The Bank of England does not directly collect EMIR reports.

q: A regulatory analyst notes that the FCA can reconcile trade data submitted by many different firms. Which system makes this cross-market reconciliation possible?
o: Quarterly corporation tax returns sent to HMRC
Monthly payroll and pension submissions made to HMRC each period
Directors' remuneration reports in the annual accounts
Annual company prospectuses filed with the FCA
Common electronic reporting standards via ARMs and repositories
w: Standardised electronic submissions allow the FCA to reconcile data efficiently across different firms and markets.

n.3: Prospectuses are not the mechanism for reconciling trade data.
n.0: Tax returns do not reconcile market reporting data.
n.1: Payroll filings are unrelated to market data reconciliation.
n.2: Remuneration reports do not reconcile transaction data.

q: A new joiner asks why firms cannot simply email reports through any channel they like but must use FCA-approved routes. What is the reason?
o: To make marketing and promotion simpler for the issuer
To keep the data accurate, secure and standardised
To raise the bonuses paid to firm directors
To cut the number of shareholder meetings needed
To reduce the corporation tax the firm owes
w: Approved channels ensure data integrity and standardisation, which are critical for regulatory monitoring.

n.4: Approved channels concern data integrity, not tax.
n.3: They have no effect on shareholder meetings.
n.0: They are unrelated to marketing.
n.2: They do not affect director bonuses.

q: A firm's data protection lead is reviewing how long client files are kept. Under the storage limitation principle, what does it require firms to do with personal data?
o: Delete all personal data after exactly five calendar years
Archive all personal data indefinitely for audit readiness
Keep personal data no longer than necessary for its purposes
Hold the data for a fixed statutory minimum of at least ten years
Retain the data until the individual requests erasure
w: Storage limitation requires firms to keep personal data only as long as necessary for stated purposes.

n.1: Indefinite retention breaches storage limitation.
n.0: No fixed five-year rule applies; retention is purpose-based.
n.4: Retention is limited by purpose, not by awaiting an erasure request.
n.3: There is no ten-year minimum; data is kept only as long as needed.

q: An adviser discovers a client's contact details on file are wrong. Under the accuracy principle, when must the firm correct the inaccurate data?
o: Without undue delay once the inaccuracy is identified
Only after receiving a formal court order
At the next scheduled annual data review
Only once the ICO has granted its formal written approval
Within three months of a verified complaint
w: The accuracy principle requires firms to rectify or erase inaccurate data without undue delay once it is identified or brought to their attention.

n.4: Correction must be without undue delay, not within three months.
n.1: No court order is needed to correct inaccurate data.
n.2: Correction cannot wait for an annual review.
n.3: ICO approval is not required to rectify data.

q: A compliance officer is listing the six data protection principles for a staff handbook. Which of the following is one of them?
o: Personal data must be stored exclusively within UK-based data centres
Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently
Personal data must be deleted every twelve months
Personal data must be encrypted using the AES-256 standard
Personal data must be anonymised before it is stored
w: The first principle requires that personal data is processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to individuals.

n.4: Anonymisation before storage is not a data protection principle.
n.0: There is no principle confining all data to the UK.
