o: Edinburgh activities, since the UK office is a permanent establishment
Only dealings with the firm's UK-based retail clients
Only dealings with the firm's UK institutional clients
Frankfurt activities, regardless of any UK connection at all
All of the firm's client dealings anywhere in the world
w: COBS applies to designated investment business carried on from the UK establishment. Frankfurt activity is subject to local EU rules instead.

n.3: Frankfurt activity is subject to local EU rules, not COBS.
n.4: COBS does not reach the firm's activities worldwide.
n.1: COBS applies by establishment, not only to UK retail clients.
n.2: COBS is not limited to UK institutional clients.

q: A firm with both UK and overseas branches asks how COBS applies across them. How does its application differ between the two?
o: COBS applies only where the clients are UK nationals
Both branches must comply with COBS everywhere in the world
COBS applies only to digital transactions, not others
UK branches follow COBS; overseas branches follow local conduct rules
Overseas branches are exempt from any conduct rules at all
w: The establishment test is key. UK branches apply COBS, while overseas establishments are governed by their home jurisdictions.

n.1: COBS does not apply globally to overseas branches.
n.4: Overseas branches follow their own home rules, not no rules.
n.0: COBS applies by establishment, not by client nationality.
n.2: COBS is not limited to digital transactions.

q: A firm assesses which of its activities bring it within the scope of COBS. Which type of client transaction is NOT sufficient on its own to bring COBS into scope?
o: Providing custody of clients' shares from a Birmingham office
Executing client equity trades from the firm's London desk
Dealing with UK clients from the firm's New York branch
Giving investment advice to clients from a Manchester office
Running discretionary portfolios from an Edinburgh office
w: Dealing with UK clients from an overseas office does not automatically bring the activity under COBS, as the firm has no UK establishment in that scenario.

n.3: Advice from Manchester is UK-establishment business, so COBS applies.
n.1: Execution from London is UK-establishment business, so COBS applies.
n.4: Managing portfolios from Edinburgh brings COBS into scope.
n.0: Custody from Birmingham is UK-establishment business under COBS.

q: A UK-authorised firm gives investment advice to clients based in Spain, but the advice is provided from its London office. Which statement is correct about COBS?
o: COBS does not apply when the advice is given remotely
COBS applies only where Spanish law expressly requires it
COBS applies, since the advice is given from a UK establishment
COBS applies only to the firm's wholesale clients
COBS does not apply because the clients are based in Spain
w: Cross-border services are still subject to COBS if carried on from a UK base. Client location does not negate FCA jurisdiction.

n.4: Client location in Spain does not remove UK-based COBS.
n.1: Spanish law does not decide whether COBS applies.
n.3: COBS is not limited to wholesale clients.
n.0: Remote delivery does not remove COBS.

q: A UK branch conducts designated investment business with a counterparty classified as an eligible counterparty and questions whether COBS still applies. Why does COBS apply in this case?
o: Because only retail clients ever fall within COBS scope
Because eligible counterparties receive full retail protections
Because place of business fixes scope before client classification
Because client classification overrides the territorial test
Because the FCA holds jurisdiction over firms worldwide
w: The establishment test applies first. Eligible counterparty classification determines the level of protection but does not remove the application of COBS to the UK branch.

n.1: ECPs get the lightest, not full retail, protections.
n.4: The FCA does not hold worldwide jurisdiction over all firms.
n.3: The establishment test applies before classification, not after.
n.0: COBS is not limited to retail clients.

q: A firm with clients in several countries is working out whether COBS applies to a piece of investment business. Which factor is decisive for COBS application?
o: Time zone in which the trade is executed
Nationality of the client
Market on which the product is listed
Currency of the transaction
Permanent place of business in the UK
w: The central criterion is whether the designated investment business is carried on from a UK establishment. Other factors are not determinative.

n.1: Client nationality is irrelevant under COBS scope rules.
n.3: Transaction currency does not change jurisdiction.
n.2: Listing venue does not decide COBS applicability.
n.0: Execution time zone is irrelevant; establishment location is key.

q: A network operates through several appointed representatives. Who holds responsibility for ensuring an AR complies with COBS?
o: The principal firm
The appointed representative itself
The representative’s clients
The FCA directly
The product manufacturer
w: Under COBS 1.1.1, an appointed representative acts under the responsibility of its principal, which must ensure compliance with FCA rules including COBS.

n.1: Appointed representatives are not directly authorised and do not bear primary regulatory responsibility.
n.3: The FCA supervises the principal, not the AR directly.
n.2: Clients cannot enforce FCA compliance on behalf of the AR.
n.4: Product manufacturers are not accountable for AR conduct under COBS.

q: An appointed representative wants to issue a financial promotion to prospective clients. How are AR financial promotions treated under COBS?
o: They are approved automatically if issued digitally
They are treated as client communications, not financial promotions
They are exempt from FCA oversight
They only need approval if targeting retail clients
They must be approved by the principal firm before communication
w: COBS 4.1 requires financial promotions issued by ARs to be approved by their principal before being made, ensuring compliance with fair, clear and not misleading standards.

n.2: AR promotions are not exempt from FCA standards.
n.3: Approval is needed for all promotions, not just retail-facing ones.
n.1: Promotions remain subject to financial promotion rules, not downgraded to ordinary communications.
n.0: Digital format does not change approval obligations.

q: A principal firm is reviewing its duties towards the appointed representatives it oversees. What is its primary obligation under COBS?
o: Ensuring they each hold direct authorisation from the FCA
Treating them as the equivalent of professional clients
Supervising their conduct and ensuring COBS compliance
Reporting them to the FCA as fully independent entities
Allowing them complete autonomy over their own conduct
w: The principal must supervise its ARs, ensuring they comply with COBS requirements for fair treatment of clients and proper conduct of business.

n.4: The principal must supervise ARs, not grant full autonomy.
n.3: ARs act under the principal, not as independent entities.
n.1: ARs are not clients; they are exempt persons under supervision.
n.0: ARs do not hold direct FCA authorisation.

q: A compliance officer needs the COBS reference governing financial promotions issued by appointed representatives. Which rule applies?
o: COBS 6.1
COBS 4.1
MCOB 3.1
ICOBS 2.2
COBS 2.1
w: COBS 4.1 sets out the rules for financial promotions, requiring them to be fair, clear and not misleading, and approved by a regulated firm if issued by an AR.

n.4: COBS 2.1 contains general client principles, not promotion rules.
n.0: COBS 6.1 concerns client disclosures, not promotions.
n.2: MCOB covers mortgage promotions, not COBS.
n.3: ICOBS 2.2 covers insurance conduct, not investment promotions.

q: A principal firm has been lax in overseeing one of its appointed representatives. Under COBS, what is the key risk the principal faces?
o: The principal is liable for breaches of COBS by the AR
The AR can transfer responsibility to another principal without FCA oversight
The AR becomes directly liable to the FCA
The AR must apply for direct authorisation immediately
Clients lose FSCS protection
w: Under COBS 1.1.1 and FCA principles, the principal bears liability for COBS breaches by its appointed representatives.

n.2: ARs are not directly liable to the FCA; accountability rests with the principal.
n.4: FSCS protection is not withdrawn due to oversight failures.
n.3: An AR does not become directly authorised unless applying formally.
n.1: Transfers of principals must be FCA-approved; ARs cannot reassign freely.

q: A principal is reviewing an AR's draft promotion before it is issued. How must that financial promotion be characterised under COBS?
o: Fair, clear and not misleading
Exempt if communicated verbally
Compliant only if aimed at retail clients
Optimistic and persuasive
Detailed but selective
w: COBS 4.1 states that all promotions, including those by ARs, must be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.3: Promotions must not be overly persuasive at the expense of accuracy.
n.4: Selective disclosure is prohibited; balance is required.
n.2: The rule applies regardless of target audience.
n.1: Verbal communications remain within scope if they are promotions.

q: An appointed representative wants to send out a promotional leaflet to prospects. What must its principal firm do before allowing the AR to distribute it?
o: Register the financial promotion with the FCA first
Submit the promotion to the PRA for prior approval
Approve the promotion to ensure it complies with the rules
Confirm the AR holds separate MiFID authorisation
Obtain the client's written consent to the promotion
w: The principal must approve financial promotions issued by ARs to ensure they comply with COBS standards before being communicated.

n.0: Promotions are not registered with the FCA in advance.
n.4: Client consent is not required to approve a promotion.
n.1: The PRA does not approve financial promotions.
n.3: An AR does not hold its own MiFID authorisation.

q: A mortgage-and-investment network takes on an appointed representative to expand its distribution. Which activity is the AR prohibited from carrying out without the principal's oversight?
o: Providing investment advice under the principal's oversight
Issuing financial promotions without the principal's approval
Meeting prospective clients on a face-to-face basis
Communicating with institutional and wholesale clients
Keeping its own internal compliance procedures manual
w: ARs cannot issue financial promotions independently; they must be approved and monitored by their principal under COBS 4.1.

n.0: ARs may advise clients under the principal's oversight.
n.2: ARs may meet clients face-to-face in the normal course of business.
n.3: ARs may communicate with institutional clients.
n.4: An AR keeping internal procedures is not prohibited conduct.

q: A compliance officer explains to the board why AR promotions must be signed off by the principal. What is the main regulatory justification?
o: To restrict ARs to dealing with professional clients
To centralise all marketing directly under FCA control
To permit ARs to use only digital advertising channels
To ensure promotions are fair, clear and not misleading
To make each AR individually accountable to the FCA
w: Principal approval ensures that AR promotions meet FCA standards, preventing misleading or unfair communications in the market.

n.1: Approval is not about centralising marketing under the FCA.
n.4: The principal, not the AR, is accountable for the promotion.
n.0: Approval does not restrict ARs to professional clients.
n.2: Approval is unrelated to limiting ARs to digital channels.

q: A mortgage network signs up a small brokerage to sell under its name and oversight. Under COBS 1.1.1, what is the regulatory status of that brokerage as an appointed representative?
o: Persons directly authorised and regulated by the FCA
Firms regulated independently of any principal firm
Clients automatically classified as professional clients
Exempt persons acting under the responsibility of their principal
Market participants treated as eligible counterparties
w: Appointed representatives are exempt persons under FSMA, acting under the responsibility and oversight of their principal firm.

n.0: ARs are exempt persons, not directly authorised.
n.1: ARs act under a principal, not independently.
n.2: ARs are not clients of a firm by status.
n.4: ARs are not classified as eligible counterparties by status.

q: An appointed representative circulates a brochure about a new investment product to prospects without obtaining its principal's approval. What breach has occurred under COBS?
o: Breach of best execution obligations
Unauthorised financial promotion
Breach of CASS custody standards
Breach of client categorisation rules
Breach of suitability requirements
w: Financial promotions by ARs must be approved by their principal before issue. Circulating without approval is an unauthorised promotion.

n.3: Client categorisation was not the issue in this case.
n.0: Best execution relates to order handling, not brochures.
n.2: CASS governs custody, not promotions.
n.4: Suitability applies to advice, not promotional approval.

q: A trainee asks how the FCA maintains oversight of appointed representatives under COBS. Through what mechanism does it do so?
o: By directly supervising each individual AR itself
By holding the principal accountable for the AR's activity
By exempting ARs from the financial promotion rules
By requiring ARs to obtain temporary FCA registration
By restricting ARs to wholesale business activity only
w: FCA supervision operates through the principal firm, which is legally responsible for the AR’s compliance with COBS.

n.0: The FCA supervises through the principal, not each AR directly.
n.3: ARs do not obtain temporary FCA registration.
n.4: ARs are not restricted to wholesale business.
n.2: AR promotions are subject to the rules, not exempt.

q: A principal discovers that one of its appointed representatives has issued misleading financial promotions. What must the principal do?
o: Take remedial action and accept responsibility for the breach
Refer the AR directly to the PRA for enforcement
Wait until the FCA opens its own investigation first
Temporarily suspend the FCA's rules covering the AR
Reclassify the clients as professional to cut duties
w: The principal must remedy breaches and accept responsibility, as ARs act under their oversight for COBS compliance.

n.3: A firm cannot suspend FCA rules.
n.1: The PRA does not enforce AR promotion breaches.
n.4: Reclassifying clients does not cure a promotion breach.
n.2: The principal must act, not wait for the FCA.

q: A principal firm asks why COBS 4.1 requires it to pre-approve every AR promotion. What is the reason?
o: To remove the need for any client categorisation
To let ARs operate fully independently of principals
To speed up the distribution of new investment products
To prevent unfair or misleading client communications
To simplify the firm's annual tax and VAT reporting
w: Pre-approval ensures that all communications meet FCA standards for being fair, clear and not misleading before reaching clients.

n.4: Approval is unrelated to tax reporting.
n.2: The aim is consumer protection, not faster distribution.
n.1: Approval keeps ARs under oversight, not independent.
n.0: Approval does not remove client categorisation duties.

q: A compliance officer is aligning the firm's controls with FCA expectations for principals overseeing ARs. Which of the following is within those expectations?
o: Regular monitoring of AR financial promotions
Allowing ARs to market unapproved overseas products
Permitting ARs to classify themselves as eligible counterparties
Leaving approval entirely to AR discretion
Requiring ARs to seek direct FCA approval
w: Principals are expected to monitor their ARs to ensure that financial promotions comply with COBS 4.1 standards.

n.3: Approval cannot be left to AR discretion.
n.4: ARs cannot directly seek FCA approval of promotions.
n.1: Promotions of unapproved overseas products are prohibited.
n.2: ECP status applies to clients, not ARs.

q: An appointed representative creates a social media advert for a new bond issue. Under COBS, what must occur first?
o: The principal must approve the advert before posting
The AR can post immediately if it targets professionals only
The AR can self-certify compliance
The AR can circulate freely as long as disclaimers are used
The advert is exempt if fewer than 50 people see it
w: All financial promotions by ARs, including digital or social media, require principal approval under COBS 4.1.

n.1: Professional targeting does not exempt approval obligations.
n.2: Self-certification is not permitted.
n.4: Audience size does not exempt promotions from COBS rules.
n.3: Disclaimers do not replace principal approval requirements.

q: A principal repeatedly lets one of its ARs issue promotions without approval. What is the likely consequence?
o: The promotions become valid through market custom
The FCA imposes sanctions on the clients involved
The FCA may take enforcement action against the principal
The PRA revokes the AR's own direct authorisation
The AR is automatically removed from the FCA register
w: Failure to supervise ARs appropriately may trigger FCA enforcement against the principal, including fines and restrictions.

n.4: There is no automatic register removal for the AR.
n.0: Non-compliant promotions do not become valid by custom.
n.1: Clients are not sanctioned for the firm's failings.
n.3: An AR has no direct authorisation for the PRA to revoke.

q: A principal firm is reviewing a promotional email sent by one of its appointed representatives. Under COBS, how should the AR's communications with clients be regarded?
o: As unregulated third-party statements
As communications of the principal firm
As personal views outside FCA rules
As exempt from FCA oversight
As marketing material only if to retail clients
w: All communications from ARs are legally treated as communications of the principal, and must therefore meet COBS standards.

n.3: AR communications are not exempt; they fall under principal responsibility.
n.0: They are regulated as firm communications, not independent.
n.2: Personal disclaimers do not override the rules.
n.4: The rule applies regardless of client type.

q: A trainee asks why principal oversight of AR promotions is treated so strictly under COBS. What is the main reason?
o: Because ARs are entirely barred from the FSCS scheme
Because ARs operate as wholly unsupervised entities
Because ARs are always treated as eligible counterparties
Because promotions directly affect retail market integrity
Because promotions to professionals are always exempt
w: Financial promotions are critical to retail protection. Principal oversight ensures compliance with fairness and prevents consumer detriment.

n.2: ARs are not classified as eligible counterparties.
n.0: FSCS access is not the reason for strict oversight.
n.1: ARs are supervised by their principal, not unsupervised.
n.4: Promotions to professionals are not always exempt.

q: An AR's financial promotion is found to breach COBS. Who is accountable to the FCA for that breach?
o: The AR individually
The client receiving the promotion
The principal firm
The marketing agency producing the material
The FCA’s promotions unit
w: Responsibility rests with the principal, which is accountable for ensuring AR compliance with financial promotion rules.

n.0: ARs are not directly accountable under FSMA.
n.1: Clients are not liable for firm breaches.
n.3: Third-party agencies are not responsible to the FCA; the principal remains liable.
n.4: The promotions unit enforces standards but does not assume liability.

q: A firm needs to send a client disclosure in a form that meets the Glossary definition of a durable medium for COBS purposes. Which of the following qualifies?
o: A poster displayed in the firm’s reception
A PDF document emailed to the client
A web banner that disappears after viewing
An advert broadcast on television
A verbal explanation recorded in a meeting
w: A durable medium must allow the client to store the information in a way accessible for future reference. A PDF meets this requirement.

n.4: Verbal explanations do not meet the definition, as the client cannot store and reproduce them reliably.
n.0: Posters are not personal or durable for the client’s use.
n.3: Broadcasts are transient and cannot be stored by the client without action.
n.2: Disappearing banners do not qualify as durable mediums.

q: A firm wants to use its website to deliver client documents as a durable medium under COBS. Which key condition must be met?
o: The website must be accessible without any password
The website must include promotional marketing videos
The website must hold at least three years of archived data
The website must be reachable only in business hours
The client is notified of the website's address and its content
w: For a website to be considered a durable medium, clients must be personally notified of the address and information made available in a retrievable format.

n.2: There is no fixed three-year archive requirement.
n.0: Password protection does not disqualify a durable medium.
n.3: Restricting access to business hours is not a condition.
n.1: Promotional videos are not a durable-medium condition.

q: A compliance officer is checking which client communications meet the durable medium test under COBS. Which of the following would NOT normally qualify?
o: PDF files downloaded and saved on the client's device
Emails retained in the client's own inbox
CD-ROMs supplied to the client with agreements
Printed contract letters posted to the client
Transient pop-up alerts shown on a trading platform
w: Transient pop-up messages cannot be stored and reproduced, so they fail the durable medium test.

n.3: A posted printed letter is a classic durable medium.
n.0: A saved PDF can be stored and reproduced, so it qualifies.
n.1: A stored email meets the durable medium test.
n.2: A CD-ROM can store and reproduce information unchanged.

q: A firm plans to send its clients key contractual information by email rather than post. Why does it matter that this electronic communication qualifies as a durable medium under COBS?
o: So clients can store and reproduce it unchanged for as long as needed
So that firms can avoid keeping any transaction records at all
So that clients receive more colourful and engaging documents
So that firms can reduce their document printing costs each year
So that the FCA can audit each client message in real time
w: Durable mediums ensure clients can retain key information unchanged, meeting the regulatory objectives of transparency and client protection.

n.3: Cost saving is not the regulatory purpose.
n.4: Real-time FCA auditing is not the purpose of durable media.
n.2: Presentation quality is not the objective.
n.1: Durable media do not remove record-keeping duties.

q: A firm wants to satisfy its disclosure obligations by making information available on its website rather than sending documents. Which condition must be met for the website to be treated as equivalent to a durable medium?
o: The site must contain the firm's financial promotions
The website must be open to every internet user freely
The firm must guarantee round-the-clock live chat support
The information stays accessible for as long as the client needs it
The site must be hosted only on servers based in the UK
w: COBS requires that the information remains accessible in an unchanged form for as long as reasonably needed by the client.

n.1: Public access to all users is not required.
n.4: UK-only hosting is not a durable-medium condition.
n.2: Live chat support is not required for durability.
n.0: Containing promotions is not a durable-medium condition.

q: A wealth manager wants to send its terms of business by posting them on its website instead of on paper. Under the Glossary, which condition must be met for a website to substitute for a durable medium?
o: The firm must update the website's content every day
The website must include interactive financial calculators
The FCA must pre-approve the website before its use
The website must be accessible without a password
The client consents to using the website instead of paper
w: Client consent is a key requirement when substituting website communication for traditional durable mediums.

n.0: Daily updating is not a Glossary condition.
n.3: Password-free access is not required.
n.1: Interactive calculators are not a condition.
n.2: The FCA does not pre-approve firms' websites.

q: A firm is deciding how to send a client their contract so it satisfies the COBS durable medium test. Which communication best meets it?
o: Flash message on a trading app that disappears instantly
Oral advice during a phone call without a record
Advertisement on social media feed
Email with attached contract in PDF format
Interactive chatbot message without storage option
w: Emails with attached PDFs meet the durability criteria: accessible, storable, and unalterable for reference.

n.0: Ephemeral pop-ups are not durable mediums.
n.1: Oral advice without a recording does not meet the test.
n.2: Social media adverts are transient and not personal.
n.4: Chatbot messages without storage cannot be considered durable.

q: A compliance officer is asked why COBS bothers to define the term 'durable medium' at all. What is the regulatory purpose of the definition?
o: To assist firms with their digital marketing campaigns
To encourage new banking technology and innovation
To ensure clients can store key information unchanged
To exempt firms' own websites from FCA supervision entirely
To reduce a firm's legal liability for its disclosures
w: The definition ensures clients can retain key disclosures and agreements in a secure, unalterable format for future reference.

n.0: The purpose is client protection, not marketing.
n.4: It is not to reduce firms' disclosure liability.
n.1: Promoting technology is not the aim.
n.3: Websites are not exempted from FCA supervision.

q: A firm wants to rely on its website to deliver terms of business as a durable medium. Which scenario would fail to meet the website conditions under COBS?
o: A firm sends the written terms in a posted letter
A firm posts terms online with consent and notification
A firm emails a PDF copy of the terms to each client
A firm hosts terms online and also emails a notification
A firm posts terms online without telling clients the web address
w: For a website to count as a durable medium, clients must be notified of the website and its content. Failure to notify means the condition is not met.

n.2: Emailing a PDF meets the durable medium requirement.
n.0: A posted letter is a valid durable medium.
n.3: Online hosting plus a notification email satisfies the conditions.
n.1: With consent and notification, the website conditions are met.

q: A compliance officer wants the firm to publish client disclosures on its website rather than post them. To meet the FCA Glossary website conditions, how must website use interact with client consent?
o: Consent is assumed where the website is written in English
Consent is optional whenever the website is publicly open
Consent is needed only for clients based in the EEA
Clients must consent to website use and be notified of availability
Consent is irrelevant if the firm provides retail services
w: Both client consent and notification of website location/content are required for website delivery to meet durable medium conditions.

n.1: Consent is required even for a public website.
n.4: Consent is not irrelevant for retail services; it is required.
n.2: Consent is not limited to EEA clients.
n.0: Consent is not assumed from the site's language.

q: A firm proposes to disclose terms only via its live website. Compliance objects that this fails the durable-medium test unless the website conditions are met. Which best explains why?
o: Because the FCA bans the use of electronic media entirely
Because websites are never reliable for regulatory disclosure
Because the FCA requires hard copies for all retail clients
Because clients need guaranteed access to unchanged information
Because website use is limited to wholesale clients only
w: The website conditions ensure clients can access information reliably and store it unchanged, matching the protection offered by a durable medium.

n.0: The FCA does not ban electronic media.
n.1: Websites can be reliable when the conditions are met.
n.2: Hard copies are not mandatory for all retail clients.
n.4: Website use is not limited to wholesale clients.

q: A firm plans to send key disclosures to clients electronically and asks what makes something a durable medium rather than an ordinary email or webpage. Which feature is essential?
o: The firm can edit the stored information at any time
The medium must be purely promotional in its nature
The information must be communicated to the client orally
The client can store and reproduce the information unchanged
The medium must allow two-way interactive messaging
w: A durable medium guarantees that the client can store, reproduce, and rely on the information in its original form over time.

n.0: A durable medium must not be alterable by the firm at will.
n.2: Oral communication is not a durable medium.
n.1: A durable medium need not be promotional.
n.4: Interactivity is not a feature of a durable medium.

q: A paraplanner is moving retail disclosures from paper to online delivery. Which approach would satisfy the FCA website conditions for replacing paper-based disclosure?
o: The firm posts the terms online without notifying clients
The firm allows access that expires after only 24 hours
The firm makes clients find the terms via search engines
The firm notifies clients, gains consent and ensures lasting access
The firm provides documents only to those who ask for them
w: Client notification, consent, and ongoing access are the core requirements for websites to qualify as durable mediums under COBS.

n.0: Posting without notification fails the website conditions.
n.1: Access expiring in 24 hours is not access for as long as needed.
n.4: Providing only on request does not meet notification duties.
n.2: Making clients search does not satisfy notification or access.

q: An adviser emails a client a PDF summary of key disclosures and asks compliance whether email counts. Why is email generally accepted as a durable medium under COBS?
o: Because emails are regulated separately from promotions
Because the content can be stored and reproduced unchanged
Because all electronic communications automatically qualify
Because email use is restricted to retail clients only
Because every email sent is automatically encrypted
w: Emails meet the durable medium definition as they can be stored and retrieved without alteration, offering a permanent record.

n.2: Not all electronic communications automatically qualify.
n.0: Separate regulation of emails is not why they are durable.
n.4: Emails are not automatically encrypted.
n.3: Email use is not restricted to retail clients.

q: A new adviser is checking which documents must be issued to a client in a durable medium. Which of the following is such an item?
o: Details of the firm's office decoration and layout
The firm's terms of business agreement with the client
General press releases issued to the news media
Internal staff job descriptions and their duties
The firm's advertising slogans and marketing taglines
w: Key contractual and disclosure documents, such as terms of business, must be given in a durable medium to ensure clients can access them reliably.

n.0: Office decoration details need not be given in a durable medium.
n.3: Internal job descriptions are not client disclosures.
n.2: Press releases are not durable-medium client disclosures.
n.4: Advertising slogans are not required in a durable medium.

q: A firm wants to provide its terms and periodic reports through its website rather than by post. Which condition must be met for such website disclosures to satisfy durable medium requirements?
o: Clients are notified in advance and can store the information
The site must offer an interactive live chat feature
The firm must have the FCA moderate the site daily
The content must appear in several different languages
The site must display promotional marketing banners
w: Durable medium conditions require notification and the ability for clients to access and retain the information in an unaltered form.

n.1: Live chat is not a durable-medium condition.
n.3: Multiple languages are not required.
n.4: Promotional banners are not a condition.
n.2: The FCA does not moderate firms' sites.

q: A firm's mobile app lets clients keep disclosures stored permanently within it. Why might this qualify as a durable medium under COBS?
o: Because the information can be retained and reproduced unaltered
Because apps always store all information fully offline
Because all mobile apps are automatically FCA-approved
Because apps are exempt from the website conditions
Because clients are unable to delete stored information
w: If the app allows clients to store and retrieve disclosures unchanged, it meets the durable medium standard under COBS.

n.2: Apps are not automatically FCA-approved.
n.1: Apps do not always store everything offline.
n.4: Durability does not depend on clients being unable to delete.
n.3: Apps are not exempt from durable-medium conditions.

q: A compliance officer compares sending a client a PDF against posting a notice on the firm's live website. Which factor makes the PDF more reliable for COBS disclosures?
o: It has an unlimited potential for wider distribution
It can always be opened without any internet connection
It can be shared easily across social media platforms
It is held by the client and cannot later be altered by the firm
It carries more colourful branding and company logos
w: Durability requires that the client can keep the information unchanged. A PDF file provided to the client achieves this, unlike a live website subject to edits.

n.4: Branding is irrelevant to durable-medium reliability.
n.1: Offline access is not what makes it more reliable for COBS.
n.0: Distribution potential is not the relevant durability factor.
n.2: Social-media sharing is unrelated to durable-medium status.

q: A firm plans to satisfy a disclosure requirement by posting the information on its own website. What is the main limitation of using a website as a durable medium?
o: Websites always require a paid subscription to view
Website disclosures are never legally binding at all
The firm controls the content and can alter it without notice
Websites cannot be accessed by clients outside the UK
Websites are prohibited outright under the COBS rules
w: Websites can be altered unilaterally, which is why conditions exist requiring notification and client access to information in a durable form.

n.3: Websites are accessible outside the UK.
n.0: Websites do not always require a paid subscription.
n.1: Website disclosures can be legally effective when conditions are met.
n.4: Websites are not prohibited under COBS.

q: During a file review the MLRO examines how disclosures were delivered to clients. Which situation is the clearest example of non-compliance with the website conditions?
o: Providing hard-copy disclosure documents to clients by post
Offering disclosures through a secure PDF portal with access codes
Sending clients an email with their signed contract attached
Posting disclosures online without notifying clients or gaining consent
Archiving the documents online with email alerts sent to clients
w: Without notifying clients and securing consent, simply posting information online fails to meet FCA Glossary website conditions.

n.2: An emailed attached contract meets the durable medium test.
n.0: Posted hard-copy disclosures are compliant.
n.1: A secure PDF portal with codes can satisfy the conditions.
n.4: Online archiving with email alerts meets notification duties.

q: A compliance officer is confirming who counts as a 'client' when the firm applies COBS 3.2. Which description best fits?
o: Any counterparty to a regulated mortgage agreement
Any ordinary member of the general investing public
Any person who merely reads a firm's financial promotion
Any person insured under a general insurance contract
A person to whom a firm provides designated investment services
w: COBS 3.2 defines a client as a person to whom a firm provides, intends to provide, or has provided designated investment business or ancillary services.

n.2: Simply reading a promotion does not make someone a client.
n.1: A general member of the public is not a client by that alone.
n.3: An insurance policyholder is an ICOBS matter, not a COBS client.
n.0: A mortgage counterparty is an MCOB matter, not a COBS client.

q: An adviser is unsure whether a prospective investor she is advising is already a 'client'. Under COBS 3.2, which of the following persons would be treated as one?
o: A retail shopper purchasing consumer goods
An unrelated individual reading the firm’s annual report
A prospective investor receiving advice from the firm
An employee under an HR benefits scheme
A borrower taking out a regulated mortgage
w: A prospective investor being advised is captured as a client under COBS definitions, as services are being provided or intended.

n.1: Annual report readers are not necessarily clients.
n.0: Consumer goods buyers are outside financial regulation scope.
n.4: Mortgage borrowers are clients under MCOB, not COBS.
n.3: Employees are not clients unless provided regulated investment services.

q: A firm is categorising the parties it deals with under COBS 3.2. Which of these does the client definition exclude?
o: A high-net-worth individual signing an advisory agreement
A professional investor acting under a discretionary mandate
An eligible counterparty acting purely as a market counterparty
A pension fund receiving portfolio management services
A retail investor receiving personal investment advice
w: When a firm treats a person as an eligible counterparty, that party is not considered a client for the purposes of the conduct rules in COBS.

n.4: A retail investor receiving advice is a client under COBS.
n.1: A professional investor under mandate is still a client.
n.3: A pension fund receiving management is a client.
n.0: An individual signing an advisory agreement is a client.

q: A trainee asks the compliance officer why it matters that someone is classified as a 'client' under COBS. What is the significance?
o: The person is restricted to wholesale business only
The person must be registered directly with the FCA
The person becomes entitled to specific conduct protections
The person must always act as an eligible counterparty
The person is entirely exempt from FCA regulation
w: Being a client under COBS brings entitlement to protections and conduct standards appropriate to the categorisation (retail, professional, or ECP).

n.4: Client status brings protection, it does not confer exemption.
n.1: Clients are not required to register with the FCA.
n.3: Being a client does not force eligible counterparty status.
n.0: Client status does not restrict a person to wholesale business.

q: A firm is reviewing several dealings to see which create client status under COBS. Which relationship would do so?
o: Distributing a general press release to journalists
Providing investment research tailored to an individual investor
Arranging a regulated residential mortgage loan
Selling a private motor insurance policy to a driver
Displaying an investment advertisement on a billboard
w: A firm providing personalised investment research or advice to an investor creates a client relationship under COBS.

n.0: A press release to journalists creates no client relationship.
n.4: A billboard advert does not, alone, create client status.
n.3: Selling motor insurance is ICOBS business, not a COBS client.
n.2: Arranging a mortgage is MCOB business, not a COBS client.

q: A firm is identifying which of its dealings involve a 'client' for COBS 3.2 purposes. Which of the following is an example of a client?
o: A newspaper reader glancing at an investment advert
A company issuing its own shares directly to the public
A consumer simply opening an instant-access savings account
A pension scheme receiving investment management services
A borrower entering into a regulated mortgage contract
w: The pension scheme is a client because it receives regulated investment services from the firm.

n.0: A reader glancing at an advert is not a COBS client.
n.2: Opening a savings account is BCOBS banking, not a COBS client.
n.4: A mortgage borrower is an MCOB matter, not a COBS client.
n.1: A company issuing its own shares is not a COBS client here.

q: A firm is deciding whether a person qualifies as a client under COBS 3.2. Which of the following is NOT required for someone to be treated as a client?
o: Having received or intended to receive investment services
Receiving portfolio management services
Reading promotional material without engaging the firm
Having executed trades through the firm
Entering into an advisory agreement
w: Mere exposure to promotional material does not create a client relationship under COBS unless services are being provided.

n.0: Service provision or intention to provide creates client status.
n.3: Execution of trades establishes client status.
n.4: Advisory agreements create a client relationship.
n.1: Portfolio management clearly establishes client status.

q: A compliance officer is training new staff on why the COBS 'client' definition matters to the firm. What is the key reason?
o: It lets the firm avoid its MiFID obligations entirely
It exempts the firm from all FSCS levy liability
It determines which conduct rules apply to each relationship
It permits the firm to skip all suitability checks
It ensures only UK nationals may receive services
w: The definition sets the scope of the rules, ensuring firms apply the right protections depending on whether a person is a client and what type of client they are.

n.1: The definition does not remove FSCS levy liability.
n.0: It does not let firms avoid MiFID obligations.
n.4: It has nothing to do with restricting services to UK nationals.
n.3: It does not let firms bypass suitability checks.

q: A paraplanner is checking the COBS definition of a 'client' before onboarding a prospect who has not yet traded. Which statement correctly summarises COBS 3.2?
o: A client is any person who happens to read one of the firm's financial promotions
Anyone the firm provides, intends to provide, or has provided investment services to
A client is only a person who has actually executed one or more trades with the firm
A client is only a person who is domiciled or resident within the United Kingdom
A client is only a person who falls within the retail client category
w: The COBS definition includes current, prospective, and past service recipients of designated investment business.

n.2: Intending clients are included; execution is not required.
n.4: Clients include professionals and eligible counterparties, not only retail.
n.0: Merely reading a promotion does not make someone a client.
n.3: Client status does not depend on UK domicile.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing who qualifies as a client under COBS. Which of the following would most clearly fall outside the definition of a client?
o: A professional investor party to a mandate
A corporate treasury department using execution services
A journalist reporting on an investment firm
A retail investor receiving portfolio advice
A pension fund under discretionary management
w: A journalist writing about a firm without receiving investment services is not a client. Clients are those to whom services are or will be provided.

n.3: Retail investors advised are clients.
n.1: Corporate treasuries using services are clients.
n.4: Pension funds under management are clients.
n.0: Professional investors receiving services are clients.

q: A new adviser at a wealth manager asks why the firm sorts every incoming client into a category before dealing. What is the core purpose of COBS 3.1 on client categorisation?
o: To guarantee that every client receives identical protections
To ensure firms apply the right conduct rules to each client type
To let firms opt out of all suitability requirements
To exempt firms from FCA oversight when facing professionals
To align the UK banking rules directly with ICOBS
w: COBS 3.1 sets the framework for categorising clients as retail, professional, or eligible counterparties, which determines the protections and rules that apply.

n.3: Categorisation does not exempt firms from oversight.
n.0: Protections differ by category; they are not identical.
n.4: Categorisation is unrelated to aligning banking with ICOBS.
n.2: It does not let firms opt out of suitability duties.

q: A firm treats retail, professional and eligible-counterparty clients differently. How does client categorisation affect the application of the COBS rules?
o: Client classification only affects the FSCS coverage level
The level of conduct protection varies with the client's classification
Every client receives an identical level of conduct protection
Retail clients may waive their classification without any effect
Client classification only matters for the client's tax treatment
w: The FCA sets varying levels of protection: retail clients receive the highest, professionals less, and ECPs the lightest conduct protections.

n.2: Protection varies by category, so it is not identical.
n.0: Classification affects far more than FSCS coverage.
n.4: Classification is not merely about tax treatment.
n.3: Changing classification has real consequences, not none.

q: A firm is onboarding a new client and setting their regulatory classification. Under COBS 3.1, which document must the firm provide before categorisation takes effect?
o: A full prospectus for each individual investment held
A PRIIPs key information document for every product
A written notice of their categorisation and its implications
A personalised suitability report for the client
An FSCS compensation scheme coverage factsheet
w: Firms must inform clients of their categorisation, explain the protections it affords, and outline the right to request re-categorisation.

n.0: A prospectus is not required for categorisation to take effect.
n.3: A suitability report is not the categorisation notice.
n.1: A PRIIPs KID is a product document, not a categorisation notice.
n.4: An FSCS factsheet is not the categorisation requirement.

q: A firm is categorising its clients under COBS 3 and lists the categories it recognises. Which of the following is NOT a formal FCA client category?
o: Retail client
High-net-worth client
Per se professional client
Eligible counterparty
Professional client
w: ‘High-net-worth client’ is not a formal COBS category. The FCA recognises retail, professional, and eligible counterparty classifications.

n.0: Retail client is a formal category.
n.4: Professional client is a formal category.
n.3: Eligible counterparty is a formal category.
n.2: Per se professional clients are defined within professional classification.

q: A new brokerage is setting up its onboarding process and must classify each incoming client. Why must firms categorise clients under COBS 3.1?
o: To determine a client's eligibility for FCA registration
To allocate clients to product distribution mailing lists
To apply proportionate rules and appropriate client protections
To decide which currency the client must transact in
To let firms charge professionals substantially higher fees
w: Categorisation ensures proportionate regulation by tailoring rules and protections to retail, professional, and eligible counterparty categories.

n.1: Categorisation is not about marketing distribution lists.
n.0: Clients do not need FCA registration; this is not the purpose.
n.4: Categorisation is not a mechanism for charging higher fees.
n.3: It does not dictate the transaction currency.

q: A professional client asks the firm to be treated as a retail client for greater protection. Which COBS rule permits a client to request re-categorisation?
o: MCOB 2.1
COBS 6.1
COBS 4.1
COBS 3.1
ICOBS 3.2
w: COBS 3.1 explicitly allows clients to request re-categorisation, subject to conditions and firm assessment of appropriateness.

n.2: COBS 4.1 covers promotions, not categorisation.
n.1: COBS 6.1 relates to disclosure of costs and charges.
n.0: MCOB applies to mortgages, not investment categorisation.
n.4: ICOBS 3.2 relates to insurance conduct rules.

q: A firm categorises a new customer under COBS 3.1 and considers the effect on its duties. How does that categorisation affect the firm's obligations?
o: It exempts the firm from its anti-money-laundering duties
It sets the firm's own regulatory capital adequacy levels
It sets which disclosure, suitability and reporting rules apply
It determines whether the firm must maintain a website
It decides whether the firm must be authorised by the PRA
w: Categorisation drives the conduct obligations under COBS, such as suitability for retail clients or limited requirements for eligible counterparties.

n.4: Categorisation does not determine PRA authorisation.
n.0: It does not exempt firms from AML duties.
n.1: It does not set the firm's capital requirements.
n.3: It does not decide whether a firm must have a website.

q: A client categorised as retail wants to understand their options over how the firm treats them. Which right does COBS 3.1 give the client in respect of categorisation?
o: To request re-categorisation and learn the protections lost or gained
To avoid every suitability assessment in all circumstances
To require the FCA itself to approve their categorisation
To opt out of the COBS conduct regime altogether entirely
To choose their categorisation on personal preference alone
w: Clients may request to be treated differently, but firms must assess appropriateness and explain the implications of changing category.

n.2: The FCA does not approve individual client categorisations.
n.4: Re-categorisation depends on tests, not preference alone.
n.3: Clients cannot opt out of the COBS regime entirely.
n.1: Clients cannot avoid all suitability assessments.

q: A firm is onboarding a new client and must categorise them at outset. What is the firm required to do at this point?
o: Obtain a suitability report from the client's other firm
Inform the client of their category and explain its impact
Automatically treat the client as a professional client
Seek FCA approval before classifying the new client
Classify the client on their account balance size alone
w: Firms must notify clients of their classification and the protections it entails under COBS 3.1, ensuring informed consent.

n.2: The default is retail, not automatic professional treatment.
n.4: Classification is not based on account balance alone.
n.3: FCA approval is not needed to classify a client.
n.0: A report from another firm is not required to classify.

q: A compliance officer is explaining how COBS 3.1 keeps client protection proportionate. Which statement best describes how it does this?
o: By exempting firms that categorise clients from their record-keeping requirements
By focusing its protections only on wholesale, and not retail, business
By allowing firms to categorise all of their clients as professionals for convenience
By varying obligations for retail, professional and eligible-counterparty clients
By mandating identical treatment and protections for every client regardless of type
w: COBS 3.1 ensures that the level of protection is calibrated to the sophistication of the client, with retail given the most protections.

n.4: Protection is proportionate, not identical for all clients.
n.2: Firms cannot simply categorise everyone as professional.
n.1: COBS protections extend to retail, not only wholesale, business.
n.0: Categorisation does not remove record-keeping duties.

q: A firm is deciding whether a new individual should be a retail client under COBS 3.4. Which description best fits a retail client?
o: A client who executes trades only on a regulated market venue
A corporate treasury holding well over EUR 20 million in assets
A client who is neither a professional client nor an eligible counterparty
A credit institution authorised under the CRD framework
A large institutional occupational pension fund scheme
w: Retail clients are defined as those not meeting the criteria for professional clients or eligible counterparties, receiving the highest regulatory protection.

n.0: Trading only on a regulated market does not make one retail.
n.1: A large corporate treasury is typically professional, not retail.
n.4: An institutional pension fund is a per se professional client.
n.3: A credit institution is a per se professional client.

q: A trainee asks why retail clients get the most conduct protection of any category. What is the reason?
o: Because they invest only in packaged retail products
Because they are presumed less experienced and knowledgeable
Because they always deal through professional clients
Because they are wholly exempt from the FCA's rules
Because they are subject to much lower transaction volumes
w: Retail clients are presumed to lack the expertise of professional or ECPs, so COBS provides them with maximum protections including disclosures and suitability.

n.4: Transaction volume is not the reason for the protection.
n.0: Retail clients are not limited to packaged products.
n.3: Retail clients are protected by, not exempt from, FCA rules.
n.2: Retail clients do not always deal through professionals.

q: A firm is categorising a new customer who is investing their own personal savings. Under COBS, which categorisation would this person normally receive?
o: A credit institution dealing in the wholesale market
An FCA-authorised investment management business
An individual investing their own personal savings
A large listed corporate meeting the professional size tests
A supranational organisation such as the World Bank
w: Individuals investing their savings fall under retail client categorisation unless they opt up and meet professional criteria.

n.0: A credit institution is a per se professional client.
n.1: An authorised investment firm is a per se professional client.
n.4: A supranational body is a per se professional client.
n.3: A large corporate meeting the size tests is professional, not retail.

q: An adviser is about to make a personal recommendation to a retail client. Which obligation applies specifically to advising retail clients under COBS?
o: Disclosure of the full costs and charges is optional
A simplified prospectus may be omitted entirely
The best execution obligation does not apply to them
The firm may simply assume the client's product knowledge
A suitability assessment must always be carried out
w: Suitability assessments are mandatory for retail advice, ensuring the recommended product meets the client’s objectives and risk tolerance.

n.3: Firms cannot assume retail clients' product knowledge.
n.2: Best execution does apply to retail client orders.
n.0: Cost and charges disclosure is required, not optional.
n.1: Required disclosures cannot simply be omitted for retail clients.

q: A private individual opens an account with an investment firm for the first time and no reclassification has taken place. What is this person's default client classification under COBS?
o: Retail client
High-net-worth professional
Institutional client
Professional client
Eligible counterparty
w: The FCA requires that individuals are treated as retail clients by default to ensure they receive maximum protections unless reclassified properly.

n.3: Professional status must be evidenced and agreed.
n.4: ECP is reserved for firms and certain institutions, not individuals by default.
n.1: ‘High-net-worth professional’ is not a formal FCA category.
n.2: Institutional is not a defined COBS category.

q: A firm is drawing up different service standards for retail and professional clients. How does the FCA's treatment of retail clients compare with that of professionals?
o: Retail clients face higher minimum investment thresholds
Retail clients have lighter disclosure rules than professionals
Retail clients get fuller disclosure and suitability requirements
Retail clients are exempt from the best execution rules
Retail clients must self-certify their own knowledge
w: Retail clients receive detailed disclosure, cost transparency, and suitability tests, reflecting their presumed lower knowledge base.

n.1: Retail clients get more, not lighter, disclosure.
n.4: Retail clients are not required to self-certify knowledge.
n.3: Best execution applies to retail clients.
n.0: There is no higher minimum investment threshold for retail clients.

q: A firm is comparing the protections owed to its retail clients with those owed to eligible counterparties. Which retail client protection is not typically extended to eligible counterparties?
o: The duty to act honestly, fairly and professionally
The rules on disclosing and limiting third-party inducements
The requirement to identify and manage conflicts of interest
The clear, fair and not misleading communication rule
A detailed suitability assessment and full risk disclosure
w: Retail clients benefit from suitability and disclosure obligations that are not required for eligible counterparties.

n.0: Acting honestly, fairly and professionally still applies to ECPs.
n.3: The clear, fair and not misleading rule still applies broadly.
n.2: Conflicts of interest rules still apply to ECP business.
n.1: Inducement rules continue to apply to ECP business.

q: A compliance officer reviews five prospective clients to set default categories. Which of these clients would always be treated as retail unless reclassified?
o: A MiFID investment firm
A large insurer managing its own funds
A government treasury department
A bank executing trades on behalf of clients
An individual investing in ISAs
w: Individual retail investors are classified as retail by default, unless formally opted up to professional under set criteria.

n.3: Banks are per se professional or eligible counterparties.
n.2: Government bodies are per se professionals.
n.0: MiFID firms are per se professional clients.
n.1: Insurers are per se professional clients.

q: A firm's default onboarding treats every new client as retail unless proven otherwise. Why is this the FCA's default position?
o: It reduces the compliance costs that firms must bear
It exempts retail clients from all AML identity checks
It promotes greater efficiency in the wholesale markets
It gives the greatest protection to those who most need it
It allows firms to limit their liability to clients
w: Defaulting to retail ensures that inexperienced investors get the maximum safeguards unless proven otherwise.

n.0: The default is about protection, not cutting firms' costs.
n.4: It does not exist to limit firms' liability.
n.2: It is not aimed at wholesale market efficiency.
n.1: Retail clients are not exempt from AML checks.

q: A firm is checking which of its account types can never fall within the retail client definition. Which of these client types is always outside it?
o: Employees using workplace ISAs
Small charities investing reserves
Pension savers in personal SIPPs
Individual retail investors
Authorised investment firms
w: Authorised investment firms are per se professional or eligible counterparties, not retail clients.

n.3: Individuals investing their savings are retail by default.
n.1: Charities are typically retail unless reclassified.
n.0: Employees using ISAs are retail.
n.2: Pension savers are treated as retail clients.

q: A discretionary manager is approached by someone acting as an agent on behalf of an underlying investor. Under COBS 2.4.1, whom should the firm treat as its client?
o: Both the agent and principal are treated as clients simultaneously
The firm may choose freely whether to treat the agent or principal as the client
Neither the agent nor the principal is considered a client
The agent is always regarded as the client
The underlying person represented by the agent is regarded as the client
w: COBS 2.4.1 clarifies that where a person acts as agent, the person represented by the agent is treated as the firm’s client for categorisation and protections.

n.3: The agent is not the client unless also receiving services for itself.
n.0: Dual treatment is not the default under COBS 2.4.
n.2: One party must be the client; it cannot be neither.
n.1: The firm does not have discretion to switch arbitrarily; rules specify the principal as the client.

q: A corporate treasurer places trades with a broker, acting as agent for the company that employs her. Under COBS, who is the broker's client?
o: No client exists in this scenario
The FCA
The treasurer personally
The company employing the treasurer
Both the treasurer and the company equally
w: The principal, in this case the company, is the client. The treasurer is acting as agent.

n.2: The treasurer personally is not the client.
n.4: Dual treatment is not recognised in this context.
n.1: The FCA is not a party to this client relationship.
n.0: A client always exists where services are provided.

q: A firm is instructed by an agent who is acting on behalf of an underlying principal. Which statement best reflects how COBS 2.4.2 treats this arrangement?
o: An agent is in every case to be categorised as a professional client
Agents are entirely exempt from the protections that COBS provides
An agent must be registered with the FCA before it is able to act
A firm may by default classify any agent as an eligible counterparty
Where an agent acts for a principal, the firm owes COBS duties to the principal
w: The rules ensure that the principal, not the agent, is recognised as the client in such cases.

n.0: Agent status does not automatically make the person professional.
n.2: Registration with the FCA is not a precondition to acting as agent.
n.1: COBS protections are not disapplied simply because an agent is involved.
n.3: There is no default eligible-counterparty classification for agents.

q: An investment adviser is instructed by a solicitor who is acting on behalf of a trust. Under COBS categorisation, who is treated as the client?
o: The trustee bank
The trust
The FCA
The solicitor personally
Both solicitor and trust
w: The trust, represented by the solicitor, is the client under COBS categorisation rules.

n.3: The solicitor is acting as an agent, not the client.
n.4: Dual treatment is not applied here.
n.2: The FCA is not a client in any transaction.
n.0: The trustee bank is not necessarily the client unless it is the principal.

q: A firm receives instructions from an agent acting for an underlying client. Why does COBS require the firm to identify the principal behind the agent?
o: So the firm can treat the agent as retail by default
So that the firm can avoid its best execution duties
So that the firm can bypass all suitability requirements
So the right level of protection and categorisation applies
So the agent bears responsibility for all client losses
w: Correct identification ensures the appropriate protections, disclosures, and obligations are applied to the ultimate client.

n.1: Identifying the principal is not to avoid best execution.
n.0: The firm looks through to the client, not treats the agent as retail.
n.4: It does not shift responsibility for losses onto the agent.
n.2: It is not a means to bypass suitability requirements.

q: A firm mistakenly treats an agent acting for an underlying principal as the client itself. What is the consequence of this categorisation error?
o: The firm becomes fully exempt from its COBS duties
The true client may not receive the appropriate protections
The agent gains its own right to FSCS compensation
The whole transaction becomes legally unenforceable
The FCA automatically voids the whole client agreement
w: If the agent is treated as the client, the actual principal could miss required protections under COBS, leaving the firm in breach.

n.4: The FCA does not automatically void the agreement.
n.0: The firm is not exempted from COBS; it may be in breach.
n.2: The agent does not thereby gain FSCS rights.
n.3: The transaction is not automatically unenforceable.

q: When an AR (appointed representative) acts as agent, who must the firm categorise under COBS?
o: Both the AR and its client jointly together
The AR's own principal firm as the client
The appointed representative itself as the client
The AR's own client, rather than the AR itself
The FCA itself, acting as the relevant client
w: The AR is acting as agent; the actual client of the AR is the party that must be categorised and protected under COBS.

n.2: The AR is the agent, not the client to be categorised.
n.0: Only the underlying client, not both parties, is categorised.
n.4: The FCA is a regulator, not the client.
n.1: The principal is not the client here; the AR's client is.

q: A firm looks past an agent to the ultimate person the agent acts for when categorising a client. Which scenario does this illustrate under COBS 2.4.3?
o: Where a firm looks through the agent to find the ultimate client
Where a firm may disregard the categorisation rules
Where a firm treats all parties as eligible counterparties
Where a firm classifies the agent as retail by default
Where a firm applies CASS in place of the COBS rules
w: COBS 2.4.3 reinforces that the ultimate person for whom the agent acts is the client, ensuring correct categorisation.

n.3: The firm identifies the ultimate client, not the agent as retail.
n.1: Categorisation rules cannot be disregarded.
n.2: Parties are not all treated as eligible counterparties.
n.4: CASS does not replace COBS categorisation rules.

q: A wealth manager takes instructions from a solicitor who is acting on behalf of a private individual. Who is categorised as the client under COBS?
o: The private client
Both lawyer and client
The lawyer
Neither party
The FCA
w: The lawyer is acting as agent; the private individual receiving advice is the client under COBS.

n.2: The lawyer is only an agent, not the client.
n.1: Dual classification does not apply here.
n.3: One party must be the client; it cannot be neither.
n.4: The FCA is regulator, not client.

q: An adviser deals with a person acting on behalf of another and must decide who the client is under the COBS agency rules. Why do these agent rules matter in practice?
o: Misidentifying the client can apply the wrong protections and cause regulatory breaches
Because they ensure the agent will always receive a fee for the introduction
Because the agent rules let firms avoid retail protections altogether
Because identifying an agent exempts the firm from the MiFID conduct rules
Because they mean that no suitability requirements apply to the transaction
w: Correct identification ensures appropriate application of disclosures, suitability, and protections. Misidentification could expose firms to breaches and sanctions.

n.2: The rules do not let firms avoid retail protections.
n.3: They do not exempt firms from MiFID conduct rules.
n.1: They do not guarantee the agent a fee.
n.4: Suitability rules still apply.

q: A retail client asks to be reclassified as professional to access more products. Under COBS 3.5.3, what must the client provide to be treated as an elective professional client?
o: A written request to opt up plus confirmation of understanding
A verbal agreement reached during a client meeting
An FCA-issued registration certificate for the client
Documentary proof of the client's UK tax residency
Evidence of an investment portfolio above GBP 1 million
w: Clients must provide a written request to be re-categorised as professional and confirm they understand the protections they may lose.

n.1: A verbal agreement is insufficient; the request must be written.
n.4: A GBP 1 million portfolio is not the elective professional test.
n.3: UK residency is not a condition for elective professional status.
n.2: No FCA registration certificate is issued to clients.

q: A firm is assessing whether a wealthy individual can be treated as an elective professional client under COBS 3.5.3B. Which of the following is one of the key tests it must apply?
o: A frequency of significant-size transactions over the past year
Holding a personal current account with a UK bank
Employment in any profession for at least five years
Being a member of an occupational pension scheme
Ownership of residential property within the UK
w: COBS 3.5.3B lists transaction frequency as one of the criteria firms must consider when assessing elective professional status.

n.2: General employment length is not the qualitative-test criterion.
n.1: Holding a UK bank account is irrelevant to the test.
n.4: Owning UK property is not part of the test.
n.3: Pension scheme membership is not a criterion.

q: A client asks to be treated as an elective professional. Which of the following must the firm assess before agreeing to this?
o: The client's personal credit score and credit rating
The client's expertise, experience and knowledge of investments
The client's nationality and their country of birth
The client's marketing and contact preferences
The client's marital status and family situation
w: Firms must be reasonably assured the client has expertise, experience, and knowledge to make investment decisions and understand risks.

n.2: Nationality is not part of the qualitative assessment.
n.3: Marketing preferences are irrelevant to the test.
n.4: Marital status is not assessed for professional status.
n.0: Credit score is not part of the qualitative test.

q: A firm applies the quantitative tests for elective professional status under COBS 3.5.3C. Which financial-instrument threshold is one of the cited criteria?
o: Minimum ISA holdings of £20,000
Mortgage borrowing exceeding £250,000
Annual salary exceeding £50,000
Portfolio value exceeding €500,000
FSCS coverage above £85,000
w: A client with a portfolio exceeding €500,000 may satisfy one of the quantitative tests for elective professional status.

n.2: Salary thresholds are not used as categorisation criteria.
n.1: Mortgage borrowing is not relevant to professional categorisation.
n.4: FSCS coverage limits are unrelated to categorisation.
n.0: ISA holdings alone do not determine client status.

q: A firm is about to re-categorise a client to a lower-protection status. What additional safeguard does COBS 3.5.3E require before doing so?
o: Prior approval obtained from the FCA for the change
A minimum annual income of at least GBP 100,000
A signed statutory declaration made by the client
Proof of at least three years' trading experience
A written warning from the firm about the protections lost
w: Firms must provide a clear written warning of the protections the client will lose and obtain confirmation of understanding before re-categorisation.

n.0: FCA approval is not required to re-categorise a client.
n.3: A fixed three-year trading requirement is not the safeguard here.
n.2: A statutory declaration is not the required safeguard.
n.1: There is no GBP 100,000 income threshold safeguard.

q: A firm is sorting new counterparties into per se and elective categories. Which of these is a per se professional client, needing no elective categorisation?
o: An authorised investment firm
An SME with fewer than 10 employees
An individual investor with a £600,000 portfolio
A pensioner investing £50,000 in ISAs
A high-net-worth individual
w: Firms and other authorised entities are classified automatically as per se professional clients under COBS 3.5.

n.2: This may qualify for elective professional, not per se professional.
n.4: High-net-worth status alone is not an FCA category.
n.3: Retail investors remain retail by default.
n.1: Small businesses do not automatically qualify as professional clients.

q: During a file review, a compliance officer checks the records kept for clients treated as elective professionals. Why must the firm retain those records?
o: To prove the client holds valid life insurance cover
To record the client's contact and marketing preferences
To provide evidence of the client's tax compliance
To monitor the firm's annual FSCS levy payments
To evidence compliance with the COBS 3.5 tests and consent
w: Firms must evidence that the criteria, warnings, and client confirmations required for elective professional categorisation have been met.

n.2: Records are not kept to evidence the client's tax compliance.
n.1: They are not kept to record marketing preferences.
n.3: They are unrelated to monitoring FSCS levy payments.
n.0: They are not kept to prove the client's insurance cover.

q: A retail investor asks to opt up to elective professional status, and the firm applies the COBS 3.5.3B tests. Which of the following is NOT one of those tests?
o: Experience in trading financial instruments
Owning a UK property valued above £1 million
Having worked in financial services for at least one year in a professional role
Carrying out an average of 10 significant transactions per quarter in the last year
Holding at least €500,000 in a portfolio
w: Property ownership is irrelevant to elective professional classification. The tests focus on financial expertise and experience.

n.4: Portfolio thresholds are part of the criteria.
n.2: Relevant industry employment is a valid test.
n.3: Transaction frequency is a recognised measure.
n.0: Trading experience is central to professional categorisation.

q: An experienced corporate treasurer, currently a retail client, asks to be treated as a professional. Why does COBS permit elective professional categorisation?
o: To ensure that all clients are able to access complex derivative products
To enable firms to place clients outside the scope of regulatory oversight
Some retail clients have enough knowledge and experience to be treated as professionals
To ensure that all high-net-worth individuals are automatically professional clients
To allow firms to reduce their disclosure obligations for every client
w: Elective professional categorisation acknowledges that some individuals or entities meet knowledge and experience standards comparable to per se professionals.

n.1: Elective categorisation does not remove regulatory oversight.
n.3: Wealth alone does not make a client automatically professional.
n.4: It does not reduce disclosure duties across the board.
n.0: It is not a mechanism to give everyone access to complex products.

q: A client asks the firm to treat them as an elective professional. What must the firm always explain before agreeing?
o: That the client must trade only through a UK exchange
That the client will now pay noticeably lower fees
That the client will gain new FSCS compensation cover
That the client will obtain useful tax advantages
The protections the client will lose against retail status
w: Firms must warn clients explicitly of the protections they will forgo when opting up to professional status, including suitability and disclosure rights.

n.1: Opting up does not guarantee lower fees.
n.2: Opting up does not add FSCS cover; it reduces protections.
n.3: There are no tax advantages from re-categorisation.
n.0: Opting up does not restrict trading to a UK exchange.

q: A large corporate wants to be treated as an elective eligible counterparty by a broker. Under COBS 3.6.4, what must it do to obtain that status?
o: Automatically qualify by holding EUR 500,000 in assets
Trade exclusively in derivative financial instruments
Be nominated for the status by another eligible counterparty
Request the categorisation in writing and get the firm's agreement
Register the elective categorisation directly with the FCA
w: A client must request elective ECP status and the firm must agree, ensuring the client understands the implications.

n.0: There is no automatic asset-threshold qualification for ECP status.
n.4: Clients do not register elective status with the FCA.
n.2: Nomination by another counterparty is not the route.
n.1: Trading only derivatives does not confer ECP status.

q: A firm wants to opt a counterparty up to elective eligible counterparty status. Which type of client may be treated this way under COBS?
o: A consumer purchasing general insurance
A professional client
A mortgage borrower
Any member of the public
A retail client by default
w: Only professional clients can be opted up to elective eligible counterparty status. Retail clients cannot be treated directly as ECPs.

n.4: Retail clients cannot be directly re-categorised as ECPs.
n.3: The general public are not automatically eligible.
n.2: Mortgage clients are categorised under MCOB, not COBS ECP rules.
n.0: Insurance consumers are governed by ICOBS, not ECP rules.

q: A firm wants to reclassify an existing client as an elective eligible counterparty. Which test must it satisfy before granting that status?
o: Confirming that the client earns over £100,000 annually
Confirming the client has traded at least 100 times in a year
Confirming the client has UK residency
Confirming the client has FSCS eligibility
Confirming that the client is already a professional client
w: A firm may only grant elective ECP status to a client already categorised as professional, ensuring a baseline of sophistication.

n.0: Income thresholds are not part of the ECP test.
n.2: Residency does not determine ECP eligibility.
n.1: Trading frequency is part of elective professional criteria, not ECPs.
n.3: FSCS eligibility is unrelated to categorisation as ECP.

q: A firm is classifying two sophisticated customers, one as an elective professional client and the other as an elective eligible counterparty. Why do COBS rules distinguish between these two categories?
o: Because ECPs are exempt from anti-money-laundering duties
Because ECPs get even fewer protections than professional clients
Because ECPs must always be established within the UK
Because ECPs are automatically retail clients in some cases
Because ECPs are required to pay much higher FCA levies
w: Eligible counterparties receive the lightest conduct protections, fewer than professional clients, so the classification requires stricter controls.

n.4: The distinction is not about FCA levies.
n.2: ECPs need not be UK-established.
n.0: ECPs are not exempt from AML duties.
n.3: ECPs are not automatically retail clients.

q: Which activities can be carried out with elective eligible counterparties under COBS?
o: Dealing on own account, executing orders, and receiving and transmitting orders
Providing regulated mortgage advice to individual borrowers
Providing cash ISAs to personal savers
Arranging regulated consumer credit loans
Offering retail general insurance products to consumers
w: ECP rules apply to core investment services such as execution and dealing. Consumer credit, mortgages, and insurance are outside COBS.

n.1: Mortgage advice is not an eligible-counterparty activity.
n.4: Retail insurance is outside eligible-counterparty business.
n.2: Cash ISAs are retail products, not eligible-counterparty activity.
n.3: Consumer credit lending is not within these activities.

q: A firm is moving a professional client up to elective ECP status. What safeguard must it provide before doing so?
o: A check of the client's minimum invested balance size
A test confirming the client's nationality and residence
A written warning explaining the loss of conduct protections
