An FCA certificate confirming the client's eligibility
A mandatory cooling-off period lasting fourteen days
w: Clients must be warned in writing about the protections they will lose when moving to elective ECP status, similar to elective professional re-categorisation.

n.3: The FCA does not issue eligibility certificates for this.
n.0: There is no minimum-balance check safeguard here.
n.4: No mandatory 14-day cooling-off period applies.
n.1: Nationality is not the relevant safeguard.

q: A compliance officer is checking which categories can be treated as elective eligible counterparties. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
o: Retail client
Corporate entity meeting professional criteria
Per se professional client
Professional client
Elective professional client
w: Retail clients cannot be classified directly as elective ECPs; only professional clients (per se or elective) may be opted up.

n.3: Professional clients can be treated as elective ECPs.
n.2: Per se professionals may elect to be ECPs.
n.4: Elective professionals may also be opted up to ECP.
n.1: Corporates qualifying as professionals may be treated as ECPs.

q: A corporate client asks to be reclassified as an elective eligible counterparty, and the firm considers why COBS restricts this so tightly. Why is elective ECP classification tightly controlled under COBS?
o: Because ECPs are entirely exempt from all FCA regulation
Because ECPs may trade only on UK-based trading venues
Because ECPs lose key protections like suitability and best execution
Because ECPs are automatically covered by the FSCS scheme
Because ECPs need FCA approval for every single transaction
w: ECPs receive the least protection; suitability and some disclosure requirements are disapplied, so firms must ensure clients are genuinely sophisticated.

n.0: ECPs are not exempt from all FCA regulation.
n.1: ECPs are not restricted to UK trading venues.
n.3: ECPs are not automatically covered by the FSCS.
n.4: ECPs do not need FCA approval for each transaction.

q: A firm agrees to treat a client as an elective eligible counterparty. What must the firm record when granting elective ECP status?
o: The client's signed waiver of all FSCS and ombudsman access rights
The client's salary, home address, and five-year investment returns
Written PRA approval confirming the counterparty reclassification decision
The client's request, the firm's consent, and warnings about lost protections
The client's tax residency and VAT registration number details
w: Firms must keep records of the client’s request, the firm’s consent, and the required warnings about reduced protections.

n.1: Personal financial data like salary is not the required categorisation record.
n.2: The PRA does not approve client categorisation; it is the firm's decision.
n.0: ECP status reduces protections but is recorded via request, consent and warnings, not a rights waiver.
n.4: Tax and VAT details are irrelevant to recording elective ECP status.

q: A firm proposes to treat a professional client as a retail client so they receive additional safeguards. Under COBS 3.7, what is meant by providing a client with a higher level of protection?
o: Treating every new client as an eligible counterparty by default
Assigning a client to a lower category to simplify the firm's compliance
Exempting professional clients from all disclosure and reporting duties
Removing FCA oversight for clients who request wholesale treatment
Treating a client in a category that gives greater safeguards than their default
w: COBS 3.7 permits firms to categorise clients at a higher protection level (e.g., treating a professional as retail), but never at a lower level without consent and tests.

n.1: Higher protection means moving up, not down to a lower-protection category.
n.3: Categorisation never removes FCA oversight.
n.2: Professional clients still receive disclosures; status does not exempt them.
n.0: ECP is the lowest protection level, the opposite of higher protection.

q: An experienced professional client asks to be treated as retail by the firm under COBS 3.7. Why might the firm agree to this re-categorisation?
o: To reduce the firm's own administrative burden in servicing the client
To exempt the client from the appropriateness test for complex products
To obtain a discount on the fees the firm pays to the FCA
To give stronger protections, such as suitability and fuller disclosures
To relieve the firm of its anti-money-laundering obligations for that client
w: A professional may be treated as retail to ensure they receive the fullest set of protections, particularly around advice and disclosure.

n.4: Re-categorising to retail does not affect AML obligations.
n.2: It does not reduce the firm's FCA fees.
n.1: It increases, not removes, protections such as appropriateness.
n.0: The purpose is stronger client protection, not less firm admin.

q: A firm is deciding how to categorise a client so as to give greater safeguards. Which of the following is an example of providing a higher level of protection?
o: Downgrading a professional to ECP to lower the firm's costs
Treating a small professional client as retail for suitability checks
Letting a client waive suitability and appropriateness requirements
Treating a retail client as an eligible counterparty for execution
Reclassifying a retail client as professional to reduce disclosures
w: Upgrading a professional to retail increases safeguards such as detailed disclosures and suitability tests.

n.3: Retail to ECP lowers protection, not raises it.
n.4: Retail to professional reduces safeguards, the opposite of higher protection.
n.2: Clients cannot waive suitability; this is not raising protection.
n.0: Professional to ECP reduces protection.

q: A client asks to be treated with more protection than his default categorisation provides. Who decides whether a client is given a higher level of protection?
o: The courts, through enforcement orders made against the firm
The relevant trade association overseeing the firm's sector
The firm, which may treat any client as belonging to a more protected category
The FCA, by issuing a special permission for each client
The client alone, by opting out of professional status at will
w: Firms have discretion to treat clients as more protected than their default categorisation. This is one-way only, from less to more protected.

n.3: The FCA does not issue per-client permissions for categorisation.
n.4: Higher protection is the firm's discretion, not a unilateral client opt-out.
n.0: Courts do not set client categorisation.
n.1: Trade associations have no role in client categorisation.

q: A compliance officer is justifying the firm's policy of treating certain professional clients as retail. What is a regulatory benefit of giving clients higher protection under COBS?
o: It removes the need for a complaint-handling procedure
It reduces the risk of client detriment by applying more stringent standards
It allows the firm to disapply MiFID conduct standards entirely
It guarantees the firm higher profitability on each account
It exempts the firm from FCA transaction reporting obligations
w: Applying stronger protections reduces regulatory and conduct risks, protecting the client and the firm’s compliance position.

n.4: Higher protection does not exempt firms from reporting.
n.2: MiFID standards cannot be disapplied by upgrading protection.
n.3: Protection level does not guarantee profitability.
n.0: Complaint handling is always required.

q: A paraplanner is checking the firm's client-categorisation policy against COBS 3.7. Which principle underpins the rule on higher client protection?
o: A firm must charge higher fees whenever it offers higher protection
A firm may exempt wholesale clients from all COBS conduct rules
A client can be upgraded automatically without the firm's knowledge
A firm may always offer more protection, but not less without a formal process
A firm must reduce protection whenever a client requests it
w: COBS permits firms to treat clients more protectively than required, but not the reverse without proper re-categorisation procedures.

n.4: Reducing protection requires tests and consent, not an automatic right on request.
n.2: Categorisation is a firm decision, not automatic without its knowledge.
n.0: There is no rule linking protection level to fees.
n.1: Wholesale clients are not exempt from all COBS rules.

q: A firm agrees to treat a professional client as retail at that client's request. What obligations then apply to the firm in dealing with them?
o: Exemption from the firm's best execution obligations
Automatic reclassification of the client as an eligible counterparty
No suitability testing, but enhanced FSCS compensation limits
Reduced reporting duties compared with genuine retail clients
Full retail conduct obligations, including suitability and disclosure
w: Once a professional is treated as retail, all obligations applicable to retail clients, such as detailed disclosure and suitability, apply in full.

n.2: Treating as retail adds suitability, it does not remove it.
n.3: Retail treatment means full, not reduced, reporting duties.
n.1: Retail treatment is the opposite of ECP status.
n.0: Best execution still applies to retail clients.

q: A firm decides to categorise a professional client as retail even though the client qualifies for professional status. Why might a firm choose to upgrade professional clients to retail in this way?
o: To avoid keeping any records of the client's categorisation
To escape the MiFID II product governance requirements
To exempt the firm from the FCA's Principles for Businesses
To manage compliance risk by applying the highest protection standards
To reduce the firm's operational and administrative costs
w: Providing higher protection reduces regulatory risk, since applying retail standards ensures compliance with the strictest requirements.

n.0: Upgrading increases record-keeping, it does not remove it.
n.2: The FCA Principles always apply.
n.4: Higher protection raises costs, it does not reduce them.
n.1: Product governance rules still apply.

q: A compliance officer wants a clear example of COBS 3.7 being applied correctly. Which of these scenarios demonstrates it in practice?
o: A corporate client is downgraded without consent
A bank is classified as ECP but treated as retail
A firm removes suitability checks for retail clients
An individual investor is classified as retail but treated as an eligible counterparty
A pension fund is classified as professional but treated as retail by the firm
w: Applying retail standards to a professional client increases protections, illustrating the use of COBS 3.7.

n.3: Treating retail as ECP reduces protections, not increases.
n.1: Banks as ECPs can be given more protection, but not less by default.
n.2: Removing suitability reduces protections, contrary to COBS 3.7.
n.0: Unconsented downgrades breach FCA rules.

q: A wealth manager decides to treat a professional client as a retail client to give them greater protection. What documentation and approach does the firm need to follow?
o: Seek prior approval from a relevant industry trade body
Record the decision and apply retail standards consistently to the client
Register the client with the PRA as a retail customer
Have the client sign a statutory declaration before a solicitor
Obtain an FCA certificate confirming the client's new category
w: Firms must document the decision to treat a client as more protected and then consistently apply the higher standard of conduct.

n.4: No FCA certificate is issued for categorisation.
n.2: The PRA does not register clients in this way.
n.0: Trade bodies do not approve categorisation.
n.3: No statutory declaration is required.

q: A firm is onboarding a client and reaches the categorisation step. According to COBS 3.3.1A, what must it do when first categorising the client?
o: Apply professional status automatically to every new client
Disclose the firm's FSCS levy contributions to the client
Register the client with the FCA as a retail investor
Notify the client in writing of their category and explain its implications
Provide the client with a PRIIPs key information document
w: Firms must inform clients of their categorisation and set out the protections it provides, in line with COBS 3.3.1A requirements.

n.0: The default is retail applied after notification, not automatic professional status.
n.2: Firms do not register clients with the FCA on categorisation.
n.4: A PRIIPs KID is product disclosure, not a categorisation notice.
n.1: FSCS levy details are not part of categorisation notification.

q: A trainee asks why the firm must send clients a categorisation notification under COBS. What is the reason?
o: To allow the firm to reduce the disclosures it must otherwise give
To exempt the firm from its best-execution obligations to the client
To enable the FCA to collect its periodic fees from the client
So clients understand their protections and right to request re-categorisation
To remove the need to carry out suitability tests for every client
w: The purpose of notification is transparency: clients must understand their categorisation and the right to request a different status if appropriate.

n.0: Notification does not reduce required disclosures.
n.1: It does not switch off best execution.
n.2: It is unrelated to FCA fee collection.
n.4: Suitability still applies where relevant.

q: A compliance officer is drafting the standard client categorisation notification. Which details must it include?
o: Confirmation of the client's eligibility to claim under the FSCS
The category applied, its implications, and the right to request re-categorisation
The client's tax residency status and national insurance number
A copy of the FCA's most recent annual report
The firm's own regulatory capital adequacy ratio
w: Notifications must set out the client’s category, what it means in terms of protections, and the right to request re-categorisation.

n.2: Tax residency and NI number are not part of the categorisation notice.
n.0: FSCS eligibility is separate from the categorisation notification.
n.4: The firm's capital ratio is not disclosed in the notice.
n.3: The FCA's annual report is irrelevant to categorisation.

q: A professional client asks a firm to re-categorise him as a retail client. Under COBS 3.3.1B, what must the firm do when acting on this request?
o: Reclassify the client as an eligible counterparty by default
Obtain the FCA's prior approval before the change takes effect
Provide a statutory auditor's confirmation of the client's status
File the change with the PRA within thirty business days
Notify the client in writing of the new category and its effects
w: Where re-categorisation occurs, firms must notify clients of the change and its consequences, fulfilling transparency requirements.

n.1: Re-categorisation does not require FCA approval.
n.3: No PRA filing is required.
n.0: Re-categorisation is not an automatic move to ECP.
n.2: No auditor confirmation is required.

q: A firm is about to notify a new individual client of the category it is being placed in. Which is the default category unless the client is properly re-categorised?
o: Eligible counterparty
Professional client
Institutional client
High-net-worth professional
Retail client
w: Retail is the default category, and firms must notify individuals accordingly unless proper re-categorisation is requested and approved.

n.1: Professional status must be formally opted into, not the default.
n.0: ECP is reserved for firms and certain institutions, not individuals by default.
n.2: Institutional client is not a formal FCA category.
n.3: High-net-worth professional is not a recognised category in COBS.

q: A firm is preparing the categorisation notice it issues under COBS 3.3. Which right must it inform the client of?
o: The right to be exempt from anti-money-laundering checks
The right to trade entirely outside UK regulatory oversight
The right to unlimited FSCS compensation on any claim
The right to request re-categorisation to a different client status
The right to waive every protection that COBS provides
w: Clients must be informed of their right to request categorisation changes, subject to meeting the relevant conditions.

n.0: AML checks cannot be waived.
n.4: Clients cannot waive all COBS protections.
n.2: FSCS compensation is capped, not unlimited.
n.1: Authorised firms' clients remain within UK regulation.

q: During an audit the firm is asked why it always notifies clients of their categorisation in writing. Why is written notification essential under COBS?
o: It replaces the need for any product disclosure documents
It allows the firm to market a wider range of products
It makes the client an eligible counterparty automatically
It provides evidence the client was informed of their category and protections
It exempts the firm from wider record-keeping requirements
w: Written records provide evidence of compliance and ensure clients understand the protections they are afforded.

n.1: Notification is about protection, not marketing scope.
n.0: Product disclosures are still required separately.
n.2: Notification does not change the client to ECP.
n.4: Record-keeping duties are not removed.

q: A broker sends a new investor a notice confirming they have been categorised as a retail client. Under COBS, what must be made clear to the client when notifying them of their categorisation?
o: That the client may only ever trade in pounds sterling
The consequences for the client's conduct protections and regulatory obligations
That the client must appoint an appointed representative
That the client is now exempt from all FCA oversight
That the client must invest solely in packaged products
w: The notification must explain the category’s consequences, including what protections apply or do not apply.

n.0: There is no requirement to trade only in sterling.
n.4: Clients are not restricted to packaged products.
n.3: Clients are never exempt from FCA oversight.
n.2: Clients need not appoint an appointed representative.

q: A firm has categorised its clients and notified them accordingly under COBS 3.3.1A/B. How should the firm document its compliance with these notification requirements?
o: Outsource all categorisation responsibility to a third party
Keep records of the notifications sent and client acknowledgements received
Publish the firm's categorisation policy in the FCA Handbook
Rely solely on verbal explanations given during meetings
Reconfirm each client's categorisation with the FCA annually
w: Firms must maintain records showing notifications were delivered and acknowledged, evidencing compliance.

n.2: Firms cannot publish in the FCA Handbook.
n.3: Verbal-only evidence does not meet record-keeping duties.
n.0: Responsibility cannot be outsourced away.
n.4: No annual FCA confirmation of categorisation is required.

q: A compliance officer is explaining the purpose of the categorisation notice to the board. What is its key regulatory objective?
o: Boosting the marketing of the firm's investment products
Collecting regulatory fees on behalf of the FCA
Simplifying the firm's product governance procedures
Streamlining the firm's anti-money-laundering compliance
Transparency and informed consent in the client relationship
w: Notifying clients ensures transparency and enables them to make informed decisions about whether to remain in or change category.

n.0: The objective is transparency, not marketing.
n.1: Firms do not collect FCA fees via categorisation.
n.3: Categorisation is unrelated to AML streamlining.
n.2: Product governance is a separate matter.

q: A MiFID firm is onboarding a client before starting investment services. What must it do regarding the client agreement?
o: Email only a summary, with full terms following within six months
Obtain a handwritten signature before making any initial contact
Record verbal consent by phone without sending anything in writing
Post a paper agreement within thirty days after the first trade
Provide the agreement in a durable medium before services start
w: MiFID firms must provide the client agreement in a durable medium before commencing services, setting out the essential terms of the service.

n.1: MiFID does not mandate a signature before contact.
n.3: The agreement must precede service, not follow the first trade.
n.0: Full terms cannot be deferred for six months.
n.2: Terms must be in a durable medium, not verbal only.

q: A client contacts a MiFID firm asking for a trade to be executed at once. When may the firm provide the client agreement immediately after starting the service?
o: If the client verbally agrees to waive all documentation
Whenever the firm is too busy to send the terms beforehand
Whenever the client is classified as an eligible counterparty
Whenever the service is discretionary portfolio management
When the client requests immediate execution via distance communication
w: If immediate service is requested using distance means that prevent prior provision, the agreement may follow immediately after commencement.

n.1: Firm workload is not a valid exception.
n.2: ECP status does not trigger the distance exception.
n.0: Documentation cannot be wholly waived.
n.3: Discretionary management is not itself the exception.

q: A firm is finalising a MiFID client agreement in a durable medium and the paraplanner queries whether the retail client must physically sign it. Which statement best describes signature requirements for MiFID client agreements?
o: A signature is not mandatory if the agreement is duly provided
No agreement is needed at all if recorded calls are kept
A signature is required only for complex instrument trades
A digital signature is compulsory for all professional clients
A wet-ink signature is compulsory for every retail client
w: MiFID focuses on provision in a durable medium with key terms; a client signature is not mandated by default.

n.4: No wet signature is mandated for retail clients.
n.3: No digital signature is mandated for professionals.
n.2: Signature rules do not turn on instrument complexity.
n.1: An agreement is still required regardless of call recordings.

q: A non-MiFID firm is about to conduct designated investment business for a retail client. How should it handle the client agreement?
o: Rely on website terms without notifying the client at all
Give a verbal summary only if the relationship is short
Send a brochure only after the first transaction settles
Enter into a written agreement before the business is conducted
Issue a fee schedule now, with full terms following later
w: For non-MiFID designated investment business to a retail client, a written client agreement must be in place before carrying on the business.

n.2: The written agreement must precede the business.
n.0: Unnotified post-trade material does not satisfy the rule.
n.4: Unnotified website terms do not satisfy the rule.
n.1: A verbal summary does not meet the written requirement.

q: A compliance officer is explaining why client agreements go out as emailed PDFs rather than casual notes. Why must they be provided in a durable medium?
o: To eliminate the firm's periodic reporting obligations
To ensure terms can be stored unchanged and later reproduced
To remove the need for any suitability assessment
To reduce the firm's printing and postage costs
To let the firm amend terms unilaterally without notice
w: A durable medium allows the client to store information unchanged and reproduce it, ensuring clarity and evidence of agreed terms.

n.3: Durable medium is about record integrity, not cost.
n.2: It does not remove suitability duties.
n.4: It does not permit silent unilateral changes.
n.0: Reporting obligations remain.

q: A firm is drafting a MiFID client agreement and checking the minimum content. Which of the following must it typically include?
o: Forecasts of guaranteed investment returns
A waiver of all client rights
Scope of services and costs/charges
Only the firm’s complaints email address
Detailed personal tax computations
w: The agreement should set out the service scope and costs/charges so clients understand what is provided and what they will pay.

n.0: Guaranteed returns are inappropriate, because agreements must present accurate terms and charges, not certainties.
n.4: Personal tax computations are beyond the minimum, because core terms and costs suffice.
n.1: Waiving all rights is incompatible with protections, because agreements must fairly set terms and costs.
n.3: A complaints email alone is insufficient, because scope and costs must be included.

q: A non-MiFID firm is onboarding a professional client and is deciding whether it must supply a written client agreement. When is it required to provide one?
o: Only after the first discretionary trade is executed
Always, before any contact is made with the client
When required by the firm's policy or the terms of the mandate
Never, because professional clients receive no documents
Only where complex instruments are being recommended
w: For non-MiFID business, written agreements are required for retail clients; for professionals, firms follow policy or mandate terms consistent with COBS expectations.

n.1: There is no rule requiring it before all contact.
n.0: It is not tied to the first trade.
n.3: Professionals do receive documents where relevant.
n.4: It is not limited to complex instruments.

q: A firm plans to deliver its MiFID client agreement electronically. Where may it be stored to meet the durable-medium requirement?
o: Only as a single paper original held at the branch
On a system where the client can store and reproduce it unchanged
On a public website with no notification to the client
In a dashboard that can edit the content silently later
Only as an audio recording of the onboarding phone call
w: Durable media include systems allowing clients to store and reproduce information unchanged, such as emailed PDFs or secure portals with download capability.

n.0: Durable media are not limited to a branch paper original.
n.2: Unnotified website posting is not durable provision.
n.3: Silently editable content is not a durable medium.
n.4: An audio-only recording does not meet the standard here.

q: A firm is reviewing which counterparties need a written client agreement for its non-MiFID business. Which client type is generally outside that requirement?
o: Retail clients
Eligible counterparties
Retail clients using execution-only services
High-net-worth retail clients
New-to-firm retail clients
w: Eligible counterparties are generally outside the non-MiFID written client-agreement requirement that is aimed at retail designated investment business.

n.0: Retail clients are the focus of the written requirement, because non-MiFID rules target them.
n.3: Wealth does not change retail status, because retail designated business still needs a written agreement.
n.4: Being new does not exempt documentation, because written agreements are required for retail designated business.
n.2: Execution-only does not remove the written requirement, because it still involves designated investment business to retail clients.

q: A MiFID client proceeds without signing the terms. How should the firm evidence the client's acceptance of those terms?
o: Retain durable-medium evidence of provision and the client's consent to proceed
Record a voicemail to the client stating the headline fees
Assume the client has consented once they log in online
Rely on internal meeting notes recorded by the adviser only
Send the terms to a generic shared company inbox
w: Firms should keep durable-medium evidence that terms were provided and that the client agreed to proceed under those terms.

n.3: Internal notes alone do not evidence client acceptance.
n.2: A login does not evidence acceptance of terms.
n.1: A fee voicemail does not evidence provision and consent.
n.4: Sending to a generic inbox is not provision to the client.

q: A client phones a MiFID firm to place an order there and then. When may the firm rely on providing the terms after the trade?
o: When prior provision is impossible on the call and the client requests execution
When the instrument being dealt in is a non-complex product
When the client is one who trades frequently with the firm
When the telephone call happens to take place outside business hours
When a third-party introducer, rather than the client, placed the order
w: If prior provision is not possible with the distance medium and the client requests immediate execution, terms may follow immediately after.

n.2: Frequent trading does not trigger the post-trade allowance.
n.3: The time of the call is not the test.
n.1: Non-complex status is not the relevant condition.
n.4: An introducer's involvement is not the test.

q: A MiFID client refuses to sign the terms of business but still wants trading to begin. What is the firm's duty in this situation?
o: Open the account but delay documentation indefinitely
Proceed if terms were provided in a durable medium and acceptance is evidenced
Refuse the service until a wet-ink signature is obtained
Take a deposit now and send the terms at year-end
Proceed relying only on the client's verbal request
w: MiFID does not mandate signatures; the firm should evidence durable-medium provision and the client’s acceptance before proceeding.

n.2: A wet signature is not required under MiFID.
n.4: A verbal request alone is not enough; durable evidence is needed.
n.0: Documentation cannot be delayed indefinitely.
n.3: Terms cannot be deferred to year-end.

q: A non-MiFID firm is about to carry out execution-only designated investment business for a retail client. Which statement aligns with the COBS rules?
o: A written client agreement must still be in place before the business
Only complex products require a written client agreement
No documentation is necessary for execution-only transactions
A factsheet sent after the trade replaces the agreement
A banner on the firm's website counts as the agreement
w: For non-MiFID designated investment business to retail clients, a written client agreement is required before conducting the business, even execution-only.

n.2: A written agreement is still required for retail designated business.
n.4: A website banner is not the agreement.
n.3: A post-trade factsheet does not replace it.
n.1: The requirement is not limited to complex products.

q: A firm is drafting a discretionary management agreement under MiFID. Which element should it include?
o: The client's full lifetime personal tax plan
A guaranteed minimum performance target for the portfolio
An annual permission letting the firm skip suitability
The mandate scope, the fee basis, and the reporting frequency
A clause excluding the firm's regulatory duties
w: Discretionary agreements document the mandate, fees, and reporting frequency to clarify authority and how the service will be delivered.

n.1: Firms cannot guarantee performance.
n.0: A lifetime tax plan is not a mandate element.
n.4: Regulatory duties cannot be excluded by clause.
n.2: Suitability cannot be waived by permission.

q: A firm intends to place its client terms on a website. How must it notify the client for this to satisfy the durable-medium rules?
o: Upload screenshots of the terms without any text access
Give targeted notice and ensure the client can store unchanged copies
Allow the marketing team to edit the terms freely
Rely only on a single link on the firm's homepage
Do nothing, since clients can find the terms themselves
w: Clients must be notified how to access and store terms in a form that can be reproduced unchanged, meeting durability expectations.

n.4: The client must be specifically notified.
n.3: A homepage link alone is insufficient.
n.2: Editable terms are not durable.
n.0: Non-reproducible screenshots do not meet the standard.

q: A MiFID firm is onboarding a professional client remotely. Which timing rule applies to providing the client agreement?
o: Provide the agreement first, unless distance constraints justify immediate post-commencement provision
Provide the agreement only after the first periodic report has been sent to the client
Provide the agreement after execution whenever the relevant market is volatile
Provide the client agreement within thirty working days of the service beginning
Provide terms only if the professional client specifically requests them
w: MiFID requires prior provision, with a narrow distance-communication exception permitting immediate post-commencement provision when prior delivery is impossible.

n.3: There is no thirty-working-day allowance; terms come before service save for the distance exception.
n.1: Terms are not deferred to after the first report.
n.4: Professional clients are still owed the agreement; it is not request-only.
n.2: Market volatility does not justify deferring terms.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing how categorisation affects agreement requirements. Which statement about client categorisation and agreements is accurate?
o: Elective professional status ends the MiFID provision duty
Retail status requires handwritten signatures for MiFID business
Eligible counterparty status requires a signed paper contract
Professional status removes all of the firm's documentation duties
Retail status strengthens the written agreement requirement under non-MiFID
w: Under non-MiFID, written client agreements particularly apply to retail designated investment business, reflecting higher protection needs.

n.3: Professional status does not remove documentation duties.
n.0: MiFID provision duties still apply to elective professionals.
n.2: ECP status does not mandate a signed paper contract.
n.1: MiFID does not require handwritten signatures for retail.

q: A MiFID firm takes on clients introduced by a third party. What must the firm still do regarding the client agreement?
o: Ensure the client still receives the firm's agreement in a durable medium
Replace the agreement with a terms webpage without notice
Skip provision entirely if the introducer is authorised
Rely on the introducer's own brochure as the agreement
Provide terms only once suitability has been assessed
w: Introducers do not displace duties; the firm must provide its client agreement in a durable medium to the client.

n.3: An introducer's brochure is not the firm's agreement.
n.2: An authorised introducer does not remove the firm's duty.
n.4: Terms come before service, not after suitability.
n.1: An unnotified webpage does not satisfy the duty.

q: A firm is deciding whether a proposed update warrants reissuing a client's MiFID terms of business. Which change would require it to issue updated terms?
o: A generic market outlook note added as an insert
An update to the firm's website colour scheme
A change to the firm's receptionist contact details
A minor branding refresh applied to the terms PDF
Material changes to the services or costs affecting the agreement
w: When material aspects of services or charges change, firms should provide updated terms so clients remain informed on the agreed basis.

n.3: Minor branding is not a material change.
n.2: Receptionist details are not material terms.
n.1: A colour scheme change is immaterial.
n.0: A market outlook insert is not a term change.

q: A non-MiFID firm upgrades a retail client to elective professional status. What should it confirm about the existing agreement?
o: That a handwritten signature is now mandatory for the client
That the prior retail terms become void automatically
That no documentation is needed from that point onward
That the documentation remains appropriate for the new categorisation
That the terms can be removed from the client portal
w: Following re-categorisation, the firm should ensure the agreement remains appropriate to status and services, updating as necessary.

n.2: Documentation is still required after re-categorisation.
n.0: No handwritten signature becomes mandatory.
n.4: Terms should not simply be removed.
n.1: Prior terms do not automatically void.

q: A MiFID firm needs to evidence that terms were provided in a durable medium before service began. Which item best does this?
o: PDF terms emailed to the client with explicit acceptance captured
A website link added without notifying the client
A voicemail left stating only the headline fees
An internal memo confirming the intention to send terms
A brochure handed to a member of the client's family
w: Emailed PDF terms, coupled with explicit acceptance, demonstrate provision in a durable medium before services commence.

n.2: A fee voicemail is not durable provision.
n.1: An unnotified link is insufficient.
n.3: An intention memo is not provision.
n.4: Handing terms to a relative is not provision to the client.

q: A non-MiFID firm is drafting a retail client agreement. What must it cover as a baseline?
o: A commitment that returns will be entirely tax-free
A disclaimer removing the client's right to complain
The services to be provided and the basis of the firm's remuneration
Predicted outperformance of the portfolio versus benchmarks
An irrevocable power of attorney over the client's affairs
w: Non-MiFID retail agreements must set out service scope and remuneration so clients understand the nature and cost of the service.

n.3: Firms cannot predict outperformance.
n.1: Complaint rights cannot be removed.
n.4: An irrevocable power of attorney is not a baseline term.
n.0: No tax-free return commitment can be given.

q: A wealth manager is moving a portfolio client from a commission basis to an ongoing percentage fee. When must the firm re-issue the client agreement to reflect this fee model change?
o: After the first invoice using the new fees is sent
Before applying the new charging basis to the client
Never, provided the website displays the change
Only at the client's next scheduled annual review
Only if the client raises a complaint about the fees
w: Material changes like fee model updates must be communicated in durable form before they take effect for the client.

n.3: Notice must precede the change, not wait for annual review.
n.0: It must be before, not after, the first new invoice.
n.2: A website display is not enough.
n.4: A complaint is not the trigger.

q: A MiFID firm onboards a client via live chat, a distance medium. Which approach satisfies the requirement before trading begins?
o: Paste the fees into the chat without the full agreement
Execute the first trade and email the terms the following week
Link to the homepage with no storage instructions given
Provide a downloadable agreement in-chat and capture consent before trading
Send a marketing flyer in the chat and then proceed
w: Providing a downloadable agreement in the chat and capturing explicit consent ensures durable provision and documented acceptance before trading.

n.1: Terms must come before trading, not a week later.
n.4: A flyer is not the agreement.
n.0: Fees alone are not the agreement.
n.2: A bare homepage link is not durable provision.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing whether unsigned non-MiFID retail agreements are valid. Which statement about signatures is correct?
o: Only complex products require any client signature
A wet-ink signature is compulsory for every retail client
A signature is not universally required; the focus is a written agreement
Professional clients must always sign the terms electronically
A signature can replace providing the written terms
w: Non-MiFID rules require a written agreement for retail designated business; they do not universally mandate a specific signature form.

n.1: No wet signature is universally required.
n.3: Electronic signature is not mandatory for professionals.
n.4: A signature does not replace providing terms.
n.0: Signature rules do not turn on product complexity.

q: A firm executed a MiFID trade before sending the terms. Which factor determines whether this post-commencement provision was allowed?
o: The length of time the client has already been with the firm
Being unable to provide terms first because of the distance medium and the client's urgent request
The level of liquidity in the relevant market on that particular day
The length of the settlement cycle applicable to the instrument
The workload of the dealing desk during a busy trading period
w: Post-commencement provision is only allowed when prior delivery is impossible due to the distance medium and the client requests immediate execution.

n.0: Client tenure does not trigger the post-commencement allowance.
n.2: Market liquidity is not the relevant test.
n.4: Desk workload does not justify post-commencement provision.
n.3: The settlement cycle is not the determining factor.

q: A MiFID client tells the firm they will not accept electronic delivery of the terms. What should the firm do?
o: Ask the introducer to send their own brochure instead
Place a trade now and post the terms later that month
Proceed to service without providing any documentation
Send a link to the firm's homepage legal footer
Provide a paper durable copy before service, or use the distance exception
w: The firm must still provide terms in a durable medium—paper if requested—before service or immediately after under the narrow distance exception.

n.2: Documentation is still required.
n.1: Terms cannot be deferred to later in the month.
n.3: A legal-footer link is not durable provision.
n.0: An introducer brochure does not satisfy the duty.

q: A firm serves clients who communicate in more than one language. Which statement best fits the MiFID language requirements in a client agreement?
o: Provide documents only in English whatever the client's preference
State that arranging translation is entirely the client's responsibility
State the languages in which the client may communicate and receive documents
Rely on machine-translated terms without telling the client
Offer only oral staff translations instead of documents
w: Agreements should specify available communication languages so clients understand in which language services and documents will be provided.

n.0: Firms must state available languages, not force English only.
n.3: Undisclosed machine translation is not compliant.
n.4: Oral translation does not replace documents.
n.1: Translation is not simply the client's burden.

q: A MiFID firm offers a bundled service combining advice and custody and is drafting the client agreement. Which practice aligns with COBS for documenting the bundle?
o: Provide the costs only on the firm's website ticker
List the components without stating the service scope
Break down the components and disclose the aggregate cost in the agreement
Describe the bundle but withhold the costs until invoicing
Provide only the annual name of the bundle
w: Client agreements should describe service components and associated costs clearly so clients understand the bundled service and charges.

n.3: Costs cannot be withheld until invoicing.
n.0: A website ticker is not adequate cost disclosure.
n.1: Scope must be stated.
n.4: A bundle name alone is not disclosure.

q: A MiFID firm plans to deliver its terms of business to clients through a secure online portal rather than by post. How should the firm properly document a client's consent to receive these terms this way?
o: Use a pop-up that disappears without being logged
Provide view-only pages that cannot be downloaded
Rely on the introducer's confirmation of consent alone
Record the client's explicit opt-in and provide downloadable, unalterable copies
Assume consent as soon as the client registers online
w: Firms should capture explicit opt-in and ensure the client can download and store unchanged copies, meeting durable-medium standards.

n.4: Registration is not explicit consent.
n.0: An unlogged pop-up does not evidence consent.
n.1: View-only pages are not durable.
n.2: An introducer's word is not the client's consent.

q: A MiFID firm is planning when to give a client information on the nature and risks of the service and the designated investments. Under COBS 2.2A, when must this be provided?
o: Only upon the client’s written request
When the client upgrades to professional status
Within 30 days after the first transaction
In good time before providing the service
At the end of the first reporting period
w: MiFID requires firms to give clients appropriate information about the nature and risks of the service and of the designated investments in good time before providing the service, so the client can make informed decisions.

n.2: Post-transaction delivery is too late, because the client must be informed before services are provided.
n.0: Provision is mandatory; it does not depend on a client request, because pre-service disclosure is a firm obligation.
n.4: Periodic reports come later; they do not replace pre-service disclosures, because clients need information upfront.
n.1: Client categorisation does not remove the timing requirement, because MiFID still expects pre-service disclosure for professionals (proportionately).

q: A MiFID firm is preparing the pre-service information pack for a retail client about to invest in a designated investment. Which item must be included in the pre-service disclosures?
o: A waiver of the client's statutory rights
The material risks of the investment and the relevant risk warnings
Only the instrument's legal ISIN code
A forecast of expected future market returns
A guaranteed illustration of the investment's future performance
w: MiFID pre-service information must describe the nature of the product and its material risks using fair, clear and not misleading language so clients understand potential losses and volatility.

n.4: Guaranteed illustrations are prohibited.
n.3: Return forecasts are not the required risk disclosure.
n.0: Statutory rights cannot be waived.
n.2: An ISIN alone is not adequate disclosure.

q: A firm is about to provide MiFID investment services to a new client. What is required regarding costs and charges before the service is provided?
o: Only the firm's headline management fee percentage
An ex-ante disclosure of all costs and charges, including third-party payments
A verbal fee summary with no durable record kept
Deferred disclosure where the product is non-complex
A generic range of fees provided after the first report
w: MiFID requires ex-ante disclosure of all costs and charges in good time before the service, covering the firm’s fees and any third-party payments, to enable comparability and informed consent.

n.0: All costs must be shown, not just the headline fee.
n.4: Disclosure must be ex-ante, not after the first report.
n.3: Non-complex products do not defer cost disclosure.
n.2: A durable record is required, not a verbal summary.

q: A non-MiFID investment firm is onboarding a new advisory client under COBS 2.2 and 6.1.1-4. Which statement about its information duties is correct?
o: Give appropriate pre-service information about the firm, its services and the risks
No pre-service information is needed where the client is dealt with on an execution-only basis
Providing a link to the firm's homepage is sufficient to meet the duty
Only clients categorised as professional require written pre-service information
The required information may be provided after the client's first trade has settled
w: For Non-MiFID designated investment business, COBS 2.2 and 6.1.1-4 require firms to give clients appropriate information in good time before business, covering who the firm is, what it will do, and the risks involved.

n.1: Execution-only clients still require appropriate information.
n.4: Information is provided before service, not after the first trade.
n.2: A homepage link is not adequate pre-service information.
n.3: The duty is not limited to professional clients.

q: A firm serves retail, professional and eligible-counterparty clients. How should its risk disclosures be calibrated under MiFID?
o: All clients must receive identical risk text for every service
They should be appropriate and proportionate to the client type and service
Retail clients should get less detail to avoid confusing them
Professional clients require no risk disclosures at all
Eligible counterparties must receive the most granular detail
w: MiFID expects firms to provide information that is appropriate for the client’s category and the service offered, ensuring clarity without omitting material risks.

n.2: Retail clients generally need more, not less, detail.
n.3: Professionals still receive appropriate risk disclosure.
n.4: ECPs receive the least, not the most, detail.
n.0: Disclosure is tailored, not identical for all.

q: A paraplanner is drafting pre-service information and must meet the 'fair, clear and not misleading' standard. Which of the following best describes that standard?
o: Balanced, accurate disclosure that avoids exaggeration and concealment
Reliance on past performance as a predictor of future returns
Complex technical jargon used to demonstrate expertise
Marketing-led wording that emphasises the product's benefits
Selective use of risk factors chosen to support the sale
w: Both MiFID and Non-MiFID regimes require pre-service information to be fair, clear and not misleading, meaning balanced presentation of features, costs and risks without omissions or undue prominence.

n.3: Benefit-led marketing bias breaches the standard.
n.2: Jargon that obscures meaning is not clear.
n.4: Selective risk disclosure is misleading.
n.1: Past performance is not a reliable predictor.

q: A firm is onboarding a client for a discretionary portfolio management service under MiFID and prepares the pre-service disclosures. Prior to providing the service, which information is required?
o: Only the name of the appointed custodian for the portfolio
A statement that risks are minimal due to diversification
The nature and risks of the mandate, the costs and charges, and reporting
The client's full personal tax projections for the year
A guarantee that the portfolio will outperform its benchmark
w: Before starting discretionary management, firms must explain the nature and risks of the service, give ex-ante costs and charges, and set expectations for reporting so clients understand how the service operates.

n.0: The custodian name alone is insufficient.
n.4: Outperformance cannot be guaranteed.
n.3: Tax projections are not the required disclosure.
n.1: Diversification does not make risks minimal.

q: A wealth firm's compliance officer is drafting the product literature a non-MiFID client will see before an investment service begins. Under COBS 2.2, what must that information achieve?
o: Enable the client to reasonably understand the product's nature and risks
Be restricted to legal terms and definitions only
Be provided only after suitability has been assessed
Maximise sales conversions through persuasive messaging
Exclude any cost implications to keep it concise
w: COBS 2.2 expects firms to give sufficient, balanced information so clients can reasonably understand a product’s nature, risks and implications before proceeding.

n.3: The aim is understanding, not conversions.
n.1: Information is not limited to legal terms.
n.2: Information comes before, not only after, suitability.
n.4: Costs must be included, not excluded.

q: Before providing a MiFID investment service, a firm gives a client its costs and charges disclosure. How should those costs and charges be presented?
o: Aggregate all costs and charges and show their cumulative effect on returns
Refer to a generic pricing webpage without figures
Disclose only the entry and exit fees to the client
Provide only separate line items with no overall total
Promise to include the totals in the first periodic report
w: MiFID ex-ante disclosures should aggregate costs and charges and illustrate their cumulative effect on returns so clients can compare and assess value.

n.3: A cumulative total is required, not line items alone.
n.2: Entry and exit fees alone are incomplete.
n.1: A figure-free webpage is inadequate.
n.4: Totals come before service, not in the first report.

q: A Non-MiFID discretionary firm is preparing pre-service information for a new client under COBS 14.3.1-10. What pre-service expectation is connected to the firm's later reporting?
o: Setting clear expectations about the service and how and when information will be reported
Advising the client at the outset that no reports of any kind will be sent
Promising that the client's risk profile will be reassessed only once a year
Requiring the client to prepare and draft their own valuation statements
Guaranteeing that the portfolio will deliver positive performance every month
w: Pre-service information should help clients understand the service and the expected form and frequency of information they will receive, aligning with subsequent client reporting obligations.

n.4: Firms cannot guarantee monthly positive performance.
n.1: Clients must receive reporting; not none.
n.2: A once-a-year-only reassessment promise is not the pre-service expectation.
n.3: The firm, not the client, prepares statements.

q: A MiFID firm receives commission from a product provider. When must it disclose these inducements and third-party payments to the client?
o: Only for retail clients, never for professionals
Ex-ante, before providing the service
Only if the client asks in writing
After the first suitability report is sent
Within 12 months after the service
w: MiFID requires disclosure of inducements and third-party payments in good time before providing the service, so the client can assess conflicts and true costs.

n.4: Twelve months later is far too late, because clients must know inducements before agreeing to services.
n.2: Disclosure is mandatory regardless of client request, because transparency is a firm obligation.
n.0: Professionals also require disclosure, although level of detail may be proportionate.
n.3: Suitability reports do not substitute for ex-ante inducement disclosures.

q: A firm is preparing pre-service disclosures for a complex financial instrument under MiFID. What must these disclosures include?
o: An exemption from risk disclosure for professional clients
Only a general statement that investments can fall in value
A forecast of the high expected returns on the instrument
A promise that risks are minimal if the product is held long-term
A clear explanation of risks such as leverage, illiquidity, and total loss
w: MiFID requires detailed, comprehensible risk disclosures for complex instruments, covering features like leverage, liquidity constraints and possible total loss.

n.1: A generic statement is not enough for complex products.
n.2: Return forecasts are not risk disclosure.
n.3: Long holding does not minimise risk.
n.0: Professionals are not exempt from risk disclosure.

q: A compliance officer is drafting the firm's conflicts disclosure to clients. What does COBS 2.2A require it to contain?
o: Disclosure made only to the firm's retail clients
Disclosure that may be omitted for experienced clients
No disclosure at all provided the firm keeps a conflicts policy
A summary of conflicts, the nature of the risks, and mitigation steps taken
Detailed disclosure given only after a conflict has arisen
w: Firms must provide a clear summary of conflicts, the nature of risks posed, and steps taken to manage them, so clients can decide whether to proceed.

n.2: A policy does not remove the disclosure duty.
n.0: Conflicts disclosure is not limited to retail.
n.4: Disclosure comes before, not only after, a conflict.
n.1: Experience does not remove the duty.

q: A non-MiFID firm is disclosing the downside of a designated investment. How should it explain the risk of loss?
o: Provide the risk detail solely for derivative products
Avoid mentioning loss so as not to deter the client
State only that values can fluctuate from day to day
State that losses are automatically reimbursed by the FSCS
Make clear that the client may lose some or all of the money invested
w: Non-MiFID disclosures must clearly set out the risk of loss so clients understand they may lose some or all invested capital.

n.1: Loss must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.2: Daily fluctuation alone understates the risk of loss.
n.0: Risk detail is not limited to derivatives.
n.3: The FSCS does not automatically reimburse investment losses.

q: An adviser asks compliance what 'good time' means for pre-service information under MiFID. Which statement best describes it?
o: Only when the client is about to make a formal complaint
Immediately after a marketing brochure has been sent
Sufficiently early for the client to consider it before being bound
Any time before the firm's first regulatory report is due
After executing a transaction but within one week of it
w: Good time means providing information early enough that clients can read and understand it before being bound to the service or investment.

n.3: Good time is before commitment, not before a report.
n.4: It must be before, not after, execution.
n.1: It is not tied to sending a brochure.
n.0: It is unrelated to complaints.

q: A non-MiFID firm is setting out its charges to a client under COBS 6.1. How should it present these cost disclosures?
o: Deferred until the end of the firm's financial year
In small-print footnotes appended after the signed contract
Orally only, during the firm's initial client meetings
By quoting industry averages rather than the actual charges
Clearly and in a durable medium, detailing the nature and amount of remuneration
w: Non-MiFID firms must disclose the nature and amount of remuneration clearly and in durable form before providing services.

n.2: Oral-only disclosure is not durable.
n.1: Post-contract small print is not adequate.
n.3: Actual charges, not averages, must be disclosed.
n.0: Disclosure cannot be deferred to year-end.

q: A firm is offering a MiFID packaged product that uses leverage. Which disclosure duty applies?
o: Give only marketing language emphasising the growth potential
Defer the explanation until after the first loss occurs
Explain how leverage works and its potential for amplified losses
Simply provide the packaged product's ISIN code
Promise that leverage boosts returns with no downside
w: MiFID requires firms to explain clearly how leverage works and that it can magnify both gains and losses, including the risk of losing more than the initial investment.

n.3: An ISIN is not a leverage explanation.
n.4: Leverage has downside; no no-downside promise is valid.
n.0: Marketing language is not risk disclosure.
n.1: Explanation must precede, not follow, losses.

q: A firm is drafting its pre-service disclosures on how it will report to clients. What does COBS 14.3 require regarding periodic reporting?
o: Reports may be withheld whenever the client seems satisfied
No disclosure of the reporting arrangements is required
Reports may be sent at random intervals without any notice
The frequency may be omitted when the client is professional
Clients must be told in advance the form, content, and frequency of reports
w: COBS 14.3 links pre-service disclosure to client reporting; clients must know how, when and what information will be reported to them.

n.0: Reports cannot be withheld on satisfaction.
n.3: Frequency is disclosed for professionals too.
n.1: Reporting arrangements must be disclosed.
n.2: Random unnotified reporting is not permitted.

q: An adviser is recommending an overseas fund priced in a foreign currency. Under MiFID, how should the firm explain currency risk?
o: Highlight that exchange-rate moves can raise or lower returns and capital
Assure the client that the currency risk is negligible
Defer disclosure until the first exchange-rate move occurs
Omit currency risk entirely for professional clients
State only that all returns are quoted in pounds sterling
w: Firms must explain that exchange rates can materially affect returns and capital value so clients appreciate the risks of cross-border investments.

n.4: Quoting in sterling does not disclose the risk.
n.1: Currency risk is not negligible.
n.2: Disclosure precedes, not follows, FX movements.
n.3: Professionals are not exempt from this disclosure.

q: A non-MiFID advisory firm earns commission that could sway its recommendations. Under COBS 6.1.4, what conflicts duty applies?
o: Inform clients of conflicts and remuneration structures that may create bias
Conflicts need not be disclosed where they appear minor
Disclose conflicts only if the FCA specifically requests it
Avoid disclosure wherever it might reduce the firm's sales
Disclose conflicts only to retail clients, not professionals
w: Non-MiFID firms must tell clients about conflicts and remuneration structures that could influence the service, supporting fair decision-making.

n.1: Even minor conflicts must be disclosed, not judged away.
n.4: Conflicts disclosure is not retail-only.
n.2: It is not contingent on an FCA request.
n.3: Sales impact is not a reason to withhold.

q: A MiFID firm will hold client assets as part of its service. Which rule applies to the information it must give about safeguarding those assets?
o: State only that the assets are safe, without any detail
Refer clients to generic FCA webpages instead of disclosing
Disclose nothing about custody unless the client asks
Provide the details only after the first annual audit
Explain how assets are held, including custody arrangements and protections
w: MiFID requires firms to give clients clear pre-service information on how their assets will be safeguarded, including custody arrangements and investor protections.

n.2: Custody must be disclosed proactively.
n.3: It cannot wait for the first audit.
n.0: A bare assurance is not adequate.
n.1: Generic webpages do not replace disclosure.

q: A financial planning firm doing Non-MiFID business is preparing a client agreement and asks its compliance officer what COBS 6.1 requires it to tell clients about commissions. What must be disclosed?
o: Only the commission rates that exceed five percent
The nature and the amount of commission the firm or associates receive
That commissions exist, but not their actual amount
Nothing at all where the commission is paid by third parties
Commissions disclosed only within the firm's periodic reports
w: Non-MiFID rules require firms to disclose clearly the nature and amount of commissions received in relation to the client service, in good time before provision.

n.2: The amount, not just existence, must be disclosed.
n.0: There is no five-percent threshold.
n.3: Third-party commissions must still be disclosed.
n.4: Disclosure comes before service, not only in reports.

q: A firm plans to deliver its MiFID pre-service information electronically. What condition must be met for this to be valid?
o: Electronic delivery removes the need for accuracy
Electronic provision always suffices with no conditions attached
The firm may alter the content without notifying the clients
Clients must consent and the format must allow durable storage and reproduction
Provision is valid only once the client prints the file
w: Electronic delivery is valid if clients consent and the format allows them to store the information unchanged and reproduce it in the future.

n.1: Conditions of consent and durability apply.
n.2: Silent alteration is not permitted.
n.0: Accuracy is always required.
n.4: Validity does not depend on the client printing it.

q: An adviser is preparing an ex-ante cost illustration for a MiFID client. Which element must the disclosure show about the cumulative charges?
o: Only the firm's initial upfront fee for the service
Nothing at all where the charges are relatively small
The overall effect of the costs and charges on the investment return
Only the performance fee, where one actually applies
A generic estimate that is not tied to the client
w: MiFID requires ex-ante cost disclosures to show not just each charge but their overall cumulative effect on returns, so clients see total impact.

n.0: The initial fee alone is incomplete.
n.3: Performance fees alone are incomplete.
n.4: A generic estimate is not client-specific.
n.1: Small charges must still be disclosed.

q: A non-MiFID firm is preparing the disclosures it gives about itself under COBS 2.2. What must these include?
o: The firm's name, its regulatory status, and its contact details
Only the firm's registered trading name for the service
No details at all of the firm's authorisation status
Just the address of the firm's registered office
A marketing strapline with no factual information
w: COBS 2.2 requires firms to provide clients with clear information on the firm’s identity, regulatory status, and contact details before services begin.

n.1: The trading name alone is insufficient.
n.3: The office address alone is insufficient.
n.2: Authorisation status must be given.
n.4: A strapline is not factual disclosure.

q: A client's structured product changes materially in the risks it carries partway through the relationship. Under MiFID, when must the firm update its risk disclosures?
o: Only when the underlying product ceases trading
Never, once the first disclosure has been provided
When material changes arise in the nature of the service or investment
Only if the FCA writes to the firm about it
Only at the client's annual review meeting
w: If the nature or risks of the service or investment change materially, firms must update disclosures so clients remain accurately informed.

n.1: Disclosures must be updated on material change.
n.3: It is not triggered by an FCA letter.
n.4: It is not limited to the annual review.
n.0: It is not limited to product delisting.

q: A non-MiFID firm is recommending a product that may be hard to sell later. How should it explain the illiquidity before service?
o: Say that liquidity risk applies only to retail clients
Describe liquidity only where the product is listed
Give the detail only after the client first has difficulty
Avoid mentioning liquidity to encourage the client to invest
State clearly that the client may be unable to sell or may face large costs
w: Non-MiFID rules require fair disclosure of material risks, including illiquidity, so clients know they may not be able to sell easily or may face high exit costs.

n.3: Illiquidity must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.1: It is not limited to listed products.
n.2: Disclosure precedes, not follows, difficulty.
n.0: Liquidity risk is not retail-only.

q: A firm wants to show a fund's track record in its MiFID pre-service documents. Which rule applies to presenting past performance?
o: Performance information is banned under all circumstances
Only the product's positive performance history should appear
Past performance may be shown fairly, over five years, with clear warnings
The firm may guarantee that past performance will continue
Warnings may be omitted where the client is professional
w: MiFID permits past performance data if presented fairly, with appropriate context and warnings that it is not a reliable indicator of future results.

n.3: Past performance cannot be guaranteed to continue.
n.1: Selective positive-only history is misleading.
n.0: Performance data is permitted, not banned.
n.4: Warnings apply to professionals too.

q: A non-MiFID firm is setting out its reporting arrangements at outset under COBS 14.3. How must the periodic statement obligations be framed?
o: Defer any explanation until after the first year
No disclosure is needed; the reports can simply be ad hoc
Send the reports solely when the client demands them
Disclose upfront how often statements are issued and what they cover
Provide only the client's cash balance in each report
w: Non-MiFID firms must tell clients before service what form, frequency, and content of reports they will receive, aligning expectations with later delivery.

n.1: Upfront disclosure is required, not ad hoc reporting.
n.4: A cash balance alone is inadequate.
n.2: Reporting is not purely on-demand.
n.0: Explanation cannot be deferred a year.

q: A firm is preparing pre-service disclosures for a derivative product. How should it explain counterparty risk?
o: State only that the relevant market is well regulated
Avoid discussing counterparty failure to reduce the client's concern
Clarify that the client could suffer loss if the counterparty defaults
Say default risk applies only in rare crises and can be ignored
Explain default risk only after a counterparty has failed
w: Pre-service disclosures should explain counterparty risk clearly so clients understand they may lose value if the contracting party fails to meet obligations.

n.1: Counterparty risk must be disclosed, not hidden.
n.0: Market regulation does not remove counterparty risk.
n.3: Default risk cannot be dismissed as ignorable.
n.4: Disclosure precedes, not follows, a default.

q: A MiFID wealth manager is onboarding a client for a discretionary portfolio service. What must the firm disclose to the client before it begins providing that service?
o: A forecast of guaranteed returns on the portfolio
Only a brief marketing statement about the service
The types of financial instruments involved and the associated risks
That any losses on the portfolio will be covered by the firm
Only the address of the appointed custodian for the account
w: COBS 6.1ZA requires firms offering discretionary management to provide detailed information about the types of financial instruments, strategies, and risks before providing the service.

n.4: The custodian address alone is insufficient.
n.0: Guaranteed returns cannot be forecast.
n.3: Firms do not cover client losses.
n.1: A marketing statement is not adequate disclosure.

q: A brokerage offers an execution-only dealing service where clients place their own orders online. Which MiFID disclosure duty still applies to the firm?
o: Disclose only to the firm's professional clients
Disclose everything only after the trade has been confirmed
Disclose the costs and charges, the risks, and the nature of the service
No disclosure is required because the client makes the decision
Disclose only the name of the product being traded
w: Execution-only services still require firms to provide clients with information on costs, charges, and risks before executing, even though suitability is not assessed.

n.3: Disclosure is still required for execution-only.
n.4: A product name alone is insufficient.
n.0: Disclosure is not professional-only.
n.1: Disclosure precedes, not follows, the trade.

q: A MiFID firm is taking on a discretionary mandate. What additional information must it disclose about the manager's authority?
o: That the manager has unrestricted power to trade without oversight
The extent of the discretion and any limits or objectives agreed
That client involvement in the decisions is not allowed
That no investment limits are possible under MiFID rules
That any limits will be disclosed only if they are breached
w: MiFID requires firms to clarify the scope of the manager’s mandate, including investment limits and objectives, so the client understands the extent of discretion granted.

n.0: Discretion has agreed limits, not unrestricted power.
n.3: Limits are permitted under MiFID.
n.4: Limits are disclosed upfront, not only on breach.
n.2: Client-agreed objectives are expected.

q: A Non-MiFID firm is setting out its fees and third-party payments to a prospective client under COBS 6.1.6. How should these costs and charges be disclosed?
o: Only in relation to services with a value above fifty thousand pounds
Only the firm's headline commission rate, with other charges omitted
Clearly, in good time before the service, covering firm remuneration and third-party payments
Only orally, and only after the first investment has actually been executed
After the end of the client's first full financial year with the firm
w: COBS 6.1.6 requires Non-MiFID firms to disclose the nature and amount of remuneration, including third-party payments, in good time before the service.

n.3: Disclosure must be in good time before service, not after the first trade.
n.0: There is no fifty-thousand-pound threshold.
n.1: All costs and charges must be covered, not just a headline rate.
n.4: Disclosure is not deferred to the year end.

q: A firm is onboarding a client for a managed account under MiFID. What must it tell the client about reporting frequency?
o: That reports will be issued at random, unannounced intervals
That the client must request each report individually
Only that periodic reports will exist at some point
How often statements will be sent and what they will include
That reports are optional for professional clients
w: COBS requires firms to inform clients before providing a management service about the form, frequency, and content of periodic reports.

n.2: The frequency and content must be specified.
n.0: Random reporting is not compliant.
n.1: Reports are not purely on request.
n.4: Reporting is not optional for professionals.

q: A MiFID firm offers certain instruments on an execution-only basis. What duty applies when providing information about those instruments?
o: Provide no details at all for professional clients
Explain whether the instrument is complex and provide risk information
Promise that execution-only removes all of the risk
Disclose only where the instrument later loses value
Wait until after the first settlement cycle to disclose
w: Firms must inform execution-only clients about the nature of the instrument, including whether it is complex, and provide appropriate risk disclosures before trading.

n.3: Disclosure is not contingent on a loss.
n.0: Professionals still receive relevant information.
n.2: Execution-only does not remove risk.
n.4: Disclosure precedes, not follows, settlement.

q: A MiFID firm is drafting its safeguarding disclosure under COBS 6.1ZA.10. Which information is required about the safeguarding of client assets?
o: Only the firm's most recent annual external audit report
Nothing, provided the client is categorised as a professional client
A marketing statement describing the expected growth of the assets
Information on custody, asset protection, and the risks of holding with third parties
A blanket assurance that the client's assets are always completely safe
w: COBS 6.1ZA.10 requires firms to provide clients with information on safeguarding arrangements, custody, and risks of holding assets with third parties.

n.0: The audit report is not the required safeguarding disclosure.
n.1: The duty is not removed for professional clients.
n.4: A blanket safety assurance is inadequate.
n.2: A growth marketing statement is not safeguarding information.

q: A Non-MiFID firm is setting up an execution-only dealing service and asks compliance what it must disclose to clients beforehand. What disclosure does COBS 6.1 require?
o: Information on the nature of the service, the costs, and the risks beforehand
Only the costs must be disclosed after the trade settles
Disclosure is required only where a complaint is later made
No disclosure duties apply to execution-only business at all
Only the name of the product traded need be disclosed
w: COBS 6.1.6 requires Non-MiFID firms to disclose information about the nature of execution-only services, the costs, and associated risks before executing trades.

n.3: Disclosure duties do apply to execution-only.
n.1: Disclosure comes before, not after, settlement.
n.4: A product name alone is insufficient.
n.2: It is not triggered by a complaint.

q: Before it begins managing a new client's portfolio, a MiFID firm sends details of its conflicts of interest policy. Why is this required?
o: Because the FCA requires the policy to appear only within marketing brochures
In order to discharge the firm's anti-money-laundering obligations
Solely to protect the firm itself from potential liability to the client
So clients understand how conflicts are managed and whether they accept the risk
So that clients can be asked to waive all of their conflict-of-interest protections
w: MiFID requires firms to disclose their conflicts of interest policy and, if necessary, summarise specific conflicts so clients can make informed decisions before service begins.

n.4: Disclosure is not a route to waiving all protections.
n.0: The policy is not confined to marketing material.
n.1: Conflicts disclosure is unrelated to AML obligations.
n.2: Its purpose is client understanding, not just firm protection.

q: A MiFID firm offers both discretionary management and execution-only services and is drafting its onboarding pack. Which statement best describes its pre-service disclosure duty across both service types?
o: Cost information may be withheld until it is set out in the client's first periodic report
Both must give clear, fair, not misleading information on nature, risks, costs and safeguards first
Only retail clients are entitled to receive the required information in a written, durable form
Execution-only business removes the obligation to provide any pre-service disclosure to the client
Management services need no disclosure at all provided the client is categorised as professional
w: Both discretionary management and execution-only services require pre-service disclosure of nature, risks, costs, and safeguards in a fair, clear, not misleading manner, tailored to client type.

n.3: Execution-only still requires appropriate information; it does not remove all disclosure.
n.4: Professional clients still require relevant pre-service information.
n.2: Durable-medium disclosure is not limited to retail clients.
n.0: Costs must be disclosed in good time before the service, not deferred to the first report.

q: A MiFID portfolio manager plans to outsource part of a client's mandate to a third party. What must it disclose to the client about this delegation?
o: Disclose the delegation only after a loss has occurred
Disclose delegation only where it exceeds half of the assets
Tell clients if parts of the mandate are delegated and describe safeguards
Omit the delegation details for the firm's professional clients
Provide no information unless the delegate is based overseas
w: MiFID requires firms to tell clients if parts of portfolio management are delegated to another entity and explain the associated safeguarding measures.

n.4: Delegation is disclosed regardless of location.
n.0: Disclosure precedes, not follows, a loss.
n.3: Professionals are told about delegation too.
n.1: There is no fifty-percent threshold.

q: A firm is onboarding a MiFID client for discretionary portfolio management. What information about valuation must it give the client?
o: Nothing about valuation need be disclosed before service
That the client must calculate the valuations themselves
That valuations are confidential to the custodian alone
How the portfolio's investments will be valued and how often
Only an assurance that the valuations will be accurate
w: COBS requires disclosure of valuation methods and frequency before providing discretionary management so clients understand how their investments will be assessed.

n.4: A bare accuracy assurance is insufficient.
n.0: Valuation method and frequency must be disclosed.
n.1: The firm, not the client, values the portfolio.
n.2: Valuations are not withheld from the client.

q: A client uses a firm's execution-only service to buy a complex product. Under MiFID, what must the firm explain to the client about appropriateness assessments?
o: That execution-only is available only for complex products
That suitability is instead assessed after the trade
That appropriateness applies only where the client is retail
That the firm guarantees the product is suitable for the client
That no appropriateness or suitability assessment is carried out
