w: Clients must be told that no suitability or appropriateness assessment is performed when they use execution-only services, placing responsibility for the decision on the client.

n.3: Execution-only involves no suitability guarantee.
n.1: Suitability is not assessed after the trade.
n.2: The point is no assessment, not a retail-only one.
n.0: Execution-only is not limited to complex products.

q: A MiFID portfolio manager is preparing its pre-service disclosures. Which information must it provide about the investment strategies it will use?
o: No disclosure of strategy is needed before service
Only the target return percentage for the portfolio
Information on the strategies used, the risks, and the instrument types
Only the name of the chosen performance benchmark
That strategies may be changed without informing the client
w: MiFID requires portfolio managers to disclose the strategies they may employ, the associated risks, and the types of instruments they will use before providing the service.

n.1: A target return alone is insufficient.
n.3: A benchmark name alone is insufficient.
n.0: Strategy must be disclosed pre-service.
n.4: Material strategy changes must be communicated.

q: A firm conducting non-MiFID business receives commission from a product provider for placing client business. Under COBS 6.1.6, how must the firm disclose this remuneration to the client?
o: In a durable medium, before the service, including its nature and amount
Omitted where the remuneration is under one hundred pounds
Only in small print at the back of the firm's brochure
Only if the FCA specifically asks the firm to disclose it
Verbally, after the first transaction has been completed
w: Non-MiFID firms must disclose in a durable medium, in good time before the service, both the nature and amount of remuneration, including inducements.

n.2: Small print in a brochure is not adequate durable disclosure.
n.4: Disclosure is before service, not after the first transaction.
n.1: There is no de minimis threshold for remuneration disclosure.
n.3: It is not contingent on an FCA request.

q: A firm is onboarding a managed-account client under MiFID. What must it explain about custody of the client's assets?
o: Who holds the assets, the risks of third-party custody, and how assets are protected
The custody arrangements only once the client has made a complaint
The custody arrangements only where the custodian is located overseas
Only a general assurance to the client that the assets are safe
Nothing, on the basis that custody is not relevant to client disclosures
w: MiFID requires firms to disclose custody arrangements, including who holds the assets, risks of third-party custody, and protections in place before service.

n.3: A bare assurance of safety is inadequate.
n.4: Custody is relevant and must be explained.
n.2: Disclosure is not limited to overseas custodians.
n.1: Disclosure is proactive, not triggered by a complaint.

q: A firm offers an execution-only service in a complex derivative to a walk-up client. What disclosure duty does MiFID impose in this situation?
o: Warn the client that appropriateness must be assessed before the trade
Guarantee that the client will not lose any money
Disclose nothing at all because it is execution-only
Provide only the product's ISIN code to the client
Omit the warning where the client is experienced
w: If execution-only involves complex instruments, the firm must assess appropriateness and warn the client if the product is not appropriate, before executing.

n.1: No no-loss guarantee can be given.
n.4: Experience does not remove the appropriateness test.
n.3: An ISIN alone is insufficient.
n.2: Complex execution-only still needs an appropriateness assessment.

q: A firm is preparing the disclosures it gives to new non-MiFID clients under COBS 6.1.6. What must it tell clients about its regulatory status?
o: That the firm is authorised and regulated by the FCA or relevant authority
That the firm has traded profitably in recent years
That the firm is expanding into several new markets
That the firm's head office is located in central London
That the firm has been in business for over ten years
w: COBS 6.1.6 requires firms to disclose their regulatory status and authorisation so clients know the protections they are afforded under FCA oversight.

n.1: Profitability is not a regulatory disclosure.
n.4: Longevity is not the required disclosure.
n.3: Location is not the required disclosure.
n.2: Expansion plans are not required disclosure.

q: A MiFID firm is setting out the costs of its portfolio management service. Which duty applies to disclosing those costs?
o: Disclose only the annual management charge after the first year
Provide ex-ante disclosure of all fees, commissions, and charges before service
Defer disclosure until the first quarterly report is issued
Disclose the retail fees but not the professional fees
Aggregate the fees only once the first trade has occurred
w: MiFID requires portfolio managers to give clients full ex-ante disclosure of all fees, commissions, and charges before starting the service, for transparency and comparability.

n.0: All charges are disclosed ex-ante, not after a year.
n.3: Fees are disclosed regardless of category.
n.2: Disclosure is not deferred to a quarterly report.
n.4: Aggregation is before, not after, the first trade.

q: A client wants to deal on an execution-only basis under MiFID. What must the firm tell them about its responsibility?
o: That the firm assumes full liability for all market losses
That execution-only removes all of the client's protections
That the firm does not assess suitability or appropriateness for non-complex products
That the firm guarantees the outcome of each trade
That execution-only applies only to derivative products
w: Clients using execution-only services must be told the firm does not assess suitability or appropriateness for non-complex products, clarifying the limits of responsibility.

n.3: No trade outcome is guaranteed.
n.0: The firm does not assume market-loss liability.
n.4: Execution-only is not derivatives-only.
n.1: Protections are not all removed.

q: A MiFID discretionary manager is preparing pre-service disclosures for a new portfolio client. What must the firm disclose about the benchmark it will use to manage the portfolio?
o: That the benchmark is disclosed only after the first year
That benchmarks are not relevant to any pre-service disclosure
Only the name of the benchmark, without any context
The benchmark chosen, why it was selected, and how it measures performance
That the portfolio's performance will always exceed the benchmark
w: COBS 6.1ZA requires portfolio managers to disclose the benchmark they will use, the reasons for its choice, and how it will be applied to assess performance.

n.2: The name alone lacks required context.
n.4: Outperformance cannot be promised.
n.1: Benchmarks are relevant and disclosed.
n.0: Disclosure is not deferred a year.

q: A MiFID discretionary manager is setting up periodic reporting for a new managed account. Which duty applies to the firm regarding these periodic reports?
o: Report only to retail clients, and not to professionals
Send the reports at irregular, unannounced intervals
Provide the reports only if the client requests them
Inform clients upfront about the content and the timing of the reports
Send reports only after the client has complained
w: Firms must disclose in advance the form, content, and frequency of periodic reports, aligning client expectations with regulatory reporting obligations.

n.2: Reporting is not purely on request.
n.1: Irregular unannounced reporting is not compliant.
n.0: Professionals receive reports too.
n.4: Reporting is not triggered by complaints.

q: A Non-MiFID firm is about to take on a new client for its portfolio management service. Under COBS 6.1.6, how must it disclose the relevant information to that client?
o: Rely on the firm's website terms without notifying the client
Provide written details of the services, costs, risks, and custody beforehand
Defer any written disclosure until after six months
Provide only oral information at the point of the first trade
Provide only the product names, with no risk detail
w: COBS 6.1.6 requires Non-MiFID firms to provide written, pre-service disclosures covering nature of services, costs, risks, and custody, ensuring clients are informed before proceeding.

n.3: Oral-only at first trade is insufficient.
n.0: Unnotified website terms do not satisfy the duty.
n.2: Written disclosure cannot be deferred six months.
n.4: Product names alone lack risk detail.

q: A stockbroker onboards a client who only wants to place their own trades with no advice. Under MiFID, what must the firm disclose about the scope of this execution-only service?
o: That execution-only lets the firm avoid all disclosure duties
That the firm will only execute orders without giving advice or management
That the firm will monitor the portfolio's ongoing performance
That the firm guarantees the suitability of all trades
That execution-only is available only for derivatives
w: Clients must be told execution-only means the firm executes orders without providing advice or management, so responsibility for the investment choice rests with the client.

n.3: No suitability guarantee is given.
n.2: The firm does not monitor in execution-only.
n.4: It is not derivatives-only.
n.0: Disclosure duties still apply.

q: A MiFID firm holds client assets in an omnibus custody account. Why must it disclose the risks of doing so?
o: Because using an omnibus account guarantees the client a higher rate of return
Because omnibus accounts are always fully insured by the FCA against loss
Because the custody arrangement makes no practical difference to the client
Because holding assets in an omnibus account removes the need for periodic reporting
Assets may be pooled, exposing clients to the default risk of another client's custodian
w: Omnibus custody accounts may pool client assets, and firms must disclose the risks, such as exposure to third-party default or shortfalls in segregation.

n.0: Omnibus accounts do not guarantee higher returns.
n.3: Reporting obligations remain regardless of custody structure.
n.2: Custody arrangements do affect client risk.
n.1: The FCA does not insure omnibus accounts.

q: A MiFID portfolio manager receives payments and benefits from third parties in connection with managing client portfolios. What disclosure duty applies to these inducements?
o: Disclose inducements only where they exceed five hundred pounds
Inform clients ex-ante of all third-party payments and benefits received
Disclose inducements only at the end of each tax year
Disclose inducements only to the firm's retail clients
Avoid disclosing inducements to protect the firm's competitiveness
w: MiFID requires ex-ante disclosure of all inducements and third-party benefits received in connection with portfolio management, to ensure transparency and manage conflicts.

n.0: There is no five-hundred-pound threshold.
n.3: Inducements are disclosed regardless of category.
n.2: Disclosure is ex-ante, not year-end.
n.4: Competitiveness is not a reason to withhold.

q: A non-MiFID firm offers a service that is narrower than clients might assume. Under COBS 6.1.6, what must it tell them about these limitations?
o: That any limitations on the service are confidential
That the service may be restricted in scope, and what those limits are
That disclosing service limitations is entirely optional
That the firm may do anything it wishes with the mandate
That limitations apply only to the firm's retail clients
w: Non-MiFID firms must disclose any limitations on their services before providing them, ensuring clients understand scope and restrictions of what is offered.

n.3: Scope limits must be disclosed, not open-ended.
n.0: Limitations are disclosed, not confidential.
n.4: Limitations are not retail-only.
n.2: Disclosure is required, not optional.

q: A MiFID portfolio manager may use leverage within the mandate. Which information about leverage must it disclose?
o: The possibility of amplified gains and losses and the impact of margin calls
That leverage risk applies only to derivative products
That leverage guarantees the client higher returns
That any losses from leverage will be reimbursed by the firm
That leverage need not be mentioned before service
w: Clients must be told how leverage affects portfolios, including that it can amplify both gains and losses and create obligations to meet margin calls.

n.2: Leverage does not guarantee higher returns.
n.1: Leverage risk is not derivatives-only.
n.4: Leverage must be disclosed pre-service.
n.3: Firms do not reimburse leverage losses.

q: A firm offering an execution-only service must make clear to clients where responsibility for the decision lies. What disclosure about client responsibilities must be given?
o: That execution-only exempts the firm from all disclosure
That the client is responsible for assessing suitability where no advice is given
That the firm guarantees the suitability of every trade
That responsibility for the decision rests with the FCA
That the client bears no responsibilities whatsoever
w: Clients must be informed that when they choose execution-only, they assume responsibility for assessing suitability because the firm does not provide advice.

n.2: No suitability guarantee is given.
n.4: The client does bear responsibility.
n.3: The FCA does not assume the client's decisions.
n.0: Disclosure duties are not removed.

q: A MiFID firm is setting out how it will report to a managed-account client. Which duty applies to disclosing the client reporting arrangements?
o: Disclose the reporting arrangements only after a full year of service has elapsed
Send reports to the client only in periods when the portfolio underperforms
Explain the reporting arrangements only to clients categorised as retail
Explain the form, content and timing of reports, including valuation and transactions, first
Provide no information about reporting until the first report actually arrives
w: MiFID requires firms to explain reporting arrangements pre-service, including how portfolios will be valued, what content reports will contain, and how often they will be issued.

n.4: Reporting arrangements are explained before service, not withheld until the first report.
n.2: The duty is not confined to retail clients.
n.1: Reports are not sent only on underperformance.
n.0: Disclosure is not deferred for a year.

q: A MiFID firm is drafting the safeguarding disclosure it gives clients under COBS 6.1ZA.9. What must it tell them?
o: That all assets are automatically protected by the FSCS
Only the annual audit results of the custody accounts
How designated investments are held, including custody and protections
Nothing at all unless the client specifically requests it
That safeguarding rules apply only to the firm's retail clients
w: MiFID requires firms to disclose to clients how their designated investments will be held, including custody arrangements and investor protections, so they understand how assets are safeguarded.

n.1: Audit results alone are not the required disclosure.
n.3: Disclosure is proactive, not on request.
n.4: Safeguarding disclosure is not retail-only.
n.0: The FSCS does not automatically protect all assets.

q: A non-MiFID firm will hold client money as part of its service. Under COBS 6.1.7, what must it tell clients about that money?
o: That client money is always segregated within the UK only
That the arrangements are confidential and not disclosed
That disclosure is needed only if the firm becomes insolvent
That client money is always guaranteed by the FCA
Where and how client money is held and the protections in place
w: Non-MiFID firms must inform clients about where their money is held, under what arrangements, and the protections afforded, so clients can evaluate custody risks.

n.3: The FCA does not guarantee client money.
n.2: Disclosure is upfront, not only on insolvency.
n.1: Arrangements must be disclosed.
n.0: Client money may be held outside the UK.

q: A MiFID firm intends to hold some client assets with an overseas third-party custodian. What must the firm disclose to clients about that arrangement?
o: That clients need not be told of sub-custody arrangements
Only where the custodian is located outside the EU
That assets may be held with third parties and the associated risks
Nothing, since custody is a purely operational matter
Only the custodian's name, without the associated risks
w: Firms must tell clients when assets may be held with third-party custodians and the risks of such arrangements, including possible insolvency or lack of segregation.

n.3: Custody risk must be disclosed.
n.4: The name alone omits the risks.
n.1: Disclosure is not limited to non-EU custodians.
n.0: Sub-custody arrangements must be disclosed.

q: A custodian firm holds several clients' securities together in a pooled omnibus account. What must the firm explain to those clients about this arrangement?
o: That pooling may expose them to default risk if a custodian fails
That pooling the assets removes all of the associated risk
That omnibus accounts always guarantee higher returns
That no disclosure is needed for professional clients
That clients are personally liable for other clients' debts
w: Omnibus accounts pool assets, and firms must disclose the risks of pooling, including exposure to other clients’ defaults or custody failures.

n.2: Pooling does not guarantee returns.
n.3: Professionals must be told too.
n.1: Pooling adds risk, it does not remove it.
n.4: Clients are not liable for others' debts.

q: A MiFID firm intends to hold some client assets outside the UK. Which safeguarding risk must it disclose?
o: That no disclosure is needed if the custodian is large
That there are no differences in protection when held overseas
That investor protections may differ and assets may fall under foreign law
That the assets are guaranteed by the local overseas regulator
That only retail clients need be told about overseas custody
w: Firms must tell clients if assets are held overseas and that protections may differ due to foreign legal regimes, which may affect recoverability in insolvency.

n.3: Local regulators do not guarantee the assets.
n.1: Protections can differ overseas.
n.0: Custodian size does not remove the duty.
n.4: Disclosure is not retail-only.

q: A non-MiFID firm's custody arrangements may allow third-party claims over client investments. What must it tell clients about liens or rights over those investments?
o: That the disclosure is required only for retail clients
That any liens are confidential and cannot be shared
That liens are irrelevant where the assets are segregated
That third parties may have rights or security interests over the assets
That liens over client assets cannot exist under UK law
w: COBS 6.1.7 requires disclosure if client assets may be subject to liens, rights, or security interests, so clients are aware of potential encumbrances.

n.4: Liens can exist over client assets.
n.0: The disclosure is not retail-only.
n.1: Liens must be disclosed, not kept confidential.
n.2: Segregation does not make liens irrelevant.

q: A MiFID firm will place client money with a bank outside the UK. Which disclosure duty applies?
o: The firm need not disclose the location if the bank is large
Disclosure is required only where the money exceeds eighty-five thousand pounds
Clients need not be informed about overseas client money
Only retail clients must be told of foreign bank locations
Clients must be told protections differ and may not match UK safeguards
w: Firms must disclose to clients if their money is held with overseas banks and that protections may differ from those available in the UK.

n.0: Bank size does not remove the duty.
n.1: There is no eighty-five-thousand-pound threshold for this.
n.2: Clients must be informed.
n.3: Disclosure is not retail-only.

q: An investment firm may appoint sub-custodians to hold client assets. What safeguarding disclosures must it make about this?
o: Firms must guarantee full recovery of assets held by sub-custodians
Clients may veto any sub-custodian the firm proposes to appoint
Sub-custody disclosure applies only to eligible counterparty clients
Sub-custody arrangements require the FCA's approval before each use
Tell clients sub-custodians may be used and explain the related risks
w: Clients must be told that sub-custodians may hold their assets and be informed of the risks, such as potential loss or different legal protections.

n.3: Firms need not obtain FCA approval for each sub-custodian appointment
n.2: The disclosure covers all client types, not only eligible counterparties
n.0: No firm can guarantee full recovery; sub-custody carries genuine loss risk
n.1: Clients have no general right of veto over the choice of sub-custodian

q: A firm holds some client money in an account that is not segregated from its own funds. Why must it explain the risk of non-segregated accounts to clients?
o: Because non-segregated money attracts a lower rate of interest
Because segregation is mandatory only for eligible counterparty clients, not retail
Because non-segregated balances must be reported to the FCA daily
Because non-segregated assets may be mixed with the firm's and lost on insolvency
Because the FSCS refuses all claims on non-segregated accounts
w: If assets are not segregated from the firm’s own, clients may lose their property if the firm becomes insolvent, so disclosure of this risk is essential.

n.1: Segregation duties protect clients generally, not only eligible counterparties
n.0: The risk is loss on insolvency, not any difference in interest paid
n.4: FSCS cover can still apply; the point is loss of assets on firm failure
n.2: There is no daily FCA reporting rule for non-segregated balances

q: A MiFID firm is drafting the terms it gives new clients whose investments it will safeguard. In relation to investor compensation schemes, what must the firm tell them?
o: That any compensation claim must be submitted within seven days
Whether clients are covered by a compensation scheme and its scope of protection
That compensation cover exists only for deposits, never investments
That the FSCS always covers every investment loss in full without any upper limit
That the firm itself guarantees any shortfall in safeguarded assets
w: MiFID requires firms to disclose if a client’s assets are covered by an investor compensation scheme and the scope and limits of such protection.

n.3: FSCS investment protection is capped, not unlimited
n.2: The FSCS also covers eligible investment business, not deposits alone
n.4: Firms do not personally guarantee shortfalls; a scheme pays out
n.0: There is no seven-day deadline for compensation-scheme claims

q: A non-MiFID adviser is preparing the account-opening pack under COBS 6.1.7 for a client whose cash it will hold. What must it tell the client about that money?
o: That all client money is at all times fully guaranteed by the FCA
That the segregation requirement applies only to clients categorised as retail
That client money may be mixed with the firm's own funds without any risk
That client money is held in a designated client bank account, segregated from firm money
That no disclosure is required where the sums of client money are small
w: Firms must disclose that client money is held in a designated client bank account, separated from the firm’s own money, to protect against insolvency risk.

n.0: The FCA does not guarantee client money.

q: A compliance officer is mapping the financial promotion rules to the Principles for Businesses. Which Principle do they most directly reinforce?
o: Principle 6: Treating customers fairly
Principle 8: Conflicts of interest
Principle 3: Management and control
Principle 10: Clients' assets
Principle 1: Integrity
w: The rules support Principle 6, which requires firms to treat customers fairly, by ensuring they receive balanced and understandable information about products and services.

n.4: Principle 1 concerns integrity, not fair treatment of customers
n.2: Principle 3 covers management and control, not customer fairness
n.1: Principle 8 addresses conflicts of interest, not customer fairness
n.3: Principle 10 concerns client assets, not customer fairness

q: A marketing manager drafting a product promotion is reminded of Principle 7. How does that Principle relate to the financial promotion rules?
o: It lets firms prioritise the benefits over the risks
It requires that all communications are fair, clear and not misleading
It applies only to investment products, and never to related services
It applies only to the firm's professional clients
It exempts digital promotions from any regulation
w: Principle 7 underlines that all client communications must be fair, clear and not misleading, which forms the foundation of the COBS 4.1 financial promotion rules.

n.0: Principle 7 requires balance, not prioritising benefits over risks
n.3: Principle 7 applies to all clients, not professionals only
n.4: Digital promotions are not exempt from the rules
n.2: The principle covers services as well as products

q: A firm is confirming the reach of the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1. Which best describes their application?
o: They apply only where the FCA pre-approves the material
They apply to all forms of client communication, whatever the medium
They apply only to the firm's printed promotional material and adverts
They apply only to advice, and not to any promotions
They apply only where the client requests them
w: COBS 4.1 applies to all communications with clients, including digital, verbal and printed, ensuring consistent consumer protection across mediums.

n.2: The rules cover all media, not printed material alone
n.3: The rules cover promotions as well as advice
n.0: The FCA does not pre-approve promotions as a condition
n.4: The rules apply generally, not only on client request

q: A trainee asks what the financial promotion rules are chiefly designed to stop. What do they primarily seek to prevent?
o: The disclosure of the product's charges and fees
The use of plain language within any advertising
Clients being misled into unsuitable investments
Firms from being able to make any profit at all
Clients from accessing benchmark comparisons
w: The rules aim to stop clients being misled into inappropriate or unsuitable investments through unclear, biased or incomplete communications.

n.3: The rules do not aim to stop firms making a profit
n.1: Plain language is encouraged, not something to prevent
n.4: Benchmark comparisons help clients; they are not prevented
n.0: Charge disclosure is required, not something to prevent

q: A firm is explaining why the promotion rules matter for Principle 6. Why is that relationship important?
o: It limits the rules to the firm's professional clients only
It removes the firm's duty to disclose its charges
It guarantees that the firm will achieve a higher overall level of sales
It lets firms omit risk information where it is positive
It ensures clients are treated fairly through transparent communication
w: Principle 6 requires firms to treat customers fairly, and financial promotion rules ensure this by mandating balanced, transparent and fair information in communications.

n.2: The link concerns fair treatment, not higher sales
n.1: Charge disclosure duties remain; they are not removed
n.0: The rules protect all clients, not professionals only
n.3: Risk information cannot be omitted; balance is required

q: A reviewer is checking a promotion aimed at retail investors against Principle 7. Which of the following would be considered a breach in financial promotions?
o: Disclosing charges in itemised and aggregate form
Translating material into plain language for retail clients
Presenting both risks and rewards with equal prominence
Using technical jargon that confuses the intended audience
Providing clear warnings about tax treatment
w: Principle 7 requires communications to be clear and comprehensible; using jargon that confuses clients breaches this obligation.

n.4: Tax disclosures are appropriate and required.
n.0: Charges disclosure is compliant, not a breach.
n.2: Balanced risk-reward presentation is required under Principle 7.
n.1: Plain language supports clarity and compliance.

q: A compliance officer links the promotion rules to the FCA's consumer protection objective. How do they interact?
o: They apply only to promotions aimed at professional investors
They ensure clients get the information needed to make informed choices
They set a fixed cap on the returns a firm is allowed to advertise
They shift responsibility for product risk entirely onto the client
They require the FCA to pre-vet every promotion before it is issued
w: The financial promotion rules protect consumers by ensuring communications are fair, clear and not misleading, helping clients make properly informed decisions.

n.4: The FCA does not pre-approve or pre-vet firms' financial promotions.
n.3: Firms must explain risks; the rules do not transfer risk to clients.
n.0: The rules protect retail clients too, not only professionals.
n.2: There is no rule capping advertised returns; balance and fairness apply.

q: A marketing manager at an investment firm is drafting a fund promotion and wants to comply with Principle 6. Which approach best demonstrates that compliance?
o: Presenting only the headline benefits to grab the client's attention
Emphasising past gains as a reliable guide to future returns
Disclosing all costs and charges to clients in a transparent way
Placing all material risk information within the terms and conditions
Quoting gross returns and leaving charges for the client to work out
w: Principle 6 requires treating customers fairly, which is demonstrated by transparent disclosure of all costs and charges so clients fully understand the impact on returns.

n.0: Showing benefits only is not fair treatment under Principle 6.
n.3: Burying risks in the terms is not clear, fair disclosure.
n.4: Charges must be shown; gross-only figures mislead on net returns.
n.1: Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future returns.

q: A firm is applying Principle 7 to its online adverts and social posts. Which is a correct application to digital promotions?
o: Letting firms play up benefits over risks on social media
Applying the fair and clear standard only to printed material
Ensuring online adverts are fair, clear and not misleading
Permitting risk warnings to be omitted from short banner adverts
Exempting social media posts from the COBS 4 promotion rules
w: Principle 7 applies equally to digital media; firms must ensure that online adverts, banners and social media promotions are fair, clear and not misleading.

n.0: Principle 7 does not relax the standard for social media.
n.3: Risk warnings cannot be dropped just because a banner is short.
n.1: The standard applies to all media, not only printed material.
n.4: Social media promotions are subject to COBS 4, not exempt.

q: A firm is confirming how far the financial promotion rules in COBS 4.1 reach. Which statement about their scope is correct?
o: They apply to all client communications, solicited or unsolicited
They apply only to products above a set minimum investment value
They apply only to prospectuses and other formal offer documents
They apply only once the FCA has given prior written approval
They apply only where the firm also provides personal advice
w: The rules under COBS 4.1 apply to all forms of communication with clients, regardless of medium or whether the client solicited the information.

n.2: COBS 4.1 covers all media, not just prospectuses or formal documents.
n.1: There is no value threshold; the rules apply regardless of value.
n.4: The rules apply whether or not advice is given.
n.3: No prior FCA approval is required for the rules to apply.

q: A compliance officer is explaining how the promotion rules serve the FCA's market integrity objective. How do they support it?
o: By preventing misleading promotions that distort market behaviour
By exempting professional clients from all conduct requirements
By helping firms maximise the profits they make on each sale
By making firms compete mainly through their advertising budgets
By limiting firms to marketing only low-risk regulated products
w: By ensuring promotions are accurate and fair, the rules prevent misleading claims that could undermine confidence and distort investor behaviour in the market.

n.2: The objective is fair markets, not maximising firms' profits.
n.4: The rules do not restrict firms to low-risk products only.
n.3: Competition on advertising spend is not a regulatory objective.
n.1: Professional clients are not exempt from all conduct rules.

q: A compliance officer reviews a draft financial promotion before it is issued. Which feature would demonstrate a breach of the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.1?
o: Setting out the product's risks and benefits with equal prominence
Giving a balanced comparison against a relevant, consistent benchmark
Disclosing charges in both itemised and aggregated form to clients
Highlighting benefits prominently but hiding the risks in small print
Stating that tax treatment depends on the client's own circumstances
w: Hiding risks in small print while highlighting benefits breaches the fair, clear and not misleading requirement central to COBS 4.1.

n.0: Equal prominence of risks and benefits is compliant, not a breach.
n.1: A fair, consistent benchmark comparison is compliant, not a breach.
n.2: Clear disclosure of charges is compliant, not a breach.
n.4: A correct tax-treatment caveat is compliant, not a breach.

q: A trainee asks how the financial promotion rules connect to Principle 6. What is the link?
o: They apply only to communications with non-retail clients
They let firms use disclaimers as their main form of disclosure
They guarantee clients a higher return on regulated products
They help ensure customers are treated fairly and are not misled
They release firms from having to disclose charges to clients
w: Financial promotion rules uphold Principle 6 by ensuring clients are not misled and are treated fairly through transparent and balanced communications.

n.2: The rules do not guarantee returns; that would itself mislead.
n.4: Charges must still be disclosed; nothing is waived.
n.0: Principle 6 protection extends to retail clients too.
n.1: Disclaimers cannot replace balanced, fair disclosure.

q: A firm publishes a misleading online advert and the compliance director warns colleagues of the likely regulatory fallout for breaching Principle 7. What is the consequence for a firm if its financial promotions breach Principle 7?
o: The firm may face FCA enforcement action and reputational damage
The promotion is disregarded by clients as soon as they see it
The FCA steps in to guarantee compensation to affected clients
The conduct rules simply do not apply to online communications
The promotion becomes valid once a disclaimer is added later
w: Breaches of Principle 7 can result in FCA enforcement action, fines, and loss of trust, as communications that mislead undermine market integrity and consumer protection.

n.1: Clients do not automatically disregard a breaching promotion.
n.2: The FCA does not guarantee client compensation for breaches.
n.4: A later disclaimer does not cure a misleading promotion.
n.3: Principle 7 applies fully to online communications.

q: A compliance officer is explaining to the marketing team how financial promotion rules connect to Treating Customers Fairly. Which statement best captures that alignment?
o: They apply only in situations where the firm is providing personal advice
They remove the obligation on firms to disclose the costs of a product
They allow firms to rely solely on a generic disclaimer to meet the standard
They allow firms to present only the positive features of a product
They require clear, balanced information so customers can decide on an informed basis
w: The rules align with TCF by ensuring clients receive the balanced, accurate information they need to make fair choices about financial products.

n.3: Promotions must be balanced, not one-sided.
n.1: Cost disclosure obligations remain.
n.0: The rules apply beyond advised sales.
n.2: A generic disclaimer does not satisfy the standard.

q: A marketing manager is checking a draft advertisement against COBS 4.1 before it is issued. Which of the following is TRUE about financial promotions under COBS 4.1?
o: They only apply to products over a certain value
They are exempt from regulation if sent by email
They must always be fair, clear and not misleading
They can guarantee investment outcomes if FCA authorised
They can omit risk disclosures if the product is low risk
w: The fundamental rule of COBS 4.1 is that all promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, regardless of medium or product type.

n.1: Email communications are subject to the same rules as all other media.
n.3: FCA authorisation does not permit guarantees of outcomes.
n.4: Even low-risk products must have risk disclosures.
n.0: The rules apply to all products, not just high-value ones.

q: A firm buried its risk warnings in small print while highlighting benefits. Under COBS 4.1, why is that insufficient?
o: Because risks must be given equal prominence to benefits
Because the FCA requires risk disclosures only for derivatives
Because clients are assumed not to read risk information
Because Principle 6 eliminates the need for disclosure
Because disclaimers automatically override FCA rules
w: COBS requires risks to be presented with equal prominence to benefits so that clients are not misled by an unbalanced impression of the product.

n.4: Disclaimers do not override FCA requirements.
n.2: Firms cannot assume clients ignore risk disclosures; they must be made prominent.
n.1: The requirement applies to all products, not only derivatives.
n.3: Principle 6 reinforces the need for disclosure; it does not remove it.

q: A marketing team drafts a promotion for an investment product and must satisfy Principles 6 and 7. Which approach best demonstrates compliance with both principles?
o: Relying on disclaimers instead of giving balanced information
Promoting only gross returns without deducting any charges
Presenting only the best-case performance scenario to clients
Providing balanced, clear and transparent financial promotions
Guaranteeing that the product will at least double in value
w: Compliance with Principles 6 and 7 requires communications that are balanced, transparent and easily understood, ensuring clients are treated fairly and not misled.

n.4: Guaranteeing gains breaches the fair, clear, not misleading rule.
n.1: Gross-only figures mislead clients about net returns.
n.2: Showing only best-case outcomes is unbalanced and misleading.
n.0: Disclaimers cannot substitute for balanced information.

q: A training officer is explaining why COBS 4.1 is read alongside Principles 6 and 7. What is the overarching regulatory objective behind linking them?
o: To protect consumers through fair treatment and clear communication
To let firms market their products in whatever way they choose
To reduce the amount of competition between authorised firms
To ease FCA supervision by cutting disclosure requirements
To guarantee investors a high return on their investments
w: The combined effect of COBS 4.1 and Principles 6 and 7 is to protect consumers by ensuring they are treated fairly and provided with clear, non-misleading information.

n.2: Reducing competition is not the aim of these rules.
n.4: The rules do not, and cannot, guarantee investor returns.
n.3: The rules increase, not cut, required disclosure.
n.1: Firms do not have free rein; promotions are tightly governed.

q: A compliance officer is checking a promotion against COBS 4.3. What is the key requirement that rule imposes?
o: They must guarantee the accuracy of the investment returns shown
They must be clearly identifiable as a financial promotion
They must be directed only to professional, not retail, clients
They may leave out risk warnings when the product is simple
They must be approved by the FCA in every single case
w: COBS 4.3 requires that all financial promotions are clearly identifiable as such, ensuring clients understand they are being presented with a promotional communication.

n.0: Returns cannot be guaranteed; that is not a COBS 4.3 requirement.
n.4: The FCA does not approve every promotion; firms are responsible.
n.2: Promotions may be directed at retail clients, not only professionals.
n.3: Risk warnings are not waived merely because a product is simple.

q: A firm is designing an advert and must make its promotional nature obvious. Why does COBS 4.3 require promotions to be clearly identified?
o: To let firms use disclaimers in place of a balanced message
To remove the need for firms to include any risk disclosures
To help firms maximise the number of products they sell
To exempt online adverts from the financial promotion rules
To stop clients mistaking promotions for impartial information
w: The rule exists to ensure clients recognise promotional content and do not confuse it with impartial advice or factual material.

n.2: Boosting sales is not the purpose of the identification rule.
n.1: Risk disclosures are still required; nothing is removed.
n.0: Disclaimers cannot replace a balanced, fair message.
n.3: Online adverts are not exempt from the promotion rules.

q: A firm is reviewing a communication for compliance with COBS 4.3. Which of the following would breach that rule?
o: Using plain language to explain features
Labelling content clearly as a promotion
Including risk warnings alongside benefits
Presenting marketing material as impartial research
Disclosing costs in both aggregated and itemised form
w: COBS 4.3 prohibits disguising promotions as neutral content such as research, as this misleads clients about the nature of the communication.

n.1: Clear labelling is compliant and required.
n.2: Balanced presentation is part of compliance.
n.0: Plain language supports clarity.
n.4: Full cost disclosure aligns with FCA requirements.

q: A firm wants to include a promotional message inside an otherwise factual client update. Under COBS 4.3, how should it present the promotion?
o: It may skip identification when the audience is professional
It must replace the factual content within the communication
It can rely on a disclaimer tucked away in the footnotes
It can be blended seamlessly with the content to seem more persuasive
It must be clearly distinguished from factual or impartial information
w: Promotional content must be separated and clearly identified so that clients can distinguish it from factual or impartial information.

n.3: Blending to persuade defeats the identification requirement.
n.0: Identification is still required even for professional audiences.
n.1: Promotion supplements, not replaces, factual content.
n.2: A hidden footnote disclaimer does not satisfy the rule.

q: A firm is considering how COBS 4.3 relates to Principle 7. What is that relationship?
o: Principle 7 removes the need to give any risk disclosures at all
Principle 7 applies only to communications with institutional clients
Principle 7 exempts firms from having to identify their promotions
Principle 7 requires clients not be misled about whether content is promotional
Principle 7 lets firms hide promotional content inside detailed factual reports
w: Principle 7 requires communications to be fair, clear and not misleading, which includes ensuring that clients understand when material is promotional.

n.2: Principle 7 reinforces, not removes, the duty to identify promotions.
n.4: Hiding promotions in factual reports breaches Principle 7.
n.1: Principle 7 applies to retail clients, not only institutions.
n.0: Principle 7 does not remove the need for risk disclosures.

q: A marketing team is preparing a promotional email campaign and wants to comply with COBS 4.3. Which of the following actions would be compliant?
o: Using small print disclaimers to identify promotional material
Implying that a promotion is FCA-endorsed
Sending out performance data without context or labelling
Labelling a marketing email subject line with ‘advertisement’
Mixing research and promotion without distinction
w: Clearly labelling marketing content, such as with ‘advertisement’, complies with the rule that promotions must be clearly identifiable as such.

n.2: Performance data must be labelled if used for promotional purposes.
n.4: Mixing research with promotions without clarity misleads clients.
n.0: Small print disclaimers are insufficient for compliance.
n.1: Promotions cannot suggest FCA endorsement.

q: A marketing team is designing a new advert and asks compliance why it must be labelled clearly as a promotion. Why does the FCA place emphasis on identifying promotions clearly?
o: To cut down the FCA's own supervisory obligations
To give firms wide freedom to design more attractive and engaging adverts
To exempt digital platforms from any regulatory oversight
So clients understand when content is persuasive rather than impartial
To restrict promotional disclosures to professional clients
w: Clients must be able to tell when information is promotional so they can interpret it as persuasive material rather than impartial guidance.

n.1: The aim is client understanding, not attractive advert design.
n.0: Identification does not reduce the FCA's supervisory duties.
n.4: Disclosure is not restricted to professional clients.
n.2: Digital platforms are not exempt from oversight.

q: A firm has issued a promotion that is not clearly identified as one. What would the FCA's concern be?
o: Clients may confuse marketing with independent advice
Institutional clients may become exempt from COBS
The cost of advertising for firms may increase
The FCA would be unable to levy its supervisory fees
Firms may lose market share to their competitors
w: Failure to identify promotions risks misleading clients into thinking the information is impartial or advisory when it is promotional in nature.

n.4: Competitive market share is not the FCA's concern here.
n.2: Advertising cost is not the regulatory concern.
n.1: Institutional clients are not made exempt from COBS.
n.3: FCA fees are unrelated to identifying promotions.

q: A firm dressed up a promotion to look like impartial research. What is the potential regulatory outcome?
o: Exemption under Principle 6
Automatic approval of the communication
The firm is allowed to continue until audited
The client bears responsibility for misinterpretation
FCA enforcement action for breaching COBS 4.3
w: Disguising promotions as research misleads clients and breaches COBS 4.3, exposing the firm to FCA enforcement action and potential penalties.

n.1: There is no automatic approval; the firm would be in breach.
n.0: Principle 6 strengthens disclosure, not exemption.
n.3: The firm, not the client, is responsible for compliance.
n.2: Firms cannot continue breaching until audited; breaches attract immediate regulatory risk.

q: A compliance officer is confirming what compliance with COBS 4.3 actually looks like. Which best describes it?
o: Making promotions persuasive enough to boost the firm's sales
Guaranteeing the investment outcomes stated in the advert
Treating online promotions as exempt from the COBS rules
Providing the required disclaimers only in the small print
Making sure clients can clearly recognise promotional content
w: Compliance means clients must be able to easily identify when content is promotional so they can treat it appropriately as marketing material.

n.0: Boosting sales is not the aim of COBS 4.3.
n.1: Investment outcomes cannot be guaranteed in adverts.
n.2: Online promotions are not exempt from COBS.
n.3: Small-print-only disclaimers do not achieve clear identification.

q: A firm is checking the exceptions to the financial promotion rules under COBS 4.8. Which of the following is a key exception?
o: Communications directed to certified high net worth individuals
All communications made to ordinary retail clients
Any communication that a firm labels as 'educational'
All communications made through social media platforms
Communications made from outside the UK directly to UK retail clients
w: One key exception under COBS and the Financial Promotion Order (FPO) is communications directed to certified high net worth individuals, provided strict criteria are met.

n.3: Social media promotions are not blanket-exempt.
n.2: Labelling something 'educational' does not create an exemption.
n.4: Overseas-to-UK promotions are restricted, not exempt.
n.1: Ordinary retail clients are not an exempt category.

q: Which statute sets out key exemptions to financial promotion rules that supplement COBS?
o: The Companies Act 2006 and its provisions on corporate communications
The Bribery Act 2010 and its offences relating to improper payments
The Criminal Justice Act 1993 dealing with insider dealing offences
The Data Protection Act 2018 governing the handling of personal data
The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Financial Promotion) Order
w: The Financial Promotion Order (FPO) made under FSMA 2000 sets out specific exemptions to the financial promotion rules that operate alongside COBS provisions.

n.0: The Companies Act does not set the financial-promotion exemptions.
n.3: The Data Protection Act governs personal data, not promotion exemptions.
n.2: The CJA 1993 concerns insider dealing.
n.1: The Bribery Act concerns bribery, not promotions.

q: An unauthorised promoter relies on an FPO exemption to send a promotion. To which client type may it be sent without breaching the rules?
o: All retail clients without restriction
Any member of the general public
Certified sophisticated investors
Clients outside the UK by default
Minors under 18 years old
w: FPO exemptions allow promotions to be directed to certified sophisticated investors who meet strict qualifying criteria, without breaching the general restriction.

n.1: The general public are protected and remain fully covered by the restriction.
n.0: Retail clients cannot be promoted to without compliance or exemption.
n.4: Minors are not a recognised exempt category.
n.3: Cross-border communication is still subject to UK regulation.

q: A compliance officer is stating the general restriction on financial promotions under COBS 4.1. What is it?
o: They may be communicated by anyone provided they are labelled clearly
They can only be made orally so as to avoid the rules
They must not be communicated unless issued or approved by an authorised firm
They may be sent to ordinary retail clients without any conditions attached
They are outside regulation whenever they are directed online
w: The general rule is that financial promotions must not be made unless by an authorised person or approved by an authorised firm, to protect consumers from unauthorised activity.

n.0: Labelling alone does not lift the general restriction.
n.4: Online promotions are within, not outside, regulation.
n.1: Oral promotions are also caught by the restriction.
n.3: Retail promotions are conditional, not unrestricted.

q: A firm is comparing the conduct standards for MiFID business against others under COBS. Which limitation applies specifically to MiFID business?
o: MiFID communications may target any retail client without restriction
MiFID communications must meet stricter disclosure and balance requirements
MiFID communications are exempt when delivered via social media
MiFID communications sit outside the fair, clear and not misleading test
MiFID communications are exempt from all financial promotion rules
w: COBS applies stricter obligations to MiFID business, requiring enhanced disclosures and balanced presentation of risks and benefits in all communications.

n.4: MiFID business is subject to more, not fewer, promotion rules.
n.3: The fair, clear and not misleading test still applies to MiFID.
n.0: Retail targeting under MiFID is restricted, not unrestricted.
n.2: Social media delivery does not exempt MiFID communications.

q: A firm wants to send a financial promotion relying on an FPO exemption without breaching COBS. Which group of recipients is permitted?
o: Clients resident outside the UK
Investment professionals
Any individual aged over 18
All retail clients
Unregulated introducers
w: The FPO allows authorised firms to send promotions to investment professionals, provided the communication is relevant and proportionate to their expertise.

n.3: Retail clients are not exempt and require full regulatory protection.
n.2: Age alone does not provide an exemption.
n.0: Communications to UK clients are always regulated, regardless of firm location.
n.4: Unregulated introducers cannot lawfully receive exempt promotions.

q: A firm's marketing manager asks how the Financial Promotion Order fits alongside the COBS rules. How does the FPO interact with COBS?
o: It provides statutory exemptions from the general restriction in FSMA 2000
It applies only to advertising placed on social media
It replaces all of the COBS rules on promotions entirely
It exempts authorised firms from the Principle 7 requirements
It lets any unauthorised person issue promotions to the general public
w: The FPO works alongside COBS by setting out statutory exemptions to FSMA’s general restriction on financial promotions, such as communications to certified investors or professionals.

n.2: The FPO works alongside COBS; it does not replace it.
n.1: The FPO is not limited to social media advertising.
n.3: The FPO does not exempt firms from Principle 7.
n.4: The FPO gives narrow exemptions, not free rein.

q: A firm is deciding whether it can rely on an FPO exemption for a particular promotion. Which of the following is NOT an exemption under the FPO?
o: Communications aimed at certified high net worth individuals
Communications aimed at certified sophisticated investors
Communications aimed at qualifying investment professionals
Communications issued or approved by an authorised person
Communications aimed at the general public without any restriction
w: Members of the general public are not exempt; communications to them must comply fully with financial promotion rules or rely on another specific exemption.

n.1: Certified sophisticated investors are a recognised FPO exemption.
n.2: Investment professionals are a recognised FPO exemption.
n.0: Certified high net worth individuals are a recognised FPO exemption.
n.3: Communications by an authorised person fall outside the restriction.

q: A compliance officer is comparing the promotion regimes for MiFID and non-MiFID business. What is a distinguishing feature of the MiFID financial promotion rules compared with non-MiFID?
o: MiFID exempts retail clients from the disclosure requirements
MiFID rules remove the need for a fair presentation of risk
MiFID rules apply only to investment firms based outside the UK
MiFID requires stricter standards for retail client communications
MiFID promotion rules apply only to printed advertisements
w: MiFID imposes stricter obligations on firms when communicating with retail clients, including detailed disclosure of risks, costs and balanced presentation of benefits.

n.0: MiFID adds retail disclosure duties; it does not exempt them.
n.4: MiFID rules apply across all media, not just print.
n.1: Fair presentation of risk is required, not removed.
n.2: MiFID applies to UK-based firms, not only overseas ones.

q: An authorised firm's marketing team is planning a new promotional campaign. Why is the existence of the FPO significant for the firm?
o: It clarifies when communications are exempt from the promotion restriction
It treats all social media advertising as outside the rules
It lets firms bypass their COBS obligations altogether
It guarantees the FCA's approval of a firm's promotional materials
It removes the need for disclosures in retail promotions
w: The FPO provides clarity on when communications fall outside the general restriction, such as promotions to certain categories of investors, without removing the overall duty to comply with COBS.

n.2: The FPO does not remove underlying COBS obligations.
n.3: The FPO does not guarantee FCA approval of materials.
n.4: Retail disclosure duties remain; the FPO does not remove them.
n.1: Social media advertising is not automatically exempt.

q: A firm wants to send a promotion to certain investors without triggering the general restriction. Which category is explicitly recognised as an exempt recipient under the FPO?
o: Any UK resident who is over 21 years of age
Members of the general public attending an investment seminar
All persons who are not resident in the UK
Certified high net worth individuals meeting the FPO criteria
All retail clients regardless of their circumstances
w: The FPO provides an exemption for communications directed at certified high net worth individuals who meet specific criteria, without breaching the restriction.

n.4: Ordinary retail clients are not an exempt recipient category.
n.0: Age alone (over 21) does not create an FPO exemption.
n.1: Seminar attendees are not an exempt category by that fact.
n.2: Non-UK residence is not itself an FPO exemption.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing which of the firm's promotions fall outside the general restriction. How do the COBS 4.8 exemptions operate in practice?
o: They allow certain communications without breaching the general restriction
They exempt all online advertisements automatically
They remove the need for all promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading
They allow firms to ignore MiFID requirements
They apply only when the FCA confirms in writing
w: COBS 4.8 exemptions clarify situations where promotions may be made without breaching FSMA’s general restriction, while still requiring compliance with fairness standards.

n.2: The fair, clear and not misleading rule always applies.
n.1: Online advertisements remain subject to full regulation.
n.4: Written FCA approval is not a requirement for exemptions.
n.3: MiFID rules continue to apply where relevant.

q: A firm is identifying communications that fall within the FPO. Which of the following is an example of an exempted communication?
o: A social media post targeted at ordinary retail clients
An email sent out to every UK household indiscriminately
A cold call made to any consumer without an exemption
A promotion directed to certified sophisticated investors
A general marketing campaign aimed at the wider public
w: The FPO recognises an exemption for promotions directed at certified sophisticated investors, provided the necessary statements and certifications are in place.

n.4: A general campaign to the public is not exempt.
n.0: Retail-targeted social media posts are not exempt.
n.2: Unexempted cold calls to consumers are prohibited.
n.1: Mass emailing all households is not an FPO exemption.

q: A firm asks whether an FPO exemption lets it sidestep MiFID's requirements. Which best explains the limitation of exemptions for MiFID business?
o: Exemptions apply only to institutional clients under MiFID
Exemptions cannot override MiFID's stricter disclosure requirements
Exemptions remove the need to comply with MiFID entirely
Exemptions permit firms to omit costs and charges from promotions
Exemptions make the giving of risk disclosures optional
w: MiFID imposes mandatory obligations on firms; exemptions under the FPO cannot remove or dilute these stricter disclosure and conduct requirements.

n.2: FPO exemptions do not switch off MiFID compliance.
n.0: MiFID exemptions are not limited to institutional clients.
n.3: Costs and charges must still be disclosed under MiFID.
n.4: Risk disclosures remain mandatory, not optional.

q: A compliance officer is testing which communications fall outside the FPO exemptions. Which of the following would NOT fall within one?
o: A communication made by an authorised person
A communication to certified sophisticated investors
A promotion disguised as impartial research
A communication directed at a certified high net worth individual
A promotion targeted to investment professionals
w: Disguising a promotion as impartial research breaches COBS 4.3 and cannot be justified under FPO exemptions.

n.3: High net worth individuals are an exempt category.
n.4: Investment professionals are covered by exemptions.
n.1: Certified sophisticated investors are recognised as exempt recipients.
n.0: Authorised persons may communicate promotions without relying on exemptions.

q: A start-up business that is not FCA authorised wants to promote an investment opportunity to the public. Which of the following correctly describes the 'general restriction' that applies?
o: Overseas promotions directed into the UK are treated as exempt from the restriction
Only retail clients are covered by the general restriction
Oral communications are excluded from the general restriction
Firms may communicate to anyone so long as they label content clearly
An unauthorised person must not communicate a promotion unless an exemption applies
w: The general restriction under FSMA 2000 states that unauthorised persons cannot make financial promotions unless an exemption under the FPO applies.

n.3: Clear labelling does not lift the general restriction.
n.1: The restriction is not limited to retail clients.
n.2: Oral communications are caught by the restriction.
n.0: Overseas-into-UK promotions are restricted, not exempt.

q: A firm is advising an unauthorised business on communicating financial promotions. Why is the FPO particularly important for unauthorised persons?
o: It gives statutory exemptions letting them make certain communications lawfully
It exempts them from all of the FCA's conduct rules
It guarantees FCA approval of the communications they make
It permits them to carry out otherwise regulated activities
It allows them to market their products to the public without any conditions
w: The FPO is essential for unauthorised persons as it provides narrowly defined exemptions to the general restriction, enabling certain lawful communications.

n.3: The FPO does not authorise regulated activities themselves.
n.1: It exempts specific promotions only, not all conduct rules.
n.2: It does not guarantee FCA approval of communications.
n.4: The exemptions are narrow and conditional, not unconditional.

q: A firm is preparing an unapproved promotion and considering which recipients fall within Financial Promotion Order exemptions. Which category is NOT typically covered by FPO exemptions?
o: Certified high net worth individuals
Employees of the firm
General members of the public
Investment professionals
Certified sophisticated investors
w: The general public is not an exempt category; promotions to them must be approved or issued by authorised persons and comply fully with FCA standards.

n.4: Sophisticated investors are recognised under exemptions.
n.1: Internal communications to employees can be exempt.
n.0: High net worth individuals can qualify under exemptions.
n.3: Investment professionals are exempt recipients.

q: A firm relies on an FPO exemption for a promotion. Which of the following is TRUE about the interaction between COBS and the FPO?
o: Exemptions under the FPO apply only to promotions issued in printed form
FPO exemptions do not remove the fair, clear and not misleading requirement
Exemptions under the FPO also remove the need to provide any risk disclosures
Exemptions under the FPO switch off all of the MiFID conduct requirements
Exemptions under the FPO permit firms to make guaranteed claims about future performance
w: Even when an exemption applies under the FPO, the overarching requirement remains that all communications must be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.2: FPO exemptions do not switch off the fair-clear-not-misleading standard.
n.3: They do not remove risk disclosure obligations.
n.0: They are not limited to printed material.
n.4: They never permit guaranteed performance claims.

q: A trainee asks what role the exemptions play in the financial promotion regime. Which best describes it?
o: They allow firms to disregard the COBS standards when marketing to retail clients
They permit firms to market their products without limit to every category of client
They are intended to encourage firms to adopt more aggressive advertising strategies
They remove the FCA's power to supervise financial promotions altogether
They carve out narrow cases where a promotion can be made without breaching FSMA
w: Exemptions allow certain promotions to be made lawfully in narrowly defined cases, but do not remove the requirement for fairness or wider FCA oversight.

n.0: Exemptions do not switch off the COBS fair-clear-not-misleading standard.
n.1: They are narrow, not a licence for unlimited marketing.
n.3: They do not remove FCA oversight of promotions.
n.2: They are not designed to encourage aggressive advertising.

q: A compliance officer is confirming the overarching standard for client communications under COBS 4. What is it?
o: Maximise firm revenue where lawful
Include full product terms always
Use FCA-approved templates only
Fair, clear and not misleading
Provide past performance for five years
w: COBS 4 requires all communications to be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.0: Maximising revenue prioritises the firm, whereas the rule centres on fairness to clients.
n.1: Full terms are not always required, while the fairness standard always applies.
n.2: Template use is not mandated, whereas fairness, clarity, and accuracy are mandatory.
n.4: Past performance is conditional and constrained, but the fairness standard applies universally.

q: An adviser needs to give a client mandatory COBS disclosures in a durable medium. Which of the following methods satisfies that requirement?
o: Recorded sales call only
Oral briefing during a meeting
Email retained by the client
Firm homepage without login
Newspaper advert
w: Email that can be stored unchanged by the client qualifies as a durable medium.

n.3: A public homepage can change without notice, whereas durable media must be stable.
n.4: A newspaper cannot ensure client-controlled retention, unlike durable electronic messages.
n.0: Recordings are firm-held, not client-retainable, unlike client-retained emails.
n.1: Oral briefings are ephemeral, not durable, whereas stored emails are.

q: A sales agent is about to cold-call prospects about an investment product. When making this non-written financial promotion, what must the caller do?
o: Identify themselves and the firm they represent
Offer to send the client a written follow-up afterwards
Quote the firm's FCA permission reference number
Read out the entire list of product risk factors
State the FSCS compensation limits word for word
w: COBS requires the caller to identify themselves and the firm in non-written promotions.

n.2: There is no rule to quote the FCA permission number on a call.
n.3: Reading out every risk factor is not the required step.
n.1: A written follow-up is not mandated for every call.
n.4: Verbatim FSCS limits are not required in the promotion.

q: A firm plans a brand image advert with no product detail. Which statement about image advertising under COBS 4 is correct?
o: It has limited exemptions from detailed rules
It is entirely outside financial promotion rules
It is allowed only on print media
It requires prior FCA approval
It must include full cost disclosures
w: Image advertising enjoys limited exemptions but must still avoid being unfair, unclear, or misleading.

n.1: It is not wholly outside scope, because fairness requirements still apply.
n.4: Full costs are not mandatory in image ads, unlike detailed product promotions.
n.2: Digital and broadcast media are also permitted; it is not print-only.
n.3: FCA pre-approval is not required; firms are responsible for compliance.

q: A firm wants to show a fund's historic returns in a financial promotion to retail clients. How must past performance be presented?
o: Be shown using only gross returns before any charges
Be presented without any benchmark comparison
Be framed as a reliable projection of the product's future returns
Include a prominent warning that it is not a guide to future results
Cover a period of at least ten years in every case
w: Past performance must include a clear warning that it is not a reliable indicator of future results.

n.0: Performance should be net of costs where possible, not gross-only.
n.4: No fixed ten-year minimum applies; up to five years is normal.
n.1: An appropriate benchmark comparison is expected, not excluded.
n.2: Past performance must not be presented as a future projection.

q: A firm's compliance officer is deciding whether COBS financial promotion standards still apply to communications aimed at different client categories. Which audience remains subject to those standards?
o: High-net-worth individuals exclusively
Sophisticated retail investors only
Overseas investors exclusively
Eligible counterparties only
Professional clients
w: Promotions to professional clients must still be fair, clear and not misleading.

n.3: Eligible counterparty category does not exclude COBS 4 duties entirely, while fairness applies to professionals.
n.2: Jurisdiction does not remove COBS standards, whereas professional clients remain covered.
n.1: Sophistication status does not nullify rules, while professional promotions still require fairness.
n.0: Wealth alone does not disapply standards, unlike the universal fairness requirement.

q: A firm plans to issue a promotion that lets clients invest straight away without further contact. Which statement best defines a direct offer financial promotion?
o: It applies only to execution-only client business
It enables the client to make an immediate investment decision
It is exempt from the promotion rules when delivered online
It can only be sent to clients through the post
It must include a Key Information Document in every case
w: A direct offer financial promotion invites and enables an immediate transactional decision by the client.

n.3: Direct offers are not limited to postal delivery.
n.4: A KID is not required in every direct offer promotion.
n.2: Online delivery does not make a direct offer exempt.
n.0: Direct offers are not limited to execution-only business.

q: An adviser drafting a retail promotion has highlighted the product's benefits, and a colleague insists the risk warnings must be equally prominent. Why must risk warnings be prominent in retail promotions?
o: To meet an FCA-mandated template of fixed, standardised wording
To allow the firm to leave out the product's costs
To balance the highlighted benefits with the material risks
To take the place of a suitability assessment
To help reduce the firm's complaint response times
w: Prominent risk warnings ensure promotions are balanced and not misleading by offsetting highlighted benefits.

n.0: There is no single FCA-mandated fixed template for warnings.
n.3: Risk warnings do not replace a suitability assessment.
n.1: Costs must still be disclosed; warnings do not excuse this.
n.4: Warnings are about balance, not complaint handling speed.

q: An appointed representative issues a financial promotion to its clients. Under the AR regime, who is responsible for ensuring that promotion complies with COBS?
o: The product manufacturer only
The principal authorised firm
The AR’s marketing contractor
The AR’s individual salesperson
The media outlet
w: The principal firm is responsible for ensuring its appointed representative’s promotions comply with COBS.

n.2: A contractor is not the regulated principal, whereas the principal bears responsibility.
n.4: Media hosts are not responsible for regulatory compliance; the principal is.
n.3: An individual salesperson acts for the AR, while the principal oversees compliance.
n.0: Manufacturers are distinct; the principal is accountable for the AR’s promotions.

q: A firm presents a fund's past performance in a client brochure and wants the comparison to comply. Under COBS 4, which practice would be acceptable?
o: Highlighting only the single best quarterly return
Using a relevant benchmark applied consistently over time
Comparing returns against unrelated asset classes
Switching to a different benchmark each year
Excluding charges when presenting the performance
w: Comparisons must be fair, using relevant and consistently applied benchmarks to avoid misleading clients.

n.0: Cherry-picking the best quarter is misleading, not compliant.
n.4: Charges should be included; excluding them misleads.
n.3: Changing benchmarks yearly undermines fair comparison.
n.2: Comparing to unrelated asset classes is not a fair comparison.

q: A firm is drafting an advertisement for a share offer that is accompanied by an approved prospectus. Under PR 3.3, what must that advertisement clearly state?
o: Where investors can obtain a copy of the prospectus
A guarantee of the investment's future performance
The daily dealing cut-off times for the offer
A personal tax illustration for each individual investor
The names of the brokers in the underwriting syndicate
w: PR 3.3 requires advertisements to indicate where the approved prospectus can be obtained by investors.

n.3: A personal tax illustration is not a PR 3.3 requirement.
n.1: Future performance cannot be guaranteed in an advert.
n.4: Naming syndicate brokers is not required under PR 3.3.
n.2: Daily dealing cut-off times are not the PR 3.3 requirement.

q: A firm advertises a securities offering for which the FCA has approved the prospectus. Which statement about that approval must the advertisement include?
o: Approval guarantees accuracy
Approval is not an endorsement
Approval ensures performance
Approval removes all risks
Approval replaces investor due diligence
w: PR 3.3 requires stating that competent authority approval should not be understood as an endorsement of the securities.

n.0: Approval does not guarantee accuracy; it is explicitly not an endorsement.
n.2: Performance is never guaranteed; approval is not an endorsement.
n.3: Risks remain present; the required wording clarifies no endorsement.
n.4: Due diligence remains necessary, since approval is not an endorsement.

q: A company preparing to list is drafting marketing advertisements to run alongside its approved prospectus. Under PR 3.3, how must those advertisements relate to the prospectus content?
o: They can emphasise projected returns
They must be consistent with it
They can rely on oral clarifications
They may simplify by omitting risks
They may pre-announce pricing changes
w: PR 3.3 requires advertisements to be consistent with the information contained in the approved prospectus.

n.3: Omitting risks would mislead, whereas consistency requires balanced content.
n.0: Emphasising projections can mislead, while consistency with the prospectus is required.
n.4: Unapproved pricing claims risk inconsistency; alignment with the prospectus is required.
n.2: Oral clarifications cannot remedy inconsistencies; written alignment is required.

q: A company is issuing shares and several parties are involved in advertising the offer. Who bears primary responsibility for the compliance of a prospectus advertisement?
o: The listing venue
Retail investors collectively
Any sell-side analyst
Financial media publisher
Issuer, offeror or applicant
w: Responsibility rests with the issuer, offeror, or person seeking admission to trading.

n.0: Venues host admissions, whereas the issuer or offeror ensures compliance.
n.3: Media outlets disseminate content; they are not the responsible party.
n.2: Analysts produce research, while the issuer or offeror is responsible.
n.1: Investors bear no publication duty; responsibility lies with the promoter.

q: A firm's advert for a bond offer emphasises the returns but plays down the risks. Why must a prospectus advertisement present risks with equal prominence to the benefits?
o: To make it easier to carry out price stabilisation
To reduce the underwriting fees charged on the issue
To prevent the advertisement giving a misleading impression
To shorten the FCA's prospectus approval timeline
To increase the level of retail investor participation
w: Balanced presentation avoids advertisements creating a misleading impression contrary to PR 3.3 requirements.

n.1: Balance is about fairness, not reducing underwriting fees.
n.4: The aim is not to boost retail participation.
n.3: It does not shorten the FCA approval timeline.
n.0: Balance is unrelated to price stabilisation mechanics.

q: An issuer's team is choosing where to place an advertisement relating to a prospectus. Under PR 3.3, which dissemination channels may be used?
o: Any medium if compliant
Only issuer websites
Only broadcast television
Only national newspapers
Only FCA-approved portals
w: Advertisements may use any medium, provided PR 3.3 content and consistency requirements are met.

n.3: There is no newspaper-only rule; any compliant medium is allowed.
n.1: Websites are not exclusive channels; multiple compliant media are permitted.
n.2: TV is not the sole route; any medium may be used if compliant.
n.4: FCA does not mandate specific portals; compliance governs.

q: A firm is preparing an advertisement that quotes performance figures taken from the fund prospectus. What must the advertisement do with that numerical data?
o: Use the same basis and source
Exclude footnotes for brevity
Present only best-case scenarios
Replace IFRS with pro-forma data
Round figures to the nearest percent
w: Consistency requires using the same basis and source as the prospectus to avoid misleading differences.

n.4: Rounding is not the requirement; consistency of basis and source is.
n.3: Changing accounting bases distorts comparability, whereas consistency is required.
n.1: Footnotes may be necessary for clarity, while consistency is paramount.
n.2: Selective best-case data misleads; alignment with the prospectus is required.

q: A firm is drafting an advertisement for a bond issue and wants investors to be able to obtain the full prospectus easily. What should the advertisement include to aid investor access?
o: Providing summaries without directions
A clear link or location details
Contacting brokers by telephone
Using QR codes only
Requiring in-person collection
w: Advertisements should tell investors exactly where to obtain the prospectus to facilitate access.

n.2: Telephone contact lacks specific access details, while a clear location enables retrieval.
n.4: Physical collection creates barriers; clear access details are required.
n.3: QR codes are optional; explicit access details satisfy the requirement.
n.0: Summaries without directions hinder access, unlike clear location details.

q: A company wishes to advertise an offer before its prospectus has been approved by the FCA. Which statement best reflects the status of that pre-approval advertising under PR 3.3?
o: It may include a legally binding offer to investors
It can state that the offer already carries the FCA's endorsement
It can contradict the disclosures in the draft prospectus
It must avoid implying that an approved prospectus already exists
It must leave out all of the product's risk factors
w: Pre-approval advertising must not suggest an approved prospectus exists and must avoid misleading impressions.

n.1: The FCA does not endorse offers; claiming so is misleading.
n.0: Pre-approval adverts should not make a binding offer.
n.4: Risk factors should not be omitted from the advert.
n.2: The advert must not contradict the draft prospectus.
