n.0: Elective professional clients can also qualify if properly classified.
n.1: Large undertakings are professional clients under MiFID and may benefit.
n.2: Institutional investors are per se professional clients, covered by the rule.

q: A compliance officer is reviewing files where suitability assumptions were relied on for professional clients. What must the firm have documented in each case?
o: The basis for classification and reliance on the assumptions
The client's weekly spend on leisure activities
The client's personal voting record history
The firm's quarterly marketing budget figures
The number of staff at each client meeting
w: Firms must record the classification and how assumptions were applied, ensuring compliance evidence if challenged.

n.1: Leisure spend is not the required documentation.
n.2: Voting records are irrelevant to classification.
n.3: Marketing budgets are not recorded for suitability.
n.4: Staff numbers at meetings are not documented for this.

q: An adviser wants to recommend that a MiFID professional client switch out of an existing holding. Under COBS 9A.2.18, what must the firm first establish?
o: That the client has not switched in six months
That the firm earns a higher commission on it
That the manufacturer has updated its marketing
That the benefits outweigh the costs and disadvantages of switching
That the rival firm has lower advertising spend
w: Switching requires a clear assessment that the new recommendation provides advantages that outweigh additional costs and potential loss of benefits.

n.2: Updated marketing is not the switch test.
n.1: Higher firm commission cannot justify a switch.
n.0: No six-month switching restriction governs suitability.
n.4: A rival's advertising spend is irrelevant to switching.

q: A compliance monitor notices an adviser repeatedly moving a client between similar funds. To decide whether this is 'churning', how is that term defined in the suitability rules?
o: Needless frequent switching that generates fees without benefit
Diversification of a client's portfolio across assets
Switching utility suppliers such as gas or electricity
Periodic rebalancing of a portfolio to its risk level
Rotation of investment staff within a firm's teams
w: Churning involves repeated switching that serves to generate fees rather than improve the client’s position, breaching suitability obligations.

n.4: Staff rotation is not churning of investments.
n.1: Legitimate diversification is not churning.
n.3: Risk-level rebalancing is legitimate, not churning.
n.2: Switching utility suppliers is unrelated to churning.

q: An adviser at a non-MiFID firm is recommending that a client switch out of an existing product into a new one. Under COBS 9.3.2, what must the firm consider first?
o: Whether the firm will gain additional market share
Whether the client loses features or benefits from the existing product
The colour of the competitor's marketing brochure
Whether the switch boosts the firm's distribution reach
The office location of the product manufacturer
w: Firms must identify and consider any loss of benefits when recommending replacement products, ensuring advice is in the client’s best interest.

n.0: Firm market share is not a switch consideration.
n.3: Firm distribution goals do not justify a switch.
n.2: Brochure colour is irrelevant to switching suitability.
n.4: Manufacturer office location has no bearing on switching.

q: An adviser is recommending that a client move from an existing personal pension into a new one. Under MiFID suitability rules, which factor must be compared between the old and new products?
o: The client's favourite financial journalist
The number of staff in the marketing team
Charges and ongoing costs of both old and new products
The firm's annual sponsorship spend total
The size of the product brochure's pages
w: A comparison of charges and costs is essential to ensure the switch delivers a net benefit to the client.

n.0: A favourite journalist is irrelevant to a switch.
n.1: Marketing team size does not affect the comparison.
n.4: Brochure page size is irrelevant to switching.
n.3: Firm sponsorship spend has no bearing on the switch.

q: A supervisor is briefing new advisers on why the FCA takes churning so seriously. What is the core regulatory concern?
o: It imposes costs without benefit, breaching the best-interests duty
It reduces the firm's profits unnecessarily each year
It limits opportunities for new client onboarding
It makes clients change their investments too rarely
It discourages firms from investing in staff training
w: Churning undermines the client’s position by creating charges without advantages, violating the obligation to act in best interests.

n.1: Churning harms clients, it does not cut firm profit.
n.2: Churning is unrelated to client onboarding limits.
n.3: Churning causes too-frequent, not too-rare, changes.
n.4: Churning is not about staff training investment.

q: A file reviewer is checking a client account for signs of unsuitable churning. Which pattern would most strongly suggest churning is occurring?
o: Tax-loss harvesting carried out at year-end
A strategic shift into assets meeting objectives
Switches aligned to goals and reduced charges
Portfolio rebalancing to maintain the risk level
Frequent switches with no clear improvement for the client
w: Switching without benefit or rationale suggests churning, as costs rise without corresponding client gains.

n.2: Goal-aligned, cheaper switches are legitimate, not churning.
n.3: Risk-level rebalancing is legitimate activity.
n.0: Tax-loss harvesting is a valid strategy, not churning.
n.1: An objective-driven shift is legitimate, not churning.

q: A paraplanner is drafting a suitability report for a recommended switch. What must the report contain to satisfy the rules?
o: The competitor's overall marketing strategy
The client's favourite stockbroker anecdotes
The firm's annual commission target figures
Clear reasons why benefits outweigh costs and risks
The firm's full list of sponsorship events
w: Reports must justify the recommendation with evidence that the switch benefits the client despite potential costs or risks.

n.2: Commission targets do not belong in a suitability report.
n.0: Competitor marketing strategy is not report content.
n.1: Anecdotes do not justify a switch recommendation.
n.4: Sponsorship events are irrelevant to the report.

q: A firm handles both MiFID and non-MiFID switching cases. How does the non-MiFID rule on switching differ from the MiFID requirement?
o: It still requires comparison but is less prescriptive on method
It allows switching purely for firm profitability
It applies only to listed equity share products
It requires FCA approval for each individual switch
It exempts firms entirely from comparing the costs
w: Non-MiFID rules mandate comparing old and new but allow flexibility, while MiFID rules are more prescriptive in methodology.

n.4: Non-MiFID rules still require cost comparison.
n.1: Switching for firm profit alone is not permitted.
n.3: No prior FCA approval is needed for each switch.
n.2: The rule is not limited to listed equities.

q: An adviser has recommended that a client move from one investment to another. What communication must the client receive?
o: An apology letter for the disruption caused
A suitability report setting out reasons for the switch
A record of the internal staff bonuses
Only a promotional marketing brochure
An oral recommendation with no written record
w: Clients must be provided with a written suitability report explaining why the switch is recommended.

n.3: A brochure does not satisfy the report requirement.
n.4: A written report, not just oral advice, is required.
n.0: An apology letter is not the required communication.
n.2: Staff bonus records are irrelevant to the client.

q: An adviser is recommending that a client switch from one pension into a replacement product that will forfeit certain guarantees. Why is it crucial to document the benefits being lost?
o: To update the firm's internal staff training manual
To satisfy the firm's marketing campaign requirements
To comply with the firm's AML identity verification checks
To show the adviser weighed disadvantages against advantages
To provide the client with competitor benchmarking data
w: Recording lost benefits ensures transparency and evidence that the adviser weighed disadvantages against gains.

n.2: AML checks are a separate obligation, not this purpose.
n.0: It is not about updating training manuals.
n.4: Competitor benchmarking is not the documentation's aim.
n.1: It serves suitability evidence, not marketing.

q: A firm is documenting a MiFID switch recommendation under COBS 9A.2.18. Which comparison is central to demonstrating the switch is justified?
o: Expected performance, risks and costs of both products
The competitor's overall staff turnover rate
The product manufacturer's sponsorship deals
The size of the firm's compliance department
The firm's year-end revenue target figures
w: The firm must compare old and new products for performance potential, risks, and costs to ensure suitability of the switch.

n.4: Firm revenue targets are not the switch comparison.
n.1: Competitor staff turnover is irrelevant to switching.
n.2: Manufacturer sponsorships do not inform the switch.
n.3: Compliance department size is irrelevant to suitability.

q: An adviser is recommending a replacement investment to a non-MiFID client. Under COBS 9.3.2, what must the assessment specifically weigh?
o: Notify the regulator ahead of the switch
Give the client competitor intelligence reports
Consider both advantages and disadvantages of the switch
Guarantee the future investment performance
Disclose the adviser's personal financial interests
w: Non-MiFID suitability requires balanced consideration of benefits and disadvantages of replacing an investment.

n.4: Disclosing adviser interests is not the switch requirement.
n.0: No advance regulator notification is required.
n.1: Competitor intelligence is not required for the client.
n.3: Future performance can never be guaranteed.

q: A discretionary manager is placing an unusually high volume of trades in a retail client's account that seem to generate little benefit beyond commission. What regulatory risk does such churning create?
o: Breach of the best-interests duty and possible enforcement
Automatic approval for new product launches
Enhanced FCA recognition and industry awards
Automatic exemption from all MiFID rules
A reduced need for compliance monitoring
w: Churning breaches best interest obligations, exposing the firm to FCA enforcement and penalties.

n.2: Churning brings sanction, not FCA recognition.
n.3: It does not exempt a firm from MiFID rules.
n.1: It does not grant automatic product approvals.
n.4: It increases, not reduces, monitoring needs.

q: A compliance officer wants proof that a MiFID switch was suitable. What is the appropriate way for the firm to evidence this?
o: Obtaining only oral confirmation from the client
A suitability report documenting the rationale and comparisons
A public press release announcing the switch decision
Logging the competitor's pricing data only
Recording the adviser's opinion in private notes
w: Written suitability reports are required to justify the switch and demonstrate compliance.

n.2: A press release is not suitability evidence.
n.0: Oral confirmation alone is insufficient evidence.
n.4: Private notes do not satisfy the report requirement.
n.3: Competitor pricing logs alone do not evidence suitability.

q: A discretionary manager routinely adjusts client portfolios and wants to be sure this is not mistaken for churning. What distinguishes legitimate rebalancing from churning?
o: Rebalancing is always driven purely by commission
Rebalancing keeps the risk profile; churning just adds fees
Rebalancing needs FCA approval every single time
Churning is limited to professional clients only
Churning always reduces charges for the client
w: Rebalancing is aligned to maintaining risk levels, while churning is exploitative and provides no client advantage.

n.0: Rebalancing serves the risk profile, not commission.
n.4: Churning adds charges; it does not reduce them.
n.2: Rebalancing does not need FCA approval each time.
n.3: Churning can affect any client, not only professionals.

q: An adviser is recommending that a client move from an existing plan into a new one and must evidence the core outcome that justifies any switch. Which client outcome must always be demonstrated in a switch recommendation?
o: That competitor firms lose market share
That the adviser earns a higher commission on it
That the firm meets its distribution quota
That the regulator's workload is reduced
That the switch leaves the client better off overall
w: Switches are only suitable if the client gains overall, considering benefits against costs and risks.

n.1: Adviser commission is not the required outcome.
n.2: Meeting firm quotas does not justify a switch.
n.0: Competitor market share is irrelevant to the client.
n.3: Regulator workload is not a switch consideration.

q: A firm is reviewing its disclosure practices as a safeguard against churning. What role does disclosure play in preventing it?
o: It fully substitutes for the best-interests obligation
It ensures clients are told of costs and disadvantages
It removes the need for written suitability reports
It exempts the firm from ongoing FCA supervision
It lets advisers prioritise their own commission income
w: Disclosing costs and disadvantages helps clients identify unnecessary switches and supports compliance with best interest rules.

n.2: Disclosure supplements, not removes, suitability reports.
n.4: Disclosure does not license commission-led advice.
n.0: It cannot replace the best-interests obligation.
n.3: Disclosure does not exempt a firm from supervision.

q: The FCA reviews a firm that has advised a client to switch investments several times in a year. What is the common breach it looks for?
o: Failure to provide annual marketing updates
Failure to justify benefits against the cumulative costs
Failure to disclose the branch opening times
Failure to report competitor product launches
Failure to expand the call centre's hours
w: The FCA views unjustified costs from frequent switches without net benefit as a breach of suitability obligations.

n.2: Branch opening times are irrelevant to switching breaches.
n.0: Marketing updates are not a suitability breach.
n.4: Call centre hours have no bearing on churning.
n.3: Reporting competitor launches is not a suitability duty.

q: A trainee asks why the same 'client best interest' test underpins both MiFID and non-MiFID switching rules. What is the correct explanation?
o: Because suitability rules flow from the overarching best-interests duty
Because it guarantees the advisers their bonuses
Because it reduces the FCA's own enforcement budget
Because it stops clients from ever seeking redress
Because it standardises all client marketing materials
w: The duty to act in the client’s best interest underpins all suitability rules, including switching assessments.

n.2: The test is about client protection, not FCA budgets.
n.1: Best interests does not guarantee adviser bonuses.
n.4: It does not exist to standardise marketing.
n.3: It supports, rather than blocks, client redress.

q: A compliance officer is coaching advisers on documenting switch recommendations properly. What should they avoid doing in the file notes?
o: A full analysis of the product's features
Detailed explanation of the charges and risks involved
A client-specific assessment of the objectives
Generic justifications that fail to compare old and new products
Transparent disclosure of the benefits lost
w: Generic documentation fails to evidence suitability; comparisons and specifics are essential to comply with COBS.

n.1: Detailed charge and risk explanation is good practice, not avoided.
n.2: Client-specific assessment is required, not something to avoid.
n.0: Full feature analysis is good practice, not to be avoided.
n.4: Disclosing lost benefits is required, not something to avoid.

q: An adviser is preparing a suitability report for a retail client under COBS 9A.3.2. What is the report's primary purpose?
o: To supply marketing material for future clients
To explain why a recommended transaction is suitable
To record the adviser's own sales performance
To advertise the firm's new product launches
To update the FCA on the firm's profits
w: A suitability report must justify why the recommendation is appropriate for the client’s circumstances and objectives.

n.3: The report justifies suitability, it does not advertise.
n.2: It is not a record of adviser sales performance.
n.4: It does not report firm profits to the FCA.
n.0: It is not marketing material for future clients.

q: An adviser conducting non-MiFID business is arranging a personal pension for a retail client and must get the timing of the suitability report right. Under COBS 9.4.1, when must the suitability report be provided?
o: Before the transaction is concluded
When the client reaches retirement age
Within 12 months of the transaction
Only at year-end audits
Only if the FCA requests it
w: Non-MiFID rules require suitability reports to be delivered before the client is bound by a transaction.

n.2: Waiting 12 months breaches the requirement for pre-transaction delivery.
n.3: Year-end audits do not set report timing.
n.4: Reports are mandatory regardless of FCA requests.
n.1: Age milestones are irrelevant; timing is tied to transactions.

q: A firm makes a personal recommendation and must decide who receives a written suitability report. Which client category is specifically entitled to one?
o: Eligible counterparties
Corporate treasury departments
Wholesale clients only
Professional clients
Retail clients
w: Suitability report obligations apply to retail clients, reflecting their need for greater protection and transparency.

n.3: Professional clients are subject to lighter rules.
n.0: Eligible counterparties are exempt from suitability obligations.
n.2: Wholesale client category does not trigger suitability reports.
n.1: Corporate treasury is typically professional or counterparty status, not retail.

q: A paraplanner is completing a MiFID suitability report for a retail client. What detail must it set out?
o: The adviser's own personal investment holdings
The client's full family tree and living relatives
How much commission the adviser earned on the sale
How the recommendation meets objectives and the risk profile
The competitor's product advertising campaigns
w: Reports must set out why the product meets objectives and is consistent with the client’s risk profile and financial situation.

n.2: Adviser commission is not required report detail.
n.1: A family tree is not part of a suitability report.
n.4: Competitor advertising is irrelevant to the report.
n.0: The adviser's own holdings are not report content.

q: An adviser is about to hand a client a suitability report and the paraplanner reminds her it must be in a durable medium. Why must suitability reports be provided in a durable medium?
o: To let the FCA control the product's pricing
So the client can refer back to the reasoning for the advice
To support the firm's client entertainment policy
To enable faster marketing distribution to clients
To reduce the firm's printing and postage costs
w: Durable mediums (e.g. paper, PDF) ensure clients can retain and revisit advice justification over time.

n.4: Durable medium serves the client, not cost saving.
n.3: It is not about speeding marketing distribution.
n.0: The FCA does not control product pricing via this.
n.2: It has nothing to do with client entertainment.

q: An adviser is writing a suitability report for a non-MiFID client under COBS 9.4.2. What must the report explain?
o: How the firm will hit its quarterly sales targets
Why the client should shun competitor products
The adviser's own employment contract terms
The basis on which the personal recommendation is suitable
The FCA's annual enforcement statistics
w: Reports must set out the reasoning for why the recommended transaction is appropriate to the client’s needs.

n.2: Adviser contract terms are not report content.
n.1: The report justifies suitability, not disparages rivals.
n.0: Firm sales targets are irrelevant to the report.
n.4: FCA statistics are not part of the report.

q: A firm is deciding when its MiFID advisers must produce a suitability report. In which situation is one required?
o: Only where the FCA instructs the firm to
Whenever a personal recommendation is made to a retail client
Only for discretionary portfolio clients
Only if the investment exceeds fifty thousand pounds
Only if the client specifically requests it
w: MiFID requires suitability reports for any personal recommendation to a retail client, regardless of size or request.

n.3: No size threshold triggers the report requirement.
n.4: A report is required whether or not the client asks.
n.2: It is not limited to discretionary portfolio clients.
n.0: It does not depend on an FCA instruction.

q: A client agrees to a transaction over the phone that must be actioned immediately. Under the non-MiFID rules, which exemption may apply to providing the suitability report upfront?
o: When the adviser is newly appointed to the firm
When the client holds professional client status
When the client requests paperless documents only
When the product itself is entirely unregulated
Where advice is by distance means and immediate action is needed
w: COBS 9.4.3 allows deferral of suitability reports where urgent action is required due to distance communication.

n.2: Paperless format does not remove the report duty.
n.1: Professional status does not create this exemption.
n.3: An unregulated product does not trigger this exemption.
n.0: A new adviser is not an exemption ground.

q: An adviser executes an urgent transaction for a client where the suitability report could not be produced beforehand. When must that deferred report be provided?
o: At the very end of the tax year
Only when the client lodges a complaint
Only if the FCA specifically requests it
At the client's next birthday each year
As soon as practicable after the transaction
w: Deferred reports under urgent circumstances must still be provided as soon as possible to maintain compliance.

n.3: A birthday is not the required deadline.
n.0: Year-end is not the deferred report deadline.
n.2: It is required regardless of any FCA request.
n.1: It is required regardless of any complaint.

q: An adviser is documenting a recommendation for a structured product aimed at a cautious client and considers why the suitability report matters so much here. Why is a suitability report especially important for complex or higher risk products?
o: It lets the firm charge the client noticeably higher fees
It stops the client transferring to another provider
It records client understanding and the adviser's reasoning in detail
It substitutes entirely for the required KYC checks
It reduces the firm's need to monitor compliance
w: The more complex the product, the more crucial it is to document reasoning and ensure the client’s objectives and risk tolerance are met.

n.0: It is not a device to charge higher fees.
n.3: It does not replace separate KYC checks.
n.4: It does not reduce compliance monitoring.
n.1: It does not restrict client provider transfers.

q: An adviser makes a personal recommendation to a retail client. What does COBS 9A.3.2 require the firm to do?
o: Record the advice in the adviser's private notes
Give a durable-medium suitability report before concluding the deal
Offer the client a rebate on the transaction fees
Wait until year-end to issue all reports in bulk
Send only a short summary marketing leaflet instead
w: Under MiFID rules, firms must provide a suitability report in durable medium before binding the retail client to the transaction.

n.2: No fee rebate is required by this rule.
n.4: A marketing leaflet is not a suitability report.
n.0: Private notes do not satisfy the report duty.
n.3: Reports must precede the transaction, not wait for year-end.

q: An adviser is drafting a non-MiFID suitability report where the client is replacing an existing investment. What must the report specifically explain about that replacement?
o: Which competitor is losing the most market share
How the client should complain if unhappy later
Why the replacement beats keeping the existing investment
How the adviser's own team is organised internally
The regulator's published annual priorities list
w: Suitability reports for replacement business must explain why the new product is more suitable than keeping the current one, highlighting costs and lost benefits.

n.0: Competitor market share is not report content.
n.3: Team organisation is irrelevant to the report.
n.1: Complaint procedure is not the replacement rationale.
n.4: Regulator priorities are not part of the report.

q: A compliance officer reviews how advisers document recommendations and notes some rely only on verbal explanations at meetings. Why must the firm issue written suitability reports to retail clients instead?
o: To let clients avoid reading any written material
To replace the firm's internal training manuals
To satisfy the FCA's product marketing obligations
To keep a permanent, reviewable record of the advice rationale
To reduce the administrative staff's daily workload
w: Written suitability reports provide a permanent, auditable record of the adviser’s reasoning and protect both client and firm.

n.2: It is not about FCA marketing obligations.
n.1: It does not replace internal training manuals.
n.4: Its purpose is a durable record, not workload reduction.
n.0: It exists so clients can read the rationale, not avoid it.

q: A pension transfer specialist is preparing a suitability report for a client leaving a defined benefit scheme. What additional requirement applies to that report?
o: They must provide FCA statistics on transfer volumes
They must include the competitor's advertising examples
They must guarantee a specific level of pension return
They must disclose the adviser's personal pension value
Explain why transferring is suitable despite losing valuable guarantees
w: Pension transfer reports must explain why giving up valuable guarantees or features is justified and in the client’s best interest.

n.1: Competitor advertising is not required in the report.
n.3: The adviser's own pension value is not disclosed.
n.0: FCA transfer volume statistics are not report content.
n.2: No specific pension return can be guaranteed.

q: An adviser needs to deliver a suitability report in a durable medium. Which of the following qualifies as a durable medium?
o: A firm's public webpage that is updated and overwritten regularly
Paper or electronic formats the client can store unchanged
Social media posts the firm can edit or remove at any time
Live phone calls the adviser summarises verbally afterwards
Text messages the firm automatically deletes after thirty days
w: Durable mediums include paper and electronic files like PDFs, allowing clients to access the report unchanged over time.

n.3: A verbal summary is not durable as it cannot be stored and retrieved unchanged.
n.0: A frequently overwritten webpage is not durable; the client cannot retrieve it unchanged.
n.4: Messages deleted after 30 days fail the durability test of unchanged future access.
n.2: Editable, removable posts are not durable media under COBS.

q: An adviser at a MiFID firm is preparing a suitability report after recommending a fund to a client. Under MiFID, what must the report explicitly link together?
o: The regulator's guidance notes to the firm's internal sales targets
The client's personal hobbies to the chosen investment strategy
The adviser's commission rate to the client's total portfolio value
The recommendation to the client's objectives and financial situation
The firm's marketing spend to the range of products it offers
w: Suitability reports must connect the advice given directly to the client’s personal objectives, financial situation, and risk tolerance.

n.2: Commission rates are not what a suitability report must link the advice to.
n.4: Marketing spend is irrelevant to the personalised suitability linkage required.
n.1: Hobbies are not the objectives or financial situation the report must connect to.
n.0: Reports link advice to the client's needs, not regulator notes to sales targets.

q: An adviser is recommending a higher-risk investment and preparing the suitability report. What obligation applies to that report?
o: Disclose rival firms' charges to justify the higher-risk choice
Limit the report to tax benefits and omit any downside scenarios
Provide detailed explanation of specific risks and why they are acceptable
Guarantee the product will outperform the lower-risk alternatives shown
Reduce written detail so the client is not put off from buying
w: Higher-risk products require clear disclosure of risks and justification of suitability despite those risks.

n.3: Firms must never guarantee performance; that would be misleading.
n.1: Omitting downside risks breaches the duty to disclose specific risks clearly.
n.4: Higher-risk products require more detail, not less.
n.0: Competitor charges do not justify suitability of a higher-risk recommendation.

q: A non-MiFID firm concludes a deal by phone that the client wants executed at once. When may the firm defer providing the suitability report?
o: When the client gives verbal consent to waive the report
Whenever the adviser's diary is full for the coming fortnight
When the amount being invested is below ten thousand pounds
When the product provider is based outside the United Kingdom
When immediate execution is necessary due to distance communications
w: Deferral is permitted only in urgent distance-selling cases, with the report delivered as soon as practicable afterward.

n.1: A busy adviser is not a permitted ground to defer the report.
n.0: A client cannot verbally waive the suitability report requirement.
n.2: There is no monetary threshold that removes the reporting duty.
n.3: The provider's location does not permit deferral of the report.

q: An adviser is preparing a suitability report and reflects on the overarching regulatory principle that requires it. Which principle underpins the suitability reporting requirement?
o: The obligation to reduce the firm's printing and postage costs
The requirement to meet the FCA's annual income and levy targets
The commitment to advance each adviser's professional career path
The EU directive setting minimum advertising and marketing standards
The duty to act honestly, fairly and professionally in the client's best interests
w: Suitability reporting is grounded in the best interest duty, ensuring clients understand recommendations and firms demonstrate compliance.

n.0: Cost-saving is not the regulatory principle behind suitability reporting.
n.1: The FCA has no income targets that drive suitability rules.
n.3: Suitability reporting stems from the best-interests duty, not marketing rules.
n.2: Adviser career development is unrelated to the suitability principle.

q: A regulator is explaining to consumers why firms must issue suitability reports. What benefit does this obligation give the client?
o: A guarantee of tax-free returns on every recommended product
Removal of the need to seek any independent second opinion
Automatic FSCS compensation cover for any investment loss
Greater transparency and ability to challenge unsuitable advice
Exemption from all product charges once the report is signed
w: Reports increase transparency, giving clients a clear rationale and ability to question or challenge advice if inappropriate.

n.0: No report guarantees tax-free returns.
n.2: A suitability report does not grant automatic compensation cover.
n.1: It does not remove the value of independent advice.
n.4: Signing a report does not exempt a client from product charges.

q: A firm is setting the timing for issuing suitability reports under MiFID rules in COBS 9A.3.2. When must the report be provided?
o: Within thirty days after the transaction has been completed
Only when the FCA specifically requests a copy of it
At the close of the firm's financial reporting year
Before the retail client is bound by the recommended transaction
At the client's next scheduled annual portfolio review
w: COBS 9A.3.2 requires that suitability reports be delivered before a retail client is bound by a personal recommendation transaction.

n.0: COBS 9A.3.2 requires it before, not 30 days after, the transaction.
n.1: It is required regardless of any FCA request.
n.4: It cannot be delayed to an annual review.
n.2: It is transaction-based, not tied to the firm's year-end.

q: A paraplanner is drafting a suitability report following a pension consolidation recommendation. Under COBS 9A.3.3, what must that report set out?
o: A record of how the client has voted at company annual general meetings
A full history of the client's personal credit score and borrowing record
Why the advice is suitable, covering objectives, risk tolerance and capacity for loss
A summary of the adviser's own career achievements and qualifications
A comparison of competitor firms' recent advertising campaigns
w: Reports must detail why the recommendation is suitable, linking to objectives, risk profile, and ability to bear losses.

n.1: A credit history is not the required content of a suitability report.
n.3: The adviser's achievements are not the point of the report.
n.4: Competitor advertising is irrelevant to suitability.
n.0: AGM voting records are irrelevant to the report.

q: A non-MiFID firm is checking the timing rule in COBS 9.4.4 for suitability reports. When must the report be provided?
o: They may be issued up to six months after advice is given
They are required only for investments above one hundred thousand pounds
They can be replaced entirely by verbal advice to the client
They must be provided before the transaction is carried out
They are optional unless the client specifically demands one
w: COBS 9.4.4 mirrors MiFID requirements: reports must be provided before the retail client is bound by a transaction.

n.0: COBS 9.4.4 requires delivery before the transaction, not six months later.
n.1: There is no such monetary threshold for the report.
n.2: Verbal advice cannot substitute for the written report.
n.4: The report is mandatory, not client-optional.

q: An adviser at a MiFID firm is preparing a suitability report following a personal recommendation. Under COBS 9A.3, which content is mandatory in that report?
o: The firm's yearly profit margin and dividend policy
The FCA's latest thematic review findings for the sector
The adviser's annual bonus and sales incentive structure
The client's preferred day and channel for future contact
The client's investment objectives and how the advice meets them
w: MiFID requires suitability reports to directly link the recommendation with client objectives and circumstances.

n.2: Adviser bonuses are not mandatory suitability report content.
n.0: Firm profit margins are not required in a suitability report.
n.1: Thematic review findings are not report content.
n.3: Contact preferences are not the mandatory objectives-linkage content.

q: An IFA is finalising a suitability report for a client following a non-MiFID insurance recommendation. Under COBS 9.4.5, which additional information must that report contain?
o: The average one-year return on the FTSE 100 index
A summary of a neighbouring client's past investment choices
The client's demands and needs and how the recommendation meets them
The number of staff in the firm's compliance team
The adviser's punctuality and timekeeping record for the year
w: Reports must explicitly address the client’s demands and needs, showing how the advice satisfies them.

n.0: Index returns are not the demands-and-needs content required.
n.4: An adviser's timekeeping is irrelevant to the report.
n.3: Compliance headcount is not report content.
n.1: Another person's history is irrelevant to this client's report.

q: An adviser completes an urgent transaction over the phone under a distance-communication arrangement and cannot give the suitability report beforehand. How soon must the deferred report follow?
o: As soon as practicable after the transaction is completed
Only in the event that the client makes a complaint
Only if the FCA later asks to see a copy of it
Within five years of the transaction being carried out
Entirely at the adviser's own discretion and timing
w: Both MiFID and non-MiFID rules allow urgent deferral but require reports to follow as soon as practicable afterward.

n.3: Five years is far too long; it must follow as soon as practicable.
n.2: It is required regardless of any FCA request.
n.4: Timing is not left to adviser discretion.
n.1: It is not conditional on a complaint being made.

q: An adviser is completing a suitability report and includes the downside risks of the recommended plan. Why must the report identify the risks associated with the recommendation?
o: So the firm can increase the client's long-term dependence on it
So the adviser can justify charging a higher rate of commission
So the client can make an informed decision balancing risks and benefits
So the firm can market related products more easily afterwards
So competing firms are placed at a clear disadvantage
w: Risk disclosure ensures clients understand potential downsides and can make informed investment decisions.

n.1: Risk disclosure is not to justify commission.
n.3: It is not a marketing device.
n.0: It is not intended to create client dependence.
n.4: It has nothing to do with disadvantaging competitors.

q: A compliance officer is confirming the MiFID rule on suitability report timing. Which statement is correct?
o: It is needed only when the client specifically asks for one
It applies only to products with a term over five years
It may always be delayed until the next quarterly statement
It must be provided before, or immediately after urgent execution
It applies solely to purchases of UCITS collective funds
w: MiFID requires delivery before the client is bound, or immediately afterward if urgent distance communication applies.

n.2: It cannot always be delayed to a quarterly statement.
n.1: There is no five-year term condition.
n.0: It is mandatory, not on request only.
n.4: It is not limited to UCITS purchases.

q: A paraplanner is checking the required contents of a non-MiFID suitability report under COBS 9.4.6. What must it include?
o: A list of the client's social media accounts and preferences
A full account of the client's schooling and educational history
The reasons why the recommended transaction is suitable for the client
An index of the relevant chapters of the FCA Handbook
A copy of the adviser's continuing professional training log
w: Reports must provide reasons why the transaction suits the client’s circumstances, objectives, and needs.

n.1: Educational history is not required suitability content.
n.4: An adviser training log is not report content.
n.3: A Handbook index is not required in the report.
n.0: Social media details are not required content.

q: A supervisor is explaining why suitability reports for retail clients cannot rely on generic templates. What is the reason?
o: Personalisation is needed to benchmark the client against rivals
Generic templates fail to demonstrate why advice meets individual needs
It removes any need to hold a best execution policy
Personalising the report lets the firm justify charging higher fees
A personalised report reduces the firm's liability to nil
w: Reports must be client-specific to evidence that the advice genuinely meets the client’s needs and objectives.

n.3: Personalisation is not about justifying higher fees.
n.0: Reports are not for benchmarking clients against others.
n.4: Personalisation does not eliminate firm liability.
n.2: It does not remove best execution obligations.

q: An adviser has told a client a transaction is unsuitable, yet the client wants to go ahead anyway. Under COBS 9.5A guidance, how is such a client described?
o: A client who refuses to give identity details for AML checks
A client who demands fees below the market average rate
A client who insists on proceeding against the adviser's recommendation
A client who insists on receiving the report only on paper
A client who will meet the adviser only outside office hours
w: An insistent client is one who, after receiving advice that a transaction is unsuitable, still requests to proceed against that advice.

n.3: Format preference does not define an insistent client.
n.1: Fee demands are not the definition of an insistent client.
n.4: Meeting times are irrelevant to the definition.
n.0: Refusing AML checks is a different matter, not insistence.

q: An adviser has told a client that a high-risk fund is unsuitable, but the client still insists on buying it. Before the firm processes the transaction, what must it ensure?
o: That the FCA has given prior written approval to proceed
That the client signs a waiver removing all firm liability
That it has clearly explained why the advice was unsuitable
That the client invests only in low-risk regulated products
That the firm secures an additional commission for the sale
w: Firms must evidence that the unsuitable nature of the transaction was explained clearly to the client before proceeding.

n.1: A waiver cannot remove the firm's regulatory liability.
n.0: No FCA pre-approval is required or available.
n.3: There is no low-risk-only restriction on insistent clients.
n.4: Securing extra commission is not a required safeguard.

q: A client insists on proceeding with an investment against the adviser's clear recommendation. Under COBS 9.5A, what documentation is critical for the adviser to retain?
o: The client's entry details from the electoral register
Records of the advice, the client's insistence and the risks explained
A copy of the firm's most recent annual report and accounts
A selection of marketing brochures produced by competitors
An up-to-date copy of the adviser's curriculum vitae
w: Clear documentation of the advice given, the client’s insistence, and risks disclosed is required to evidence compliance with COBS 9.5A.

n.2: The firm's annual accounts are irrelevant to insistent-client files.
n.0: Electoral register details are not the critical documentation.
n.3: Competitor brochures are not required records.
n.4: An adviser CV is not the documentation needed.

q: A client insists on proceeding against the adviser's recommendation. Why should the firm still provide a suitability report?
o: To market a range of other products to the client
To replace the firm's ongoing monitoring obligations
To remove the need to carry out any AML checks
To protect the adviser's entitlement to sales commission
To evidence the advice given and highlight risks of proceeding
w: Even if the client insists, a suitability report must document the adviser’s reasoning and highlight the risks of proceeding contrary to advice.

n.3: The report is not to protect commission.
n.0: It is not a marketing tool.
n.2: It does not remove AML obligations.
n.1: It does not replace ongoing monitoring duties.

q: An adviser has recommended against a transfer, but the client insists on going ahead anyway. Under COBS guidance on insistent clients, what must the adviser clearly communicate before proceeding?
o: The risks and disadvantages of proceeding against advice
The adviser’s personal opinion of competitor firms
The potential for the adviser to earn higher commission
The average market return over the past decade
The client’s obligation to write their own suitability report
w: Insistent clients must be made aware of the risks and disadvantages of ignoring professional advice before proceeding.

n.1: Competitor opinions are irrelevant.
n.2: Commission is not to be discussed as justification.
n.3: Market averages are not a substitute for suitability disclosure.
n.4: The firm, not the client, is responsible for reports.

q: An adviser has warned a client against a course of action, but the client wishes to proceed regardless. How should the firm properly evidence the client's insistence on its file?
o: By retaining an internal staff duty rota for that week
By filing competitor product brochures with the record
By obtaining a signed statement confirming the client's decision
By keeping only the adviser's own informal personal notes
By citing recent FCA enforcement cases in the file
w: Firms should seek a signed statement or record of the client’s decision to proceed despite advice, evidencing informed insistence.

n.3: Informal notes alone are weak evidence; a signed statement is expected.
n.0: A staff rota does not evidence client insistence.
n.4: Citing enforcement cases does not evidence this client's decision.
n.1: Competitor brochures do not evidence insistence.

q: A firm processes an insistent client's request but fails to follow the relevant guidance. What regulatory risk does it face?
o: The firm will be barred from using any marketing slogans
The firm's clients become professional clients automatically
The firm may face enforcement for unsuitable advice and weak records
The firm may lose its access to FCA press releases
The firm will forfeit its annual staff training budget
w: Failing to follow insistent client guidance risks FCA enforcement for unsuitable advice and failure to evidence compliance.

n.3: Losing press-release access is not a regulatory consequence.
n.0: There is no marketing-slogan ban.
n.1: Clients are not reclassified automatically.
n.4: Training budgets are not a regulatory sanction.

q: A client insists on proceeding against the adviser's recommendation, and the firm agrees to transact. Why is recordkeeping especially important in such insistent client cases?
o: Because it removes the need for ongoing client communication
Because it guarantees the investment's future performance
Because it ensures advisers receive larger annual bonuses
Because regulators may scrutinise the firm's justification for proceeding
Because it exempts the firm from routine FCA oversight
w: Detailed records are vital as insistent client cases attract heightened regulatory scrutiny to ensure compliance with suitability standards.

n.2: Recordkeeping is unrelated to adviser bonuses.
n.0: It does not remove communication duties.
n.1: Records cannot guarantee performance.
n.4: It does not exempt the firm from oversight.

q: An adviser wants to respect a client's wishes while meeting regulatory duties when the client insists on unsuitable action. How should the adviser handle this?
o: Allow the client to waive the firm's suitability obligations
Refuse every request an insistent client makes as routine
Defer to a competitor firm's advice instead of your own
Respect the client's decision but fully document the advice and risks
Place the firm's profitability ahead of the client's suitability
w: Advisers must respect client autonomy but comply with obligations by documenting advice, risks, and client insistence.

n.1: Automatic refusal is not the required balanced approach.
n.4: Prioritising profit over suitability breaches the rules.
n.0: Suitability obligations cannot be waived by the client.
n.2: Deferring to a competitor is not an appropriate response.

q: A compliance manager is explaining the thinking behind COBS 9.5A guidance on insistent clients. What is the key regulatory principle?
o: Clients bear full responsibility for outcomes once they insist
Firms should avoid giving any advice to such clients at all
Advisers should decline to document clearly unsuitable cases
Clients must be protected even if they choose to act against advice
Clients must pay a higher fee whenever they insist on a deal
w: The principle is to maintain client protection by documenting risks and advice, even if clients insist on unsuitable actions.

n.0: Insistence does not shift all responsibility onto the client.
n.1: Firms should not refuse to advise insistent clients.
n.2: Unsuitable cases must be documented, not left undocumented.
n.4: There is no higher-fee rule for insisting.

q: A firm offers non-advised sales and must apply the appropriateness rules. What is the primary purpose of those rules?
o: To establish suitability against objectives and risk appetite
To assess client knowledge and experience for the service or product
To confirm the client's tax residency for regulatory reporting
To verify the client's overall financial resilience to losses
To allocate client orders to the best execution venue available
w: Appropriateness rules test whether a non-advised client has sufficient knowledge and experience to understand the product’s risks.

n.3: Financial resilience is not what appropriateness assesses.
n.2: Tax residency is unrelated to appropriateness.
n.0: That describes suitability, not appropriateness.
n.4: Order allocation is a best-execution matter, not appropriateness.

q: A broker is deciding whether a client can trade a product on an execution-only basis without an appropriateness test. Which product is generally treated as non-complex?
o: Warrants on individual equities
Structured UCITS with capital protection features
Units in a plain UCITS scheme
Contingent convertible bonds
Exchange-traded options on indices
w: Plain UCITS are typically non-complex, permitting execution-only where other conditions are met.

n.1: Structured UCITS can embed derivatives, making them complex and outside execution-only without appropriateness.
n.3: CoCos are complex due to loss-absorption features, requiring appropriateness rather than execution-only treatment.
n.0: Equity warrants are derivative instruments and therefore complex, requiring an appropriateness assessment.
n.4: Exchange-traded options are derivatives and complex, so appropriateness must be assessed.

q: A client wants to buy a complex product on a non-advised basis but declines to answer the appropriateness questions. How should the firm proceed?
o: Treat the client as an elective professional to skip the test
Warn appropriateness cannot be assessed; proceed only if the client insists
Decline all business until a full suitability assessment is done
Rely on best execution disclosures to satisfy the rules here
Proceed with no warning because execution-only always applies
w: If information is insufficient, the firm must warn the client that appropriateness cannot be assessed; it may then proceed if the client insists.

n.2: Suitability is not required for a non-advised complex sale.
n.4: A warning is required; execution-only does not always apply to complex products.
n.0: A firm cannot unilaterally reclassify a client to skip the test.
n.3: Best execution disclosures do not satisfy appropriateness.

q: A non-MiFID firm sells complex products to clients without giving advice. Why does COBS 10.1 apply to these sales?
o: To cap product and service charges on an annual basis
To ensure clients understand complex risks before execution
To require a personal recommendation in all transactions
To impose a statutory cooling-off period for every product
To require a KID to be delivered for all packaged products
w: COBS 10.1 ensures clients in non-advised settings have sufficient knowledge and experience to understand risks, especially for complex products.

n.4: COBS 10.1 does not mandate KIDs for all packaged products.
n.0: It does not cap charges.
n.3: It does not impose a cooling-off period on every product.
n.2: Non-advised sales, by definition, have no personal recommendation.

q: A firm is identifying which MiFID clients fall within the appropriateness regime under COBS 10A.2.1. Who is in scope?
o: Eligible counterparties transacting in their normal business
Only retail clients receiving a personal recommendation
Clients dealing solely through discretionary mandates
Clients given MiFID services other than advice or portfolio management
Clients buying non-investment general insurance contracts
w: COBS 10A.2.1 applies appropriateness when a MiFID service is provided other than advice or portfolio management.

n.1: Personal recommendations engage suitability, not appropriateness.
n.2: Discretionary portfolio management is outside appropriateness.
n.0: Eligible counterparty business is outside these appropriateness rules.
n.4: General insurance is outside MiFID appropriateness scope.

q: A client wishes to buy a non-complex product on an execution-only basis with no assessment from the firm. What must the mandatory warning communicate to the client?
o: That the client waives all of their best execution protections
That the firm guarantees no capital loss will ever occur
That the firm will not assess whether the product is appropriate
That the tax consequences have been independently reviewed
That the transaction carries a statutory cooling-off period
w: The warning must state the firm is not required to assess appropriateness for execution-only non-complex transactions.

n.0: Execution-only does not waive best execution protections.
n.1: No firm may guarantee against capital loss.
n.4: No cooling-off guarantee is part of the warning.
n.3: The warning does not concern tax review.

q: A trainee is comparing the suitability and appropriateness assessments. How do they differ in the information the firm must gather?
o: Suitability requires only the client's risk appetite details
Appropriateness requires evidence of the client's tax planning
Suitability covers objectives and finances; appropriateness only knowledge
Appropriateness requires a full affordability analysis first
Both require only the client's knowledge and experience data
w: Suitability considers objectives and financial situation alongside knowledge; appropriateness looks solely at knowledge and experience for non-advised services.

n.4: Suitability also needs objectives and finances, not just knowledge.
n.3: Appropriateness does not require affordability analysis.
n.0: Suitability needs far more than risk appetite alone.
n.1: Appropriateness does not require tax-planning evidence.

q: A retail client buys listed shares online through the firm's platform with no advice given. Which assessment, if any, applies?
o: Appropriateness always, because shares are complex instruments
No assessment at all, since retail clients may simply opt out
Confirmation of the client's eligible counterparty status first
No appropriateness if execution-only conditions for non-complex apply
A full suitability assessment before each and every transaction
w: Listed shares are generally non-complex, so the firm may use execution-only if all conditions and the warning are satisfied.

n.4: Suitability applies to advice, not execution-only dealing.
n.0: Listed shares are generally non-complex, so appropriateness is not always required.
n.1: Retail clients cannot simply opt out of the framework.
n.2: Retail buyers are not eligible counterparties.

q: A client contacts an execution-only broker and, during the call, the dealer suggests a particular fund the client then buys. Which circumstance defeats the execution-only exemption under MiFID rules?
o: The order is placed through the firm's mobile trading app
The client is UK resident and over eighteen years old
The client selects the firm's default market venue
The firm suggests a specific product, which amounts to advice
The product manufacturer has produced a KID for it
w: Any personal recommendation constitutes advice, so execution-only conditions are not satisfied and appropriateness or suitability obligations change.

n.0: The channel used (an app) does not defeat the exemption.
n.1: Residency and age do not defeat the exemption.
n.4: A KID existing does not defeat execution-only.
n.2: Choosing a default venue does not defeat the exemption.

q: A client wants to buy a complex product on an execution-only basis with no advice. Under COBS 10.1, when must the firm carry out an appropriateness assessment?
o: When a client requests a statutory cooling-off period
When carrying out suitability assessments for advised sales
When the firm's best execution arrangements are disclosed
When offering basic deposit accounts to retail clients
When providing non-advised services involving complex products
w: Non-MiFID appropriateness under COBS 10.1 applies in non-advised sales involving complex instruments to ensure the client understands the risks.

n.3: Basic deposit accounts do not trigger appropriateness.
n.1: Advised sales engage suitability, not appropriateness.
n.0: A cooling-off request does not trigger appropriateness.
n.2: Best execution disclosure is unrelated to appropriateness.

q: A firm is running an appropriateness assessment under MiFID for a non-advised trade. Which factor does it consider?
o: The firm's compliance with statutory cooling-off rules
The client's knowledge and experience of the relevant instrument
The client's overall wealth and available liquidity profile
The firm's market share in the instrument being offered
The client's annual tax liability and country of residence
w: Appropriateness considers only the client’s knowledge and experience with the instrument or service, not their finances or tax status.

n.4: Tax liability is not an appropriateness factor.
n.3: Market share is irrelevant to appropriateness.
n.2: Wealth and liquidity relate to suitability, not appropriateness.
n.0: Cooling-off compliance is not an appropriateness factor.

q: A non-MiFID firm is selling a complex product to a client on a non-advised basis. What must it obtain from the client?
o: Independent legal advice obtained before the transaction
Confirmation of the client's income, assets and liabilities
A signed suitability report justifying the recommendation
Documentary evidence of the client's insurance coverage
Information on the client's knowledge and experience of the product
w: COBS 10.1 requires assessing the client’s knowledge and experience in non-advised complex product sales.

n.1: Income and assets relate to suitability, not appropriateness.
n.2: A suitability report is not required for non-advised sales.
n.0: Independent legal advice is not required.
n.3: Insurance evidence is not required.

q: A client wants to trade one of several products without advice, and the firm must decide which requires appropriateness testing under MiFID. Which is complex and triggers it?
o: Ordinary shares in a large FTSE 100 listed company
UK Government gilt-edged fixed-interest securities
Units in a plain vanilla UCITS collective scheme
A contract for difference, a leveraged derivative product
A fixed-term deposit account held with a UK bank
w: CFDs are derivative instruments and always complex, so appropriateness must be assessed under MiFID rules.

n.0: FTSE 100 shares are non-complex, so no appropriateness is triggered.
n.2: UCITS units are deemed non-complex.
n.1: Gilts are non-complex instruments.
n.4: A bank deposit is not a complex instrument.

q: A firm cannot complete an appropriateness assessment because the client has given incomplete information. What must the firm do?
o: Apply best execution as a substitute for appropriateness
Proceed without comment if a KID has been provided
Warn the client and allow them to proceed if they wish
Refuse to transact under all circumstances
Automatically reclassify the client as professional
w: If information is insufficient, the firm must warn the client that appropriateness cannot be determined, though the transaction may proceed at the client’s insistence.

n.3: Refusal is not mandated; a warning is required instead.
n.4: Reclassifying a client requires strict criteria, not lack of appropriateness information.
n.1: A KID is not a substitute for appropriateness testing.
n.0: Best execution relates to order handling, not client knowledge and experience.

q: An adviser gives a personal recommendation and wonders why no separate appropriateness assessment is needed. What is the reason?
o: Because execution-only exemptions are triggered
Because suitability rules apply instead
Because a KID is always provided
Because tax implications are assessed
Because the client is always a professional
w: When advice is given, suitability rules apply, which are broader than appropriateness, so no appropriateness assessment is required.

n.0: Execution-only applies to non-complex instruments without advice, not to advised sales.
n.4: Clients may be retail; professional status does not exempt advised sales from suitability.
n.2: KIDs are separate disclosures and not the reason appropriateness is unnecessary.
n.3: Tax analysis is not a reason for appropriateness being displaced by suitability.

q: A retail client asks to trade a complex derivative on an execution-only basis, with no advice. Under COBS 10A.2.1, what is the firm's obligation?
o: Assess the client’s creditworthiness for lending purposes
Offer execution-only services without any warnings
Provide a full written suitability report
Reclassify the client automatically as an elective professional
Assess appropriateness based on knowledge and experience
w: For MiFID business, appropriateness must be assessed in non-advised sales of complex derivatives by evaluating knowledge and experience.

n.2: Suitability reports are for advised services, not non-advised appropriateness.
n.1: Execution-only cannot apply to complex derivatives without the warning and other conditions.
n.3: Elective professional status requires explicit procedures, not automatic reclassification.
n.0: Creditworthiness is not the focus of appropriateness; knowledge and experience are.

q: A compliance officer is listing what triggers an appropriateness assessment. Which of the following is NOT a trigger?
o: Client initiates a trade in a complex product without advice
Client receives a personal recommendation
Firm executes an order in a derivative at client request
Client purchases a structured note directly online
Firm provides access to an online CFD trading platform
w: Personal recommendations trigger suitability, not appropriateness; appropriateness applies to non-advised services involving complex products.

n.0: Non-advised trades in complex products do trigger appropriateness.
n.4: CFD platforms involve complex products, so appropriateness applies.
n.3: Structured notes are complex and require appropriateness testing if non-advised.
n.2: Derivatives are complex and require appropriateness assessment if non-advised.

q: A firm is dealing with per se professional clients on a non-advised basis. How do the MiFID appropriateness rules apply to them?
o: Professional clients are presumed to hold the necessary knowledge
Professional clients must sign a waiver to skip the test
Firms must do both suitability and appropriateness for them
Execution-only services are banned for professional clients
Professional clients are always exempt from suitability rules
w: Professional clients are presumed to understand products, so appropriateness tests are not generally required.

n.4: Professional clients are not automatically exempt from all suitability.
n.2: Firms are not required to run both tests for professionals.
n.3: Execution-only is not banned for professionals.
n.1: No waiver signature is required; the presumption applies by status.

q: A retail client fails the appropriateness test for a complex product they want to buy. What is the firm's required response?
o: The firm must warn the client that the product may be inappropriate
The firm must reclassify the client as a professional one
The firm must compensate the client for any future losses
The firm must provide a full suitability report instead
The firm must block the transaction from taking place at all
w: Where a retail client is found not to have sufficient knowledge or experience, the firm must warn that the product may be inappropriate. The client may still proceed at their discretion.

n.4: The firm warns but need not block; the client may still proceed.
n.1: The firm does not reclassify the client.
n.3: A suitability report is not required in non-advised sales.
n.2: There is no automatic compensation obligation.

q: A non-MiFID firm wants to know when it can skip appropriateness checks. In which circumstance may they be omitted?
o: Advised purchases of structured investment notes
Discretionary portfolio management mandates
Bespoke tailored private equity investment schemes
Complex over-the-counter derivative transactions
Execution-only dealing in non-complex instruments
w: Execution-only services involving non-complex instruments under non-MiFID are exempt from appropriateness checks.

n.1: Discretionary management is a separate regime, not an appropriateness skip.
n.0: Advised sales engage suitability, not an appropriateness exemption.
n.3: Complex derivatives require appropriateness, not exemption.
n.2: Bespoke private equity is complex and not exempt.

q: A firm is classifying MiFID products for the appropriateness exemption. Which product is always treated as non-complex?
o: A non-UCITS retail scheme (NURS) holding
Units in a UCITS collective investment scheme
A leveraged exchange traded note product
An exchange-traded commodity future contract
A collateralised debt obligation instrument
w: UCITS schemes are explicitly deemed non-complex, qualifying for appropriateness exemptions.

n.4: CDOs are complex instruments.
n.3: Commodity futures are complex derivatives.
n.2: Leveraged ETNs are complex.
n.0: NURS are not automatically deemed non-complex like UCITS.

q: An adviser asks why certain shares are exempt from appropriateness checks under MiFID. What is the reason?
o: They guarantee fixed income
They hedge market volatility
They include complex derivatives
They trade on regulated markets
They are bespoke products
w: Shares admitted to trading on regulated markets are defined as non-complex.

n.0: Shares do not guarantee fixed income; complexity classification is key.
n.2: Shares with derivatives are complex, requiring appropriateness checks.
n.4: Bespoke products are complex and never exempt from testing.
n.1: Volatility hedging is irrelevant; exemption relies on regulatory classification.

q: A firm wants to rely on the appropriateness exemption for a transaction. Which condition must be satisfied?
o: The service is non-advised, execution-only and non-complex
The firm is acting as discretionary portfolio manager
The client signs a formal appropriateness waiver
The service involves bespoke product structuring
The product involved is a highly complex derivative
w: Only non-advised execution-only services with non-complex instruments are exempt from checks.

n.2: A waiver does not create the exemption.
n.4: A complex product removes, not enables, the exemption.
n.1: Discretionary management is a different regime.
n.3: Bespoke structuring implies complexity, not exemption.

q: A non-MiFID firm is checking which instrument qualifies as non-complex for the exemption. Which one does?
o: Unregulated offshore scheme
Commodity option contract
Collateralised loan obligation
Private equity investment
Listed government security
w: Listed government securities without derivatives are non-complex and exempt under COBS 10.4–10.6.

n.0: Unregulated offshore schemes are complex, requiring appropriateness checks.
n.3: Private equity is complex and always subject to assessment.
n.1: Commodity options are derivatives requiring appropriateness checks.
n.2: CLOs are complex securitisations that require full checks.

q: A broker is deciding whether an appropriateness test is needed before selling a plain vanilla corporate bond with no embedded derivatives. How does COBS classify such a bond?
o: Always complex instruments
Complex when listed abroad
Non-complex if no derivatives
Complex when traded electronically
Complex if government issued
w: Plain vanilla bonds without embedded derivatives are deemed non-complex and exempt from appropriateness checks.

n.0: Not all bonds are complex; plain vanilla may be exempt.
n.1: Foreign listing does not change non-complex classification.
n.3: Electronic trading does not affect complexity status under COBS.
n.4: Government issuance alone does not determine complexity status.

q: A firm offers execution-only dealing but must know when appropriateness is still mandatory under MiFID. In which case must it always be tested?
o: Listed bond purchases
Execution-only UCITS trade
Regulated market equities
Sale of complex products
Simple share transactions
w: Complex products require appropriateness testing regardless of execution-only status.

n.1: UCITS are non-complex and exempt when execution-only.
n.4: Simple shares are non-complex when traded execution-only.
n.0: Listed bonds may be exempt if non-complex.
n.2: Regulated equities are classified non-complex and exempt.

q: A trainee asks why the execution-only exemptions are limited to particular instruments. What is the reason?
o: They are bespoke structured
Risk levels are lower
They use hidden derivatives
They include leverage features
They guarantee fixed profits
w: Exemptions are limited because non-complex instruments carry lower risks and are easier for retail clients to understand.

n.4: No instrument guarantees fixed profits; exemption is about risk clarity.
n.3: Leverage increases complexity and requires appropriateness checks.
n.0: Bespoke products are complex, not eligible for exemptions.
n.2: Hidden derivatives make instruments complex and unsuitable for exemptions.

q: A firm reviews its product lines to see which activity always requires appropriateness testing. Which one does?
o: Execution-only sales of UCITS collective funds
Simple exchange traded fund transactions

n.0: Legislative jurisdiction rests with Parliament, not the FOS.
