w: DISP 2.2 requires a complainant to have a direct relationship with the firm about the service or product in dispute.

n.2: Holding listed shares is not required to complain.
n.4: A complainant need not be FCA authorised.
n.0: Proof of the firm's profits is irrelevant to eligibility.
n.3: No prior court judgment is needed to lodge a complaint.

q: A firm is checking whether a complainant qualifies to use its complaints process under DISP 2.7. Which of the following is NOT an eligible complainant?
o: A small charity under the income threshold
A large multinational corporation above the limits
An individual retail consumer of the firm
A micro-enterprise with fewer than 10 staff
A trust with net assets below £5 million
w: Multinational corporations are too large and fall outside DISP eligibility criteria.

n.3: Micro-enterprises are eligible complainants under DISP 2.7.
n.0: Small charities below the threshold are eligible complainants.
n.4: Trusts under £5m net assets are eligible complainants.
n.2: Individual retail consumers are eligible complainants.

q: An authorised investment firm collapses and cannot meet claims from its retail clients. Under COMP 3.2, when will the FSCS pay compensation?
o: When a consumer complains about a firm to the FOS
When a firm delays the launch of a new product
Whenever an authorised firm breaches an FCA rule
When an authorised firm cannot meet claims against it
When a bank introduces new charges on accounts
w: COMP 3.2 states that FSCS compensation is payable when an authorised firm is unable, or likely to be unable, to meet claims.

n.2: A rule breach alone does not trigger FSCS compensation.
n.0: An FOS complaint does not itself trigger FSCS payment.
n.4: New account charges do not trigger FSCS compensation.
n.1: A delayed product launch is not an FSCS trigger.

q: A retail customer of a failed authorised bank asks the FSCS what it can claim for. Under COMP 4.2.1, which type of claim is covered?
o: Government grants
Corporate tax refunds
Shareholder rights
Company dividends
Protected deposits
w: COMP 4.2.1 confirms that FSCS covers claims relating to protected deposits held by authorised firms.

n.3: Dividends are corporate matters, not FSCS-protected claims.
n.0: Government grants are outside FSCS coverage.
n.1: Tax refunds are managed by HMRC, not FSCS.
n.2: Shareholder rights are corporate law matters, not FSCS claims.

q: A depositor asks how much of their protected deposit the FSCS would pay out if their bank failed. Under COMP 10.2.1, what is the correct level of cover?
w: COMP 10.2.1 states FSCS covers 100% of protected deposits up to £85,000 per eligible claimant per firm.

n.3: FSCS deposit cover is 100% up to £85,000, not 90% to £50,000.
n.4: The limit is £85,000 at 100%, not 75% up to £100,000.
n.0: Deposits are covered at 100%, not 50%, up to £85,000.
n.2: FSCS pays 100%, not 80%, up to the £85,000 limit.

q: A client is pursuing an FSCS claim after their authorised investment firm fails. Under COMP 10.2.3, what percentage does the FSCS pay for protected investment business?
w: COMP 10.2.3 specifies that FSCS pays 90% of claims in respect of protected investment business, up to £85,000.

n.0: 100% applies to deposits, not investment business.
n.3: 75% is not a coverage percentage under COMP rules.
n.4: 80% is not recognised in FSCS investment cover.
n.2: 50% is not a valid FSCS protection percentage.

q: A claimant approaches the FSCS after a firm collapses. Under COMP 4.2.2, which condition must be met before compensation is paid?
o: The firm has FCA approval
The FOS authorises the claim
The firm is in default
The client has High Court consent
The PRA issues a waiver
w: COMP 4.2.2 requires that a firm is declared in default before FSCS can pay compensation.

n.0: FCA approval alone does not trigger FSCS payments.
n.3: High Court consent is not needed for FSCS payments.
n.4: PRA waivers do not activate FSCS claims.
n.1: FOS authorisation is separate from FSCS compensation.

q: A saver is checking whether their bank balance is covered by the FSCS. Which deposits are eligible for protection?
o: Deposits in cryptocurrency exchanges
Deposits with UK authorised firms
Deposits with foreign governments
Deposits with unregulated lenders
Deposits with shareholder funds
w: FSCS protects deposits held with UK-authorised firms under COMP rules.

n.3: Unregulated lenders are not covered by FSCS.
n.2: Foreign government deposits are not FSCS-protected.
n.4: Shareholder funds are not deposits under COMP.
n.0: Cryptocurrency exchanges are unregulated and not FSCS-protected.

q: An investor asks when the FSCS will cover an investment business claim. When does cover apply?
o: When a firm is in default
When profits fall
When dividends are cut
When shareholders complain
When FCA sets new rules
w: Investment business claims are covered when the authorised firm is declared in default under COMP 4.2.3.

n.1: Falling profits alone do not trigger FSCS cover.
n.3: Shareholder complaints are not FSCS claims.
n.2: Dividend cuts do not activate FSCS protection.
n.4: New FCA rules do not themselves trigger FSCS claims.

q: A customer wants to know how much the FSCS protects for deposits per person per firm. What is the compensation cap?
w: COMP 10.2.1 provides full protection for deposits up to £85,000 per person per firm.

n.1: £75,000 was the previous limit before being raised.
n.2: £100,000 exceeds the statutory FSCS deposit cap.
n.0: £60,000 is not a recognised FSCS deposit limit.
n.3: £50,000 was an earlier FSCS limit, not current.

q: A couple hold a joint account with a bank and ask how the FSCS treats it. What coverage applies to joint accounts?
o: £75,000 per account
£85,000 total per account
£100,000 total per account
£50,000 total per account
£85,000 per person
w: Joint accounts are covered up to £85,000 per person, so two account holders receive £170,000 protection in total.

n.1: Coverage is per person, not capped at £85,000 per account.
n.3: £50,000 is an outdated limit and incorrect today.
n.2: £100,000 is not the statutory FSCS joint account protection.
n.0: £75,000 reflects a prior limit, not the current level.

q: An investor whose authorised firm has defaulted asks how the FSCS calculates an investment business claim. How is it worked out?
o: 90% of loss up to £85,000
75% of loss up to £100,000
80% of loss up to £70,000
100% of loss up to £85,000
50% of loss up to £60,000
w: COMP 10.2.3 provides 90% protection of investment business losses up to £85,000 per person per firm.

n.3: 100% applies only to deposit claims, not investment claims.
n.1: 75% is not an FSCS-recognised protection level.
n.4: 50% is not valid under FSCS compensation rules.
n.2: 80% is not a recognised FSCS coverage rate.

q: A client worries about what would happen to their money if their investment firm collapses. Under COMP 3.2, what triggers FSCS compensation payments?
o: Client dispute
FCA fine
Market volatility
Dividend suspension
Firm default
w: FSCS compensation is triggered when a firm is declared in default under COMP 3.2.

n.1: An FCA fine does not itself trigger FSCS payments.
n.2: Market volatility does not activate FSCS cover.
n.0: Client disputes are addressed by the FOS, not FSCS.
n.3: Dividend suspensions are corporate decisions, not FSCS events.

q: A treasury team reviewing FSCS deposit cover asks which category of depositor is excluded from protection. Which of the following is excluded?
o: Money held in a personal joint account
Deposits held by a registered charity
Deposits held by credit and financial institutions
Personal savings held by an individual
Deposits held by a small or medium enterprise
w: Deposits held by large corporates are excluded from FSCS protection under COMP rules.

n.3: Individuals' personal savings are protected by the FSCS.
n.0: Joint account balances are protected, each holder up to £85,000.
n.4: SME deposits are eligible for FSCS protection.
n.1: Charity deposits are eligible for FSCS protection.

q: A client who has just received house-sale proceeds asks how the FSCS treats a temporary high balance. How much is protected, and for how long?
o: £500,000 for six months
£1 million for six months
£250,000 for one year
£2 million for three months
£750,000 for nine months
w: FSCS provides £1 million protection for temporary high balances for up to six months.

n.2: £250,000 for a year is not a statutory FSCS limit.
n.0: £500,000 is below the correct £1 million temporary balance limit.
n.3: £2 million exceeds the statutory FSCS temporary balance cover.
n.4: £750,000 is not a recognised FSCS compensation threshold.

q: An investment firm is explaining FSCS coverage to a corporate treasurer. Which deposits qualify for 100% FSCS protection regardless of the limit?
o: Insurance company deposits
Client money accounts
Personal pension deposits
Corporate current accounts
Shareholder equity funds
w: Client money accounts are protected in full under FSCS rules without a monetary limit.

n.2: Personal pension deposits follow normal FSCS deposit limits.
n.3: Corporate current accounts are subject to standard FSCS caps.
n.4: Shareholder equity is not treated as a protected deposit.
n.0: Insurance company deposits are not fully covered regardless of amount.

q: An investor is preparing an FSCS claim for investment business under COMP 4.2.3. What must the claimant prove?
o: That the losses arose from a market downturn
That a dispute with the FOS is still unresolved
That the firm has breached a specific FCA rule
A valid claim against an authorised firm in default
That a court judgment has already been obtained
w: Claimants must prove a valid claim against an authorised firm in default under COMP 4.2.3.

n.2: A rule breach alone is not what claimants must prove.
n.0: Market-downturn losses are not covered by the FSCS.
n.1: An unresolved FOS dispute is not the FSCS test.
n.4: No prior court judgment is required for an FSCS claim.

q: A retail client holds a large cash balance with a single authorised bank and asks their adviser how much would be protected if the bank failed. What is the maximum FSCS compensation for deposits at one bank?
o: £100,000 per person
£200,000 per person
£150,000 per person
£85,000 per person
£50,000 per person
w: FSCS covers deposits up to £85,000 per person, per authorised bank.

n.2: £150,000 is not a current FSCS deposit limit.
n.0: £100,000 exceeds the statutory FSCS cap.
n.4: £50,000 was a historic FSCS limit, not current.
n.1: £200,000 is not a recognised FSCS compensation threshold.

q: A saver holds deposits with two brands owned by the same authorised bank and asks how the FSCS treats them. How are they covered?
o: Added together under a single £85,000 limit
Covered in full with no upper monetary limit
Protected up to £85,000 for every branch used
Protected up to £85,000 for each separate brand
Protected up to £85,000 for each account held
w: Deposits across different brands of the same authorised bank are aggregated under a single £85,000 FSCS limit.

n.3: Brands of one bank share one limit, not £85,000 each.
n.4: Cover is per firm, not £85,000 per account.
n.2: Cover is per firm, not per branch.
n.1: FSCS deposit cover has an £85,000 limit, not unlimited.

q: An investor whose authorised broker has failed asks whether the FSCS will cover their losses. Which type of activity is protected under the FSCS investment rules?
o: Regulated investment business by an authorised firm
The exercise of shareholder voting rights
Mergers and acquisitions between companies
Unregulated investment schemes based overseas
Betting and gambling on financial markets
w: FSCS covers regulated investment business provided by authorised firms under COMP rules.

n.3: Unregulated overseas schemes are not covered by the FSCS.
n.4: Gambling on markets is not protected investment business.
n.1: Shareholder voting is not an FSCS-covered activity.
n.2: Corporate mergers are not covered by FSCS protection.

q: A client asks an adviser where the money comes from to pay FSCS compensation when an authorised firm fails. How are FSCS payouts funded?
o: From the reserves of the Bank of England
By contributions collected from consumers
From damages awarded by the High Court
By levies on authorised firms across the industry
By funds provided directly by the taxpayer
w: The FSCS is funded through levies on authorised firms across industry sectors.

n.4: The FSCS is not funded directly by the taxpayer.
n.0: Bank of England reserves do not fund the FSCS.
n.1: Consumers do not fund the FSCS.
n.2: The FSCS is not funded by High Court awards.

q: A customer of a defaulted firm wants to claim from the FSCS. What must they demonstrate to access compensation?
o: That they hold a tax compliance certificate
That they own shares in the failed firm
A record of past employment with the FCA
That the government has approved the claim
That they are eligible claimants under the COMP rules
w: Claimants must demonstrate eligibility under COMP rules to receive FSCS compensation.

n.1: Owning shares in the firm is not the FSCS eligibility test.
n.3: Government approval is not required for an FSCS claim.
n.0: A tax compliance certificate is irrelevant to FSCS claims.
n.2: FCA employment history is not needed to claim from the FSCS.

q: A consumer group believes a market feature is harming customers and wants to raise it formally with the FCA. Who is permitted to submit a super-complaint?
o: Serving judges of the High Court
Any individual retail client of a firm
Large corporates authorised in the UK
Institutional investors in the markets
Consumer bodies designated by the Treasury
w: Only designated consumer bodies may submit super-complaints to the FCA under the statutory framework.

n.1: Individual retail clients cannot lodge a super-complaint.
n.2: Large corporates cannot submit a super-complaint.
n.3: Institutional investors cannot make a super-complaint.
n.0: High Court judges do not submit super-complaints.

q: A designated consumer body is preparing a super-complaint to the FCA. What is the purpose of a super-complaint?
o: To flag features causing systemic consumer detriment
To request a tax exemption for consumers
To help set the level of UK interest rates
To challenge the FCA's rule-making powers
To appeal against a decision made by the FOS
w: Super-complaints are designed to alert the FCA to practices causing systemic consumer detriment.

n.3: A super-complaint does not challenge FCA rule-making.
n.4: It is not a route to appeal a FOS decision.
n.1: It does not request tax exemptions for consumers.
n.2: It has no role in setting UK interest rates.

q: Which legislation provides the framework for super-complaints?
o: Consumer Credit Act 1974 governing lending
The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000
Pensions Act 2004 governing occupational schemes
Banking Act 2009 dealing with bank resolution
Companies Act 2006 governing corporate matters
w: The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 provides the framework for super-complaints to the FCA.

n.4: The Companies Act does not provide the super-complaints framework.
n.2: The Pensions Act 2004 is not the framework.
n.3: The Banking Act 2009 concerns bank resolution.
n.0: The Consumer Credit Act 1974 governs lending, not super-complaints.

q: A designated consumer body submits a super-complaint to the FCA about a market-wide issue. What must the FCA do on receiving it?
o: Provide a public response
Refer immediately to FOS
Impose direct fines
Approve new rules instantly
Request court enforcement
w: The FCA must provide a public response within a defined timescale when a super-complaint is received.

n.1: Super-complaints are not referred to FOS; they are reviewed by the FCA.
n.3: New rules are not instantly approved upon complaint receipt.
n.4: Court enforcement is not the FCA’s first action; assessment comes first.
n.2: Direct fines are not imposed as an automatic response to super-complaints.

q: A consumer body identifies that thousands of customers may have been sold an unsuitable product by several firms. What is such an alert to the FCA called?
o: An alert about a bank's liquidity shortfall
A disciplinary decision issued by the FCA
A recommendation about future tax policy
A referral of a single client's dispute
An alert to the FCA about widespread consumer harm
w: A mass-detriment reference alerts the FCA to widespread consumer harm requiring regulatory attention.

n.3: A mass-detriment reference concerns widespread, not single, harm.
n.0: It is not an alert about a bank's liquidity.
n.2: It is not a recommendation on tax policy.
n.1: It is not an FCA disciplinary decision.

q: Evidence of widespread consumer harm is emerging across many similar complaints against firms. Who may make a mass-detriment reference?
o: An institutional investor
The Financial Ombudsman Service
A company's board of directors
Any individual complainant
A serving High Court judge
w: The Financial Ombudsman Service may refer evidence of widespread consumer detriment to the FCA.

n.3: Individual complainants cannot make a mass-detriment reference.
n.4: High Court judges do not make mass-detriment references.
n.0: Institutional investors cannot make such a reference.
n.2: Company directors do not make mass-detriment references.

q: A designated consumer body wants to raise a super-complaint with the FCA about a widespread industry practice. What must accompany the submission?
o: Plans for a proposed corporate merger
A full list of the FCA's named supervisors
Details of the bank's capital ratios
Court papers seeking an injunction
Evidence of systemic detriment to consumers
w: Super-complaints must be supported by evidence showing systemic consumer detriment.

n.1: A list of FCA supervisors is not required with a super-complaint.
n.3: Court injunction papers are not part of a super-complaint.
n.2: Bank capital ratios are not required to support it.
n.0: Corporate merger plans are irrelevant to a super-complaint.

q: A mass-detriment reference has been made highlighting systemic harm to consumers. What outcome may follow?
o: PRA intervention
Automatic compensation
Court appeal
FCA investigation
Parliamentary review
w: A mass-detriment reference can prompt the FCA to launch an investigation into systemic harm.

n.1: Automatic compensation is not granted; FCA first investigates.
n.4: Parliamentary review is not an immediate outcome of mass-detriment references.
n.2: Court appeals are separate legal processes, not FCA responses.
n.0: PRA intervention concerns prudential issues, not mass detriment.

q: A consumer body lodges a super-complaint with the FCA about widespread harm in a retail product market. What must the FCA do within 90 days of receiving it?
o: Publish a response
Award compensation
Approve new boards
Change statutory law
Impose firm closure
w: The FCA must publish a reasoned response within 90 days of receiving a super-complaint.

n.1: Compensation awards are not part of FCA’s super-complaint duties.
n.3: The FCA cannot change statutory law; only Parliament can.
n.4: Firm closures are enforcement actions, not super-complaint responses.
n.2: Board approvals are corporate governance matters, not FCA obligations.

q: A policy analyst is comparing two routes for raising systemic consumer issues with the regulator. What is the main distinction between super-complaints and mass-detriment references?
o: Super-complaints require FCA rule change
Mass-detriment references are criminal cases
Super-complaints involve court judgments
Mass-detriment references come from shareholders
Super-complaints are from consumer bodies
w: Super-complaints are raised by designated consumer bodies, while mass-detriment references are raised by the FOS.

n.3: Shareholders cannot submit mass-detriment references.
n.0: Super-complaints do not require FCA to change rules.
n.1: Mass-detriment references are not criminal proceedings.
n.2: Court judgments are not involved in super-complaints.
